en: The Śūraṅgama Sūtra:
The Scripture on the Ultimate Meaning of the Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause for Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas;
translated by the Indian śramaṇa Paramiti.

"India" (Tianzhu) is the general name for the kingdoms of the Western Regions. "Śramaṇa" is translated here as "Diligent Cessation," meaning to diligently practice wholesome dharmas and to cease unwholesome conduct.
"Prajñāmitra" means "Limitless" (Jiliang); this is the name of the translator. A "translator" (yìzhě) is one who transcribes Sanskrit characters into Chinese characters.
The sovereigns of the Five Indias held this sutra as their most precious treasure, keeping it secret and not transmitting it. Prajñā... [text continues]
The Secret Truth was intended to be transmitted to China; it arrived from the land of Mlecchas, but was ultimately captured and sent back.
Later, he transcribed it using fine hair on delicate silk, and having cut open his arm, he concealed it within his flesh. Sailing across the ocean, he reached Guangzhou.
At that time, in the first year of the Shenlong era of the Tang Emperor Zhongzong, the Chancellor Fang Rong was in Guangzhou and requested that the text be translated at Zhiyi Temple.
The śramaṇa Migaśika from the country of Udyāna translated the words.
"Udyāna" means "garden" (yuàn) in this language; it was formerly the royal park of a great kingdom located in Northern India. As for Migaśika:

This is titled *Neng Jiangfu* (Able to Subdue). It is a translation of the original language, specifically a "translating-and-measuring" (*duyu*) work, meaning that the correct principles of both sides were weighed and measured to render the Sanskrit language into Chinese.
Transcribed by Fang Rong, a disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts who served as Vice President of the Secretariat and the Chancellery during the Tang dynasty.
"Bodhisattva Precepts" refers to those who, as high-ranking officials, have received the Bodhisattva precepts. "Disciples" refers to those who take the Triple Gem as their Great Teacher.
"Together" means jointly. "Chancellery and Secretariat" refers to both internal offices; that is, the residences of the Left and Right Ministers.
"Pingshangshi" (Ministers of State) means to harmonize and clarify the administration of the state. "Pen-shou" (Scribe) refers to the one who records the translation.
If the phrasing was occasionally clumsy, he would take up the brush to refine and embellish it. During the translation assembly, Minister Fang also concurrently held this office;
thus, his achievements were displayed alongside those of the two masters.
Preface to the Śūraṅgama Sūtra:

The Śūraṅgama Sūtra is the life-force of wisdom for all Buddhas, the path to realization for all sentient beings, the grand mainstay of the net of teachings, and the essential gateway of the Chan school.
Since the World-Honored One attained enlightenment, throughout his dispensation in five periods, every teaching was none other than for this one purpose.

This is a great causal nexus. Seeking that which universally encompasses the capacities of those to be transformed, it points directly to the essence of the mind and proclaims the nature of true ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

It discerns and establishes the truly perfect penetration, enabling people to master external objects as the Tathāgata does and, with a mere snap of the fingers, transcend the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Nothing surpasses the *Śūraṅgama* for this purpose. To explain its name: all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid; this is what is meant by "penetrating to the very bottom of the Dharma."

The Source is unmoving and indestructible; yet the secret cause of the Tathāgata and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas all derive their beginning from this and find their ultimate consummation in this.
Examining what it elucidates: it expounds the perfect principle to clarify true nature and opens up the perfect practice to demonstrate true cultivation.
As for its nature, both essence and function are manifest together; as for its cultivation, effect and cause are harmonized as one. Thus it traces the origin and examines the end.

This concludes the discourse on the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). It is truly because practitioners turn their backs on the truth and follow after delusion that they fail to achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.

Some cherish the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and consider a mere trifle sufficient; others fail to eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and thus allow their learning to become a source of fault.
Therefore, taking Ānanda’s extensive learning and his erroneous attachments as conditions, the Great Teaching was profoundly manifested. The World-Honored One first addressed him, saying:
"The continuous succession of birth and death among all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of nature that is pure and luminous."
"By means of various deluded thoughts, these thoughts being unreal, there is cyclic existence. It further says:

"There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown, the King of Śūraṅgama, which fully encompasses the myriad practices and is the path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.
Is this not the fundamental principle for both theory and practice? From this, the clinging to the seven locations is refuted, and the two [truths] are distinguished.

This plants the fundamental roots. Because of seeing, the mind is revealed; because of the mind, seeing is revealed. Although mind and seeing manifest one another, the primary manifestation resides in the mind.
It is like using a blind person staring into the darkness as a metaphor for how seeing is not the eye; it is like bending the fingers to trace a flying light to verify that seeing is immovable;

it is like using the observation of the river to confirm that it does not change, and comparing the hanging of the hands to show there is nothing omitted. Thus, one distinguishes the eight returns and selects among all things. It is not...

It is neither expansion nor contraction; it is neither right nor wrong. This causes one to realize that the true mind is pure and perfect, and that what is falsely perceived as form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing is merely delusion.

Having realized that these are delusions, one may still suspect they are intermingled and confused; therefore, he further refutes the notions of spontaneity and causal conditions to demonstrate that the "seeing of seeing" is not actually seeing.

By combining the individual karma (*bipakṣa-karma*) with the collective karma (*sabhāga-karma*), he points out the locus where false seeing arises, using the experience of one person as an analogy for many.
Taking one nation as an example for all nations, this collectively reveals that the vessel-world, the sense organs, and the physical body are all equally illusory.

From the shallow to the deep, and from the narrow to the broad, although various methods are employed to reveal their illusory nature, that which is revealed is solely the True. Therefore, the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are further cited.

Extensively encompassing the seven great elements, they are gathered into the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, causing one to realize that things and self share the same root, that right and wrong are of one essence, and that delusion has no inherent nature;
the entire body is thus the Truth itself. All phenomena of the ten realms, both the environment and its inhabitants, are merely manifestations arising in accordance with karma.

Having realized their identity with the Truth, yet still remaining deluded regarding these karmic manifestations, he therefore further answers the challenge concerning mountains, rivers, and the great earth, profoundly [elucidating the matter].

It exhaustively investigates the origin of the arising of life. It is like empty space, which does not reject the manifestation of various forms. It reveals the true, wondrous, awakened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm;
where the one and the many respond to each other, the small and the large contain one another; it is both essence and function, neither mundane nor sacred.
Reaching the point of departing from "is" and "is-not," and being both "is" and "is-not," then the wondrous nature of the hidden mind transcends all names and words. Furthermore...

The metaphor of a madman running while holding up a mirror illustrates that delusion has no cause. This concludes the reprimand for mere erudition and exhorts the cultivation of the outflow-free (anāsrava) path.

Generally speaking, all of these pertain to the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*). Although understanding may be perfect, it cannot be realized without practice; therefore, the two definitive meanings are further elucidated.
First, he examined the initial arousal of the bodhicitta on the causal ground and the subduing and severing of ignorance as the essentials of cultivation.

Next, he examined the root of afflictions and the selection of the faculty of perfect capacity as the basis for initiating practice. Thereupon, he determined the relative superiority and inferiority of the six faculties, causing one to enter deeply through a single gate.

He struck a bell to verify the permanence of the auditory faculty and tied a cloth to demonstrate the nature of knots. He then set forth the Dharma-gates realized by the twenty-five sages, and issued [the following] command:
Selecting the faculty of hearing as the expedient means for the beginner, he further instructs in the rules for collecting the mind and establishing the site of practice (*maṇḍala*).
Thereupon, one hears the four kinds of precepts and the divine mantra from the light on the crown of the head. Generally speaking, these are all practices of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanxing*).

Even proceeding through the three stages of advancement to accomplish the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi—though this discusses the stages of realization—it does not yet exhaust the subject.

The practice of causes consists of cultivating the karma of precepts regarding the emotional perceptions of the seven realms of existence, and maintaining meditative concentration against the demonic deceptions of the five aggregates;
there is nothing that does not pertain to the gates of practice. One must aim for the perfection of Bodhi and return to the state of non-attainment;
only then is it called the ultimate, steadfast realization. Thus, based on the principle of ultimate steadfastness, one establishes ultimate steadfastness.
The practice of ultimate and steadfast conduct; the realization of ultimate and steadfast principle. Such, in general, is the purport of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*.
Those who have categorized the scripture take the principle and its practice as the orthodox teaching (*zhengzong*), and divide that which departs from the orthodox teaching into five sections:

first, the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); second, the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); third, the Realization of the Fruit (*phala-prāpti*); fourth, the Conclusion of the Scripture; and fifth, the Aids to the Path. This means that one cultivates after having seen the path.

The Way: one cultivates the path and subsequently realizes the fruit; this is merely the conventional sequence. However, when investigating the cultivation and realization of those of superior faculties, it is as stated after the revelation of the *tathāgatagarbha*:
"Without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one attains the Dharma-body. This occurs prior to being invited to enter the jeweled hall.
This refers to the elimination of doubt and the mind’s awakening to the true reality (*dharmatā*), and so forth; how could such matters be confined to the mundane?

Now, for those who wish to give rise to the truth and return to the source, clarifying the mind and seeing the nature (*prakṛti*), they should devote their utmost effort to this. Therefore, I have collected the excellent commentaries of various masters to produce this *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation).
Compiled in the *Renwu* year of the Yuan Zhi Zheng era by the śramaṇa Wuite (Tianru) of Luling:
Dharma Master Weike of Xingfu, Dharma Master Hongyuan of Zizhong, Dharma Master Renshuo of Wuxing,
Dharma Master Chongjie of Zhijie, Dharma Master Hongmin of Xilei, and Chan Master Xiaoyue of Letan.
The *Preface to the Original Text of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by Dharma Master Zixuan of Changshui, Dharma Master Zhizhuan of Gushan, and Chan Master Jiehuan of Wenzheng states:
"The wondrous nature of True Suchness (bhūtatathatā) is called the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. Its great samādhi is firm and solid; this is named Śūraṅgama. From beginning to middle..."

Ultimately, there can be no difference; across the past, present, and future, they cannot be distinguished. Looking back, the path of universal penetration (samantamukha) leads to but one destination;
yet cultivation and realization must necessarily rely upon the myriad practices (*sāhasra-caryā*). Thus, employing the fruit as the cause is called the "Secret Cause" (*guhyahetu*);

attaining the fruit by means of this cause is termed the "Definitive Meaning" (*nītārtha*). Only by practicing this can one become a Buddha; without understanding this, there is no way to compile a sutra. Now, Śāriputra has obtained the secret...

The record of *nirvāṇa* encompasses both *pratyekabuddhas* and *śrāvakas*, presenting them all together. Although Ānanda requested the initial expedient means, both the internal concealment and the external manifestation were omitted.
This is because, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the work was completed and his rank was already supreme; it thus recounts retrospectively the path traversed midway.

In the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, he pursued his studies with a forward-looking resolve, pre-emptively severing the notion of the "burnt-out city" (*tāpasa-pura*) to benefit those with clear vision through the compilation.

Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): having discarded the minor and raised up the essential, the exposition of the principles does not await their conclusion; the opening of the scripture has already revealed its ultimate point.
Within the fifty-five stages, by means of the few words concerning the Bodhisattva’s skillful transcendence, the Dharma of Perfect Penetration has already been manifested previously.
Within the twenty-five sages, we select six venerable ones—Maudgalyāyana and Kauṣṭhila—to represent them; how could those who have attained perfect penetration lie outside of these?

Throughout antiquity and the present, renowned masters have formed groups to establish their doctrines, exhausting their efforts to investigate the subtle. Yet, the meaning and principles remain profound and deep.

It is not easy to find those who can truly comprehend [the scriptures]. Even among those whose literary expressions are clever and refined, many remain obscure. Recently, there was Dharma Master Sanhuai, whose eloquence was unimpeded, yet he did not annotate a single sutra.
When people asked him the reason for this, he said: "How would I dare to annotate a sutra when I am not proficient in literary composition?"
"If one cannot help it, using the brush of a scholar to act as the tongue of the Sangha may serve as a mutual aid. How profound these words are!

They approach the state of non-self (*anātman*). Now, if the subtlety of literary composition is already such that the sutras are difficult to understand, how much more so must the profound analysis of principle and the subtle essentials of the mind be?
To summarize their general outline, they can be briefly described: birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The root of this has two aspects: the conditioned mind is the coarsest, while the karmic consciousness is subtle. How could it be permissible to treat them as entirely distinct? On the path to Bodhi, there are not many stages;
when the true mind is alone revealed, the deluded views are naturally eliminated. How could both be maintained simultaneously without one being discarded?

By turning back from delusion, one attains the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). That which is turned back is surely the mind that was previously destroyed in seven stages, which abandons the profound stillness to reach a state of immovability.

That which is abandoned is precisely the boundary between the eight consciousnesses. When does "seeing the seeing" occur? It is at the moment when the Tathāgata illuminates the ignorance of the arising-phase (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).
What dharma is "heard by hearing"? This is the gate of quiescence prior to views into which the Bodhisattva enters.
By refuting [the views of] self, other, both, and causelessness, one awakens to the fact that birth and extinction are fundamentally non-existent;

thus it is called hearing, reflection, and cultivation, and like an illusion. One realizes the unimpeded nature of perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vyūha*). However, while present karma can only be extinguished through practice, past transgressions cannot be countered except by mantras.
Since these emerge from the crown of the head, they are the Buddha-body itself. Upon their appearance, evil spirits flee; how could they be demons?
The title states: "Thought has already been severed; realization remains. The distinctions between the sudden and gradual approaches prior to the Equal and Wondrous [Stages] are naturally clear.

However, regarding the degrees of depth after the Stage of Dry Wisdom, many people confuse them. Since the grounds of the various devas are not yet true, how can they be entrusted with the sages who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment]?
Since the paths taken by the Two Vehicles are not mistaken, how could they fall into the stream of false views? This is the awakening at these various stages.
This delusion concerns the clarity or obscurity of the entire scripture. Not daring to underestimate my own dullness and ignorance, I have vainly hoped for faith and understanding.

Having spent five years in research and dwelling in the search of various canonical texts, I [encounter] the middle son of Layman He, whose innate wisdom and eloquence are profound, whose heart is deeply committed to extensive learning, and who formerly resided at the White Gate.

The lectures were delivered numerous times. Later, while serving in the provincial office of Min for forty days, I peeled back the layers of this scripture to discern its causes and effects, and analyzed the similarities and differences among various teachings.
It was as clear as observing fruit and as joyful as the plucking of a flower. I considered that what was harbored within my mind would not have been proclaimed had it not been for my brush;
yet, fearing it might be lost or forgotten, I exerted myself to compile these notes. After several revisions of the draft, the work was finally completed.
The lay practitioner came to Chu. Having carefully examined the weighty matter, he was humbly granted approval.
Taking the phrase from the Sūtra, "as it is spoken," he thus titled it *Yúshuō* (As Spoken).
Written by the Buddha’s disciple Zhong Xing (courtesy name: Bojing) of Jingling on the next day, the Jiǎzǐ year of the Míng dynasty.

Regarding the "New Sequence of the Buddha’s Teachings" as it is spoken: the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma does not involve speaking apart from the Dharma; he merely speaks in accordance with the Dharma itself. As for later people...
When explaining a sutra, one should not offer interpretations that deviate from the text; one should simply explain it as the sutra itself states.

There are those who, seeking more than what is said, either select one or two characters from the sutra to establish a coherent thread of meaning, or dissect preceding and succeeding passages to clarify the structural divisions.
Such explanations suffer from the disease of fragmentation (*zhīlí*). Indeed, regarding this fragmentation...

In the sutras, [the truth] is already not as they claim. Some take what they have acquired through their own studies or what has been transmitted by their teachers, and without inquiring whether it accords with the actual intent of the sutras, they insist on forcibly aligning it with their own views. The flaw in their discourse lies in their forced harmonization.
To force [the teachings] into alignment with texts outside the sūtras is nothing less than a grave error. How excellent is Master Zhou Neng’s exposition of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;
it is rooted entirely in the Tathāgata. Indeed, this single sūtra begins with the inquiry into the mind and culminates in the vision of seeing and the contemplation of observing.

The essential instructions for investigating the Chan school are fully contained herein. From the ritual regulations of the *dōjō* through the fifty-five stages of realization, it cuts off all seven realms of existence;
both realization and cultivation are presented together, and cause and effect are manifested simultaneously. The Dharma taught therein is more complete than that of other sutras.
Finally, it discerns the various demons who enter the path of heterodoxy with the utmost thoroughness, ensuring that future students may simply follow [this method].

The wording of the sutra and the intent of its teaching are already beyond exhaustive investigation; how, then, can one allow the proliferation of fragmented and contrived interpretations to be added therein?
There have been dozens of schools that have previously commented on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, yet none of their explanations is entirely correct or free from error.
They were distinguished by what was consistent with reality and what was not; how could such a distinction possibly be mistaken?

In the past, Lord Zhong Bojing extensively searched for materials and synthesized them, selecting only the refined and avoiding the erroneous. He took up only the meaning, without naming the individuals.

He titled it "As Spoken" (Rushuo). Master Zhou deeply accords with this sutra; there is nothing that can surpass this teaching. He therefore had it carved into woodblocks and newly published for circulation in the world.
Indeed, it is not merely the teaching of Zhou, but the teaching of Zhong; nor is it merely the teaching of Zhong, but the teaching of all other masters;
nor is it merely the teaching of those masters, but the teaching of the Buddha; and furthermore, it is not merely the teaching of the Buddha, but the teaching of all other sutras as well.
The exposition in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is as it is in the sūtra; it is like the Dharma itself, reaching the ultimate point and beyond which nothing can be added.
Whether regarding this suchness or that suchness, one cannot find any difference or identity between them.
To employ this teaching and apply it to explain other sūtras is likewise the same.
Presented as a Jinshi Graduate, Provincial Administration Commissioner of the Shanxi Provincial Administration Commission, disciple of the Buddha of Xie Li, Wang Ting,
respectfully inscribed this on the tenth day after the Double Ninth Festival of the ninth lunar month in the eighteenth year of the Kangxi era,
for the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (The Great Buddha-Crown Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Ultimate Meaning of All Bodhisattvas).
In the first fascicle of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Myriad Practices*, concerning the fruit-body of the Tathāgata as described therein:
its essence is inherently so; why rely upon secret causes? The functional application of the Bodhisattva path is non-active;
what, then, are the myriad practices? Without cause and without practice, there is no cultivation and no realization, no awakening and no lack thereof—neither great nor small.
Names and marks are entirely non-existent; this is the true Śūraṅgama, which is ultimately firm and solid.
It is simply because the Tathāgata is hidden within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of sentient beings that he is not revealed without the secret cause.

Because sentient beings and bodhisattvas have sunk into the seven realms of existence, they do not cultivate the myriad practices. Therefore, the Buddha of Enlightenment manifested the Great Dharma for them, so that they would not be deluded.
Within the minor paths, one silently attains the essence that is without exterior;
this is illustrated by the metaphor of the Buddha’s crown, so that one does not become obstructed by the perception of forms, but reaches the wondrous pinnacle of the unsurpassed state.

It points to the Tathāgata’s secret cause, so that one may clarify the fundamentally wondrous mind and know that all Buddhas of the three periods of time take this as their primary cause. It clarifies the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization, so that...

Awakening to the ultimate Dharma, one knows that all sages rely upon this to realize the fruits [of their practice], even unto the Bodhisattvas who are fully endowed with the ten thousand pure practices.
Among all phenomena, there is nothing that does not reach ultimate consummation; reaching the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is firm and indestructible.
Therefore, it is named the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata, the Definitive Meaning of Cultivation and Realization, for all Bodhisattvas.
The Ten Thousand Practices. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. This sutra begins with the Tathāgata’s Unseen Crown Mark emitting light and proclaiming a mantra.
The Tathāgata first designates that there is a samādhi called the "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-uṣṇīṣa*).
This refers to the Bodhi and Nirvāṇa—the fundamentally pure essence, the Tathāgatagarbha mind. Because this essential mind contains and exhales the ten voids, it pervades and encompasses all things.
The myriad phenomena cannot have their forms seen by the five eyes, nor can their characteristics be described by the four types of eloquence.
Only our Great Awakened One, upon beholding the morning star, opened the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; he gazed directly at its summit, and thus this Dharma is named the "Supreme Summit Dharma.
The phrase "The Tathāgata’s secret cause, the definitive meaning of cultivation and realization" reveals the reason for this Dharma.
It is the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa. "As" (Tathā) means unchanging; "coming" (Āgata) means following conditions.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle are "as" but do not "come"; ordinary beings "come" but are not "as. Only I, the Great Awakened One, am both "as" and "come," and is thus named Tathāgata.

That which is known and seen alone is called "Secret" (Guhyaka); that which gives birth to the fruit of sainthood is called the "Cause" (Hetu). This refers to the Great Awakened One relying upon this Uṣṇīṣa.

The Dharma serves as the cause for the arising of the myriad practices. To refine, polish, and cultivate these habits is called "cultivation" (*xiū*). To forget the mind and attain silent resonance is called "realization" (*zhèng*).

This means that the Great Awakened One, relying on this "Summit Dharma," severed delusions and realized the Truth. To exhaustively investigate everything without exception is called "perfection" (*liǎo*).
To transcend words and thought is called the "Ultimate Meaning" (*yì*). This refers to the Great Awakened One’s realization of this First Ultimate Meaning.

The Truth. This Great Matter of causal conditions has appeared in the world, and now it has been fully investigated and exhausted without remainder; therefore, it is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*).
Truly, because the karmic consciousness of sentient beings is vast and boundless, entirely devoid of awakening, they transmigrate through birth and death with no end in sight.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle merely guard the illusory city, indulging in the bliss of cessation and halting midway, unable even to—

Even if a Bodhisattva reaches the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there is still a path ahead; as long as one has not yet reached the state of ultimate perfection, it is ultimately not yet fully realized.

Only the Great Awakened One (*mahābuddha*) has exhausted all hindrances and emptied all delusions, having reached the end of causes and fulfilled the fruits, such that his enlightened activities are complete and no further tasks remain.
Only when every single principle is fully understood and no further principles remain does one finally attain full realization and achieve unsurpassed awakening (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas, *Śūraṅgama* refers to the fact that from the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*),
one takes this "Crown Dharma" as the cause for practicing the six perfections, severing ignorance bit by bit and realizing the True Principle bit by bit.
Thus, ascending through the sacred stages of a Bodhisattva, one is able to tread upon the steps of the Buddha at every step and achieve steadfastness in every matter.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove Monastery, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all of whom were stainless Great Arhats, sons of the Buddha who maintained the teachings.
He has excellently transcended all realms of existence. He is able to manifest majestic deportment within the lands, following the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma.

Wondrously worthy of being entrusted with the legacy, he strictly purifies the *vinaya* and establishes a grand model for the three worlds. With infinite response-bodies, he delivers sentient beings and rescues those of the future.
They had transcended all worldly entanglements. Their names were:
the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, Subhūti, Upāliśata, and others, who served as their leaders.

Such scriptural teachings were heard by me from the Buddha. "At one time" is synonymous with "at that time. "The Buddha was at such-and-such a place" means he was together with such-and-such individuals.
This includes the manner of the questions and answers, up to the point of "faithfully accepting and practicing"—this is the general formula for the compilation [of the sūtras].
The term "bhikṣus" excludes those who are minor; it refers to the assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty followers who constantly attended him. There are three outflows (*āsrava*), namely:

The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*): being free from these three types of leakage is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
An Arhat is the ultimate fruit of the Śrāvaka. Because the various Bodhisattvas conceal their great practices within while outwardly appearing as Śrāvakas, they are designated by this [Arhat] name;

yet, when their conduct is fully enumerated, they are capable of succeeding to the Buddha-dharma and are thus called "Sons of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*), dwelling in the family of the Dharma-king and maintaining it.
The Dharma-wheel is called "abiding and maintaining. To "transcend" means not to be bound by anything; it is to transcend without leaving the triple world, which is called "skillful transcendence.

"All existences" refers to the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the existence of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the existence of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*); these collectively indicate the places of birth within the triple world.
Dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) is the standard of conduct. Being fully endowed with dignified deportment, one can achieve self-perfection and also bring others to perfection.
When the intention for ethical conduct resides within, it turns the wheel; this is a metaphor for how the Buddha-dharma can destroy the obstacles of delusion and transport one out of birth and death.
Although he received the final testament, he truly forgot the marks of self and other, subject and object. He preached the Dharma as an illusion and delivered sentient beings as being like space;
thus he was called Miaokan (Wondrously Capable). *Vinaya* refers to the precepts. In terms of the body, it is called "rigor"; in terms of the mind, it is called "purity.
The four chapters on purity in the sixth fascicle and the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa* in the seventh fascicle are all subsumed herein. Thus it is seen.

The phrases "excellently transcending all realms of existence" (*sukhena sarvabhavān atikrāntaḥ*) and "establishing a broad model for the threefold world" (*traidhātuka-vinaya-prakāśaka*) both take this as their fundamental basis;
thus, this sutra regards the precepts (*śīla*) as paramount. Śāriputra—here translated as "Partridge"—is the name of his mother;
he is not her son. He was named after his mother and is foremost in wisdom. Maudgalyāyana is his clan name; his personal name is Kolita. He is foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Kauṣṭhila was formerly the brahmin Dīrghanakha, who was foremost in extensive learning. Pūrṇa means "Full";

Maitrāyaṇī is his father's name, meaning "Compassionate," and Maitrāyaṇī is his mother's name. Because he is named after both his parents, he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, or "Son of Full Compassion."
He is foremost in preaching the Dharma. Subhūti—here called "Born of Emptiness" (Kōshō) and also named "Well-Appeared" (Zen-gen)—is foremost in understanding emptiness.
Upānisaṭa—here called "The Nature of Dust is Empty"—awakened to the nature of form among the six sense objects.
In the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is said that he receives the prediction of attaining Buddhahood; this account proceeds from the perspective of the two vehicles but ultimately returns to the One Vehicle.
Therefore, when opening this sutra to praise its virtues, it first mentions the śrāvakas and only subsequently reaches the bodhisattvas.

The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* speaks of the "initial expedient means," setting aside the two vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and directly denouncing them as practicing in a confused and erroneous manner.
It is listed at the end of the ten types of false views. This is because the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* discusses exclusively the Supreme Vehicle from beginning to end, without mentioning anything else;
thus, when extolling virtues, it begins directly with the untainted Great Arhats, which is already discourse concerning the ultimate pinnacle.
Śāriputra and the other six are all included among the twenty-five sages of Perfect Penetration.
Opening this scroll reveals the clear exposition of Perfect Penetration as a model for all.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable Pratyekabuddhas who had attained the stage of no-more-learning, along with those at the initial stage of the path, who all came together to the Buddha’s presence.

At that time, while the Bhikṣus were observing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at the end of the summer retreat, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions sought to resolve their doubts and, out of reverence for His compassionate yet majestic authority, sought to inquire about the profound meaning.

Immediately, the Tathāgata arranged his seat and sat in tranquil repose. For the sake of those in the assembly, he proclaimed the profound and mysterious Dharma. The pure multitude at this Dharma banquet attained what they had never experienced before.
With the *kalaviṅka* voice of an immortal, his sound pervaded the worlds of the ten directions, and Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges gathered at the site of enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī is the foremost [of these].

Pratyekabuddhas—here translated as "Solitary Realizers" (Dujue) or alternatively as "Conditioned Realizers" (Yuanjue)—possess faculties slightly sharper than those of Śrāvakas, because they are able to erode and sever their residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Those who have attained the stage of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) are those for whom reality is truly exhausted and delusions are utterly ended. As for the initial mind, it refers to the stage of investigating reality and severing [delusions].

Regarding those who are deluded: at the beginning of the summer retreat, a bhikṣu enters the *varṣā* (rainy season) by binding his feet (*pāda-bandha*) and observing the *anupakhajja-vāsa* (the settled residence), refraining from begging for alms;

this is called the "cessation of the summer. At the conclusion of the period, on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or sixteenth day of the seventh month, he performs the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to admonish).
If one knows of one's own faults, one may freely confess them; if one does not know of one's faults, one allows the Saṃgha to raise them. This is the proper procedure.
This is the meaning of the purification of the *vinaya*. It further demonstrates that the precepts are of paramount importance.

Regarding the request for the profound meaning and the reasons for reverently receiving [the teaching], it is not merely to resolve and penetrate doubts and obstructions; rather, one seeks the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of esoteric cultivation and esoteric realization.
"At this very moment" refers to preaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of the audience. *Kalinga* is a celestial bird whose voice is subtle and wondrous.

The Buddha’s voice was like this: its sound pervaded the entire world. Even when Maudgalyāyana exerted his supernatural powers and listened to the Buddha’s voice as far as the worlds of the western direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it was as if he were face-to-face with him.
At that time, King Prasenajit was observing a fast on the anniversary of his father’s death.

He invited the Buddha to the inner palace and went himself to welcome the Tathāgata, providing an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed, exquisite flavors. Furthermore, he personally extended invitations to the great Bodhisattvas.

Within the city, there were also elders and lay devotees who were simultaneously feeding the Sangha, waiting for the Buddha to come and respond to their offerings. The Buddha then commanded Mañjuśrī to lead and distribute the Bodhisattvas.

[Sa]. As for the Arhats and those who should serve as the masters of the *zhāi* (fasting) rites, the Buddha’s four-line injunction clarifies that one should practice universal compassion in this manner, opening up and expounding the unobstructed path of mindfulness and conduct.
Only Ānanda had previously accepted a separate invitation; having traveled far and not yet returned, he was unable to join the assembly in its proper order.
Since there was neither an elder nor an ācārya, he returned alone on the road. On that day, no offerings were available, so Ānanda immediately took up his alms-bowl.
As he wandered through the city, begging from door to door in due order, he first sought out his final donor to serve as the host for his midday meal.

Without regard for whether they were pure or defiled, whether they were of the noble Kṣatriya caste or the lowly Caṇḍāla, he practiced universal compassion, making no distinction between the humble and the base.
He has resolved to bring to full completion the immeasurable merits of all sentient beings.
Ānanda already knows that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, rebuked Subhūti and Mahākāśyapa for being Arhats whose minds were not impartial, and he looks up to the Tathāgata with deep reverence.

He proclaimed the unobstructed [Dharma], delivering all who were subject to doubt and slander. Passing through the city moats, he walked slowly toward the outer gate, his deportment solemn and dignified, reverently observing the rules of purity.
At that time, Ānanda, while on his almsround, passed by a brothel and encountered a great illusionist.
The Mātangī woman, using the *sāvikāra* mantra of the former Brahmā-deva, drew him into her bedchamber;
as she touched his body with lustful intent, he was on the verge of destroying his precept-body.
This is the reason for such an error. If Ānanda does not follow the Tathāgata when attending to the offerings of kings, he will fall behind the senior monks (*sthavira*) in rank.
If he does not join the great assembly when attending to the homes of various patrons (*dānapati*), he will fall behind the *ācāryas* in rank.
*Ācārya* here means "preceptor" or "teacher of discipline," one who is able to correct his disciples. The *kṣetra*... [text fragment]

Whether they be kṣatriyas, caṇḍālas, or those such as prostitutes, drunkards, and butchers—if from the very beginning they seek within their hearts immeasurable merit, this is the most excellent point of Ānanda’s resolve.
It is later stated that he vowed to enter the evil world of the five turbidities first.
This is similar to the initial thought one first seeks within the mind; however, at this stage, while abiding in the conditioned mind, there is no clear sense of mastery or direction.
Later, upon awakening to the true mind, one has already accumulated the necessary provisions. The power of the realization in these two stages cannot be forcibly equated.
Subhūti abandoned poverty to follow wealth because it was easier for him to practice giving; Mahākāśyapa abandoned wealth to follow [poverty]...
Poverty was the cause he planted for that [result]. The standing of these two men is exceedingly high. Ānanda was rebuked by the Buddha for his uneven mind;
he desired to seek the unobstructed (*asaṃvara*), which is the power of a great vow. Ultimately, it was due to this that he encountered the calamity of the Mātangī woman.
Because he sought the unobstructed, he fell into error. Because he fell into error, he finally attained the Great Samādhi. In the end, this is...
It is reached through the power of one's vows, yet the karmic conditions are also subtle.

If the mind has not yet been fully transformed and integrated, such that one cannot achieve unimpeded mastery in all matters, then one may enter the pure realms but not the defiled ones; one may enter the state of a Buddha but not the realm of Māra.
The Tathāgata, knowing that she had employed the arts of seduction, returned immediately after the meal was finished.

The king, along with his ministers, elders, and householders, all followed the Buddha, wishing to hear the essential points of the Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness.
From within the light, a thousand-petaled precious lotus emerged, upon which a transformation-body Buddha sat in the full-lotus posture and proclaimed a divine mantra.
He commanded Mañjuśrī to take this mantra and go forth to provide protection; thus, evil spells were extinguished.
He then exhorted Ānanda and Mātaṅgī to return to the presence of the Buddha.
There is no goodness not fully possessed; hence it is called "the hundred treasures. There is no evil not utterly destroyed; hence it is called "fearlessness.

When the Original Buddha manifests silence while the Transformation Buddha speaks, the intent is to signify that the Dharma of the Buddha is primordial: there is neither speaking nor showing, yet through formlessness it manifests forms;

there is neither speaking nor showing, yet through non-speaking it reveals speech. In this single truth of profound stillness, the myriad transformations are darkly interconnected. Thus he uplifts and guides Ānanda and—
Mātanga, upon seeing the World-Honored One, was universally delivered by the power of His compassion;

upon seeing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, Ānanda saw the Buddha, prostrated himself, and wept with grief, lamenting that from time immemorial he had been devoted solely to extensive learning, yet had failed to perfect his spiritual power.
With earnest devotion, he entreated the Tathāgatas of the ten directions for the initial expedient means by which they attained bodhi—the wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna.
At that time, there were also Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the great Arhats of the ten directions.
The Pratyekabuddhas and others all wished to hear [the teaching] with joy; they withdrew to sit silently and received the holy command.
When the aforementioned text was about to destroy the essence of the precepts, it was Rāhula who desired to destroy them. If Ānanda had possessed his own fundamental capacity...
When he beheld the Buddha, it was not because his precept-body was about to perish that he prostrated himself and wept with grief;

rather, it was because the practitioner, having reached this point, still could not escape the affliction of evil states. This meant that the Way was not yet complete, and thus he lamented and repented with sorrow, seeking the Great Samādhi.
Ānanda, regretting his own excessive learning which had failed to prevent his erroneous fall, did not realize—
The illness of excessive learning arises from the ear-faculty. Therefore, we first select the ear-faculty as the initial expedient.
This is because the illness is formed by following after sounds; thus, one must cause the hearing to turn back upon its own mechanism in order to restore its profound stillness.
The medicine and the disease depend upon one another; this is the mark of a masterful hand. Bodhi is the ultimate end of the ocean of fruition.

Wondrous śamatha, samādhi, and dhyāna are the causes; they constitute the intermediate stage on the path to bodhi and are the primary task within the causal phase, marking the very beginning of the arousal of bodhicitta.
In the following text, one should [discuss] the stages from the beginning to the end, with the intermediate [stages].

The phrase "forever free from any trace of deviousness" clarifies that the eternally abiding true mind and the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) constitute the mind for the causal stage.
Later in the text, when only *samādhi* is mentioned, it refers directly to *samādhi* as the Great Samādhi;
when only *śamatha* is cited, the same principle applies. Indeed, the triad of *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā*, and *samādhi* constitutes "concentration" (*samādhi*) within this sutra.
This is the collective name for these extraordinary concentrations. By prefixing them with the word "wondrous," they become wondrous śamatha, wondrous samādhi, and wondrous dhyāna.
"Wondrous" implies that taking up one is equivalent to possessing all three.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You and I share the same life-force; our feelings are equal to those of brothers born of the same parents.
When you first resolved your mind, what superior signs did you perceive within my Dharma that caused you to suddenly renounce the deep and heavy affection for the world?

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "I saw the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, which were supremely wonderful and peerless. His physical form was translucent and radiant, like lapis lazuli. I constantly reflected upon this."
This appearance was not born of sensual desire. Why is this? The breath of desire is coarse and turbid;
it is foul-smelling and produced through sexual union, a chaotic mixture of pus and blood, incapable of giving rise to the supreme, pure, wondrous, and luminous mass of purple-gold light.
Therefore, out of thirsting aspiration, he went forth from home under the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
The phrase "seeing what superior sign" (見何勝相) contains the intent of pointing toward the nature of seeing that appears in the subsequent text.

Otherwise, it would simply have to say, "By what causes and conditions do you suddenly abandon the world," and so forth. It would not be a great error for the arising of the resolve [to seek awakening] to be based on "seeing signs.
The Buddha’s exclamation, "Excellent! was because [Ānanda] had not yet sought deeply. Ānanda’s point of failure does not lie in this section; rather, it lies in the world—
Venerable One, I have come here merely to pose a question, seeking only to ascertain where that mind resides.

Ānanda, you should know that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have undergone the continuous succession of birth and death solely because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature.
By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not true, [birth and death] exist.
The two types—the revolving cycle of birth and death, and the initial arousal of the eternally abiding true mind and deluded thoughts—are hereby revealed as the primary purport of the entire sutra.
Ānanda admires the Buddha’s wondrous samādhi; yet this wondrous samādhi is not that which is cultivated by the consciousness-mind. You must first cause him to awaken to this.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is not the mind; one must seek the true mind separately. Therefore, the subsequent text proceeds from the shallow to the deep, gradually revealing it.
From this point until the end of the third fascicle, the entire section consists of refuting the false to manifest the true. However, there are two types of refutation:
that which is ultimate, such as saying "brass is not gold"—once the brass is completely refuted, it is no longer used; and that which is non-ultimate, such as saying "there is sand within the ore."

It is like wishing to extract pure gold from ore; thus, one breaks through [the delusions] by means of manifestation. In the Sūtras, regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), they completely refute its falsity while largely manifesting its reality, with only a slight refutation of its falsity.
Regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), they refute the falsity and manifest the reality in each and every instance.
Regarding the seven great [elements], they largely manifest their reality. There are three kinds of false imaginings that are not real, because sentient beings...
Thus, three layers of deluded attachments are formed: first, although it is fundamentally not the mind, it resembles the mind; therefore, one is deludedly attached to it as being the mind.
Second, although it fundamentally has no substance, it seems to have substance; therefore, one is deludedly attached to it as having substance.
Third, although it fundamentally has no location, it seems to have a location; therefore, one is deludedly attached to it as having a location.

In this context, I do not directly refute the claim that the mind has no substance. First, I strip away the locus of the mind as it is grasped by him, compelling him to examine each point individually so as to reveal that it has no place of abiding whatsoever.
I wish for him to realize its falsity through his own self-awareness; he will certainly not awaken to it on his own until his attachments regarding these seven locations are exhausted.
Only then will I reprimand him for his "non-mind" and clarify that it lacks any substantial essence.
Now that you wish to investigate supreme bodhi and truly illuminate the nature of clarity, you should respond to my questions with a straightforward mind.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions follow one and the same path; they all depart from birth and death by means of a straightforward mind. Because their minds and words are straightforward, [they attain liberation].
In this way, it continues until the final stage; throughout the interval from beginning to end, there are never any signs of deviation or complication.

Regarding the statement that "from beginning to end, throughout the interval there are never any signs of deviation or complication," it means that this arises from a cause that is neither produced nor extinguished.
One attains the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing, directly realizing Bodhi without traversing the various realms of external paths or the Lesser Vehicle.
Ānanda, I now ask you: when you first resolved your mind upon the thirty-two marks of the Tathāgata, what did you see?
Who was it that felt such love and joy? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, such love and joy arose from using my own mind."
Eyes. Because one beholds the sublime marks of the Tathāgata with the eyes and the heart gives rise to love and joy, one thus resolves to leave birth and death behind.
This is "arousing the mind by virtue of seeing the marks. [The Buddha] uttered the two characters "eyes" (xu) and "mind" (xin) to provide a handle for expounding the sutra, Ānanda.
It is stated directly that what is seen by the eyes is entirely the cognitive vision of sentient beings. The subsequent passages repeatedly reveal this truth;
it is nothing more than a transformation of the cognitive vision of sentient beings into the cognitive vision of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "What you have said is truly what one cherishes and delights in. It is because of the mind and the eyes.
If you do not know where the mind and the eyes reside, then you will be unable to subdue worldly afflictions. It is like a king who has been invaded by bandits."
I shall mobilize troops to suppress and eliminate them. These troops must first know the location of the bandits. It is your own wandering that causes this;
your mind and eyes are at fault. I now ask you: where, precisely, are your mind and eyes located right now?

"Only the mind and the eyes—where are they now? This refers to the "investigation of the mind. Thereafter, no such interrogative phrasing occurs again; so how can it be called the "seven investigations"?
If one says there are seven rounds of refuting locations, that would suffice. Do not overlook this as a mere passage:
it is an analogy for a king whose kingdom is invaded by bandits and who dispatches troops to eliminate them, necessitating that he know the location of those bandits. (The subsequent text follows.)
There are seven locations where the mind resides; pursue it thoroughly until the thief has no place to hide.
It is clearly stated that you are made to wander in saṃsāra because the eyes and the mind are at fault. Therefore, he asks: "Where are this mind and these eyes now?
Thus, the "mind" that the Tathāgata interrogates is the thief—it is not the [true] mind, but the deluded mind; it is not the true mind. Ānanda...
If one were to know that the deluded mind is a thief, one would naturally answer that its whereabouts are unknown, and instead simply request the true mind.
It is precisely because one habitually employs the deluded mind and protects it with all one's might that, upon seeing the Tathāgata point it out as a thief, [one feels such resistance].
Though he does not speak with his mouth, his mind does not believe. He points out seven locations one by one.
If it is said that there are specific locations, how can he be hastily called a thief? Later, Ānanda says: "In performing all difficult dharmic practices, I always employ this mind. He further says:
"As for what I have realized regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, I currently do so with the conditioned mind (*ālambana-citta*)."
That which one reveres and looks up to is, in fact, the underlying state of the deluded mind that protects its own falsehoods and mistakes a thief for its son;
this is what first emerges. The Buddha stated repeatedly that such a thing is impossible, and only thereafter did he directly rebuke him, saying, "This is not your mind.
He declared that this mind is a thief and not a son, without needing to seek out its specific location. As for the eternally abiding true mind, however—
"Then it may reside within the seven apertures; it may not reside within the seven apertures;

it may neither reside nor not reside. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: 'World-Honored One, all ten types of ordinary beings in the world alike take their consciousness and mind to dwell within their bodies.
Even when gazing at the Tathāgata’s blue-lotus eyes, they are likewise seen to be on the Buddha’s face. Now, as I observe this floating [consciousness]...'"
The sense organs and their four objects reside only on my face; yet this consciousness-mind truly dwells within the body.
That the mind resides within the body is what all sentient beings habitually cling to—what is known as the state of turbid confusion.

This is what is meant by taking the mind-nature as the [true] mind. "Once deluded, it becomes the mind; one is certain to be confused, thinking it resides within the physical body"—this is precisely it.
As for the other six [theories], they were merely forced into alternative calculations after being refuted by the Buddha at one time.
The Buddha said to Ānanda, "As you now sit here in the Tathāgata’s lecture hall, look at the Jeta Grove; where is it now?
"World-Honored One, this great multi-storied pavilion and pure lecture hall is within Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, while the Jeta Grove is actually outside the hall.
"Ānanda, what did you first see when you were inside the hall? "World-Honored One, while I was inside the hall, I first saw..."
The Tathāgata next observes the great assembly; looking outward in this manner, he finally gazes upon the grove and garden.

Focusing on the scene before his eyes, he discerns the internal and external realms in their sequential order of perception. [He] lowers his gaze to the ground—[marking] the seven locations of the World-Honored One.
He raised many difficult questions based on his views, which also contained the notion that the nature of seeing is the mind and not the eye.
"Ānanda, when you gaze upon the groves and gardens, by what means does this seeing occur? "World-Honored One, this great lecture hall has its doors and windows wide open."
Therefore, as I stand here in the hall, I am able to behold you from afar. At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, extended his golden-hued arm and stroked Ānanda’s crown.
He then announced to Ānanda and the entire multitude: "There is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown."
"Śūraṅgama King, complete with the myriad practices, is the wondrous path of sublime adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend by a single gate.
Listen attentively now! Ānanda prostrated himself and humbly received the compassionate instruction."

Ānanda requested instruction on the Great Samādhi. The Buddha first shattered his conditioned mind; having first broken through the mind, even before the question and answer were concluded, he urgently pointed out the existence of samāpatti, and so forth.
This was likely to steady his soul, which had momentarily returned to its original state.

This comforts the intent of his initial inquiry. It is like a destitute son who, upon seeing his father, is first told of the family treasures so that he may know in advance where his food and clothing will come from;
once his alarm has subsided and his spirit is calmed, he may gradually inquire further, thereby concluding the passage on the "Seven Breaks."

Later, the Great Samādhi is examined in detail. "Transcending through a single gate" refers to the Path of Wondrous Adornment, which corresponds to the subsequent "Entering deeply through a single gate.
"Entering deeply through a single gate" is the cause; it is the initial expedient means.

"Transcending through a single gate" is true Bodhi, the ocean of wondrous adornment—the ultimate fruit of the Buddha. Because one proceeds toward it by means of the Great Samādhi, it is called a "path."
The Buddha told Ānanda, "It is as you have said. While your body is in the lecture hall, with its doors and windows wide open, you can gaze far out at the groves and gardens;
yet there are sentient beings within this hall who do not see the Tathāgata, but see those outside the hall. Ānanda replied:
“World-Honored One, it is impossible that one who is inside a hall could see the groves and springs but not see the Tathāgata.

“Ānanda, you are just like this. Your mental faculty is all-knowing and clear. If the mind that is currently clear and aware were truly within your body, then you should first be able to perceive the interior of your own body.
Is there any sentient being who first sees what is inside their body and only afterwards observes what is outside?”
Regarding external objects: even if one cannot see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach, one certainly ought to understand clearly that nails grow, hair lengthens, tendons turn, and pulses throb.
How can you not know this? If you do not know what is within, how can you claim to know what is without?
Therefore, you should know that your assertion—that the mind capable of conscious awareness dwells inside the body—is impossible.
"Perhaps it is still acceptable. To question this is to resolve that [the heart] cannot be so. The heart, liver, spleen, and stomach are deep-seated;

the growth of nails and hair, the turning of tendons and the throbbing of vessels are more superficial—these too are places of origin within the skin. All of these belong to what is "inside. Once the heart is pierced, it is no longer "inside.
By this single piercing alone, any who hear it should be startled into awakening and fall prostrate. Try to examine this for yourself.
"Among the worldly scriptures, is there anyone who says that the mind does not reside within? This is a true lion’s roar!
Ānanda bowed his head to the ground and said to the Buddha: "Having heard such a teaching from the Tathāgata, I have realized that my mind truly resides outside the body.
Why is this? It is like a lamp burning inside a room; that lamp must necessarily..."
First it illuminates the interior of the room; from the door of that room, it subsequently reaches the courtyard.
All sentient beings do not see within their own bodies, but see only outside their bodies, just as a lamp placed outside a room cannot illuminate the interior. This principle must be clear.
May there be no further delusion; may this accord with the Buddha’s definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and not be erroneous.
To seize the internal while clinging to the external is the way of common sentiment. The analogy of the lamp follows from the previous point that the mind resides within the body;

one must necessarily know the internal body. This is like a lamp inside a room being able to illuminate the room; now, [the case where it is] outside the room serves as an analogy for the mind being [outside].
"Externally, they cannot see internally.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "These bhikṣus have just now come from the city of Śrāvastī, begging for alms-food along the way."
We have returned to the Jeta Grove; I have already finished my midday meal. "Observe these bhikṣus," [the Buddha said]. "When one person eats, are all the people satiated?
Ānanda replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Although these bhikṣus are arhats, their bodies and lives are not the same.
How could one person cause the multitude to be satiated? The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you were to awaken and understand..."
When you see it, the mind is actually outside the body; since the body and mind are external to one another, they do not interfere with each other.
Thus, what the mind knows, the body cannot perceive; what the body perceives at its own boundaries, the mind cannot know.
I now show you my hand, as soft as *tūla* cotton. When your eyes see it, does your mind discern it? Ānanda replied, "It is so, World-Honored One. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "If..."

Regarding those who claim it is "outside": how could that which perceives and knows be situated outside the body? Therefore, you should know that your assertion—that the mind capable of cognition dwells outside the body—is impossible.
That food cannot satisfy this; how could the external mind know the body? This second point refutes the notion that the mind exists outside.
When you see with your eyes, does the mind not discern? This also implies that it is the mind, not the eye, that intends.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said, because it does not see within, it does not reside inside the body;
yet because the body and mind know one another and are not separate, it does not exist outside the body. As I now reflect, I know that it must reside in a single location.
The Buddha asked, “Where, then, is this location? Ānanda replied, “This consciousness that knows: since it does not know what is within, yet is able to see what is without...”
As I reflect upon it, the faculty is hidden within the root, much like a person who takes a lapis lazuli bowl and covers both eyes with it;
although there is something covering them, it does not obstruct vision. That faculty perceives according to what is seen and immediately discriminates accordingly.
Yet, as for this mind of mine that is conscious and capable of knowing, it does not perceive what is internal because it resides in the faculty; it gazes clearly at the external without obstruction.
Because its root is latent within, it is able to see external objects by virtue of not seeing the internal. Contemplating this mind, one finds it resides beneath the faculty of the eye;
the faculty of the eye does not obstruct the mind’s vision, just as crystal does not obstruct the eye’s vision.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "As you have said, that which is hidden within the roots of the eyes is like lapis lazuli.
Suppose that person were to cover their eyes with a lapis lazuli mask; would they see mountains and rivers, and yet not see the lapis lazuli? "Yes, World-Honored One;
if that person were to cover their eyes with a lapis lazuli mask, they would indeed see the lapis lazuli. The Buddha told Ānanda: "If your mind were united with the lapis lazuli in this manner..."

If one can see mountains and rivers, why does one not see the eye? If one were to see the eye, the eye would be identical to its object, and thus could not function as that which follows [the object].
If it cannot be seen, how can you say that this cognizing mind is latent within the faculty, like a crystal joined [to it]?
Therefore, you should know that your claim—that the mind capable of conscious awareness dwells hidden within the sense organs like a crystal casket—is impossible.
When a crystal covers the eye, the eye sees the crystal; but when the faculty of sight covers the mind, the mind does not see the eye. Even if one were to grant that it could see:
The eye. It is through the eye that an object is constituted as such. Now, can an object itself ever see an object?
Your claim that "the faculty follows what is seen, and immediately thereafter performs discrimination" is logically untenable. Third, it is refuted that the mind does not reside within the faculties.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I have now further reflected as follows:

In the body of this sentient being, the viscera and organs are within, while the orifices are situated on the outside. Where there are internal organs, there is darkness; where there are orifices, there is light.

Now, when I am facing the Buddha, I open my eyes and see light, which I call 'seeing the external'; when I close my eyes and see darkness, I call it 'seeing the internal. What is the meaning of this?"
Because there are apertures, there is light; thus, when the eyes are opened, one sees light. Because there are cavities, there is darkness; thus, when the eyes are closed, one sees darkness.
Seeing light is termed "seeing the external," though one need not insist that it refers to something external to the body and mind.

Seeing darkness is termed "seeing the internal," though one need not actually see the heart, liver, spleen, or stomach. Although "internal" and "external" are listed side by side, this is merely a figurative use of the term "external."
This manifestation within the body still reverts to the original attachment that it exists within. Therefore, the Buddha refutes only its existence within.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "When you close your eyes and perceive darkness, is this realm of darkness facing your eyes?"
If it does not face the eye, yet when it is in front of the eye, how can darkness in front of one's eyes constitute the "internal"?

If it were internal, then while you are in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps, this entire darkness within the room would be your own internal organs. If, on the other hand, it does not face the eye...

How could this constitute the "burning furnace" (*jiaofu*)? The *jiaofu* refers to the internal organs. If darkness were already present before one's eyes, how could what is in front possibly be considered "internal"?

If that which is immediately before one were defined as internal, then a dark room directly in front of one’s eyes could be called the *jiaofu*; would that not be absurd? If this appearance of darkness...
If the eye were in opposition to darkness, then this eye should not be in conjunction with it; how then could one see darkness before the eyes?
Thus, whether the eye is in opposition to darkness or not, in either case, it cannot be established as being internal.

If you claim that apart from external seeing there is internal seeing established by opposition—such that closing the eyes and seeing darkness is called "seeing within the body"—then when opening the eyes and seeing light, why do you not see your own face?
If you do not see your face, then internal seeing is not established. If seeing your face were established, then this cognizing mind [would be self-evident].
Furthermore, if the visual faculty were located in empty space, how could it be said to be "within"? If it were in empty space, it would not be your own substance;
in that case, when the Tathāgata now looks at your face, that [vision] would also be your body. Your eyes already perceive this, yet your body should not be aware of it.
If you insist that there are two cognitions—one from the body and one from the eye—then this single body of yours would necessarily become two Buddhas.
Therefore, you should know that your claim that seeing darkness is called "seeing the internal" is untenable.
The realm before one's eyes is called "external," while the realm within the body is called "internal. Previously, because it was opposed to the eye, it could not be established as internal.
Now, even if it were separated from the external to become an internal counterpart, this would mean the eye is capable of looking back upon itself.
If it can look back upon the body when closed, then when open, it should likewise be able to look back upon its own face. If this were not the case, the principle would not hold.
If seeing were accomplished upon meeting [the object], then the one who sees would reside in empty space. To reside in space would mean to be separated from your own body.
If you further insist that it is your own essence, then the Tathāgata would likewise be separate from your body when he sees your face;
would he then also be your own person? If you do not allow that the Buddha’s body is you, then your mind and eyes are also not you. Your eye—
It is in empty space. It is already known that within empty space, the body is conjoined with it yet there is no sensation.
If you insist that both possess consciousness, then this single body of yours should have two cognitions: one in empty space and one in your body, making you two Ānandas today.
"In another day, you shall become two Buddhas. Having thus explained and clarified this point by point, there is no principle of looking back;
since one cannot perceive darkness as seeing within, the fourth [point] refutes the notion that the mind resides within.
Ānanda said, "I have often heard the Buddha teach the fourfold assembly that because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
and because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise. As I now contemplate this very essence of contemplation, it is truly my own mind-nature.
Wherever it conjoins with something, the mind appears accordingly; yet it is not located within, without, or in between—none of these three places."
Because the mind arises, various phenomena arise; phenomena do not arise of themselves. Because phenomena arise, various minds arise; the mind does not arise of itself.
This means they are falsely manifested through mutual dependence, both lacking an essence of arising; thus, both mind and phenomena are empty.
Ānanda cited this to prove that the mind exists in accordance with whatever it encounters, yet regardless of what object it grasps—
The Dharma is precisely the place where the mind resides. "In between" refers to within the aforementioned sense organs. Ānanda did not mean that the mind must necessarily have a physical substance;

he meant precisely that the mind has no substance yet is capable of uniting. This "uniting" is the very location of the mind. Below, it is distinguished that where there is union, there must be a substance;
if there were no substance, there could be no union, and if there were no union, there would be no location.

The Buddha told Ānanda: "As for what you have just said—that because dharmas arise, various minds are produced, and that wherever they encounter conditions, the mind follows and exists—this mind has no substance;
thus, there would be nothing with which it could encounter. If it were possible to encounter conditions while lacking any substance,"
Thus, the nineteen realms arise from the conjunction of the seven particles; this principle is not so.

If they possess a substantial body, then when you prick that body with your own hand, does the mind that perceives it emerge from within, or enter from without? If it emerges from within, [how could it perceive what is outside?]
If you look back into your own body, [the mind] would have to come from the outside; in that case, it should first meet with the face.
For things to meet, they must be like a lid meeting a box—there must necessarily be substantial entities on both sides before a meeting can occur.
Now, the thinking mind you contemplate is originally but a floating thought; it truly has no self-substance, and thus there is no place for it to meet. In the world, there are only ten...
The eight elements and the six objects—these nine and seven [together] are merely names for emptiness. Since emptiness cannot be joined, it is said that this interpretation is incorrect;
only that which possesses a substance can truly join. If the mind has a substance, where would it be located? Test this by pressing against the body:
it is not seen within the body, nor does it emerge from within. It is not perceived beforehand.
The face does not enter from without. This mind is ultimately without substance; how could it exist in accordance with conjunction?
To exist in accordance with conjunction and yet be restlessly turbulent and confused—this is still to mistake it for the true mind. This exhaustively describes the deluded state of worldly people.
Ānanda said, "I see with this eye, but my mind knows that it is not the eye; therefore, 'seeing' does not have the meaning of [the eye's] function.
The Buddha said, "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see? Furthermore, all those who are already dead still possess eyes;
they should all be able to see objects. If they could see objects, how could they be called dead?"
The Master [Sengzhao] previously stated that because the mind does not perceive its own locus, one says the mind is not there.

Therefore, Bian’s claim that "seeing is the eye" and his refutation based on the premise that "knowing is not the eye," yet holding him accountable for the act of seeing, is incorrect in meaning. How could he know that the capacity to see resides in the mind, while the eyes themselves do not see?
It is not only the knower that is not the eye; the seer is likewise not the eye. If the eye were able to see, then it would be as follows:
If a door has apertures, there should likewise be seeing; why then is it not possible? Furthermore, observe those who are already dead:
this serves as proof that the eyes alone cannot see. Seeing must necessarily belong to the mind. This also implies the intention that it is the mind, and not the eye, that sees.
Ānanda, furthermore, as for this mind of yours that is conscious and capable of cognition: if it must have a substantial body, does it consist of a single entity or many entities?
Now, while residing within your body, does it pervade the entire body or does it not pervade it?

If it were a single entity, then when you prick one limb with your hand, the other three limbs should feel it. If all [limbs] were to feel it, then the pricking would have no specific location. If [you say] it is pricked...
If [the self] were a single entity, it could not constitute itself as "you. If it were multiple entities, it would constitute many people; which entity, then, would be you?
If it were a pervasive entity, it would be the same as the aforementioned pinching. If it were not pervasive, then when you touch your head, you would also be touching your foot;
yet while the head has sensation, the foot would be without consciousness. This is not the case for you. Therefore, one should know that according to where...
That the mind should exist wherever there is a point of conjunction is impossible.
One should know that the essence of the mind is neither one nor many, and neither pervasive nor non-pervasive; thus, one knows that the mind has no fixed substance.
How, then, could there be conjunction? This is the fifth refutation: that the mind does not follow conjunction.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I have also heard the Buddha and Mañjuśrī and the other Dharma Princes conversing on the time of the True Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
At that time, World-Honored One, you also said: 'The mind is not within, nor is it without.

As I reflect upon this, there is nothing seen within, and there is no mutual cognition without. Because there is no cognition within, its existence within is not established. Yet, body and mind do cognize one another."
The external is not the object [of the mind]. Since it is now known through mutual perception, yet there is no seeing within, it must reside in between.
What the World-Honored One said—that it is neither internal nor external—was intended to show that the mind has no fixed location; it was not meant to say that the mind resides in the space between.
Ānanda again clung to this as being "in the middle," failing to realize that the very moment one designates something as "middle," a fixed location has already been established. Therefore...
He further examined whether [consciousness] resides in the body or in the sense-object. He thought: "If it were within, one would not see the internal organs;
if it were outside, the body and its parts would not be aware of one another. Since neither of these two positions holds, it must reside between the sense organ and the object.
The Buddha said, “Regarding what you call the ‘middle,’ the middle must not be confused; it cannot be without a location. Now, as you investigate this middle, where does it reside?

Does it reside in a place, or does it reside in the body? If it resides in the body, then being on the periphery it would not be the middle, and being in the center it would be the same as the interior.

If it resides in a place, is that place something that can be indicated, or is it something that cannot be indicated? If it cannot be indicated, it is the same as non-existence. If it can be indicated, then...”
It is not fixed. Why is this? For example, when a person uses a gnomon as a marker, it is west when viewed from the east, and north when observed from the south.
