Dragons are all swift and rapid. Those born from a womb have much emotion and little thought; because their emotions are heavy and their thoughts are many, they sink downward and cannot rise lightly.
Those born from moisture do not depend on parents; rather, when their emotional thoughts combine with moist vapors, they immediately undergo birth.
Transformational birth also arises from thought: by contemplating a superior place and feeling affection for that realm, one immediately undergoes transformational birth.

The four propositions regarding feeling and perception further clarify that the four modes of birth undergo constant transformation and are not fixed. Sometimes feeling transforms into perception; union transforms into separation; there is no fixed karma.
An egg-born being may change into one born from a womb; moisture-born beings may change into those born by transformation; there is no fixed substance.
The karmic retributions they receive may involve ascending or sinking; there is no fixed realm of rebirth. Such are the causes for the continuous succession of sentient beings.
Pūrṇa, when conceptualization and craving form a single bond, and craving cannot be severed, then throughout the worlds, fathers, mothers, sons, and grandsons are born in an uninterrupted succession.

These are rooted in desire and greed; as craving and love nourish one another and greed cannot be halted, then throughout the worlds, those born from eggs, transformations, moisture, or wombs, according to their relative strength or weakness, devour one another in turn. These are rooted in killing.
Greed is the root. Because humans eat sheep, when the sheep dies it becomes a human; when the human dies, they become a sheep. Thus it continues through ten types of births.
Death after death and birth after birth, they prey upon one another. These evil karmas arise together, persisting until the end of the future.
Such beings take the greed for theft as their root. "You owe me my life; I shall repay you with my debt. For these reasons and conditions, [the cycle] continues through the *sūtra*.
For hundreds of thousands of kalpas, you have constantly remained within birth and death. You loved my heart, and I cherished your form;

because of these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas we have constantly remained bound in entanglement. Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the three fundamental roots; by these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue in succession.

Sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) pervades all four modes of birth (*yoni*). Now, let us examine this in relation to human beings. "Conceiving through craving" (*saṃjñā-rāga-saṃyojana*) refers not exclusively to the moment of taking birth;
it is likewise so while one is in the world. "Growing together through craving" means that both body and life-force are equally dependent upon nourishment.

Regarding humans and sheep, who come and devour one another in the cycle of birth and death, this is called "thieving greed"; it is both killing and stealing. To seize [another's]— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "奪," which corresponds to "to seize" or "to rob."]
Wealth belongs to theft; how much more so the taking of one’s life? Life belongs to killing, and debt belongs to theft; affection belongs to desire. You must repay me for my life-debt;
the textual meanings are thus mutually evident. It is the same for the mind and form, and for affection.
Desire-greed, killing-greed, and theft-greed are all called "roots"—the roots of the cycle of birth and death. Thus, one knows the flow of the triple world.
It revolves. There is only craving and attachment. If one cuts off craving and attachment, one immediately transcends the triple world.
Pūrṇa, these three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of awakened clarity;

they arise from the functioning of this knowing-nature, which, through its capacity for cognition, gives rise to appearances. From deluded vision, the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena arise, flowing and shifting in succession. Because of...
This is false and illusory; it ends and begins again.
Just as with the karmic fruits of sentient beings in the worlds above, these three kinds of inverted states continue in succession.

All of them arise from the clarity of original enlightenment (benjue) as a deluded manifestation of awareness; because of this awareness, appearances emerge, and from delusion, birth is perceived. As the previous question asked:
Why do mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Why do all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) undergo successive transformations and flux, ending only to begin again?
The answer now is that they all arise from false imaginings (*abhūtaparikalpa*) and are produced by what is known through delusion.

Pūrṇa said: "If this wondrous enlightenment—the original wondrously enlightened luminosity—is neither increased nor diminished from the Tathāgata’s mind, then how did the mountains, rivers, the great earth, and all conditioned phenomena suddenly arise without cause? Now that the Tathāgata has attained this wondrous, empty, luminous enlightenment..."
"Mountains, rivers, the great earth, conditioned phenomena, habitual tendencies, and outflows—when will these ever arise again? The Buddha told Pūrṇa:
"Suppose there is a person who is lost, and in a certain village, he mistakes south for north. Does this delusion exist because of delusion, or does it emerge because of awakening?
Pūrṇa replied: "Such a lost person neither exists because of delusion nor because of awakening. Why is this so?"
Delusion has no fundamental root. How can it arise because of delusion? Awakening does not give rise to delusion. How can it arise because of awakening? The Buddha said:
"Pūrṇa, suppose that while a person is in a state of delusion, another person who has suddenly attained awakening points out the way and causes them to awaken.
Pūrṇa, what do you think? Even though this person was previously deluded, would they become deluded again regarding this village? "No, World-Honored One. "Pūrṇa," [the Buddha continued].
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise so. This delusion has no fundamental basis; its nature is ultimately empty.

Originally there was no delusion, yet it appears as if there were a perception of delusion. When awakening perceives delusion, the delusion is extinguished; once awakened, delusion is never produced again. It is also like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky.

"When the cataract disease is removed, the flowers vanish into the empty space. Suppose there were a foolish person who, in that empty space where the flowers had ceased to exist, waited for the flowers to be born again.
Do you consider such a person to be foolish or wise? Pūrṇa replied, "In emptiness, there were originally no flowers."
To perceive the arising and ceasing of delusive visions, and to see the flowers vanish into emptiness, is already an inversion. To then command them to emerge once more is truly madness.
How can such a madman be called either ignorant or wise? The Buddha said:

"According to your understanding, why do you ask how the wondrously enlightened, luminous emptiness of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas could ever again give rise to mountains, rivers, and the great earth? Furthermore..."
Gold ore mixed with refined gold, once that gold has become pure, can no longer be mixed again;
just as wood turned to ash cannot become wood again, so it is with the Bodhi and Nirvana of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
The awakening-nature of sentient beings is no different from that of the Buddha.

That, without cause, various conditioned phenomena suddenly arise is a point that even Tathāgatas—who have already realized the awakening of emptiness—might wonder when these conditioned states could ever arise again; it is a matter of constant delusion for ordinary people, and thus this question was specifically raised.

In the beginning, there was fundamentally no delusion; this is not because sentient beings had not yet engaged in false conceptualization. Precisely at the moment of delusion, no delusion can be found.
It is like one who has lost their sense of direction: the directions themselves have not actually shifted. Where there is no delusion, there is likewise no awakening;

it is as if there were delusion and one subsequently awakens to it. Therefore, if there is no non-awakening, that is that; but once one awakens to delusion, delusion is instantly extinguished, never to arise again.
Arising? Indeed, when one is deluded, there is already no delusion to be found; how much less could delusion arise after awakening? Delusion is fundamentally unarisen;

its formation did not begin with the Buddha, nor was it extinguished by him. Reality is fundamentally unchanging; it did not begin to arise upon becoming a Buddha. Within the realm of sentient beings, there is already neither arising nor change;
how much less could there be arising or change for one who has attained Buddhahood? These four metaphors encompass [the meaning].

This citation serves to show that although delusion and enlightenment are illusory, they do not preclude cultivation and realization. For the ground is fundamentally unchanging, and space is fundamentally devoid of flowers;
this points to the state of being "pure and original. Just as ore must be smelted and wood must be burned, these words direct one toward the practice of spiritual work.
"Delusion" is a metaphor for afflictions never arising again; "flowers" are a metaphor for birth and death never continuing; and "gold" is a metaphor for [the true nature].
Bodhi is eternally imperishable; the analogy of ashes for nirvana signifies that there is no returning.
Pūrṇa, furthermore, you asked: "The natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally interfused and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
I doubt that the natures of water and fire do not mutually overcome or extinguish one another. You also questioned how empty space and the great earth both pervade the Dharma-realm without...
They are mutually compatible. Pūrṇa, it is like empty space: its essence is not composed of various phenomena, yet it does not obstruct the manifestation of those various phenomena.
Why is this so? Pūrṇa, when the sun shines upon that great void, it becomes bright; when clouds gather, it becomes dark; when the wind stirs, it moves;
when the sky clears, it becomes pure; when vapors condense, it becomes turbid; when dust accumulates, it forms a haze; and when water settles, it becomes clear.
"Ying, what do you think? Regarding these various conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) in different directions, are they produced because of that [sun], or do they exist independently of it?
If they were produced by that, Pūrṇa, when the sun shines, since it is the light of the sun, throughout the worlds of the ten directions—"
It is the same solar light; why then is a round sun seen again within the sky? If this were the luminosity of space itself, space should illuminate itself;
why then does it not produce such radiance during the midnight hours when clouds and mist prevail? One should know that this luminosity is neither the sun nor the sky.

It is no different from the sun in the sky. When one contemplates their characteristics, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out or described; it would be like seeking flowers in the sky and binding them into a fruit of the sky.

How can one then interrogate them regarding the meaning of their mutual subjugation and extinction? When one contemplates their nature, it is fundamentally true—nothing but wondrous, enlightened clarity. This mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity...
Previously, they were neither water nor fire; why then do you ask again about those that are mutually incompatible? True, wondrous, enlightened clarity is also like this:
if you manifest it through space, then space appears; if you manifest it through earth, water, fire, or wind, then each of these respectively appears.
If both are illuminated, then both appear. How do they appear together? Pūrṇa, it is like the reflection of the sun appearing in a single body of water.

When two people look at the sun in the water together and walk in opposite directions—one to the east and one to the west—each person perceives a sun following them, one to the east and one to the west.
Since there was originally no fixed standard [for their positions], you should not raise the objection that "this sun is but one."
If each [element] acts individually, then since each day is already dual, how can they manifest as one? This is a circular and false argument that provides no basis for reliance.
The following answers Pūrṇa’s second question. The essence of empty space is not the various phenomena; it does not refuse to manifest them.

This is a metaphor for the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is not the various great elements (*mahābhūta*), yet it is not obstructed by their following conditions. This has already exhausted the general meaning; below follows the detailed explanation.

To clarify: "different regions" refers to the manifestation [of these elements] wherever they may be. When those [passages] mention the sun, clouds, and so forth—specifically from the "sun reaching the sky" to the "single instance of solar light"—they cite the luminosity of the sun as an analogy for the six delusions;
this is intended to show that they lack substantial reality. Since the great elements have no inherent substance, how could they mutually overcome or extinguish one another?
Furthermore, when we contemplate the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, although it possesses names such as "true fire" and "true water," [it remains ultimately devoid of such distinctions].
The primordial, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind is, in reality, devoid of the characteristics of solidity, obstruction, moisture, burning, or dryness.

How could there be anything that is not mutually compatible? That emptiness is luminous and emptiness manifests is because it appears as the characteristic of emptiness following the karma of emptiness, just as emptiness emerges when one digs a well.
That each is luminous and each manifests is because each follows its own karma and each respective realm appears, just as when one seeks fire in a particular place.
In one place fire emerges; in another, one seeks water; and in yet another, water emerges. All are clear and manifest;
they appear as objects alike according to their respective karma. This is like the grasping that pervades the Dharma-realm, arising so as to fill the Dharma-realm.

It precisely represents the subtlety of responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the measure of what they know. The second fascicle reveals the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it uses the true moon [as its metaphor].

This is an analogy for the True. Taking the moon’s reflection as the false, this reveals that the Tathāgatagarbha is unchanging while following conditions, and follows conditions while remaining unchanging.
It cannot be fully described by borrowing the image of the sun’s reflection in water;

rather, one should observe how the Tathāgatagarbha manifests simultaneously with the seven elements, just as a single reflection of the sun appears wherever it moves—east or west—and its wondrous nature will naturally become apparent.
Pūrṇa, you have used the characteristics of form and emptiness to oppose and displace one another within the Tathāgata-garbha;

yet the Tathāgata-garbha, in accordance with them, manifests as form and emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, the wind moves and the sky clears, the sun shines and the clouds darken.

Sentient beings become deluded and distressed, turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the dust of the senses; thus they give rise to worldly toil and manifest the signs of the mundane world. I, by means of wondrous clarity and...
Cessation does not arise; it is merged with the Tathāgatagarbha. Now, the Tathāgatagarbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, within it, the one becomes the infinite, and the infinite becomes the one. Within the small, the large appears; within the large, the small appears.

Without moving from the site of enlightenment, it pervades the worlds of the ten directions. It contains the inexhaustible voids of the ten directions within its body, manifesting [all things] upon a single tip of a hair.

In the Jewel-King lands, sitting within a single mote of dust, he turns the Great Dharma Wheel; by extinguishing the dust and merging with awakening, he gives rise to the wondrously enlightened nature of true thusness (*tathatā*).
The characteristics of the seven elements described above are such that their mutual sublation or extinction cannot be questioned. Regarding these seven elements—
The nature is likewise so. One cannot inquire into that which is mutually incompatible. Nevertheless, for what reason do the seven elements exist?

It is because your *karmic consciousness* is not empty and the distinction between subject and object (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi*) has not been destroyed. Following the karma of form and emptiness, they compete with and usurp one another within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* itself manifests as emptiness or as form in accordance with your karma. Therefore...

One perceives that the emptiness of form pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Yet, at the moment of opening one's eyes, one sees only a dense array of material objects and defilements filling the field before one, such that it appears entirely as a defiled land.
One does not realize that these appearances are fundamentally empty and have no basis for reliance.

This is truly because sentient beings are internally obscured by ignorance and driven by the power of karma; their minds are naturally bewildered and distressed, and they do not understand this for themselves.

Turning one's back on pure awakening and uniting with delusive objects, one gives rise to worldly toil and perceives the signs of the mundane world, failing to see the wondrously enlightened nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Thus, the entire nature is transformed into signs. I, however, have exhausted ignorance and emptied the karmic consciousness;
there remains only the essence of pure, wondrous, and luminous wisdom, with nothing else whatsoever. By means of this wondrously luminous wisdom—

The essence merges with the Tathāgatagarbha; yet the Tathāgatagarbha is seen only as the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind pervading the worlds of the ten directions, without a single thing acting as an obstruction or impediment.
Therefore, within this, all things are unimpeded. Thus, the totality of phenomena (lakṣaṇa) constitutes the nature (dharmatā).
One should know that when the mind exists, the realm of Sahā appears; when the mind does not exist, the Flower Treasury (Puṣpakuṭa) merges with space.
"One becoming two" refers to the mutual compatibility of the one and the many. "The small containing two" refers to the non-obstruction of the broad and the narrow.
"Without moving" refers to the one being immeasurable. "The body containing two" refers to the immeasurable being one.

Regarding "a land appearing on the tip of a hair," this is the appearance of the container within the contained. Regarding "a wheel turning within a mote of dust," this is the appearance of the contained within the container; that is, within the small.
This refers to the manifestation of the Great. All of these are the manifestation of the realm of *yathābhūta-pramāṇa* (as-it-is) within the wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness).

The Tathāgatagarbha is like the substance of a mirror; the wondrously enlightened clarity is like the light of the mirror; and the perfect illumination of the *dharmadhātu* is like the images appearing in the mirror.
Though three, they are one; though one, they are three. "One becomes the immeasurable," and so forth—all of these reveal this very meaning.
Yet the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind; it is neither mind nor emptiness, neither earth nor water, neither wind nor fire;
it is neither eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, nor mind; it is neither form, sound, smell, taste, touch, nor mental objects; it is not the sphere of visual consciousness.
In this manner, it extends even to: not the element of mental consciousness; not clarity nor ignorance, nor the exhaustion of clarity and ignorance. In this manner, it extends even to:
not aging nor death, nor the exhaustion of aging and death; not suffering nor its origin, not cessation nor the path; not knowledge nor attainment.
It is not dāna; it is not śīla; it is not vīrya; it is not kṣānti; it is not dhyāna; it is not prajñā; it is not pāramitā.
Thus, it extends even to not being tathāgata, not being arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha, or mahāparinirvāṇa;
it is neither permanence, nor bliss, nor self, nor purity. Because all these are non-existent, it transcends both the mundane and the supramundane.
Regarding worldly phenomena: the Tathāgatagarbha is the fundamental luminosity of the wondrous mind. It is the mind itself and it is emptiness. It is earth and it is water; it is wind and it is fire.
It is the eye, and it is the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. It is form, and it is sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects.
It is the sphere of visual consciousness, and so on, up to the sphere of mental consciousness. It is clarity and ignorance, and the exhaustion of both clarity and ignorance. Thus it is.
...up to and including aging and death; up to and including the exhaustion of aging and death. It is suffering, it is the origin, it is cessation, it is the path.
It is wisdom, it is attainment. Just as with *dāna*, so too with *śīla*, *vīrya*, excellent *kṣānti*, *dhyāna*, *prajñā*, and the *pāramitās*. Thus, up to and including the *Tathāgata*, the *Arhat*.
Samyak-saṃbodhi is precisely Great Nirvāṇa; it is permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

Because these are all identical, and because they encompass both the mundane and the supramundane, it is the wondrous, luminous, fundamental mind of the Tathāgata-garbha. It is free from identity and free from non-identity; it is both identity and non-identity.

Although it is said that by extinguishing dust one unites with awakening, and that the one and the many, the small and the large, mutually encompass and contain one another to give rise to great spiritual power, within the Tathāgatagarbha not even a speck of dust is established; thus, it is not "all.
Yet, although it is not all, all myriad dharmas are fully contained therein; thus, it is "all. Furthermore, they mutually vanish and mutually exist in an inconceivable manner. Why do you doubt?

All the great elements pervade the Dharma-realm without encroaching upon or displacing one another. "Mind" extends to the fire element; these are the seven great elements and the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
Mind is the consciousness-element (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which subsumes the five aggregates. "Eye" extends to the consciousness-element;

these are the eighteen realms (*dhātus*), which likewise subsume the twelve bases (*āyatanas*). The aforementioned are the worldly dharmas. From ignorance through old age and death, they constitute the realm of the *pratyekabuddhas*. Suffering...
The aggregates, cessation, and the path constitute the realm of the śrāvaka. Wisdom and attainment constitute the realm of the two vehicles. The six pāramitās constitute the realm of the bodhisattva.
The tathāgata, up to and including permanence, bliss, self, and purity, constitute the realm of the Tathāgata. The above are supramundane dharmas;
the mundane consists of the six classes of ordinary beings, while the supramundane consists of the four types of noble ones. This is both non-identity and identity—what is called "also identical."
Nor are they identical. "Illumination" (vidyā) refers to the ignorance that arises from true illumination.
Dāna means "generosity. Śīla means "the cessation of evil"; it is the general name for ethical discipline.
Vīrya means "diligence. Kṣānti means "patience. Dhyāna means "meditative concentration. Prajñā means "wisdom."
Prajñā-pāramitā. This is translated as "reaching the other shore. Only when the six perfections are perfected can one be called "having reached the other shore";

therefore, they are explained individually. Regarding the phrase "and so forth" (*yāvat*): since the categories of supramundane dharmas—teachings, principles, practices, and fruits—are numerous, it is impossible to describe them all in detail;
thus, the text proceeds by leaping over them until reaching the ten titles of the Buddha, which are not [included] below.
These are the names that designate the one who realizes [the truth]. *Tathāgata* means "Thus-Come One" (*Rulai*). *Arhat* means "Worthy of Offerings" (*Yinggong*).
*Samyaksaṃbuddha*—that is, *Samyaksambodhi*—means "Perfectly Complete Enlightened One" (*Zhengbianzhi*).
These are three of the ten titles of a Buddha; they are not Great Nirvāṇa itself. These are the names that designate the dharma realized. Nirvāṇa is the essence; it is eternal.
Bliss, self, purity, and permanence are the four virtues of nirvāṇa. Immortality is called "permanence. The absence of suffering is called "bliss. Possessing the eight masteries is called "self.
Freedom from defilement is called "purity. These are "neither identical nor different": they are shown as the Tathāgatagarbha in terms of ultimate truth; yet they are also "identical."

According to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the Tathāgatagarbha is revealed; the principle of the Garbha is that which is non-existent yet existent, wherein the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are perfectly manifest.

How then can the sentient beings of the three realms of existence in the world, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who have transcended the world, with their minds of objective cognition (*jñeya-citta*)...
To fathom the unsurpassed bodhi of the Tathāgata by means of worldly language and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is like a lute, a harp, a *konghou*, or a *pipa*:
though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers, they can never produce music. You and all sentient beings—

It is likewise so. The precious, awakened true mind is perfectly complete in each and every one. Just as when I press my finger, the Ocean-Seal manifests its radiance, so too, when you momentarily stir your mind, the afflictions of worldly toil arise first.
This is because you do not diligently seek the unsurpassed path of enlightenment, but instead cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a small attainment sufficient.

In the preceding passage, it was said that by extinguishing the dust and uniting with awakening, one gives rise to the wondrously awakened clarity of True Suchness, such as "one becomes immeasurable," which refers to "when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light.

In the preceding passage, it was said that by turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the dust, one gives rise to worldly afflictions and mundane appearances, such as "if you momentarily raise your mind, the toil of delusion arises first. In the preceding passage...
This is the Dharma; this is the analogy. As for the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgarāmudrā):

just as all forms and images existing in Jambudvīpa are reflected as imprints within the great ocean, so too does the nature-ocean of the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya universally manifest the appearances of all worlds.
Pūrṇa said: "My true, wondrous, pure mind—the precious, perfectly luminous awakening of the Tathāgata—is non-dual and complete with it.
Yet, in the past, I encountered beginningless delusion and have long remained in saṃsāra; though I have now attained the Holy Vehicle, I am still not yet ultimate."
World-Honored One, all delusions have been completely extinguished within You; You alone are wondrous, true, and eternal. I venture to ask the Tathāgata:
for what cause do all sentient beings harbor delusions, thereby obscuring their own wondrous clarity and undergoing this drowning in saṃsāra?
"This [passage] exhaustively seeks the false cause in order to determine it. 'I and' (the following) refers to the root above—the precious, awakened true mind—which is each perfectly complete.

'Yet I' (the following) refers to receiving the preceding [explanation of] delusion as being clarity and awareness. 'World-Honored One' (the following) refers to receiving the analogies of gold and ore, and wood and ash.
'May I venture to ask' (the following) is the formal request regarding the false cause. It states that having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, [the meaning] is already known."
The wondrously luminous true mind is non-dual with that of the Buddhas. I already know that because of my deluded thoughts, I have long remained in saṃsāra;
whereas because the Buddhas have extinguished delusion, they alone possess the wondrous, true, and eternal. I only do not yet know what causes this delusion to exist.
Previously, you asked how that which is fundamentally pure and still could suddenly arise. The World-Honored One answered that it arises because of delusion.
Now you ask what causes this deluded brightness to arise; this is what is meant by "directly investigating to the very bottom."
The Buddha told Pūrṇa: "Although you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain unexhausted.
I shall now question you again by means of various matters present in the world. Have you not heard of Yaśodara in the city of Śrāvastī, who one morning suddenly looked at his face in a mirror?
He became attached to the head in the mirror, whose eyebrows and eyes were clearly visible, and grew resentful toward his own head for not being able to see its face."
[He] took them for *chīmèi* (goblins and specters) and ran about wildly without cause. What do you think? For what reason did this person run about wildly without cause?
Pūrṇa said, "This man’s mind was deranged; there was no other cause. The Buddha said, "The wondrous awakening is perfectly bright, and its fundamental nature is perfectly bright and wondrous.
Since it is called 'delusion,' how could it have a cause? If it had a cause, how could it be called delusion? From [here].
All deluded thoughts arise through mutual causation; from confusion they accumulate further confusion, passing through as many kalpas as there are motes of dust.

Though Buddhas may illuminate them, they still cannot turn back. Such causes of delusion exist inherently due to delusion itself. When one recognizes that delusion has no cause, then the false has nothing on which to rely.
Since it never had birth, what is there to extinguish? One who attains Bodhi is like a person awake recounting the events of a dream; their mind...
Even with great discernment, for what cause or condition could one take hold of things from a dream? How much more so when they are without cause and fundamentally non-existent?
It is like that person in the city, Yan Rudatuo, who ran away in fear of his own head; though he suddenly recovered from his madness, his head was not obtained from outside.
Even if he had not ceased his madness, what would he have lost? Pūrṇa, such is the nature of delusion; for what reason [would one seek it]?
This is to clarify, by means of these phenomena, that delusion is fundamentally without cause and arises suddenly.

You have already understood that the continuity [of existence] arises from deluded luminosity, and that the seven elements are nothing but the true nature. Thus, when the Tathāgata attains wondrous, luminous awakening, it does not give rise to [delusion].
Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—yet you still do not know that this delusion is fundamentally without cause. Therefore it is said: "Though you have removed your doubts, other delusions remain.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, your head was never lost; you were no *chi-mei* (goblin) yourself, yet suddenly you took yourself to be a *chi-mei* and ran about wildly and pointlessly.
From what cause did this madness arise? Pūrṇa should have understood clearly at once, and replied: "This..."
The human mind becomes deranged and runs wild; there is no other cause for this. The Buddha said:

"The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is inherently perfect, inherently luminous, and inherently wondrous. It has never possessed delusion. Since it is called 'delusion,' how could it have a cause?
If it had a cause, it would be called 'real. How then could it be called 'delusion'? When one investigates its present state..."
This is one's own deluded imagination, arising through mutual succession without any fixed origin.
If you trace its root and beginning, it is simply one confusion accumulating upon confusion, spanning across kalpas as numerous as motes of dust; yet even now, it has no cause.
Previously, I explained this to you, yet you were still unable to seek it within yourself and instead sought the source of delusion from others. Such a cause for delusion is itself delusion.

It exists within your own inherently perfect and wondrous mind; there is nothing else besides it. If you recognize that this delusion is fundamentally without cause, then your false thoughts have originally no basis upon which to rely.
Although you are currently beset by these false thoughts and have long been wandering in saṃsāra, [they are ultimately groundless].
Since there is not even birth, how can it be said that the World-Honored One has completely extinguished all delusions, leaving only the wondrous, true, and eternal?
How could one seek the root of delusion within the self? Although I have now attained Bodhi, I can only say that this delusion originally has no cause;
how could I possibly extract a causeless delusion to show it to others? It is just like a person who, having awakened from sleep, recounts the events of their dream.
There is no other method [to find its cause] than to take an object from a dream and show it to others.

Even though objects in a dream appear to have causes, they cannot be grasped; how much less so for deluded thoughts that are fundamentally non-existent—how could one possibly seek their originating cause?
This delusion is causeless, just like the madness of Devadatta; it is not something original.
There is madness. Originally, it arises from being deluded about one's own head and identifying with its reflection; how could its cause have a fixed location?
You need only not follow the threefold continuity of worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings. When these three conditions are severed, [madness ceases].
When the three causes do not give rise [to delusion], then the madness of your own mind’s Yantradatta will naturally subside.

This subsiding is itself Bodhi—the supreme, pure, and luminous mind—which is fundamentally coextensive with the Dharma-realm and is not obtained from others. What need is there for arduous toil or laborious cultivation and realization?
It is like a person who has tied a wish-fulfilling jewel within his own garment, yet remains unaware of it. Wandering through foreign lands in poverty and exposure, he runs about begging for food;
though he is truly destitute, the jewel has never been lost. Suddenly, a wise person points out the jewel to him.
Your wishes will follow your mind, leading to great abundance; only then will you realize that the divine pearl is not obtained from without.
This is the instruction on the method for ceasing madness. "Not following" is the first step in ceasing madness.
"Discrimination" refers to the discrimination of the two attachments. It means: "You need only not follow the three kinds of discrimination regarding worldly karma, its fruits, and sentient beings."
The continuity of the mind in its active manifestation consists of three types of continuity in active manifestation that cease simultaneously and instantaneously;
that is to say, when conditions are severed, the cause does not arise. Furthermore, in response to the question concerning the beginning and end of flux, there are three conditions:

the conditions of the world, sentient beings, and karmic retribution; and the conditions for the world itself, such as "the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness, which interact to produce agitation," and so forth.

"To clarify that delusion is not something else: 'The fault lies in the clarity of awareness,' and so forth. The craving for existence, the craving for sensual desire, the craving for killing, the craving for stealing, and so on, serve as the causes and conditions for sentient beings;

these constitute the causes and conditions for karmic results. Furthermore, borrowing the example of Pūrṇa’s madness—mistaking his head for a reflection—to illustrate the madness of Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra:
mistaking clarity for an objective realm. Although the specific acts of madness differ, the mad mind is no different. This madness is one..."

Rest! Realize bodhi in this very moment without expending further effort. Then you will know that the supreme, pure, and wondrous mind is inherently all-pervasive and is originally your own possession;
why rely on clinging to skin and bone, undergoing toil and hardship for eons to cultivate and realize it?
The robe is a metaphor for ignorance; the pearl is a metaphor for the supreme, pure, and luminous mind. Although it is said that this supreme, pure, and luminous mind exists—
The mind is enveloped by ignorance and thus fails to perceive what exists. As for the wish that one’s desires follow the heart and lead to great abundance:
whether manifesting as sensory objects or as buddha-lands, nothing occurs contrary to one's intent.
At that moment, Ānanda prostrated at the Buddha’s feet amidst the great assembly, then rose and addressed the Buddha:

“World-Honored One, you have just explained that because the three conditions for the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are severed, the three causes do not arise; thus, Cūḍāpanthaka’s madness has naturally subsided within his mind.”
"Cessation is itself Bodhi; it is not obtained from others. Thus, the nature of causes and conditions is clear and manifest.
Why, then, does the Tathāgata suddenly discard causes and conditions? I have attained awakening of mind through causes and conditions.
World-Honored One, is this principle applicable only to us junior śrāvakas in training? Within this assembly now, there are Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Subhūti—"

Pṛthivībandhu and others, having heard from the aged brahmin the causal conditions of the Buddha, gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, attained awakening, and achieved the state of being free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Now, if you say that bodhi does not arise from causal conditions, then the doctrine of spontaneity (*svayambhū*) taught by Kauṣṭhila and others in Rājagṛha would constitute the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
We pray only that you will grant us great compassion to dispel our confusion and delusion.
Pūrṇa’s inquiry having reached completion, Ānanda is again brought forward to pose questions; this still accords with the immediate capacity of the audience.

Regarding killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, he cites the causes and conditions of karmic results, encompassing both the causes and conditions of the world and the causes and conditions of sentient beings—these are "sudden abandonment" phrases.

"The cessation of the finger is itself Bodhi; what need is there for words such as 'cultivation' or 'realization'? This was Ānanda’s third adherence to the doctrine of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
It necessarily involves the notion of spontaneity (*svabhāva*); for if one were to say that causes and conditions are now abandoned, then the heterodox teaching of spontaneity would be correct.
What is meant by "spontaneity" here is the claim that after eighty thousand kalpas, one spontaneously attains the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "It is just like the case of the city dweller Yantradatta. If the causal conditions for his madness were to be extinguished, then his non-mad state would naturally emerge.
Causal conditions and spontaneity reach their ultimate limit in this principle. Ānanda, Yantradatta’s head was originally spontaneous;
it was inherently so from the beginning. There is no spontaneity that is not inherent. For what causal reason, then, would he have been terrified of his own head?"

He runs about wildly. If his head were natural, why would it run wild due to causes and conditions? Why would it not be natural? It is lost due to causes and conditions, yet the original head is never lost.
This wild panic is a false projection; it has never undergone any change. Why rely on causes and conditions?

If the original state were naturally wild, and if wild panic were originally present, then before the onset of madness, where would that madness have been hidden? If the non-mad state were natural, then since the head was originally without delusion, why [would there be this running]?
He ran about wildly.
Ānanda did not maintain that madness is spontaneous, but maintained that it arises from causes and conditions. The Buddha said: "If you do not claim it is caused by conditions, then let it be;
but if you say that the nature of madness can be extinguished through causes and conditions, then at the very moment it is being extinguished, one would no longer be mad."
The nature [of things] simply emerges spontaneously. This is the principle that the fundamental is spontaneous and, conversely, falls back into spontaneity;
the logic of the spontaneity of causes and conditions reaches its ultimate limit here. Below, Ānanda wipes his head, yet this is not spontaneous.
If one were to say the head is fundamentally spontaneous, then it would have been so from the beginning. It ought to be perpetually spontaneous. Why, then, does he suddenly fear losing it?
"And yet they run about wildly. These two characters, "yin" (因) and "yuan" (緣), are simply the character "gu" (故). According to the proper principle of the Dharma, it should be stated:

"If the original nature were something that exists spontaneously, sentient beings should constantly perceive their own nature. For what reason, then, are there those who are deluded and turn away from it?"

It can be seen that Bodhi does not belong to spontaneity (*svabhāva*). If it were to descend spontaneously, then the clearing away of madness would not be due to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

If the head were mad by way of causes and conditions, then it should likewise lose its nature through causes and conditions; yet now, the original head has not been lost. Madness and fear are merely false manifestations.
At the time of madness and fear, the original head is truly without change; thus, when the madness ceases, one realizes its presence.

Head. What need is there for causes and conditions? According to the Dharma, it should be said: "The nature is fundamentally never lost; it is only through groundless delusion and turning away that it seems lost.
At the time of such delusion and turning away, the nature undergoes no change. Thus, when delusion is shattered and the nature is seen, what reliance can there be on causes and conditions?
It can be seen that Bodhi does not belong to causes and conditions. Regarding the phrase "originally mad" (*beng kuang*): this negates that madness is not natural.

In the preceding passage, it was stated that madness is not caused by conditions; fearing that one might then argue that madness belongs to nature (*ziran*), he refutes this with the present statement.
The principle of the Dharma should be expressed thus: "Pure and fundamentally so, originally free from deluded thoughts. Regarding the phrase "not mad": this negates that non-madness is not natural.
[This is] also [the case]. "Non-insanity is natural" responds to the preceding passage on how the nature of non-insanity emerges spontaneously.
Fearing that one might further conceptualize non-insanity as being "natural," he therefore uses this [statement] to refute that.
If one awakens to the original head and recognizes the deluded running about, both the causal conditions and spontaneity are merely conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Therefore, I say that when the three conditions are severed, it is itself the bodhicitta. When bodhicitta arises, the mind of arising and ceasing ceases; yet this is still merely arising and ceasing.

When both cessation and arising are exhausted, there is the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*). If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*), then it would be clear that a spontaneous mind arises and an arising-and-ceasing mind ceases;
yet this too is arising and ceasing. That which is without arising or ceasing is called spontaneity.

It is like the various phenomena of the world that, through mutual blending, become a single entity—this is called the nature of combination (*saṃyoga-svabhāva*); that which is not a combination is termed the original nature (*prakṛti-svabhāva*).
Fundamentally it is not so; in harmony it is not joined. It is detached from both "joined" and "so"; it is neither "detached" nor "joined.

Only this phrase may be called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Awakening and nirvana are still far off; they are not to be realized through your arduous cultivation and verification over kalpas.

Even if one were to memorize and uphold the twelve divisions of the sutras and the pure, wondrous principles of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, it would only increase frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Hereafter, the correct meaning is revealed: the characters "awakening" (*wu*) and "knowing" (*zhi*) are the wondrous secret for ceasing madness. This is because one awakens to one's original head.
It is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions. Only then does one know that frantic running is neither spontaneous nor caused by conditions;
one awakens to the original head and only then sees that the original face is truly real. Knowing the frantic running, one realizes for the first time that rushing outward in search is delusion.
You say you are yourself lost to the family treasure and rush outward in search; clinging to conditions and clinging to the self is something you cannot avoid.
If one were to personally see the original source, the deluded mind would suddenly cease;
then one would know that both "causes and conditions" and "spontaneity" are merely conventional fabrications (*prapañca*) and not the ultimate reality.

When I say that because the three conditions are severed, it is the Bodhicitta, this refers to the method of ceasing delusion to awaken to the source—how could it be approximated by either causes and conditions or spontaneity? Nevertheless, if one clings to the deluded mind...
Cease. That which gives rise to the mind of Bodhi is likewise dependent on causes and conditions; it is likewise a deluded mind and a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

It remains subject to arising and ceasing; it is not alone in this regard. Even if one reaches the state of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga*) where both arising and ceasing are exhausted, if there is still something "spontaneous" and one forms the thought of spontaneity, this is called the spontaneous arising of the mind. When the mind that arises and ceases is extinguished, [this is the true cessation].
This is also conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is also a deranged mind, and it is also subject to arising and ceasing. Why is this?
Because it takes arising and ceasing as its causal conditions, whereas that which is without arising or ceasing is the spontaneous nature (*svabhāva*).

It is like how, in the world, when various things are blended together to form a single entity, it is called a "composite nature" (*saṃghāta-svabhāva*); in contrast to such a composite, that which is not composite is termed "original spontaneity" (*tathatā*).
Nature is precisely this "original suchness" (*prakṛti*). This is a dharma of opposition; it is not the true original suchness. Therefore, it is likewise like conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Only when one reaches the point where "original suchness is not original suchness" and "conjunction is not conjunction," and both are utterly transcended—transcending both transcendence and non-transcendence—is [the truth realized].
When both [positions] are simultaneously negated, only then is it the correct statement; only then is it the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Yet, fearing that one might take mere intellectual understanding as realization, he strikes a decisive point: "Even when you have reached this stage, Bodhi and Nirvana are still far off.
The moment you grasp the phrase is precisely when you first resolve to attain enlightenment (*bodhicitta*); it is then that you must properly practice and advance toward Bodhi. If...

This is not something realized through cultivation over kalpas. Although one may uphold many sutras and their wondrous principles, these merely add to frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and have no connection whatsoever with the fundamental matter.
This sutra is for the practice of seeing one's nature, which does not rely on extensive learning or intellectual understanding.
Ānanda has already awakened to the wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind. Below, he secretly requests instruction on its cultivation; thus, principle and practice are in profound accord.
Although you have discoursed upon both conditioned causality and spontaneity with definitive clarity, among men you are acclaimed as the foremost in extensive learning.
If, despite the熏習 (vāsanā) from extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas, one cannot escape the calamity of Mātanga’s daughter, why wait for my Buddha-Usnīṣa Divine Mantra?
The lustful fire in Mātanga’s daughter’s heart was instantly extinguished, and she attained the stage of Anāgāmin within my Dharma.
The Forest of Diligence is perfected and the River of Craving is dried up, bringing you liberation.

Therefore, Ānanda, though you have for kalpas retained the Tathāgata’s secret and wondrous adornments, it is not equal to practicing untainted karma for a single day and remaining far removed from the two sufferings of worldly hatred and love.
Just as Mātanga, who was formerly a courtesan, had her lustful desires dissolved through the power of the divine mantra.
Among those in the Dharma, she is now named the Bhikṣuṇī Śīlā. Together with Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula, they simultaneously awakened to their past causes.

Knowing the causes throughout successive lifetimes—that craving and attachment are suffering—they cultivated untainted goodness for a single thought-moment, and thus some were able to transcend the bonds of existence.
"Or perhaps you have received a prediction of enlightenment; why then do you deceive yourself by still lingering here to listen?
The following passage speaks in extreme terms of the faults of mere erudition to spur you toward diligent cultivation. It says:
'Your discourse on natural causes and conditions is definitive, clear, and entirely without error. Among the assembly of śrāvakas, you are ranked foremost for your extensive learning.'"
This is the foremost [remedy]. Yet, despite using this extensive learning and practicing it through the accumulation of kalpas, one cannot distance oneself from the perils of sexual arts.

If extensive learning were truly capable of liberating one from suffering and severing bonds, why would it be necessary for the power of secret mantras and spiritual assistance to cause Daṅga’s lustful fire to suddenly cease and for her to immediately realize the third fruit, no longer being born in the realm of desire? If that were so, you too would have been liberated. However, [it was not so]. Therefore—
Know that the power of incantations and the power of extensive learning increase tenfold with each passing day and kalpa.
Although you may remember and uphold the Tathāgata’s Secret Sublime Array, it is not equal to a single day of earnestly practicing the Secret Sublime Array;

by doing so, you can immediately distance yourself from the two sufferings of hatred and attachment. These two sufferings arise from the moment of conception: they exist wherever one perceives difference as hatred and sameness as attachment.

This [affliction] arises simultaneously with birth and is extremely difficult to eliminate; yet if one is willing to practice untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for even a single day, one can sever it forever—how much more so for other [virtuous deeds]?
It is only feared that one will not be willing to advance in cultivation. Furthermore, he cites the benefits gained by those of inferior capacity to rebuke him sternly:
"A single moment of perfuming cultivation is not merely verbal talk. "Emerging from the entanglements" refers to [the case of] Dhanika, who was granted a prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).

I am referring to Yaśodharā. Yaśodharā’s body was already that of one with a delicate constitution, yet even she attained great benefit through cultivation for a single thought-moment. As for the courtesan Tiṅga, her faculties were even more inferior;
yet she too gained great benefit through a single moment of cultivation. You, however, being a man and a teacher to the multitude, instead become confused and bewildered yourself.
You remain attached to frivolous discourse and refuse to cultivate untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*). This is truly self-deception.

Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s instruction, saw their doubts and delusions eliminated; their minds awakened to the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), and their bodies and minds became light and at ease, attaining what they had never experienced before.
Weeping again with deep sorrow, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O Unsurpassed One of Great Compassion, Pure and Precious King! You have skillfully opened our minds, enabling us to [understand] these various..."
Through causes and conditions and skillful means, you have exhorted and uplifted us, leading those submerged in darkness out of the ocean of suffering. World-Honored One,

although I now receive such sounds of the Dharma and know that the Tathāgata-garbha— the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind— pervades the worlds of the ten directions and contains within it the pure,
jewel-adorned lands of the Tathāgatas, the buddha-fields of the Wondrous Enlightened Kings, the Tathāgata further rebukes me for the lack of merit in my much-hearing.
I have not yet attained the practice. I am now like a traveler who has suddenly been granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King;
though I have obtained this great residence, I must enter through its gates.

I only pray that the Tathāgata will not abandon his great compassion, but show the path of the original aspiration to all those of us in this assembly who are still shrouded in darkness, so that we may renounce the Lesser Vehicle and ultimately attain the Tathāgata’s nirvana without remainder.
"May those in training, by what means, subdue their past objects of attachment, attain dhāraṇī, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision?
Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and, with single-minded devotion within the assembly, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate instruction.
The true mark is markless; it is the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha, pervasive throughout the ten directions, pure by nature, transcending names and free from marks.
In the previous fascicle, the Buddha rebuked the śrāvakas for failing to penetrate the true mark and permitted those cultivating the Mahāyāna to do so.
Now, through repeated and layered explanations, delusions are dissolved and the mind awakens. [As for] "losing one's nature":...

While traveling and lodging abroad, one may see the nature of reality as if it were a magnificent mansion; yet if one sees this nature but does not cultivate it, it is like having found the house but failing to enter.

Therefore, he requests the path of the Tathāgata’s original aspiration to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). *Nirvāṇa without remainder* is the perfect fruit, while the path of the original aspiration is the perfect cause.
Since he has already seen his own nature, he further seeks to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; thus, the gate of seeing is opened.
To demonstrate that cultivation leads to awakening and entry, one must enter through a gateway; this gives rise to the intention to penetrate deeply through the final gateway.

As for "the攀緣 (pān-yuán) of former times," it refers to the攀緣心 (pān-yuán xīn,攀緣心) mentioned in the first fascicle. Here, one no longer regards it as having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet one does not yet know by what means to subdue it.

The first fascicle provides a definitive discernment of the true and the false, elucidating the nature of enlightenment (*bodhi-svabhāva*), and even proceeds to profoundly exhaust the myriad dharmas, providing a definitive...
This removes doubts and obstructions, enabling faith and understanding to become authentic and true, serving as the mind of the causal stage.

Once the causal stage is truly established, one can then perfectly accomplish the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage. The above constitutes the section on the Path of Vision; below begins the distinct section on the Path of Cultivation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas in the assembly who were not yet masterful regarding the bodhicitta,
and for the sake of sentient beings of the final dharma period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa who have resolved upon the bodhicitta, opened the gateway to the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
This path of sublime practice is proclaimed for Ānanda and the great assembly.
You all must resolutely resolve to attain Bodhicitta and never grow weary in the pursuit of the Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi. You should first clarify the initial mind that awakens to enlightenment.
Second, the meaning of the definitive realization (*niyata-artha*).

"Awakening" (*pratibodha*) refers to the arising of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) from fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). "Initial mind" (*ādi-citta*) refers to the mind first giving rise to the resolve for cultivation.

"Definitive meaning" (*niyata-artha*) means that which is fixed and cannot be altered. The first meaning causes one to examine thoroughly the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*).

As a foundation for further cultivation, he points to the five turbidities as the root of birth and death—that which is the cessation of delusion and the arising of existence—and causes them to discern and revolve [the mind] so that they may achieve accomplishment by relying on the perfectly湛 (zhan) and unarisen, undying nature.
Next, the second meaning is to cause them to examine the root of afflictions so that they know what must be subdued, thereby attaining the state of a Tathāgata; and he points to the six...

Using the analogy of a thief who uses a root as a medium to plunder a house, he proceeds by means of the principle of the mutual interpenetration of the world to fully reveal the quantities and relative merits of the six faculties, so that one may know which to choose.

Once one has attained the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing as the mind for the causal ground, one further examines the root of afflictions and selects a single faculty of perfect capacity to enter deeply; thus, all six faculties are simultaneously subdued.
One may then perfectly realize the awakening of the stage of fruition.
How are the two meanings of the initial mind determined? Ānanda, as for the first meaning:

if you wish to cast aside the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, cultivate the Bodhisattva vehicle, and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully examine the mind generated at the causal stage in relation to the fruit.

"Are the stages of the earth identical or different? Ānanda, if, at the stage of the causal ground, one takes a mind subject to arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, yet seeks the Buddha-vehicle of non-arising and non-ceasing, such a thing is impossible.

For this reason, you should clearly observe that all conditioned phenomena within the vessel-world are subject to transformation and extinction. Ānanda, observe the conditioned things in the world..."
Regarding the nature of dharmas, who could cause them not to decay? Yet, one never hears of empty space rotting or decaying. Why is this? Because space is not something that can be produced;
thus, from beginning to end, it is without decay or extinction. Therefore, within your own body, that which has the characteristic of solidity is earth;

that which is moist is water; that which has the sensation of warmth is fire; and that which moves is wind. By means of these four entanglements, they divide your profoundly still, perfect, wondrously enlightened clarity.
The mind functions as seeing and hearing, as sensing and discerning. From beginning to end, these five faculties become turbid. What constitutes this turbidity?

Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is pure and pristine by nature. Yet, when dust, soil, ash, or sand—substances that are inherently obstructive—are introduced, the two entities remain distinct by their very nature;
their essences do not harmonize. Suppose there were a person in the world who took some of that soil and dust and threw it into the water.
In pure water, when the earth loses its restraint and the water forfeits its clarity, its appearance becomes turbid; this is called "turbidity.
Your fivefold turbidity is likewise thus.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the aforementioned ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), which is identical to the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.

If you wish to abandon the Small Vehicle and cultivate the Great Vehicle to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, you should carefully and minutely examine whether this mind of the causal stage and the awakening of the fruition stage are the same or different;
for the final secure barrier does not depart from that very first thought-instant.

What Ānanda had previously employed were all minds subject to arising and ceasing through causes and conditions. Now, wishing to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, he was first instructed to conduct a thorough investigation;
only by taking the mind that is neither born nor extinguished as the causal condition for the Great Matter can one truly enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
As for "arousing the mind," it refers to this awakened mind, which is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

It is merely because one is entangled by the two obstacles that [this mind] remains suppressed and does not arise. If this mind is developed and brought forth, what difficulty could there be in awakening to the fruit of Bodhi?
If one does not take this as the mind of the causal ground, yet continues to employ that which is perfumed by names and words, [then awakening will remain impossible].
To take the arising and ceasing of the mind, produced by the seeds of karma, as the fundamental cause while seeking the awakening of the Buddha-fruit—how could this possibly be achieved?
From here on, he causes [the practitioner] to carefully observe within the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) what is subject to destruction and what is not.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the world are subject to change and decay; only empty space (*ākāśa*) is indestructible, for it is devoid of volitional construction (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). Thus...
One knows that only by taking non-arising and non-ceasing as the cause does one attain the adamantine, indestructible body.
If one takes arising and ceasing as the cause, after many kalpas, it will ultimately result in decay and ruin. Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-vehicle must carefully examine the causal mind.
Yet this mind of non-arising and non-ceasing is not separate from the present consciousness of arising and ceasing; it is merely obscured by the four great elements and the six sense faculties.
It is turbid and cannot be seen; therefore, I have caused you to observe it closely. As for the four entanglements (*catvāraḥ paryavasthānāḥ*), they are the four great elements (*mahābhūtāni*).

You possess a profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind that is pure and fundamental by nature. Yet, when it is entangled by the four great elements, it is no longer all-pervasive;
when it is split into the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatanāni*), it is no longer fundamental; and when it is turned into the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), it is no longer pure. Why is this?

"What is below? This metaphor clarifies the characteristics of turbidity. Clear water is a metaphor for the pure awakening; dust and soil are metaphors for the four great elements and the six sense organs.
The pure mind of awakening fundamentally has no interaction whatsoever with the four great elements and the six sense organs.

Due to the sudden arising of a single initial thought, the distinction between subject and object is created, whereby the pure mind of awakening becomes turbid and is no longer perceived. (The first fascicle states "each"...)
This is a confused and erroneous practice. First, one distinguishes between the arising and ceasing of the causal ground and that which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.

Having taken the攀緣心 (the mind that clings to objects) as the root of birth and death and the cause of arising and ceasing, one then points out the *vijñāna-śuddhi-mūla-prakāśa* (the fundamental clarity of consciousness) as Bodhi and Nirvana, the originally pure essence, and takes it as the cause of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, [one confuses] arising and ceasing with non-arising and non-ceasing. Regarding their causes...
The result is perfectly clear. As for the various points mentioned here, why do they not appear again? It is said that the essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous;
although it belongs to the nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is like a second moon—within the true, there is the delusive.

What is the "true"? It is the profoundly still, perfect, wondrous, awakened, and luminous mind. What is the "delusive within the true"? It is the four entanglements that divide this mind into the faculty of sight.

Listen to this observation: from beginning to end, there are the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). One must clarify and remove these five turbidities so that no further delusion exists within the truth;

only then can it be called "indestructible" and only then does one attain the fundamental, luminous awakening. This is the nature free from arising and ceasing, serving as the mind for the causal stage. This is truly because cause and effect are made clear;
therefore, even before entering the stage of faith, one has already attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). In the following text, first...
To discern the root of birth and death is not the "conditioned mind" refuted in the first fascicle; rather, it refers to "revolving the delusion to subdue the source.

This means clarifying and removing that fraction of delusion carried within the fundamental luminosity of the *vijñāna*-essence. This is what is refuted at the end of the sutra regarding the sphere of the *vijñāna-skandha*.
The previous question asked, "From where does one restrain and subdue grasping? This answer replies: "By revolving the delusion to subdue the source. [This is the function of] karma.
When consciousness is completely penetrated, the conditioned mind will subside of its own accord without the need for deliberate suppression.
Ānanda, you perceive empty space pervading the ten directions; space and seeing are not distinguished. Space exists but has no substance; seeing exists but has no awareness.
These interweave to form a delusion; this is the first layer called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Your body currently manifests as a composite of the four great elements.

It constitutes their substance. Sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition are congested and obstructed; water, fire, wind, and earth are rotated into states of cognition. These interweave and falsely form [this world].

This second layer is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, within your mind, memory, consciousness, recitation, and study give rise to the nature of knowing and seeing, which allows the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) to appear.
Apart from the objects there are no marks; apart from cognition there is no nature. These interweave and falsely form [this world]. This is the... [third layer].
The third is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, you arise and perish morning and evening without ceasing;

your perceptions and views constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts the lands. These weave together to form delusion; this fourth stage is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).
Your seeing and hearing originally possess no different natures; yet, separated by the various sensory dusts, they give rise to unaccountable differences. Within the nature...

They recognize one another, yet in their midst they turn against each other; identity and difference lose their standard, and through mutual entanglement, delusion is formed. This fifth stage is called the turbidity of life.

The first turbidity relies upon the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). As for the term "empty vision" used in reference to the aggregate of form alone: it is the very beginning of deluded confusion. There is only...
The characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*). Due to the seeing-faculty (*darśana*), it is drawn in and coagulated to become form (*rūpa*).
The deluded vision of inert emptiness and [form] blend together as one; this is called "non-distinction. As stated previously, even empty space possesses names and appearances.

This is because emptiness originally possesses a pure essence (*svabhāva*); now, being mixed with the characteristic of seeing, emptiness becomes a turbid emptiness, and its essential nature as emptiness is lost.
Previously it was said that seeing is not empty; this seeing is fundamentally the clear and lucid awareness.

Now, when it becomes mixed with the characteristic of emptiness, seeing becomes a state of murky vision, and the awareness of seeing is lost. This is what is meant by "earth losing its quality of resistance."
Water lacks purity. Second, delusion gives rise to birth and death without ceasing; they are densely entangled, possessing the sense of being woven together.
In Sanskrit this is called *kalpa*, which here means "time-period. Since sentient beings have, from time immemorial, obscured themselves and taken darkness for emptiness, this very time is impure;

hence it is called the turbidity of the kalpa (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). Regarding the passage "Your body... and below: the turbidity relies upon the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); as for sensation...
To receive and experience is its meaning; "coagulation" (*tuan*) refers to sensation. Within the profound and perfect nature, there is originally no physical form;
it is coagulated by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The nature itself is without obstruction, yet it becomes obstructed by the congestion of the four great elements.

The four great elements themselves have no cognition, yet they become endowed with cognition through being whirled by the nature. This whirling and this congestion are interwoven so densely that they cannot be separated.

Because it is apprehended through seeing, it is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). Furthermore, from the passage "you [should know] below," the turbidity relies upon the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
recollecting the past, cognizing the present, and rehearsing what has not yet occurred—all these are perceptions. By the power of perceptual ideation, the nature of knowledge and vision is activated.

This nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises from the six sense faculties; this characteristic of mental consciousness manifests within the six sense objects. Thus, apart from the sense objects, it does not exist.

The characteristics of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): apart from the sense organs, there is no nature of consciousness. When the three—organ, object, and consciousness—intermingle as one, greed, anger, and other afflictions arise;

this is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*). Furthermore, in the passage beginning "Moreover, morning and evening," turbidity depends upon the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The constant shifting and flowing from moment to moment is called "formations. Here, cognitive perception is the master, while karmic movement constitutes good and evil. This...
The body is the master that maintains it, yet it is helpless before the shifting power of karma; it cannot act as its own lord.

That which one wishes to retain departs because of the movement of karmic force and cannot remain forever; that which one wishes to move away remains because the master holds it back and cannot depart immediately.
Since this operation of karma is the common basis for the birth of sentient beings, it is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). You all—

Below. The turbidity depends upon the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Its nature is but one; it is only because the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) differ that they draw forth the six consciousnesses.

Hence it is said: "The various objects are separated and distinct, yet they arise differently without cause. "They know each other within their nature" refers back to the fact that the original nature is without difference.

Functioning through mutual opposition, they cite the lack of a fixed pattern among ordinary beings; yet when speaking of sameness, their functions oppose one another, and when speaking of difference, their natures and characteristics coincide.

Having never possessed a definitive standard, these elements intertwine to falsely constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Consciousness abides and life remains; consciousness departs and life fades away.
Lacking self-mastery, it is therefore called the turbidity of life-force. The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is solely a single, profound, and perfect stillness.
Since the self-obscuration that became emptiness, it has been externally turbidified by the vessel-worlds of the ten directions, resulting in the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*);

internally turbidified by the characteristics of the four great elements of the body, resulting in the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*); and further turbidified by the reflected images of the six sense objects, resulting in the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Consequently, through the intermittent flow of continuity, it has been turbidified by birth and death, resulting in the...

The turbidity of sentient beings causes the various defilements to become obstructed and stagnant; the six sense faculties no longer function with harmonious clarity, resulting in the turbidity of life.

These five layers of turbidity cause one to completely lose the nature of profound stillness and perfect roundness. To restore this profound stillness and perfect roundness, one must seek the method for clarifying the turbid waters.

Ānanda, if you now wish to cause seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition to reach far back in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity, you should first select the root of birth and death, and establish yourself upon the nature of the non-arising and non-ceasing, perfect and profound stillness.

By means of this profound stillness, turn back its false arising and ceasing, and restore the original awakening. Attaining the originally luminous awakening, which possesses a nature free from arising and ceasing, let this serve as the mind for the ground of practice. Only then—

The cultivation and realization that perfects the stage of fruition is like settling turbid water by storing it in a still vessel. When it remains deep and motionless, the sand and silt sink to the bottom and clear water appears before one;

this is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). When the mud is removed and pure water remains, this is called the eternal severance of fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
When the marks of clarity are refined and pure, all transformations and manifestations do not constitute afflictions, as they are all in accord with [the nature of reality].

Nirvana is pure and wondrously virtuous. When one is deluded regarding the Truth, delusions arise; through seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition, one may turn back from delusion and return to the Truth—the state of permanence, bliss, selfhood, and purity. Question:

If one examines the causal mind, why is it that this causality depends upon seeing, hearing, awareness, and cognition? Answer: It is because of these four entanglements that your profound, perfect, and pervasive nature is divided.

The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind functions as seeing, hearing, observing, and cognizing; therefore, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are entirely the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind.
Since turbidity is formed through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it must be clarified through seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing.
To look at the ordinary from the perspective of the sage is why it is called "distant. "Selecting" means selecting away that which is not to be used.

The root of birth and death is precisely the karmic activity of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). The nature of perfect stillness, beyond arising and ceasing, is precisely what is referred to in the second fascicle as the "perfectly complete nature of bodhi, beyond arising and ceasing.
"Perfect" refers to the fruit; "basis" refers to the cause. By using this stillness to revolve back the false and extinguish arising and ceasing, one returns once more.

Original enlightenment (*yuanjue*) is the effort that eradicates the causes of birth and death. When one attains original luminous enlightenment (*yuanyang jue*), which possesses the nature of being beyond arising and ceasing, then Bodhi is perfected.
To take this as the mind of the causal stage is to use the fruit as the cause; thus, it is both cause and fruit.

As stated in the second fascicle: "At the time of seeing the seeing, the seeing is not [ordinary] seeing"—this refers to the moment of illuminating and perceiving the ignorance of the arising aspect (*shengxiang wuming*).
This is the point where delusion is turned back into truth; it is the time for advancing toward the severance of the ignorance of the "arising phase" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).
