All transformations and manifestations are exclusively pure functions; therefore, it is said that they do not constitute afflictions. Because function is identical with essence, it is said that all are in accord with *nirvāṇa*.
Such was the intention behind the Tathāgata’s exhortation to Ānanda to cultivate untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).

Regarding the second meaning: if you truly desire to resolve upon the bodhicitta and give rise to great courage and vigor within the Bodhisattva Vehicle, you must decisively abandon all conditioned characteristics and carefully examine the root of afflictions from time immemorial.
Regarding the initiation of karma and the moistening of rebirth, who creates them and who receives them?

Ānanda, as you cultivate Bodhi, if you do not carefully examine the root of afflictions, you will be unable to know the false nature of the sense faculties and their objects, nor where delusion resides.
If you do not even know the locus [of delusion], how can you subdue it and attain the rank of a Tathāgata?

All conditioned characteristics (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*)—the provisional practices cultivated by those of the Lesser Vehicle—are what "initiate karma and moisten birth," which refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This is because the point where karma is not initiated is true initiation of the mind; the point where birth is not moistened is true non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Therefore, it is made clear that one must carefully examine who initiates and moistens karma and who performs and receives it; this intends to reveal that the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) themselves act and themselves receive the results. Since...

If one knows that the consciousness of karma creates karma and receives retribution, then one knows that it is by transforming this consciousness of karma that one can first resolve to attain enlightenment and realize the fruit.
Ānanda, observe those in the world who untie knots: if they do not see what was knotted, how could they know how to untie it?
Have you never heard that empty space cannot be torn asunder by you? Why is this? Because emptiness has no form or appearance; thus, there is neither knotting nor untying. Therefore, your present...
The preceding five—eye, ear, nose, tongue, as well as body and mind—these six act as intermediaries for thieves, plundering the family treasures within.
Because of this, sentient beings have been bound by entanglements throughout beginningless worlds; thus, they are unable to transcend the vessel-world (the physical environment).

True emptiness is without knots; yet because the six sense faculties interact with the world, one becomes entangled in afflictions and unable to transcend them—this constitutes the formation of knots.
This is precisely the locus of the delusions of the false faculties and objects.
Are not the six faculties the very root of affliction? You ought to untie them. A thief must have a go-between: the six external objects and the six internal [faculties].
Consciousnesses are all induced by the union of the eyes and other faculties, which afflict and harm the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;

therefore, it is said that "the six [faculties] act as intermediaries for thieves, who plunder the family treasure. Thus, one knows that these six sense organs are truly the root-source of the knots of birth and death.
Ānanda, what is meant by the "world of sentient beings"? "World" (*loka*) refers to the flow of time; "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial direction.
You should now know that east, west, south, north, southeast, southwest, northeast, northwest, above, and below constitute the realms;
the past, future, and present constitute the worlds. There are ten directions and three periods of time. All sentient beings are woven together by delusion.

They form one another. Within the body there is exchange; worlds intersect with one another. Yet the nature of these realms, even if extending through the ten directions, has its fixed positions clearly defined.

The mundane world merely designates east, west, south, and north; above and below have no fixed positions, and the center has no fixed direction. The four numbers must be clear as they intersect with the mundane world:
three times four and four times three, revolving to twelve, flowing and transforming through three cycles, making ten and one.
One hundred thousand. To summarize from beginning to end: within the six sense faculties, each possesses one thousand two hundred merits.
By intermingling the four realms and the three periods of time—taking three times four and four times three—they both become twelve;
this constitutes the first layer. Taking these twelve, each transforms into ten, resulting in one hundred and twenty; this is the second layer.
"Layering" refers to these one hundred and twenty [dharmas], each of which transforms into a hundred, resulting in one thousand two hundred; this constitutes three layers.
Within the world, sentient beings see, hear, know, and perceive, arising and ceasing incessantly from moment to moment.
The characteristics of the coarse and the subtle are as described above. That the six sense organs are able to discern their respective objects is considered a merit;
however, this refers only to what is possessed by ordinary worldlings. If the six are resolved and the one is forgotten, their number would be immeasurable.
Ānanda, you must further determine the relative superiority and inferiority among these. It is as when the eye perceives: the rear is dark while the front is bright;

the front is entirely bright while the rear is entirely dark; and when looking to the left and right, two-thirds of the field is visible. Generally speaking, the meritorious function it performs is incomplete.
Of the three parts of its functional capacity, one part lacks virtue. You should know that the eye possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the ear...
Listening pervasively, it reaches all ten directions without omission. When active, things seem near and yet far; when still, there is no boundary.

You should know that the faculty of hearing is complete with one thousand two hundred merits. As for the nose smelling odors, it passes through inhalation and exhalation; though there is out-breathing and in-breathing, it lacks the interval between them.
Examining the faculty of the nose, it is deficient by one-third; you should know that the nose possesses only eight hundred merits. As for the tongue...
To proclaim and disseminate all mundane and supramundane wisdom, its expression is methodical and its principle is inexhaustible.

You should know that the faculty of the tongue is endowed with one thousand two hundred merits. Just as the body perceives touch—distinguishing between the disagreeable and the agreeable—it is aware when there is contact, but does not know when separated;
it perceives the single when separated and the pair when joined. By examining the faculty of the body, one finds that three parts are lacking one. You should know this.

The body possesses only eight hundred merits; yet it silently and wondrously accommodates all mundane and supramundane phenomena throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether saintly or ordinary—embracing them all without exception to their very limits. You should know that the faculty of mind possesses one thousand two hundred merits.
Ānanda, if you now wish to go against the current of the desire-stream of birth and death and trace back to the root of that flow, [you must rely upon this].
Up until the state of non-arising and non-ceasing, one should examine these six faculties of sensory reception: which are joined and which are separated; which are deep and which are shallow;

which constitute the faculty of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), and which are not yet perfected. If one can awaken to the faculty of perfect penetration among these, one will turn back the beginningless flow of delusory karma and attain the circulation of perfect penetration.
Compared to those with imperfect faculties, this progress is multiplied by as many days as there are eons. I shall now fully reveal this for you.
The six sense bases are profoundly still, perfectly luminous, and constitute the fundamental merits; their number is thus.

According to your careful discernment of which you may enter, I shall clarify them for you, causing you to advance. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have each practiced within the eighteen realms.
All have attained the perfect, unsurpassed Bodhi; among them, there is neither superiority nor inferiority.
It is only because you are of inferior capacity that you have not yet perfected sovereign wisdom therein; therefore, I proclaim this so that you may enter deeply through a single gate.
Entering into one state without delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
The preceding section explained the beginning of the false clarity and the knots of the faculties; this section distinguishes their relative merits so that one may know which to choose.
"Two-thirds" means that, out of three parts, only two parts are attained. When in motion, they seem near yet distant; when at rest, they have no boundaries.
Following its movement, there appears to be distance and proximity; yet within my stillness, listening is all-pervasive and boundless.
That which lacks the intermediate conjunction is like regulated breathing: when the breath has fully exhaled, it pauses briefly before entering again.

The tongue is capable of speaking, regardless of whether it tastes flavors. As for "separating the one and uniting the two": if separated, one does not know; this is because one part is lacking. When conjoined, [it is complete].

At that time, there is the capacity for awareness. There is both opposition and compliance; this constitutes the two aspects. When the mental consciousness arises alone, it universally perceives all phenomena, and is thus called "silent acceptance.
The flowing roots are precisely those that are wondrously clear and immovable. If one allows them to emerge and flow outward, rushing toward objects, it is called the "flow of birth and death.
If one moves against this current and enters within, returning the flow to its original unity, it is called "non-arising and non-ceasing. This is what is meant by "receiving."

Taking in the sensory objects is "reception" (*vedanā*). Bringing forth meritorious qualities is its "function. "Combined" refers to cognition within contact; "separated" refers to cognition without contact.
When separated, the object is distant and thus "deep"; when combined, the object is near and thus "shallow. To be pervasive and complete in a single intent is "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*);
to have a deficiency in function is "incomplete. In selecting the faculties, one chooses the deep and perfect "separated" mode and discards the shallow "combined" mode.

[Text missing]. It merely says, "Awakening to perfect penetration. This is an abbreviated expression. That "days and kalpas multiply each other" refers to the vast difference between slow and swift progress in one's practice.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how can one flow against the current by entering deeply through a single gate, such that all six faculties become purified simultaneously?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "You have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna; you have already extinguished the multitude of [defilements] within the three realms..."

Although one has given rise to the afflictions abandoned through seeing in this world, one still does not yet know that within the faculties there is an accumulation of births as vast as empty habituation.
Those habits must be eliminated through cultivation; how much more so, then, the specific portions and enumerations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing?
One wishes to counteract the flow of desire within birth and death and reach the state of non-arising and non-extinction;

yet, not knowing what constitutes this flow of desire in birth and death that one must counteract, and since the merits of the six sense faculties vary in degree, each faculty differs from the others.
How is it that by entering deeply through one gate, all six gates attain purification? The Buddha first answers regarding the characteristics of the current against which one must flow:

the *srotāpanna* (here translated as "entering the stream"). This refers to one who has entered from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into the state of a noble one (*ārya*), realizing the first fruit and thus entering the stream of the noble ones.

Consequently, the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) are also called the "stream of views. This refers to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) engaging with mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*).
These are the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-moha*). Because of these views, one transmigrates through the three realms and is unable to achieve liberation;

therefore, by severing these delusions of view, one realizes the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) and enters the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). The accumulated, beginningless, empty habitual tendencies within the faculties are the delusions of thought (*bhāvanāmoha*).

Since these tendencies must be severed primarily through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the second and third fruits are called the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). [This applies to] the three realms.
There are nine stages. In each stage, there are nine grades of afflictions of thought (*klesha*), totaling eighty-one grades.

All of these are abandoned by those who have attained the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). When these afflictions are completely eliminated, one realizes the fourth fruit and is named an Arhat; this is designated as the Stage of No Further Learning (*aśaikṣa-bhūmi*).

In this context, the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within the sense bases (āyatana) refer to the afflictions severed by Bodhisattvas, which constitute the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) beyond the realms.

It says: "Although you have already severed the outflows of views and attained realization of the first fruit (srotāpanna), you still possess the afflictions of thought (bhāvanā-kleśa) within the realms."
If you have not yet been able to exhaust these within, how much less could you perceive the objects of the realms outside? These are all that you must oppose.
Now, you should first observe the six sense faculties before you: are they one, or are they six? Ānanda, if you say they are one, why does the ear not see?
Why does the eye not hear? Why does the head not tread? Why do the feet not speak? If these six faculties are definitively...
"Thus they become six. Just as in this assembly of mine, I proclaim the subtle and wondrous Dharma-door for you; among your six sense organs, which one comes to receive it?
Ānanda replied, "I hear with my ears. The Buddha said, "It is your ears that hear. What concern is there for the body or the mouth?

It is the mouth that asks about the meaning, and the body that rises to show reverence. Therefore, you should know that they are not one, yet they ultimately constitute six; they are not six, yet they ultimately constitute one. Ultimately..."
"It is not that your faculties are fundamentally one or six, Ānanda. You should know that these faculties are neither one nor six;

rather, due to the inversion and confusion since beginningless time, the concepts of 'one' and 'six' have arisen within the perfectly湛 (zhan) and pure [nature]. You, as a Srotāpanna, although you have attained the dissolution of the six, have not yet eliminated the 'one.
It is like the great void of space which accommodates a multitude of vessels; because the shapes of the vessels differ, they are given different names."
"Space. When one contemplates space by setting aside its vessels, space is said to be one. How could that great void be either identical to or different from you?
How much less can it be called 'one' or 'not one'? Thus, your awareness of the six faculties and their functions is also like this."
Although you have attained the dissolution of the six, you have not yet lost one. It simply requires the use of the original, fundamental language. As the Sutra says:

"Originally relying on one brilliant essence, it is divided into the six harmonious combinations. Now that the six harmonious combinations have been dissolved, you must instead preserve that one brilliant essence.

One removes the vessel to contemplate emptiness; how could one wish to remove the emptiness itself? It is not that one is ill at ease with emptiness, but rather that one is ill at ease with the attachment to a single emptiness.
Attachment to a single, pure spirit is likewise the same. Only when both [the spirit and its attributes] are simultaneously extinguished does one realize the substance of the mind.
Space has no difference; yet because vessels have squareness or roundness, the space within those vessels also appears to have the differences of squareness or roundness.
It is only after removing the vessels that one speaks of "oneness. How could space itself possess oneness? Sameness is oneness; difference is diversity.
If one knows the sameness and difference, the right and wrong of space, and realizes that nothing can be established, then [the concepts of] "one" and "six" [are transcended].
They perish together, and the perfect clarity becomes undifferentiated. Ānanda had not yet understood the teaching that "one enters and the six become pure.

The Buddha said that because the empty habits accumulated over many lifetimes have not yet been cultivated and severed, it is natural that he does not yet know this; it is difficult for him to resolve the distinction between one and six.
[The Buddha] causes him to know that the fundamental nature of the faculties is originally devoid of one or six, so that when the "one" is resolved, the "six" immediately vanishes.

Due to the mutual conditioning of the two aspects of light and darkness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adhered to and gives rise to seeing. The essence of seeing reflects forms, and by binding these forms, the sense organ is formed.
The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the substance of the eye; it is shaped like a cluster of grapes.

The four sensory objects float upon the faculties, and the mind flows and rushes toward forms. Through the mutual impact of the two aspects of movement and stillness, within the wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness becomes adhered to, giving rise to hearing.
The essence of hearing reflects sound, and by coiling back the sound, it forms the faculty. The source of this faculty is termed the "pure four great elements."
Therefore, it is named the substance of the ear, like a newly unfurled leaf. The four sensory objects float upon the root-faculty; as they flow and disperse, they rush toward sounds.

Through the two conditions of openness and obstruction, [the faculty] is activated. Within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to smelling. The essence of smelling reflects fragrance, and by receiving fragrance, the sense-organ is formed.
The source is designated as the pure four great elements; hence it is named the substance of the nose. Like a pair of hanging claws, the peripheral faculties (the four dusts) float upon it.

They rush toward fragrances with flowing dissipation, due to the intermingling of the two aspects of tranquility and transformation. Within the wondrous perfection, turbidity adheres to stillness and gives rise to the sense of taste.

It constantly refines and reflects flavors, condensing the essence of flavor to form its root. This root-source is termed the "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*), and for this reason it is named the "tongue-body.

It is shaped like a newly curved crescent moon; as a floating root among the four sensory objects, it flows outward and rushes toward flavors. Through the two types of friction—separation and conjunction—it perceives them.
Within this wondrous perfection, the clarity of stillness coagulates to give rise to awareness. The essence of awareness reflects upon contact, and by grasping that contact, it forms the sense organ.

The fundamental source of this organ is termed the "pure four great elements," and for this reason it is called the body. Like the head of a waist-drum, the peripheral organ floats amidst the four sensory objects; its faculties flow outward and rush toward contact.

Through the two kinds of continuity—arising and ceasing—within the wondrous perfection, the clarity becomes adherent and gives rise to cognition. The essence of cognition reflects the dharmas, and by grasping these dharmas, the sense-faculties are formed.
The fundamental source of these faculties is termed the "pure four great elements," which, because they give rise to mental activity, are called "thought. This is like seeing within a dark chamber.
The floating faculties scatter toward the four objects, rushing headlong toward dharmas;
this clarifies that the fetters of the faculties arise from the objects. The profound, perfect, and wondrous mind is fundamentally free from attachment, just like a bright mirror.
All images manifest within it. Due to the movement of a single thought of delusion, they immediately become the two sensory objects of light and darkness, which adhere to it;
thus, the nature of stillness is smeared, triggering the nature of seeing. However, this has not yet formed a root-knot (*mūla-granthi*).
Subsequently, the essence of seeing again reflects back and forth with the two sensory objects of light and darkness, merging into a single place, and finally coalesces into a knot.

The two types of particles constitute the ultimate sense-faculties (*paramārtha-indriya*). These faculties are composed of the primary four great elements (*mahābhūta*) in their initial state of purity;

however, they are so subtle and difficult to manifest that they can only be perceived by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Therefore, their substance is illustrated by the metaphor of a cluster of grapes.
"Flowing and rushing toward forms" means that this essence of vision relies upon those two types of objects and flows outward.

From "due to movement" (*yòu dòng*) below, the knot of the ear is explained. "Striking" (*jī*) has the meaning of stirring or vibrating. "Encompassing" (*juǎn*) refers to not excluding either the clear or the turbid. From "due to penetration" (*yóu tōng*) below, the knot of the nose is explained.

"Emitting" (*fā*) means to induce or trigger. "Accepting" (*nà*) means receiving both the fragrant and the putrid. From "the realm of tranquility" (*jiè tián*) below, [the knot of the tongue is explained].
"Jie" (knot) refers to the tongue. "Can" (interpenetration) means the mutual entry of the five flavors; "jiao" (chewing) means chewing their flavor finely.
These arise from the separation [of the tongue] below; they explain the "knots of the body. "Mo" (rubbing) means the intersection of cold and warmth; "bo" (grasping) means to seize and take hold.

These arise from the birth [of the mind] below; they explain the "knots of the mind. The nature of the mind is deliberation and reflection. The floating root of the mind is a single aperture within the physical heart-mass. It is the most...
At the initial moment of absorbing the vital essence and blood of the parents, the mind immediately attaches itself to this [embryo] and rushes toward its destiny.
Yet, within the body, it cannot be seen by people; therefore, the character "si" (thought) is used to clarify that there is a locus of deliberation, which is precisely where it resides.
Being in a place of light, it cannot see darkness; being in a place of darkness, it can see light. The locus of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) is profound and obscure.
This is the locus for the preceding five sense organs. Because they employ schemes and deploy strategies, the state of knowing is illustrated by the metaphor of the dark chamber;
this refers to the previous passage stating that because this world gives rise to entanglements, one cannot transcend the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
What is called "knots" is identical to the knots themselves. Since the preceding text states that it is neither one nor six, then what [is it]?
It is from this that the distinctions of the six sense organs arise; therefore, he here reveals their origin. One perceives that within the wondrously perfect nature, there are fundamentally not six;
it is only because of the false attachment that light is emitted, leading eventually to outward dissipation.

Ānanda, it is thus with these six faculties. From that awakened clarity, there arises a clarity that is itself awakened; yet they lose that essential discernment, and through clinging to delusion, they emit light.

Therefore, at this moment, when you are neither in darkness nor in light, the substance of seeing does not exist; when you are neither in motion nor in stillness, the essence of hearing is fundamentally absent.
Without penetration and without obstruction, the nature of smelling does not arise; being neither changing nor tranquil, tasting has no outlet; [the faculty of touch] does not depart...
This is not correct. Contact is fundamentally non-existent; it neither ceases nor arises. To understand this is to know where [the mind] rests.

These six sense organs all derive from the essence of the nature-awareness, which is profoundly luminous. Through a single movement, they transform into the "luminous awareness" that seeks to illuminate.
Consequently, one loses the essence of the pure, clear, and cognizant awareness. From this, it becomes attached to light and darkness, giving rise to the faculty of vision.
The binding together of movement and stillness constitutes hearing and the other faculties; "light" here refers to the essential radiance of the six sense organs.
This is what is meant by "stirring up the dust to form a knot. Apart from light and darkness, there is no seeing-nature; apart from movement and stillness, there is no hearing-essence and so forth.
This is what is meant by "apart from the dust, there is no knot. Nevertheless, the seeing-nature, the hearing-essence, and the rest are the consciousness-natures within the six sense organs.
One cannot speak of "knotting" [the mind]. Knotting depends upon the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*). When one is detached from sensory objects, the nature of consciousness perishes;

yet, when the light of delusive attachment ceases, the knot perishes. This is precisely what is meant in the third fascicle of the *Jiandao fen* (Section on Realizing the Way): "Ultimately there is no substance.
That treatise reaches the ultimate point regarding the fundamental substance, whereas this treatise reaches the ultimate point regarding the practice of cultivation.

If you simply do not follow after these twelve characteristics of conditioned existence—movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and agitation, penetration and obstruction, birth and death, light and darkness—then by pulling out any single root, you will detach from clinging and settle within; settling back into the original reality, you will give rise to the fundamental radiance.

The luminous nature manifests and clarifies itself. As for the other five attachments, they should be uprooted and completely liberated; they do not arise from the cognitive perceptions triggered by external objects.
Clarity does not follow the sense organs, yet it relies upon the organs to manifest. Consequently, the six faculties function interchangeably for one another.

The following passage teaches that by distancing oneself from sensory objects, the one is understood and the six vanish; fundamentally, there is neither one nor six. "Not to follow" (bùxún) means not to pursue.

The character "not" (bù) serves as the bridle and rein that restrains the galloping toward forms and sounds, and it carries the same meaning as the characters "contrary" (nì), "reverse" (fǎn), and "revolve" (xuán) used previously.
However, this word is profoundly subtle; it is what is called "resting is itself bodhi. It says: you who wish to...

One should cause the six faculties not to follow the six objects in their constant flux. One must select a single faculty with a perfect capacity as the point of entry, and apply all one’s strength to it first to uproot it.

If one faculty is made to detach from the external and subside within, such that the faculty and its object no longer couple together, then the familiar will gradually become unfamiliar and the unfamiliar will gradually become familiar; thus, one will naturally return to and settle into the original luminosity of fundamental awakening.

This is the essence, namely the fundamentally luminous awareness (*mūla-vidyā*), which serves as the mind for the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi-citta*). From this point onward, it no longer clings to delusions when emitting light;
externally it does not depend on sense objects, and internally it does not follow the faculties. The constant light manifests before one, possessing the power of discerning reflection.
It merely provisionally relies upon those faculties to manifest the appearance of illumination. Although it does not alter the functions of the ears and eyes, it remains so.
Yet, seeing and hearing actually do not depend on the ears and eyes; thus, a single faculty can perform the functions of all the faculties.
This is precisely entering the state of non-delusion in one thing, whereby those six cognitive faculties are simultaneously purified.
Ānanda, do you not know that within this assembly, Aniruddha sees though he has no eyes; the Naga Baddhanta hears though he has no ears;
the goddess of the Ganges smells fragrances though she has no nose; Gavāmpati knows tastes through his extraordinary tongue;
and the Śūnyatā-deva perceives touch though he has no body? They have been made to appear momentarily by being reflected within the light of the Tathāgata. Since they have...
The nature of wind is fundamentally non-existent. So it is with all states of cessation and the śrāvakas who have attained tranquility;
for instance, Mahākāśyapa here in this assembly has long since extinguished his mental faculty, yet he perceives with perfect clarity without relying on thought.
The six individuals, such as Śāriputra and the others, were either ordinary beings experiencing the retribution of karma or small sages who had attained realization through cultivation;
these were all powers of delusion that did not even rely upon their physical faculties, let alone the state of perfect liberation—how could they not possess mutual functioning?
Ānanda, if your faculties were now completely uprooted, their inner radiance would shine forth.
Then these superficial phenomena, as well as all the changing appearances of the vessel-world, would—like ice melting in hot water—be transformed at that very thought into supreme awareness. Ānanda!

It is like those people of the world who, when their eyes are gathered together and suddenly closed, perceive only the appearance of darkness; their six sense faculties become darkened, and their heads and feet appear indistinguishable.
If such a person were to run their hand over the exterior of the body, although they do not see it, they would distinguish between the head and the feet.

Cognition is the same; it takes seeing as its condition and light as its cause. When darkness arises, it constitutes non-seeing. If non-light were to manifest spontaneously, then all appearances of darkness could never obscure it.
Since the faculties and their objects have already dissolved, how could the luminous awareness not become perfectly wondrous?
True wisdom is like hot water; delusive objects are like ice. To realize that delusion is itself truth is for it to transform into enlightened awareness (*jñāna*).
What was previously called "being unable to transcend the vessel-world" can now be said to be transcended.

The cases of Aniruddha seeing despite being sightless and others demonstrate that true awakening does not depend upon the sense organs. This demonstrates that true awakening does not rely upon external conditions (*pratyaya*). This is enlightened awareness.
As for this point of identity: the awareness within darkness is no different from what is seen in the light.

If even ordinary beings can possess discernment without depending on the condition of light, how much more so for the true awakening of a sage—what need would there be for external conditions to trigger it?
The above concludes the explanation of the faculties and the practical methods; however, it has not yet specifically identified which faculty serves as the gateway for universal penetration.
I shall explain these two meanings. The former meaning provides a brief indication of the complete efficacy of cause and effect, enabling one to know in advance the ultimate, final fruit.
This present meaning provides a detailed exposition of the expedient means for the beginner, enabling one to clearly understand the practical techniques for applying oneself to practice.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, if one wishes to seek the permanently abiding mind through the ground of practice, it must correspond in name and designation with the state of fruition.
World-Honored One, within the state of fruition, there are these seven names:

Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, True Suchness (Tathatā), Buddha-nature (Buddhadhātu), Āmalaka-consciousness, the Empty Tathāgatagarbha, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Although these seven designations differ...”
It is distinct. It is pure and perfect; its essential nature is firm and solid, like a diamond king, eternally abiding and indestructible.
If this seeing and hearing were to exist apart from light and darkness, motion and stillness, or openness and obstruction, they would ultimately have no substance.

They would be just like the thinking mind, which, when separated from external objects, fundamentally has nothing at all. How can you take that which is ultimately subject to annihilation as a cause for cultivation, desiring thereby to attain such [a state]?

"World-Honored One, when one comes to dwell in the seven fruits of permanence, if one leaves behind both light and darkness and perceives ultimate emptiness, then—just as there are no external objects before one—the nature of thought itself ceases.
Through repeated cycles of investigation, whether advancing or retreating, one minutely seeks and finds that fundamentally there is neither a self-mind nor the mental factors associated with a self.

With whom, then, could one establish a cause for seeking supreme enlightenment? The Tathāgata previously spoke of the profound, pure, perfect, and eternal; this contradicts your truthful words. [End of passage]
This results in conceptual proliferation. How is it that the Tathāgata speaks words of truth? May you deign to show great compassion and dispel my ignorance and hesitation.
Having received the teaching on the correspondence between the causal stage and the resultant stage within the primary meaning (*paramārtha*), Ānanda again raised this difficult question.
The Buddha experienced the dream of striking a bell and pounding [grain]; these events verify that hearing is not severed. Only then is the primary meaning perfected.

That which all Buddhas attain is called *bodhi* (enlightenment); that which is quiescent, eternal, and blissful is called *nirvāṇa*; that which is non-deceptive and unchanging is called *tathatā* (suchness).

To be free from faults and severed from all that is non-existent is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature). To discern all things while remaining without defiled attachment is called *amala-vijñāna* (the immaculate consciousness).
When not a single dharma is established and afflictions are utterly exhausted, it is called the *śūnya-tathāgatagarbha* (the empty womb of the Tathāgata).

To penetrate and illuminate the myriad dharmas without distinction is called the *ādarśa-jñāna* (great perfect mirror wisdom). These seven are all states of fruition; once accomplished, they are forever accomplished, never to change again.

Regarding the seeing and hearing faculties: by citing two, all six are encompassed. Regarding the objects—light and darkness, motion and stillness, penetration and obstruction—by citing these six, all twelve are encompassed.
This is to say that the faculties have no substance apart from their objects. As for "the mind of recollection," this refers to the consciousness-mind of the six sense bases.

Previously, the Buddha refuted that the consciousness-mind has no substance apart from its objects; now it is shown that the six faculties likewise have no substance apart from their objects. Thus, they are identical to the conditioned mind.
There is no difference. Therefore it is said, "It is just like the mind of mindfulness," and so forth.

If one sets aside the two phrases regarding light and darkness and speaks solely of the essence of seeing, this is because, in the first fascicle, the essence of seeing was used to refute the conditioned mind. "The absence of the mind" refers to the absence of the substance of the mind;
"the absence of mental factors" refers to the absence of the locus of the mind. Since there is no seeing apart from objects, it is then identical to—

The deluded mind that clings to objects has no substance and no location; this is identical to what the Tathāgata previously challenged when asking, "Who is it that cultivates and realizes the Dharma of Non-arising Patience?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata previously designated this essence of seeing as the "pure, subtle, perfect, and constant."

Is this not mere conceptual proliferation? In the preceding section, there was doubt that cause and effect were inconsistent; in the passage following "If one departs from light and darkness," there is doubt that the Buddha’s words are inconsistent with one another from beginning to end.
Ānanda’s intention is that while the knots may be eliminated, the six sense faculties cannot be discarded.

As the Buddha has taught regarding seeing, hearing, and so forth, if these are devoid of substance apart from their objects, then the six sense organs and the攀緣心 (the mind that clings to conditions) are both things subject to arising and ceasing; they should both be decisively abandoned.

Furthermore, the World-Honored One has instructed me to follow the faculty of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) among the six faculties, entering deeply through a single door, thereby seeking the unarisen within the causes of arising and ceasing.
Regarding the fruit of cessation: would it not be inconsistent with the names and designations of cause and effect? [The Buddha replied:

"You do not realize that while the six sense organs adhere to the illusory light and thus undergo birth and death, the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within those six organs has never, from the beginning, undergone birth or death.
It is certainly incorrect to identify the six organs as the primordial luminous awareness; yet, to claim that there exists a primordial awareness separate from the six organs is likewise incorrect."
To say "luminous awareness" is also not permissible. Regarding the World-Honored One’s karmic occasion concerning the striking of the bell: it precisely concerns the gateway of the six sense organs.

Before the light of delusive attachment has yet arisen, there is only the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, vividly and constantly present, which demonstrates the nature that is without birth or extinction.
This nature without birth or extinction exists within the six sense organs, like gold within ore; thus it is seen.
In the *Dàofēn* (Section on the Path), fearing that Ānanda might mistake ore for gold, [the Buddha] points out two kinds of deluded vision within the essence of seeing.
In the *Xiūdàofēn* (Section on Cultivating the Path), fearing that Ānanda might fail to see the gold apart from the ore, he reveals a segment of the nature of hearing within the six sense faculties—
what is called "revolving away from delusion to subdue the source"— which is nothing more than smelting the ore to produce gold.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Though you have studied much and possess great learning, you have not yet exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).

In your mind, you merely know the causes of inversion, but when true inversion actually manifests before you, you truly cannot recognize it. I fear that despite your sincere heart, you have not yet attained full faith and submission.
I shall now test you with matters of the mundane world to remove your doubts. Thereupon, the Tathāgata commanded Rāhula to strike the bell once.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "Do you hear now? Ānanda and the great assembly replied together, "We hear.
When the bell had ceased and there was no sound, the Buddha asked again, "Do you hear now? Ānanda and the great assembly replied together, "We do not hear.
Then Rāhula struck it once more. The Buddha asked again, "Do you hear now? Ānanda and the great assembly replied together once more, "We hear."
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "How do you hear? How do you not hear? Ānanda and the great assembly together replied to the Buddha, "If the bell is struck, then I hear it.
When the striking has long ceased and the sound has faded, when both the resonance and the echo have utterly vanished, that is called not hearing."
The Tathāgata again commanded Rāhula to strike the bell and asked Ānanda, "Is there a sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly both replied, "There is a sound. After a short while, the sound faded away. The Buddha asked again, "Is there a sound now?
Ānanda and the great assembly answered, "There is no sound. Then Rāhula came forward once more and struck the bell. The Buddha asked again, "Is there a sound now?"
Ānanda and the great assembly all said, "There is sound. The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In what way is there sound? In what way is there no sound?
Ānanda and the great assembly all addressed the Buddha, saying, "If the bell is struck, it is called 'having sound. When the striking has ceased and the sound has faded, [it is called 'no sound']."
When both sound and resonance are utterly transcended, it is called "no-sound. The Buddha addressed Ānanda and the great assembly:
"Why do you now speak with such deceptive confusion? The great assembly and Ānanda simultaneously asked the Buddha: "In what way, sir, do we speak with deceptive confusion?"
The Buddha said, "I asked you whether you heard, and you said you heard. Again I asked about the sound, and you said it was a sound.
Since your responses regarding 'hearing' and 'sound' were not fixed, how can this not be called evasive confusion? Ānanda, when the sound has vanished, there is no resonance."
"You say there is no hearing. If, in truth, there were no hearing, then the nature of hearing would have already ceased, like a withered tree. When the bell is struck again, how could you know it?
Whether one knows 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' depends on whether the object of sound itself is present or absent;

how could that nature of hearing be subject to existence or non-existence for you? If hearing truly did not exist, who would be there to know its absence? Therefore, Ānanda, within the act of hearing, the sound..."

Birth and cessation belong to the sounds themselves; they do not pertain to your hearing. It is not that the arising and ceasing of sound cause the nature of your hearing to become existent or non-existent.
You are already inverted and deluded, mistaking sound for hearing; how then can you be surprised that, in your confusion, you mistake the permanent for the intermittent?
One should never say that apart from movement and stillness, or closure and openness, hearing has no inherent nature—just like a person in deep sleep, lying soundly upon their bed and pillow.
In his household, while he was sleeping, someone was pounding silk and husking rice.

In his dream, the man heard the sound of the pounding and husking, yet he perceived it as something else—either as the beating of drums or the striking of bells. While still dreaming, he wondered at himself that the bells were making sounds like wood or stone.
Suddenly waking up, he immediately recognized the sound of the pestle and told his family: "While I was dreaming..."

Confused by this sound of pounding, you take it to be the resonance of a drum. Ānanda, while this person is in a dream, would they recall whether [the door] was still or shaking, open or closed, or whether sounds were penetrating or blocked?

Although their body is asleep, the nature of hearing is not obscured. Even if your physical form were to dissolve and the radiance of your life were to pass away, how could this nature be extinguished for you?
Ānanda takes the permanent to be the intermittent. The Tathāgata, taking the matter at hand as his witness, explains it by verifying that the faculty of hearing is truly permanent.
In the passage, "knowing existence and knowing non-existence," the character *zhī* (to know) is emphasized.

Since it says one "knows existence and knows non-existence," it is evident that existence and non-existence are the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*), and how could they concern the nature of hearing? If the nature of hearing were actually non-existent, then that which "knows non-existence" would likewise...

"Who is it? When the bell is struck, there is sound; this is verified by movement. When there is no sound, it is verified by stillness. Furthermore, he cites the state of sleep to verify that [the nature] is detached from both movement and stillness.
Even if one mistakenly strikes a mortar for a drum or bell, one simply takes up the hearing-nature which is not obscured.
The four lines beginning with 'Even if your form were to dissolve' mean that it is not only unobscured during dreams, but remains unobscured even after death. Thus he asked.

Whether in motion or stillness, or in birth and death, the nature of hearing is neither obscured nor extinguished. Why then does the Tathāgata say that it is "separate from motion and stillness," as if it originally lacked the substance of hearing?
Answer: To say it lacks substance when separated from objects means that when hearing is gathered into the ear, it forms a substance of stagnation and obstruction.
If this physical substance were to perish, then the hearing-nature that pervades the entire Dharma-realm would be fully revealed; how could it possibly become annihilated?
What was previously stated—that there is no substance apart from objects—and what is now stated—that there is a substantial essence apart from objects—are not contradictory in their meaning.

Because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have followed after forms and sounds, flowing along with every thought without ever awakening to the pure, wondrous, and eternal nature of their own being;
failing to follow that which is constant, they pursue birth and death, whereby they undergo birth after birth, transmigrating through defilement.

If you abandon arising and ceasing and maintain the true and eternal, the light of eternity will manifest before you; the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and the mind will, at that moment, dissolve away.
Conceptualization and its signs are the dust, and the clinging of consciousness is the defilement; when both are left far behind, your Dharma-eye will, at that moment, become clear and bright.
Why would one fail to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?

Why would one fail to awaken to the true and eternal, instead of following it, but rather flowing outward and rushing toward the dust of sensory objects? Thus, one undergoes defiled transmigration, and the fruits of suffering will never end.
To abandon birth and death and maintain the true and eternal is precisely to turn the faculties back and reflect inward; then the constant light will manifest.

Thereupon, one immediately submits to and returns to the primordial truth, giving rise to the radiance of the fundamental luminosity. The faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind dissolve at that very moment;

this is precisely the sign of the sixfold liberation. Since the faculties, objects, consciousness, and mind—which are capable of defiling, obstructing, and obscuring prajñā—are now distanced from, one perceives the illumination of the Dharma and will certainly achieve perfect enlightenment.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Fascicle Four.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the fifth fascicle:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, although the Tathāgata has explained the second gateway of meaning,
when I observe those in the world who attempt to untie knots, if they do not know the origin from which the knot was tied, I believe that such persons will ultimately be unable to untie it.”
"World-Honored One, it is the same for me and the śrāvakas in this assembly who are still in training. Since beginningless time, we have arisen and ceased together with various forms of ignorance.
Although we have attained such roots of goodness through extensive learning and are called 'those who have left the home life,' we are like those suffering from quotidian malaria.
We only pray that the Great Compassionate One will take pity on us who are drowning in affliction. Regarding our bodies and minds today, what constitutes these fetters, and from what are they named?"
"Understand this! May you also cause sentient beings suffering in future kalpas to escape saṃsāra and not fall into the three realms of existence.

Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the great assembly, raining down tears with uplifted sincerity, awaiting the unsurpassed instruction of the Buddha-Tathāgata.
In the previous fascicle, the Tathāgata revealed the second determination, first instructing [Ānanda] to carefully examine the root of afflictions.
He then said: "Observe those in the world who untie knots; since they do not see what was knotted, how can they know how to untie it?
The root of affliction is precisely that which is knotted. Because Ānanda wished to understand this knot deeply, he requested the World-Honored One to clarify and reveal it.

"Origin" (*yuan*) means "fundamental source. It refers to the original source first established at the very beginning. This has both a remote and a proximate sense. The remote refers to the establishment of an object based on the cause of illumination;

once that object is falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. The proximate refers to the essential clarity of the consciousness-essence (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which pervades all the sensory gates.
This is called the root of all fetters. From beginningless time, it has arisen and ceased simultaneously with all forms of ignorance;
this is termed "co-emergent ignorance" (*sahaja-avidyā*), and it is precisely this very thing. Therefore, this root of bondage is of the utmost gravity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Ānanda and all those in the assembly who were still in training,
and also for the sake of all sentient beings of the future as a cause for transcending the world and as eyes for the ages to come, [extended] his hand of Jambūnada gold and purple light.
He touched Ānanda’s crown; immediately, the Buddha-worlds throughout the ten directions shook in six ways.
From the crowns of every Tathāgata dwelling in those worlds, rays of precious light issued forth, and at that same moment, those lights appeared in those worlds.
They came to the Jeta Grove and poured [water] over the Tathāgata’s crown. This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before.

Thereupon, Ānanda and the entire assembly together heard the Tathāgatas, as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, speaking with one voice in different tongues, addressing Ānanda:

Excellent, Ānanda! If you wish to recognize and understand the co-arising ignorance that causes you to revolve in birth and death as the root of bondage, it is none other than your six sense faculties;

there is no other thing. Furthermore, if you wish to know the unsurpassed Bodhi, which enables you to swiftly realize peaceful liberation and the wondrous, eternal tranquility, it is likewise your six sense faculties and nothing else.
That this sutra is titled "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" precisely means that it reveals and elucidates the unsurpassed Uṣṇīṣa-dharma.

Sentient beings inherently possess the ultimate fruit; that which is the fundamental object of veneration is the primordial clarity of the essence of consciousness, which transcends the realm of principle.

Those who perceive the Way perceive this; those who cultivate the Way cultivate this; and those who realize the Way realize this. It is for the purpose of revealing and elucidating this that [the teaching] is set forth.
This Dharma was first indicated by touching the crown of the recipient’s head.

As for the fact that each of the Buddhas further emitted light from their own crowns to consecrate the Tathāgata’s crown, the intent is to clarify that the primordial luminosity within the essence-consciousness of the recipient is identical to the ultimate luminosity of the Tathāgata’s state of fruition;
they share the same "crown-dharma. The method of its representation is thus most thorough and exhaustive.
The Tathāgata has already manifested this for you through his form and further clarified it for you with these words:
"Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, afflictions and bodhi—all are the six sense faculties; there is nothing else.

This is sufficient as a resonant utterance to illuminate the fundamental knot and serves as the preliminary introduction for revealing how to untie that knot. Ignorance is itself the knot. It is ignorance that is said to be "together with..."
Birth. When one perceives the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*), there is immediately ignorance (*avidyā*). Question: What constitutes this bondage? Answer: It is precisely your six sense faculties.
Question: From what is liberation named? Answer: It is likewise your six sense faculties. This is a definitive exposition based on the present body and mind;
apart from these, there is no further source of bondage, and apart from these, there is no further place of liberation.
Although Ānanda had heard such sounds of the Dharma, his mind was still not yet clear.
He bowed his head to the Buddha and said, "How is it that my cycle of birth and death and the wondrous, eternal bliss are both the same six sense faculties and nothing else? The Buddha told Ānanda:
The faculties and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. The nature of consciousness is illusory, like flowers in the sky.

Ānanda, knowledge arises from the objects, and characteristics exist because of the faculties. These characteristics and the seeing-nature have no inherent substance, being like two reeds leaning against each other.

Therefore, when you now establish a knowing within your seeing and hearing, this is the very root of ignorance. When there is no seeing within your seeing and hearing, this is precisely Nirvana—untainted, truly pure. How so?
Within this, other things may further be accommodated. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Fearing that Ānanda might mistakenly grasp the six faculties as being bound by the drifting and escaping of sense objects, the Buddha said:

'These faculties and their objects are both the same as the profoundly still, perfect, and wondrously enlightened mind. When deluded, water freezes into ice; when awakened, the ice returns to water. Thus it was said.

It is said that bondage and liberation are non-dual. Fearing that Ānanda might mistakenly cling to the six sense organs as the source of consciousness and thereby rob himself of his own family treasure, the Buddha stated that the substance of consciousness is entirely empty;
thus, not only are bondage and liberation non-dual, but it has never been bound in the first place.
The two lines concerning the nature of consciousness clarify the emptiness of the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).

The four lines concerning objects clarify the emptiness of both the image-seeing portions (*nimittabhāga* and *darśanabhāga*). "Knowing" refers to the seeing-portion; "image" refers to the image-portion. With the sense organs and objects as conditions, consciousness arises between them.
The seeing-portion appears to be induced by the organs, yet it cannot arise without objects. The image-portion appears to originate from objects.
However, apart from the faculties, one cannot grasp characteristics. Thus, apart from characteristics there is no seeing; apart from seeing there are no characteristics.
They are utterly devoid of self-nature and are fundamentally illusory. To cling to knowing and seeing as truly existent is called "establishing knowing and seeing";
this is the deluded mind. To realize that knowing and seeing have no nature is called "non-knowing and non-seeing"; this is the true mind. This is clarified at the very place of knowing and seeing.

The form of darkness and delusion: when the clarity of stillness becomes sticky, vision is triggered; as it flows outward and rushes toward forms, this very faculty of knowing and seeing becomes the root of ignorance.

When, within this faculty of knowing and seeing, one does not follow after external objects, detaches from stickiness and retreats inward, and when the inner luminosity radiates light, this very faculty of knowing and seeing becomes the root of nirvana.
Ānanda asked: "What is this bondage? From what is it named?"
To understand: when one establishes knowledge within what is known and seen, that is bondage; when one knows and sees without seeing, that is liberation.
True nature is empty of the conditioned, for it arises through conditions and is thus like an illusion. The unconditioned has no arising or ceasing; it is unreal, like flowers in the sky.
False speech reveals the various truths; yet both the false and the true are equally false. Since it is neither true nor not-true, how can there be a seer and that which is seen?

Between them there is no real nature; therefore, they are like reeds leaning against one another. Both bondage and liberation share the same cause: for the sage and the ordinary person, there is no second path.
Observe the nature within the intersection: it is neither emptiness nor existence. When obscured by delusion, it is ignorance; when clarified through illumination, it is liberation.

The two characters for "true nature" (zhenxing) are identical in their source to the character for "source" (yuan) used previously. From the discussion on conditioned phenomena being empty up to the simile of the sheaves of reeds, these verses demonstrate that the nature of consciousness is illusory.
Since true nature is fundamentally empty, how could all conditioned dharmas arise? They all arise by depending upon conditions.
What is its substance? It is merely like an illusion. Because it is like an illusion, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Because it is unconditioned, it has no arising or ceasing.
Because it has no arising or ceasing, it is like a flower in the sky. That which is called "true nature" (*tathatā*) is likewise manifested only through the delusion of words.

The false and the true are both equally false. Since even the true cannot be established, how much less so the false? This is an extreme statement asserting that the false must necessarily be non-existent.
As for "the true is not true," the two characters "true" and "false" refer to the seeing as the faculty (the root) and the seen as the object (the dust).
Since both truth and falsehood are equally non-existent, how can there be a seer or that which is seen? Whether it be the characteristic or the vision, both lack any real nature;

are they not like two bundles of reeds leaning against one another, while their interior is actually empty? Below, regarding "knotting and untying," this verse praises the fact that bondage and liberation are non-dual.
The cause of this refers to the six sense faculties. Knotting constitutes being an ordinary person; untying constitutes becoming [an enlightened one].
"Sage. The binding and liberation of sages and ordinary beings do not depart from the six sense faculties; therefore, it is said they share the same cause, for there are no two paths.

You should observe the nature of their intersection. This reiterates the previous metaphor: if you say it is empty, the reeds possess external forms; if you say they exist, the interior of the reeds is fundamentally empty.
This metaphor illustrates that while the deluded attachments of the faculties and objects appear to exist, their essence is originally empty. Delusive obscuration is precisely ignorance.
What is called "losing that essential clarity" can be bound; what is called "revealing the fundamental luminosity" can be liberated.
"Revealing" means overturning delusion to give rise to awakening; "luminosity" means transforming obscurity into clarity.

The four lines concerning true nature collectively reveal that the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is itself the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). "The conditioned" refers generally to the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.
Previously, it was said that one must definitively abandon all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). It was also said: "You need only not follow the twelve conditioned phenomena.
Ānanda, thinking that there is a separate unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) apart from these conditioned phenomena, asked in doubt:

"How can these be the same as the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and nothing other than them? The Buddha said: "You now distinguish between the false and the true, yet you have not yet fully realized the nature of the faculties."

It is merely the source of defilement. What is this source? It is the true nature (*dharmatā*). When viewed through the lens of the true nature, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are empty in their very essence;
they are entirely unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). One cannot find their arising or ceasing, nor can one find their truth or falsity.
Why then must one seek liberation by abandoning bondage, seek deliverance by abandoning fetters, or seek the unconditioned by abandoning the conditioned?

The sequence for unraveling the knots follows a specific order; when the six are unraveled, even the one perishes. By selecting the faculty that is perfectly penetrating, one enters the stream and attains true enlightenment.
The *ālayavijñāna* is a subtle consciousness; its habitual tendencies form a violent torrent. Fearing that people might confuse the real with the unreal, I have never openly expounded it.
The self-mind grasps the self-mind; that which is not illusion becomes illusory phenomena. If one does not grasp, there is nothing that is not illusion.
Since even non-illusion does not arise, how can illusory phenomena be established? This is called the Wondrous Lotus, the Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening, and the Illusion-like Samādhi.
With a snap of the fingers, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning. This Abhidharma is the single path to Nirvana for the Bhagavans of the ten directions.
This section follows upon the meaning of the preceding "untying the knots" and introduces the subsequent text on "perfect penetration.

"Cause" refers to the sequence of untying the knots. When the six knots are untied, the faculties are uprooted; when the one [knot] is lost, there is profound stillness and perfection. By selecting the perfect faculty, one enters the state of sainthood.
"Flowing. One attains perfect enlightenment. Regarding "Ādāna" (below): both [terms] follow from "entering the flow" and "attaining perfect enlightenment. How is it called "flowing"?
It is because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of Ādāna constitute a violent torrent. What is "entering the flow"? It is not grasping at the notion that there is "non-illusion," and so forth.
What is "attaining perfect enlightenment"? It is the lotus and so forth. *Ādāna* is translated here as "grasping."
"Upholding" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). It contains seeds as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and accumulates waves of consciousness as a violent torrent.

It is from this that the depths are divided and it is from this that fetters arise. This consciousness arises based upon True Suchness (*tathatā*), existing in the interval between the true and the delusive.
If one takes it to be truly real, one fears becoming confused by delusive habits and thus misleading oneself; yet if one takes it to be not truly real, one fears...
Deluded regarding their own nature, they seek outwardly; thus, it is neither the right time nor the right capacity [for them].

How could I fail to expound that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone? Yet within this, they grasp and cling, falsely forming the knots of the sense-roots. This is the self-mind grasping the self-mind.

It is not that illusory phenomena are produced by illusion; rather, it is due to false grasping that there is both the illusory and the non-illusory. If one does not grasp falsely, even the non-illusory does not exist.
If the non-illusory itself is absent, how can illusory phenomena exist? Then the sense organs and their objects are suddenly purified, and perfect penetration manifests before you.
These two characters, "non-grasping," are the method for entering the stream. This is what is called below "attaining true enlightenment."
These characters refer to the Dharma-gate of non-grasping. Because it takes the fruition-awakening as its cause, it is neither attached to the pure nor defiled by the impure;
thus it is named the "Wondrous Lotus. Ultimately firm and solid, the fetters of the sense-bases and the delusions of the objects of perception dissolve upon encountering it.
Each Vajra King awakens to the state where both truth and falsehood are extinguished; neither the illusory nor the non-illusory is grasped. This is called the Samādhi of Illusion-like Appearance.
By relying on this for the cultivation of the path, one may, in the space of a single finger-snap, transcend the stage of No-More-Learning and enter the Perfect Position (*avasthā*).
That the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have utterly transcended birth and death and swiftly realized quiescent permanence is entirely due to this.
Therefore it is said: "The Bhagavāns of the ten directions / Have but one path to the gate of Nirvāṇa. Wherever the Holy Feet tread, the vehicle is non-dual; hence it is called "the one path.
This verse elucidates the meaning of being like an illusion: first, it presents dependent origination as being like an illusion;
next, it clarifies that both bondage and liberation are equally illusory; finally, by taking the self-mind with the self-mind, it accomplishes the samādhi of being like an illusion.

The meaning [is as follows]. Next, in the fascicle on Avalokiteśvara’s illusory-like permeation through hearing (*śrutavāsanā*), one can see that this verse has already implicitly selected the Dharma-gate of Avalokiteśvara.
Furthermore, the subsequent fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi are likewise concluded with the theme of being "illusory-like."

Thereupon Ānanda and the great assembly, having heard the unsurpassed compassionate instructions of the Buddha Tathāgata—consisting of geyas and gāthās that were interwoven, refined, exquisite, pure, and lucid—felt their hearts and minds opened to clarity and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. Ānanda joined his palms in reverence.
He prostrated and addressed the Buddha: "I have now heard the Buddha’s unobstructed great compassion, the pure, wondrous, and eternal true Dharma-words;

yet my mind has not yet attained the state where the six are resolved and the one is forgotten. Pray, out of your great kindness, show further pity for this assembly and explain the sequence for unraveling these knots."
As well as for those to come in the future, he bestows the sound of the Dharma to wash away deep-seated defilements.

This was requested because, although [the meaning] had been understood, there were still points that remained unclear. *Geya* (祇夜) means "Verses in Response" (*saṃgīti*), so called because they are verses that correspond to the preceding prose (*gadya*).
*Gāthā* (伽陀) means "Recited Verses," so called because they do not correspond to prose but arise independently as recitations.
"Beautiful" refers to its praise. "A blend of the refined and the brilliant" means that the two verses together clarify [the meaning] such that nothing lacks refinement or penetration.
"Unobstructed great compassion" describes its universal salvation. "Naturally pure, wondrous, and eternal" refers to the true words of the Dharma;

it is discourse that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). "Sinking defilements" refers to subtle fetters and delusions. At this point, Ānanda finally believed that the faculty-nature (*indriya*) is for the purpose of cultivation.
Regarding the gate of realization, they no longer harbor any doubt; they merely request the sequential order and the selection of a single gate.
At that moment, the Tathāgata, upon the lion throne, adjusted his nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī robe, gathered his saṃghāṭī robe, and took up a seven-jeweled desk.
He reached his hand over the table and took the flowered silk scarf offered by the deva Kāpila.
Before the great assembly, he tied it into a single knot and asked Ānanda, "What is this called? Ānanda and the entire assembly replied to the Buddha together, "This is called a knot.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata folded the flowered silk scarf again and tied another knot, asking Ānanda once more, "What is this called?"
[And so forth. Ānanda and the great assembly again addressed the Buddha, saying: "This is also called a 'knot.

Thus, by successively folding and overlapping this flowered handkerchief, six knots were formed in total. As each knot was completed, [the Buddha] took the knot formed in his hand and held it up, asking Ānanda:
'What is this called? Ānanda and the great assembly likewise responded to the Buddha in succession: 'This is called [a knot]. "
[The Buddha] tied [the cloth]. The Buddha said to Ānanda: "When I first knotted the headcloth, you called it a 'knot. This folded flower-cloth was originally a single strip;
as for the second and third [folds], why do you all again call them 'knots'? Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."

This precious layered flower has been woven together to form a headcloth. Although they were originally of one substance, as I contemplate it, when the Tathāgata makes one fold, it receives the name of "one knot";
if one were to make a hundred folds, it would ultimately be called "a hundred knots. How much more so in this case, where the headcloth has only six knots?
"It will never reach seven, nor will it remain at five. Why then does the Tathāgata permit only the first [knot], while the second and third are not called knots?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "Regarding this precious flowered cloth, you know that this cloth originally consists of only a single strand."
"When I tied it six times, there were six knots. You should examine this closely: the substance of the cloth is the same, yet distinctions arise because of the knots.
What do you think? When the first knot was formed, it was called the 'first'; in this manner, up until the sixth knot was produced."
"I now wish to change the name of the sixth knot to 'the first. Is this possible? "No, World-Honored One. As long as the six knots remain, this name 'sixth' can never become 'first.
Even if I were to exhaust my eloquence throughout successive lifetimes, how could I cause these six knots to change their names?
The Buddha said, "It is so. The six knots are distinct; yet, when tracing them back to their original cause, they were all fashioned from a single piece of cloth."
If they were allowed to become disordered, they would ultimately never achieve completion. Thus, your six faculties are also like this:
within ultimate sameness, there arises ultimate difference.
*Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* is called the "inner robe. *Saṃghāṭī* is called the "great robe" (*dàyī*). *Kāpāla* is called "time-portion," which refers to the Yāma Heaven.
*Puṣpa-paṭa* (folded-flower) is the silk fabric of the Western Heaven; it is woven with a profusion of floral patterns and is especially precious when offered by the gods.

To speak of them as identical is because the nature of the One Truth is fundamentally without difference, like the substance of a headcloth. To speak of them as different is to refer to the six... [the six realms/phenomena].
The essence of the faculties differs in its functional application, just as the knots in a cloth. To address each instance individually clarifies that if there is no binding, there is no knot;
once bound, a knot must necessarily form. This is a metaphor for how the six sense objects adhere to the translucent stillness, thereby giving rise to the six faculties.

The World-Honored One, based on their mutual correspondence within the fundamental nature, questioned how it could be that the six become one. Ānanda, based on their mutual divergence in terms of function, replied.
The six knots cannot be confused in name; that "six become one" refers to the mutual functioning of the six sense organs.

That "within ultimate sameness there arises ultimate difference" means that prior to the tying of the knots, they were originally a single entity, fundamentally devoid of either difference or sameness.
Once the knots were tied, each possessed its own boundaries and divisions, such that they could no longer function interchangeably. This concludes the sequence of the knots.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "If you find these six knots unsatisfactory and wish for them to become one, how can that be achieved?
Ānanda replied, "As long as these knots persist, disputes will arise; within them, the notion will naturally emerge that 'this knot is not that,' or 'that knot is not this.
If the Tathāgata were to untie them all today so that no knots remain, then there would be neither 'this' nor 'that. Furthermore—
"It cannot be called one. How, then, can the six become so? The Buddha said, "When the six are resolved, the one vanishes; it is just like this.
The Buddha asked, "If you insist on reversing difference into sameness and would have the six become one, by what means could this possibly be accomplished?
Ānanda replied, "If the six knots still exist, then each has its own fixed position. If one were to take the six..."

First, if one insists on this, arguments will arise like sharpened blades and a resolution can never be reached; it is better to release [these attachments], so that fetters and delusions do not arise, and distinctions between identity and difference are perfectly extinguished.
The essence of the six sense faculties is fundamentally the nature of the One True Reality; it is only because they follow conditions that they appear as such.
In the eye, it is called the essence of seeing; in the ear, it is called the essence of hearing.

If you can, according to your capacity, extract [the consciousness] from one faculty, detaching it from its adhesions and causing it to settle within, then the six will merge into one, and that one will likewise vanish. This vanishing of "one" does not mean that the true substance itself perishes;
rather, when it no longer confronts the six knots, it naturally ceases to establish itself as a singular reality.

Because your mind-nature has been deluded since beginningless time, false perceptions have arisen; as these false perceptions continue without ceasing, the wearying faculty of sight gives rise to dust.
It is like having blurred vision, where one perceives floating flowers in the midst of clear, brilliant clarity, arising chaotically without cause.

All worlds—mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana—are all merely the inverted, delusory appearances of those floating flowers born of weariness. Ānanda said: "This..."
The knot was the same as before. How might it be undone? The Tathāgata took the knotted cloth in his hand and pulled the left side taut.
He asked Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One. He then turned the cloth over and pulled the right side taut.
Again he asked Ānanda, "Is it untied like this? "No, World-Honored One. The Buddha told Ānanda, "I have now with my hand [pulled] the left..."
Each pulled on their respective ends, yet they could not untie them. "Employ a skillful means; how can they be untied?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, if one were to untie them at the very center of the knot, they would immediately fall apart. The Buddha told Ānanda, "So it is, so it is.
If you wish to remove a knot, you must do so at the center of the knot."

As for "madness and confusion": within the pure mind, one fails to perceive the arising of the mind and thus possesses these thoughts, which subsequently form the *karmic consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
As for "the false emergence of knowledge and vision": from the karmic consciousness, it transforms into the "seeing-division" (*darśana-bhāga*).

As for "exhausted seeing giving rise to dust": from the seeing-division, the "image-division" (*nimitta-bhāga*) is further produced. All the mountains, rivers, and great earth of the mundane world are precisely this image-division. Thus they arise.

Death and nirvana are both aspects of perception (*darśana-bhāga*). If one clings to the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*) as being existent and thereby falls into the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), this constitutes saṃsāra.
If one regards the aspect of appearance as non-existent and thereby falls into the view of phenomena (*dharma-dṛṣṭi*), this constitutes nirvana.

Within the profound nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*), not a single dharma can be found. Every name and category, whether mundane or supramundane, is merely a flower of deluded toil.
This is the characteristic of a knot. Ānanda said, "The toil of seeing arises from the toil of dust; it is simply a knot formed from a single cloth.
I do not know what kind of effort is required to untie it. The World-Honored One demonstrated this by pulling at both ends, left and right, yet being unable to untie it.
This illustrates how ordinary beings cling to existence and those of the Two Vehicles adhere to emptiness—both using a knot to remove a knot, exhausting themselves in vain.
They belong to the category of partiality and perversion; none can unravel them. One must apply oneself from the point where the knots are formed at the heart; only then can they be untied.
This "heart-knot" refers to the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is the core of the root-knots.
