Ānanda, I teach that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions; it does not grasp at the coarse, composite characteristics of the world.

The Tathāgata illuminates both mundane and supramundane phenomena, knowing their fundamental causes and how they emerge according to their respective conditions. Thus, even down to a single drop of rain beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he knows its specific count.
Before his eyes, he discerns every variety—whether pines are straight or thorns are crooked, whether cranes are white or... [black].
Wu Xuan: "All this is understood from its fundamental cause. Therefore, Ānanda, follow your own mind to select one of the six faculties.
If the knots of the faculties are untied, the appearances of sensory objects will naturally cease. When all delusions have been eliminated, what need is there to wait for the unreal to vanish?"

Having already explained that one should resolve the knots at the very place where they are tied, and wishing now to select the faculties for the cultivation of the perfect practice, he demonstrates that the Buddha-dharma arises from causes and conditions.
If it were merely the causes and conditions of the four great elements, it would be a coarse phenomenon of worldly conjunction; therefore, such things are to be entirely rejected.
The present causes and conditions, however, are intended to select the faculty of perfection so that one may enter deeply through a single door and bring forth illumination.

This is a matter of great significance. What the world calls the six realms of ordinary beings, and what the world-transcending teachings call the four classes of noble ones—know that these ten realms all attain their respective fruits according to what is cultivated;
this is what is meant by "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*). One foreknows the falling of raindrops beyond the realms, as well as the original causes of pines, thorns, cranes, and crows.
Whether sentient or insentient, one clearly perceives and understands all such various causes and conditions without any obscuration. This is the Buddha.
If wisdom is thus, then how could the selection of faculties and the unraveling of knots explained here—the causes and conditions for perfect cultivation—be erroneous?
This concludes the method for loosening the knots.
"Ānanda, I now ask you: regarding this *karpāsa* cloth, these six knots appear before us;
could they all be untied simultaneously? No, World-Honored One. These knots were originally tied in succession; today they must be untied in succession.

Although the six knots share the same substance, the knots themselves were not tied at the same time. Therefore, when the knots are untied, how could they be removed all at once? The Buddha [continued].
He said: "The liberation of the six sense faculties is likewise so. When this faculty is first liberated, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

When the nature of emptiness is perfectly luminous, it constitutes the liberation from phenomena (*dharma-vimokṣa*). Once liberated from phenomena, both [person and phenomenon] are empty and do not arise; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) from within samādhi."
The sequence for untying the knots is contained within the selection of the faculties and the selection of the characters. One faculty comes first;
once its knot is untied, the remaining five faculties are eliminated in succession, each serving as a function for the others.

The six knots are not untied simultaneously, which is a metaphor for the six faculties not being in the same state at once. Just as the knots cannot be untied all at once, so too the faculties cannot be [perfected] simultaneously.

All is extinguished. This section below clarifies the functional efficacy obtained through the resolution of knots. One who attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) has no attachment to a self and destroys the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

When the nature of emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, one achieves liberation through the Dharma and thus destroys the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), attaining the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
As for "both being empty," it means that both person and phenomena are empty, and even this "emptiness of both" is itself empty; only then does one truly attain it.
"Neither arising nor ceasing, it serves as the mind for the causal ground; upon entering the Abiding of the Initial Resolve, this is called attaining the Patience of Non-arising.
Ānanda and the great assembly, having received the Buddha’s instruction on the perfect penetration of wisdom and awakening, were freed from all doubt.
At once they joined their palms, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Today our bodies and minds are radiant and clear; we have attained great joy."
We are unobstructed. Although we have realized that the "one" and the "six" are both lost in meaning, we have not yet reached the fundamental root of perfect penetration.

World-Honored One, we have drifted and wandered through kalpas, left alone and exposed for ages. With what heart or what concern could we have anticipated becoming fellow members of the Buddha’s celestial family? We are like infants who have lost their mother's milk.

Suddenly I have encountered my compassionate mother. If, through this, I may encounter the Way and achieve its realization, then the secret words I receive shall be identical to my original awakening;
they will be no different from never having heard them before. I only pray that you will bestow your great compassion and grant me these sublime secrets, fulfilling the Tathāgata’s final instruction.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, withdrawing into the secrecy of his intent, hoping for the Buddha’s silent transmission.
Having received the gift of a magnificent residence as mentioned above, he requested permission to enter. The Buddha set forth two definitive meanings.

Furthermore, within those definitive meanings, he revealed the perfect penetration of wisdom and enlightenment, leading him to realize that when "one" and "six" are lost, their meaning vanishes. Yet, he had not yet clearly understood the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
He then reflected: "For many kalpas I have wandered aimlessly; what is the significance of my encountering the Buddha now? This may truly be called a marvelous occasion."

Furthermore, if this present encounter is called "attaining the Way," yet the secret words obtained are merely the same as those previously understood regarding the meaning of "one and six perishing," then one still does not know the fundamental root of perfect penetration; how would this differ from not having received the instruction at all?
Therefore, I pray that you will further bestow the profound and solemn teaching to fulfill this final instruction, for I hope that the Buddha will point directly to that One.
This gateway allows for profound entry; it is called the fundamental root of perfect penetration.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed all the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats free from outflows within the assembly.
"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats have been born within my Dharma and have attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). I now ask you:

regarding your initial aspiration for enlightenment and your realization of the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), which among them constitutes perfect penetration? By what means did you enter into *samādhi*?"
The aggregates, bases, sense-fields, and elements are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness of the Tathāgatagarbha.

Desiring to manifest the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the foremost of the myriad practices of all bodhisattvas, the Buddha utilized the selection of the faculties to enable twenty-five sages to each open the gates to manifold wonders.
This clarifies that all these constitute correct cultivation. All phenomena do not transcend the eighteen realms; indeed, the eighteen [realms] sufficiently manifest the myriad dharmas.
As for the necessary presentation of the seven elements, the seven elements serve as the general category, while the eighteen realms serve as the specific categories.

Whether taken collectively or individually, all may enter the Dharma-realm. Regarding the places where the twenty-five sages realized perfect penetration, they all arose from within the three aggregates and the seven elements;
they did not come from the sense organs, nor were they produced from objects, nor did they emerge from space, and so forth.

To realize that all phenomena do not arise from themselves, do not arise from others, and do not arise without cause, and to attain the wondrous state of perfect penetration and omnipresence—responding to the minds of sentient beings according to the scope of their knowledge—is precisely the stage of perfect penetration (*yuantong*).
This school of the Gate of the Patriarchs clarifies that this was brought forth by all the sages. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* asks: "In truth, there is no dharma named Arhat..."
Han: Furthermore, it is said, "I do not harbor such thoughts as: 'I am an Arhat who has transcended desire.
Why then do the various sages repeatedly speak of what they have attained and realized? Answer:

At the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One stated that all the great disciples were those who secretly maintained [the truth] within while manifesting [otherwise] without, acting as assistants in proclaiming the Great Teaching. Now, at the assembly of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, [the Buddha] specifically questions Pūrṇa...
The reason is that they desire to transmit the teaching to Bodhisattvas; thus, the various sages dare to speak freely of their own experiences.
From immeasurable kalpas past, they have planted various roots of goodness; this manifestation of the body and preaching of the Dharma is not performed with a mind seeking personal attainment.
The five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"While we were in the Deer Park and at the Kukkuṭārāma, we witnessed the Tathāgata first attain the Way. Through the Buddha’s voice, we realized and clarified the Four Noble Truths.
When the Buddha asked the bhikṣus, 'Have you understood? I was the first to declare that I had understood. The Tathāgata confirmed me by naming me Ajñāta. This was the Sublime Sound.
Mili Yuan said: "Regarding sounds, I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, sound is the foremost.
This was through the sense-object of sound. Kauṇḍinya—here called 'Fire-Vessel'—in a previous life was a fire-worshipping outsider."
The Way (Dào). His descendants later took this as their surname. The Five Bhikṣus were those whom the Buddha first brought across [to liberation].

When the Buddha left home, his father, the King, ordered three men from his own lineage and two from his mother’s lineage to follow and protect him. Later, they fled to the Deer Park and practiced the ways of non-Buddhist teachers.
After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he went there and turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths for them three times. He asked them, "Do you understand? They replied, "No. (Cén)

He answered, "I have understood. The Buddha then addressed Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya—this word means "understood" (ājñāta). Because he heard the Four Noble Truths, he realized that the nature of sound is empty, and that there is only the Tathāgatagarbha.
"Sublime Sound" refers to the true reality (dharmatā) of sound. "Secretly Perfect" means he secretly awakened to the perfect principle through the teachings of sound.
The Four Noble Truths are Suffering, Accumulation, Cessation, and the Path. Suffering is the fruit of suffering.

"Accumulation" (*samudaya*) is the cause of suffering. Because karmic actions have accumulated since beginningless time, it is called "accumulation. Through the cause of karma, the fruit of suffering is summoned;
this is the causal relationship of the mundane world. "Cessation" (*nirodha*) is quiescence; by extinguishing the accumulation of suffering, one realizes *nirvāṇa*.

The "Path" (*mārga*) consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). By cultivating these factors of enlightenment, one attains the realization of cessation; this is the causal relationship of the supramundane.
Upāliṣada immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I too, when observing the Buddha’s initial attainment of the Way, contemplated the mark of impurity and gave rise to great wearying detachment.

I realized the nature of all forms, seeing that from the impure white bones and subtle dust, they return to empty space. When both emptiness and form are non-dual, one achieves the path of no-more-learning. This is the Tathāgata’s seal.”
My name is Niṣadha. Once all coarse forms were exhausted, wondrous form became subtle and perfect. Through these characteristics of form, I attained arhatship.
When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration of the faculties, according to what I have realized, the faculty of form is supreme.
This [realization] entered through the sense-object of form (*rūpa*). *Upaniṣad* is here translated as "near" or "slight," and also as "the nature of the object.
This means that a subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) is a minute portion of form. Because he attained awakening by means of the object, he received this name. In the past, he was full of lust;

the Buddha instructed him to practice the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Through this contemplation, he realized that the very nature of the object of form is the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, it is called "awakening."
All forms are empty. Since illusory forms are already empty, even emptiness does not abide; therefore it is said that form and emptiness are both non-existent.
When illusory defilements are forever extinguished, one realizes the mark of reality; thus it is said that when the dust of form is exhausted, wondrous form is mysteriously perfect.

Initially, taking form as a disease, the nine contemplations and emptiness served as the medicine. Reaching this point, both medicine and disease are eliminated, and one suddenly awakens and enters [enlightenment].

The nine perceptions are: first, the perception of bloating; second, the perception of livid discoloration; third, the perception of decay; fourth, the perception of being smeared with blood; fifth, the perception of festering pus;
sixth, the perception of being devoured by worms; seventh, the perception of scattering; eighth, the perception of bones; ninth, the perception of burning.
The youth Gandhahastin immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“I heard the Tathāgata instruct me to carefully contemplate the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena. At that time, having taken leave of the Buddha, I was dwelling in quiet seclusion and pure fasting.
I saw bhikṣus burning aloeswood incense; the fragrance was serene as it entered my nostrils. I contemplated this scent and realized it was neither wood nor empty space.”

It was neither smoke nor fire; when it departed, there was no place of attachment, and when it came, there was no point of origin. Through this, my conceptual mind dissolved, and I realized the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).
The Tathāgata conferred upon me the title "Incense-Veneration" (*Gandhāra*). In an instant, the dust-like vapors were extinguished, and a wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive.
Through this Incense-Veneration, I attained Arhatship. When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, Incense-Veneration is supreme.

He entered through the sensory object of fragrance; by means of fragrance he attained the Way. Realizing that the nature of fragrance is empty, he attained firm concentration. Therefore, he was named "Incense-Veneration" (Gandhavimala). Having first realized the path of awakening, his physical form was complete yet subtle; thus he was called a "Child" (Kumāra). "Secluded retreat" refers to sitting peacefully with the mind merged in the profound. "Pure fasting" refers to a quiet chamber. It is signless. Contemplating that fragrance has no source, the characteristics of the mind are likewise exhausted; thus it is said that "by this, the mental constructs dissolve and the deluded mind suddenly ceases.
When the outflow-free state is revealed, one directly perceives the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Since defiled illusions are empty, the true mark abides eternally;
thus it is said that "the turbid vapors vanish in an instant, and the wondrous fragrance is subtle and pervasive."

The two Dharma princes, Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, together with five hundred Brahmās present in the assembly, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Throughout kalpas beginningless in the past, we have served as skilled physicians for the world.
We have tasted every herb, wood, metal, and stone of this Sahā world; there are generally one hundred and eight thousand such names, all of which we know thoroughly."
Whether tastes be bitter, sour, salty, bland, sweet, or pungent; whether they be compounded or innate, transformed or otherwise;
whether they be cold or hot, poisonous or non-poisonous—he is able to know them all thoroughly. Serving the Tathāgata, he understands the nature of taste to be neither empty nor existent.
It is neither identical to body and mind, nor is it separate from body and mind. By discerning the cause of this flavor, one attains awakening.
Having been sealed by the Buddha-Tathāgata with the names of us two brothers, the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, we are now Dharma princes within this assembly.

By means of clarity through the sense of taste, one attains the stage of a Bodhisattva. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, I testified that the sense of taste is supreme among my realizations.
This entry is through the object of taste; it consists of the six flavors—bitter, sour, and so forth—which together constitute what is called "harmony."
To adopt [the flavors] as they are is called "co-nascent" (*sahaja*); to refine them through the "fire of cultivation" is called "transformation.

One who has tasted the medicinal herbs of the world is the peer of Shen Nong; one who serves the Buddha and hears the Dharma understands, within the nature of flavor, the cause of non-arising, thereby realizing that emptiness and existence are one.
Flavor is not empty, and thus it is not separate from body and mind; flavor is not existent, and thus it is not identical to body and mind.
Bhadrapāla, together with his sixteen companions, Bodhisattvas, immediately rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, under the Buddha King of Majestic Sound, we heard the Dharma and left the household life. At the time when the monks were bathing,"

Following the custom, he entered the room and suddenly awakened to the cause of water: it neither washes away dust nor washes away the body; in the midst of this, he was at ease and attained a state of non-possession.
Without forgetting his past training, he has followed the Buddha into the homeless life until the present day, attaining the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
That Buddha was named I-bhadrapāla. Through the manifestation of sublime touch, he attained the station of a Buddha’s son.
When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, the faculty of touch is the supreme cause.

This [consciousness] enters through the sense-object of touch. Bhadrapāla—here translated as Xiànhù (Worthy Protector) or Xiànshǒu (Worthy Guardian)—is so named because he is able to protect himself and is not turned by external things;
thus he has attained this name. He destroys all ignorance and first awakens to the Buddha-enlightenment.
Therefore, he is called a Bodhisattva. When Vīradhvaja perceived the Truths, that was his initial resolve. Now, following Śākyamuni, he has realized the profound stage [of enlightenment].

As for external objects and the internal essence—both internal and external are non-existent. How could there be an intermediate state acting as water to wash? "Touching" is the meaning [of the term];
it receives its name through the interaction between water and the self. Now that both are absent, where can the fruit of touching reside? It does not exist.
Contact is contact; yet in reality, contact is non-contact. Contact is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa); contact is awakening (bodhi). Therefore, it is called "sublime contact.
Mahākāśyapa, the Bhikṣuṇī Suvarṇaprabhāsā, and the others immediately rose from their seats and prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "In a past kalpa, within this world-system, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa.
I was able to draw near to him, hear the Dharma, and practice its study. After that Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, I made offerings to his relics and lit lamps to maintain the light."

"Because they applied purple-gold light to the images of the Buddha, from that time forth, in life after life and birth after birth, their bodies have always been perfectly complete as a mass of purple-gold light.
These bhikṣuṇīs of Purple-Gold Light and the others were my own retinue; we simultaneously resolved our minds [for enlightenment]."

I observe that the six sense-objects in the world are subject to change and decay; by cultivating cessation through emptiness and stillness alone, my body and mind were able to pass through hundreds of thousands of kalpas as if it were the snapping of a finger.
By means of the dharma of emptiness, I attained arhatship. The World-Honored One declared me the foremost among those who practice dhūta.
Through the illumination of the wondrous Dharma, all outflows have been extinguished. When the Buddha asks about perfect penetration, this is what I have realized.
The Dharma-cause is supreme.
This cause enters through the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Mahākāśyapa—here translated as "Great Drinker of Light"—is his clan name.
His body was golden in color, its radiance eclipsing the sun and moon. His personal name was Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja. He had a retinue of kinsmen and provided offerings while living as a householder.

The passage beginning with "He enshrined the relics" describes his past causes. Observing that sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are subject to decay and transformation, he realized the emptiness and quiescence of all phenomena (*dharma*).

He subsequently cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to extinguish the faculty of mind (*manas*), so that it no longer took sensory objects as its object. Thus attaining the state beyond arising and ceasing, he transcended hundreds of thousands of kalpas in the space of a finger-snap.
Wearing a golden *kāṣāya*, he entered meditative absorption on Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await the descent of Maitreya.
This is the proof thereof. The section on the six sense objects concludes. As for why the six sense objects are all called "wondrous," it is because they do not bind one to the objects.
Then Aniruddha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "When I first left the household life..."
I was constantly fond of sleep. The Tathāgata rebuked me, saying I belonged to the class of beasts.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s reproach, I wept and reproached myself, remaining awake for seven days until I lost both my eyes. The World-Honored One then revealed to me the Vajrasamādhi of Delightful Vision and Illumination.
I do not rely on the eye to perceive the ten directions; with refined and true clarity, I see them as plainly as looking at fruit in the palm of my hand.

The Tathāgata certified me as an Arhat. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, according to what I have realized, by turning back the faculty of sight and following its source, this is the foremost method.
This enters through the eye-consciousness. Āniruddha—here called *Yìrúì* (Asaṅga)—was the Buddha’s younger cousin.
In the past, he offered a meal to a Pratyekabuddha and, as a result, experienced the bliss of his wishes for ninety-one kalpas.
While the Buddha was preaching the Dharma at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, Āniruddha fell asleep; the Buddha then spoke this verse: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? Like a snail..."
Regarding species such as oysters and clams: they sleep for a thousand years without hearing the name of the Buddha.
Their joy in beholding illumination is roughly similar to practicing the visualization of the sun in the Pure Land. Although their eyes do not see, they joyfully behold with the mind’s eye.
Suddenly attaining illumination, their essence is never darkened; nothing can obscure it. It is neither lost nor destroyed; therefore, it is called "vajra" (diamond-like). It is the refined and true.
"Penetratingly clear" means that within the true nature, the refined radiance manifests and shines forth, such that one sees the great trichiliocosm as clearly as a fruit in the palm of one's hand.
At that moment, Cūḍapanthaka rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I lack the capacity for recitation and retention, and am devoid of the nature of extensive learning. When I first encountered the Buddha, I heard the Dharma and left the household life; yet I can only remember a single verse of the Tathāgata."

"Oṭṭha, for one hundred days, I was able to leave the former while grasping the latter, and leave the latter while grasping the former. The Buddha, pitying my folly, instructed me to dwell in retreat and to regulate the inhalation and exhalation.
As I then observed the breath, I thoroughly investigated its subtle aspects—its arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—and the momentary nature of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
My mind suddenly opened wide, attaining great non-obstruction. Eventually, with the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), I became an Arhat and sat upon the Buddha’s seat."

[He] attained the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), [Ānanda] said: "According to what I have realized, reversing the breath to follow emptiness is the foremost method.
This was entered through the faculty of the nose. Pāṇṭaka means "Successor of the Path" (*jìdào*); he was so named because he was born by the side of a road. Zhou...
This was to benefit his elder brother. As they were twin brothers, he included the elder brother’s name as well.

In the past, he had been a great Dharma master who was secretive and stingy regarding the Buddha-dharma, refusing to teach others; consequently, he received the retribution of being dull-witted. However, due to his past roots of goodness, he encountered the Buddha and left the household life.
The Buddha instructed him to regulate his breath and collect his mind, whereby he attained realization that both the exhalation and inhalation possess the four characteristics (*catvāraḥ lakṣaṇāni*).
Initial arising is called "birth" (*jāti*). Non-interruption is called "abiding" (*sthiti*). Gradual attenuation is called "change" (*anyathātva*). Having ceased is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).

These are the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which are the flux of these four characteristics. Although dullness and ignorance have remote causes, their immediate conditions also arise from mental confusion.
By regulating the breath and maintaining composure, one avoids the interference of other conditions; thus the mind becomes suddenly clear, and concentration can give rise to wisdom. Conversely—
"Breath follows emptiness. This means that when one traces the breath back to its source until it reaches the point of extreme subtlety, it likewise returns to emptiness.
Kauṇḍinya then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I possess oral karma."
In past kalpas, I mocked śramaṇas; consequently, in life after life, I suffered from the disease of rumination (bovine eructation).
The Tathāgata showed me the Dharma-gate of the Single Flavor of the Pure Mind-Ground. Having attained the cessation of the mind, I entered samādhi and contemplated the cognition of flavors.

Neither a substantial entity nor a material object, one should contemplate so as to transcend all worldly outflows (*āsrava*). Internally, one is liberated from body and mind; externally, one leaves behind the world.
Far removed from the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), like a bird escaping its cage, one is freed from defilement and dust, the Dharma-eye becomes pure, and one attains the state of an Arhat.

The Tathāgata personally certified me as having attained the path of no-more-learning. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied: "According to what I have realized, by returning to the flavor and revolving it back into the faculty of cognition, this is the foremost method."
This [faculty] enters through the tongue-root. Kauṇḍinya—here translated as "the Cow-chewer"—is so called because even when not eating, a cow makes a hollow sound like chewing;
in the past, seeing an old śramaṇa who was toothless yet still eating, he remarked that he resembled a cow, and thus he has experienced this retribution life after life.
To prevent such slander, the Buddha granted him a rosary, instructing him to constantly recollect the Buddha, sever all miscellaneous conditions, and remain single-mindedly focused.
Pure. Having attained the *nien-fo samādhi*, he further contemplates the nature of taste. It is not known by means of a substance, for it does not follow the sense organ;

it is not known by means of an object, for it does not cling to the sensory field. Although the sensory field of taste is raised up, it merely manifests on the tongue; that which is able to know is the tongue itself.
The Buddha, wishing to instruct him in the perfect penetration of the tongue-root, first causes him to cease distraction and enter stillness, and subsequently instructs him to emerge from stillness.

Arising illumination, one observes and tastes the fundamental nature; both sense organs and objects are forgotten, and the hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha) is suddenly awakened to. Thus, all outflows (āsrava) are instantly exhausted.

Internally, one is liberated from body and mind—this is liberation of the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*). Externally, one leaves behind the world—this is liberation of the secondary retribution (*adhiṣṭhānaphala*).

Far removed from the entanglements of the triple realm, one is like a bird escaping its cage, moving without obstruction wherever it goes. Free from defilement and dissolving the dust, clarity [is attained].

Through the merit of severing delusions, the Dharma-eye becomes pure. One clearly attains the meaning of the fruition; "returning to the flavor" and "revolving back to knowledge" means that the stream of returning to the flavor revolves back toward the awakening of True Suchness (Tathatā).
Pilingyavatsa immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I first resolved to attain enlightenment, I followed the Buddha to enter the Path. I frequently heard the Tathāgata speak of the many things in the world that are not to be enjoyed.

While begging for alms in the city, my mind was contemplating the Dharma-gates; unaware, a poisonous thorn pierced my foot on the road, causing my entire body to ache with pain. As I reflected upon this—"
I understood. I understood this profound suffering. Although my awareness perceived pain, my awareness of the pure mind was free from any perception of pain.
I further reflected: how could there be two simultaneous perceptions within this single body? Before long, as I focused my mindfulness, my body and mind suddenly became empty.

Within twenty-one days, all outflows were exhausted, and I attained Arhatship. I received the Buddha’s personal seal of approval and realized the state of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). The Buddha asked about the perfection [of my realization].
"Penetration is as I have realized it: pure awakening that leaves the body behind; this is the foremost.
This enters through the faculty of the body. Pindola Bharadvāja—this is translated as 'Residual Habit. For five hundred lifetimes he was a Brahmin;
his lineage was arrogant, and his residual habits have not yet been forgotten. That which is unpleasant in the world is precisely suffering."
This is the Truth. When one contemplates suffering in accordance with the teaching, encountering a painful circumstance becomes the very condition for entering the Way.

Wood and stone are devoid of consciousness; thus, whether they are cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, they remain entirely unaware. I alone possess consciousness, and therefore I am aware of this pain.
Although there is awareness that perceives this pain, my fundamental awakened mind is originally pure and free from pain. This is because it is the pure awakening.
The mind cannot reach [the sensation of] pain. Furthermore, regarding this single body, how could there be two simultaneous perceptions?

There is only the pure, true awakening (*tathatā-jñāna*); fundamentally, there is no deluded perception that perceives pain. Since truth and delusion cannot coexist, the body and mind suddenly become empty;
this is precisely the point of enlightenment. Because the body is empty, there is no one who suffers pain; because the mind is empty, there is no one who perceives the pain. (Excerpted)
"Mindfulness" refers to the true awakening that accords with painless purity; it does not refer to the deluded awakening that pursues the perception of pain.
"The exhaustion of all outflows" means that the nature of the treasury of true awakening manifests before one, while deluded awakening can no longer be found.
The pure awakening leaves behind the body; there is only the single, perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening, with no further marks of a physical form.
Subhūti immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Throughout kalpas past, my mind has attained non-obstruction. I recall my births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; even when first in my mother’s womb, I already knew emptiness and stillness."
Thus, even unto the ten directions, all things are realized as empty. I also cause sentient beings to realize the nature of emptiness;

through the Tathāgata’s awakening to the true emptiness of their own nature, their emptiness becomes perfectly luminous, and they attain Arhatship. They suddenly enter the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness, sharing the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and are sealed as those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Liberated into the emptiness of nature, I am supreme. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the faculties, [I replied] as follows:

That which I have realized is that all marks enter into non-existence; where there is no "non-existence," even that is exhausted. Turning back from phenomena to return to the Unconditioned—this is the foremost.

This enters through the faculty of mind. Understanding emptiness does not cease with a single lifetime; while in the womb, one knows emptiness, and the wisdom of emptiness is not deluded by the aggregates of the womb.
Upon birth, one is immediately able to discourse on emptiness and enables sentient beings to realize emptiness as well. Although...

To "understand emptiness while afflictions are not yet exhausted" means that although one has attained awakening, there are still residual delusions. "To bring forth" means to illuminate this for them.

"Intrinsic awareness is true emptiness" refers to the emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Entering the ocean of precious luminosity, one shares the same knowledge and vision as the Buddha, realizing the Tathāgata-garbha of emptiness and thereby possessing its non-empty virtues.
"All marks enter non-existence" means that all phenomenal characteristics enter into the state of being without characteristics. This is not a place of... [non-existence].

It is not that they are exhausted; even the characteristic of emptiness is empty. As phenomena revolve back into non-existence, non-existence is itself emptiness. This concludes the section on the six sense organs. Regarding the omission of the ear organ:
this was a deliberate choice to suit the specific capacity of the audience, leaving it for last. Among the five organs, four contain the characters "revolving" (xuan) and "returning" (fan).

Within the gateway of the faculties and their natures, there is the principle of the faculties turning back and detaching from objects; this is distinct from the relationship between objects and consciousness.
Śāriputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "Since the beginningless kalpas, my mental vision has been pure.
Thus have I undergone births as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, manifesting various transformations both mundane and supramundane. One...
Upon seeing him, my vision was unobstructed. I attained freedom from hindrance. On the way, I encountered the Kāśyapa brothers following one another as they expounded upon causes and conditions;
I realized the boundlessness of the mind and left the household life under the Buddha. Seeing that enlightened clarity is perfect and complete, I attained great fearlessness and became an Arhat.
As the eldest son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma, when the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the senses, it was as follows:
That which I have realized is the mind’s vision that emits light; this light is the ultimate knowledge and insight, and it is the foremost.
This enters through the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). This mental vision is precisely the eye-consciousness—pure and without obstruction.
It encompasses all mundane and supramundane realms of both ordinary beings and sages. Because the eye-consciousness is clear and sharp, one penetrates everything upon a single glance.
This is called the Dharma-eye. Kāśyapa spoke in verse: "All phenomena arise from conditions, And likewise they cease through conditions.
Our Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, Constantly teaches this very truth. Arising and ceasing from conditions— Arising is non-arising, And ceasing is non-ceasing.
By awakening to this, One attains a mind without bounds, Directly perceives the sign of freedom from thought, And acquires the wisdom-eye."
Thus, as the clarity of awakened perception becomes perfectly full, illusory consciousness is already dissolved, and true awakening manifests in its entirety. One attains great fearlessness;
this is the thorough penetration of seeing. With wisdom foremost and name and virtue preeminent, one is called the "eldest son.

Because the Tathāgata has revealed the wondrous Dharma, it is said that he follows from the mouth and from the Dharma, thereby obtaining the Buddha-eye. The vision of the mind emits light, and this light reaches the ultimate limit of knowledge and insight.
From visual consciousness, the light of wisdom is manifested. That which is the ultimate limit of the light of wisdom is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
At that moment, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I have previously served as a Dharma prince for Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Among the disciples of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, I am the one whom they instruct regarding the faculties of bodhisattvas."
I shall cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra; my name shall be established from this. World-Honored One, with a mind of hearing, I shall discern all the knowledge and views of sentient beings.

If, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in other directions, there is a single sentient being who brings forth the realization of the conduct of Samantabhadra within their heart, at that time I shall mount the six-tusked elephant, manifesting hundreds of thousands of bodies, and arrive at that place. Even if they...
Their obstructions are deep; they have not yet attained the vision of me. I personally place my hand upon their heads in the darkness to protect, comfort, and bring them to fulfillment.

When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration, I declare its fundamental cause: the illumination of the hearing-faculty of the mind, through which discernment becomes sovereign—this is the foremost.

This enters through the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). To traverse the entire Dharma-realm is called "Universal" (*Samantabhadra*); to occupy a station adjacent to the ultimate sages is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*).

There is no practice not cultivated and no virtue not fulfilled. Generally, those who possess the great faculties and cultivate the path of the Bodhisattva are all said to perform the conduct of Samantabhadra.
"Hearing with the mind" refers to the manifestation of the ear-consciousness. The elephant symbolizes a gait that is calm and dignified; it is constant...
His conduct is not violent. The elephant has six tusks, symbolizing that the practices of Samantabhadra pervade the six perfections.

"White" is the source of all colors, symbolizing the principle of the single truth as the foundation of myriad practices. He provides protection so that demons cannot disturb him, and offers consolation so that the mind does not retreat.
"The mind-hearing becomes manifest" refers to internal realization; "discrimination is sovereign" refers to external function.
This refers to the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of auditory consciousness, not to the discursive conceptualization of the mental consciousness.
Sundarananda then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Since I first left the household life and entered the Path under the Buddha, although I am fully possessed of the precepts, my mind has remained constantly distracted and agitated regarding *samādhi*, and I have not yet attained [liberation]."
"O World-Honored One, you have instructed me and Cūḍapanthaka to contemplate the white at the tip of the nose.

When I first applied myself to this contemplation, after twenty-one days had passed, I saw the breath entering and exiting through my nostrils like smoke. My body and mind became inwardly luminous, and the world appeared as a perfectly open void, everywhere pure and empty like crystal.
As the appearance of smoke gradually faded away, the breath at the nose became white. My mind opened and my outflows were exhausted. Thus he spoke regarding all that entered and exited.
Cessation transformed into radiance, which illuminated the worlds of the ten directions. I attained Arhatship, and the World-Honored One prophesied to me that I would surely attain Bodhi.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "I attained it through cessation; through long practice of cessation, illumination was revealed. This illumination became perfect and extinguished all outflows. This is the foremost."
This [scent] enters through the nose-consciousness. *Sundarī* means "beautiful and beloved," which is the name of his wife; *Nanda* means "joy," which is his own name.
To distinguish him from Nanda the cowherd, he is identified by mentioning his wife's name along with his own. He was the Buddha’s own younger brother.
First, it was explained that because their desire-minds had not yet been forgotten, their minds remained constantly distracted and agitated even at the time of entering meditative absorption.

Kūṭadanta was of a sharp and quick-witted nature, yet his wild intelligence was excessive and his mind was likewise distracted. The Buddha instructed them both to contemplate the white [light] at the tip of the nose, fixing the mind there and not allowing for other objects.
Respiration arises from wind and fire, which stirs up the turbidity of the afflictions; its appearance is as follows:
It is like smoke: as pure contemplation gives rise to illumination, afflictions gradually dissolve. With internal clarity and external emptiness, the smoke vanishes and becomes white.
Upon the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), where no further afflictions remain, the inner radiance emits light, and the light of transformative activity subsides.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since the beginningless kalpas, my eloquence has been unimpeded; I have proclaimed suffering and emptiness and deeply penetrated the true mark of reality.
Thus, even regarding the secret dharma-gates of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have skillfully revealed them within the assembly, attaining fearlessness."
The World-Honored One knew that I possessed great eloquence; with the wheel of his voice, he instructed me to proclaim it forth.

In the presence of the Buddha, I assisted the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma. Through this lion’s roar, I attained arhatship. The World-Honored One certified me as being unsurpassed in the preaching of the Dharma.
The Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way. I, by means of the Dharma-sound, subdue demonic adversaries and extinguish all outflows;

this is the foremost method. This entry is through the consciousness of the tongue. There are four kinds of eloquence: first, eloquence of phrasing; second, eloquence of doctrine; third, eloquence of meaning; and fourth, eloquence of joyful exposition.
"Unyielding and inexhaustible," both are termed "unimpeded. "Proclaiming the lower [teachings]" refers to the Dharma of the Hīnayāna.
"Thus" and so forth indicates the meaning of the Mahāyāna. Regarding the "secret dharma-gate": it may refer to a teaching that the Tathāgata long kept silent and did not proclaim;

or a teaching that is half-clarified and half-obscured; or a teaching where the words point east while the intent points west. "Subtly revealing" means to exhaustively manifest [the truth] through indirect means.

He clarifies their intent in order to penetrate the source of the Dharma; thus, he has no fear. The section above, beginning with "The past deeds of the Buddhas," describes the Buddha’s activities of the past.
The section below, beginning with "The World-Honored One," describes his activities of the present. Regarding the "wheel of sound": this refers to the sound of preaching the Dharma.

The term "sound-wheel" is a metaphorical expression for the teaching, which can destroy the obstacles of affliction and bring about the attainment of the supreme transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); therefore, the sound of the Dharma is likened to a wheel. It instructs me to arouse [the aspiration].
"Promoting" means causing others to assist the Buddha in promoting his transformation of beings. "I, at the lower [level]" clarifies the attainment of the fruit through merit.

"The Buddha asks, etc. concludes the meaning of the present inquiry. Although preaching the Dharma pertains to the faculty of the tongue, chewing the flavor of the Dharma involves the gustatory consciousness (*jihvā-vijñāna*).

However, preaching the Dharma requires the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). That he employs the gustatory consciousness here indicates that his preaching of the Dharma is spontaneous and effortless, requiring no deliberation.
Upāli immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I personally followed the Buddha when he left the city to renounce the world;
I personally witnessed the Tathāgata’s six years of diligent austerity; I personally saw the Tathāgata subdue all Māras and restrain all non-Buddhists;
and I personally received the Buddha’s teachings on the precepts for the sake of liberation from the worldly outflows of greed and desire—thus it was, even unto the third [rainy retreat]."

The thousand modes of deportment and the eighty thousand subtle natures of karma—both obstructive and neutral—are all completely purified. Body and mind are stilled and extinguished; I have become an Arhat.

Among the assembly of the Tathāgata, I am the leader. My own mind has been personally sealed by the Buddha. Upholding the precepts and cultivating the body, I am acclaimed by the assembly as unsurpassed.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I began with the mastery of the body, and then sequentially mastered the mind. The mind...
One attains thorough penetration; thereafter, body and mind become entirely supple and proficient.

This is the foremost [attainment]. This enters through body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). Whether it be close following, close observation, or even receiving the teachings, all are matters of body-consciousness.
Upāli, this is called "the Foremost," because he maintains the precepts as the guiding framework for the assembly. It is also called "the Close Attendant," for the Buddha [relied upon him].
At the time he was a prince, because of his close association with the ministers who attended to him, the *Samādhi Sūtra* states:
Once the Prince had attained the Way, he moved the heavens and shook the earth, emitting a great radiance that eclipsed the palaces of Māra.
King Māra Pāpīyān, struck with terror and anxiety, led eighty billion demonic armies of various forms and strange appearances to come and cause disturbance and harm. He disturbed...

When [the Buddha] remained unmoved, the mind of Māra was finally subdued. As for the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*): after the Buddha attained enlightenment, he traveled and transformed beings throughout various kingdoms.
The six teachers of the non-Buddhists were widespread throughout the five regions of India; each teacher had three types of followers, totaling eighteen schools.

All of them were erudite and widely learned, yet they all had their heterodox minds shattered and followed his transformation. By subduing Māra and restraining the non-Buddhists, he clarified the Buddha’s wisdom and virtue, leading to liberation.

The "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*) clarifies the Buddha’s virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). The phrase "following the Buddha" below correctly clarifies the cause of awakening. Regarding the "three thousand dignified conducts" (*sāhasra-īryāpatha*):
these consist of the two hundred and fifty precepts of a bhikṣu; for each of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—there are two hundred and fifty, totaling one thousand.
Regarding the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā*), they form three thousand [precepts]. "Majesty" (*veṣa*) refers to a dignified and upright bearing;
"demeanor" (*īryā*) refers to the outward manifestation of conduct, wherein seeing, hearing, speaking, and moving are all in accord with the Dharma. As for the "eighty thousand" and so forth:

by again applying the three thousand [precepts] to the seven branches of body and speech, they become twenty-one thousand; these are then further applied to the four categories of afflictions, resulting in eighty-four thousand [precepts].

One thousand. Now, to cite the general number, it is called eighty thousand. "Natural karma" (*prakṛti-karman*) refers to that which is created by the nature of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying.

"Prohibited karma" (*pratikṣepaṇa-karman*) refers to secondary transgressions; these were prohibited because they arise from faults. "Sealing the mind" means sealing the pure mind of one who maintains the precepts and practices cultivation.
Because consciousness exists dependent upon the body, one first clings to the body and subsequently clings to the mind. "The intelligent and sharp-witted" refers to those who are discerning.
This is the realization of perfect penetration. Regarding the three clusters of precepts: the cluster of gathering wholesome dharmas involves accumulating every good deed without exception;

it gives rise to the practice that aids the Path and is the cause for the virtue of wisdom, through which the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is cultivated and perfected. The cluster of restraining from misconduct involves abandoning every evil without exception; it gives rise to the practice of the True Path.

This is the cause for the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*); through its cultivation, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is perfected. It encompasses sentient beings; there are none among those born who are not saved.

It gives rise to the practice of the non-abiding path (*apratiṣṭhita-mārga*); this is the cause of liberation (*vimukti*). Through its cultivation, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is perfected. The seven branches [of misconduct] consist of three of the mind—greed, hatred, and delusion—and four of the mouth:
false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh abuse. The four divisions of afflictions (*kleśa*) are excessive greed, excessive hatred, and so forth.
[This refers to] delusion and the [other] equal parts.
Mahāmaudgalyāyana then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I was first on the road begging for alms, I encountered the three Kāśyapas—Uruvilvākāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and Nadīkāśyapa—and they proclaimed the Tathāgata..."

Regarding the profound meaning of causes and conditions, I suddenly gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and attained great penetration. The Tathāgata bestowed upon me a *kāṣāya* robe which I wore upon my body, and my beard and hair fell away of their own accord.
As I traveled through the ten directions, I attained unimpededness; my supernatural powers were manifested and proven supreme.
I attained arhatship. Not only the World-Honored One, but all Tathāgatas of the ten directions have praised my spiritual power as perfectly clear, pure, sovereign, and fearless.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I replied that by returning to the stillness of the ocean-like mind, the light of the heart was manifested and proclaimed, like clearing away the turbidity from a flowing stream.
Having long ago attained purity and clarity, he is the foremost.
He entered through the mental consciousness. Maudgalyāyana is his clan name; this is translated as "the Clan of the Mung Bean Gatherer. Kolita—
"Isi" is translated here as "the Unfettered Tree. "Uruvilvā" is translated as "Papaya Grove.
"Gayā" is translated as "City. "Nadī" is translated as "River"; each was named after its respective location. The elder brother had five hundred disciples.

Each of the two younger brothers had two hundred and fifty followers. Because the Buddha had subdued the fire dragon and disciplined them through various holy sites, the three brothers, together with their one thousand disciples, followed the Buddha into the homeless life. Such is the profound significance of these causal conditions.
This is not a coarse phenomenon resulting from worldly conjunction; rather, it elucidates the meaning of the emptiness of all dharmas.

Being unimpeded throughout the ten directions, it truly manifests the foremost of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). That which cannot be fathomed is called "spiritual" (*shen*); that which is unimpeded is called "penetration" (*tong*).

Whether appearing or disappearing, gathering or dispersing, whether one or many, large or small, or shifting and transforming back and forth—whether suddenly hidden or suddenly manifest—all such states are beyond the reach of cognition and are thus termed "supernatural power."
However, this is merely the trace. If one investigates its source, it is originally the light inherent in my wondrously enlightened true mind.
"Revolve the stillness" means to revolve the mental consciousness and return to wondrous stillness; that is, to transform the mental consciousness and realize the Tathāgata-garbha mind.

The radiance of the mind is manifested; this is the wondrous function of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). This concludes the discussion of the six consciousnesses. How are consciousness and the sense organs distinguished? Let us consider the eye for a moment.
When the eye illuminates an object, there is not a single thought of movement; it is like a mirror that makes no further analysis or distinction.

This is the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*), termed the function of the eye-organ (*cakṣur-indriya-vṛtti*). Subsequently, it encounters various appearances—black and white, large and small, good and evil—and perceives them with vivid clarity.

Discrimination (*vikalpa*) is precisely visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). From this sequence of pointing and indicating, the conceptual calculation of distinctions is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) belonging to the eye.
The other four [senses] should be understood by analogy.
Ucchuṣma joined his palms before the Tathāgata, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I constantly recall that in the distant past, many kalpas ago, I was by nature full of lust. At that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Śūnyarāja."

He spoke of those who indulge excessively in lust as being like a mass of fierce fire. He instructed me to contemplate throughout my entire body—the hundred skeletal parts, the four limbs, and all the cold and warm vital energies—so that the divine light might coalesce within and transform this lustful mind into the fire of wisdom.
From that time on, all the Buddhas have called me by the name Huotou (Fire-Head). By the power of the Fire-Light Samādhi, I attained Arhatship and made a great vow.
When the Buddhas attained the Way, I was a powerful warrior who personally subdued the demonic enemies. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied:
"By clearly observing that the warmth and touch within my body and mind flow unimpededly, all outflows were extinguished; thus, a great jewel-flame arose, and I ascended to supreme enlightenment."
This is the first.
This [deity] enters by means of the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*). Ucchuṣma—here translated as "Fire-Head"—is named according to his attribute.
The reason he is not described as arising from a seat is that, manifesting a vajra body as a protector and attendant, he does not employ a formal throne. Regarding this:
To describe his awakening, he first sets forth his delusion. Since awakening is attained through delusion, delusion is the cause of awakening.

Lust arises from the pressure of warmth and tactile contact; life is the fire of desire, and death is the fire of karma. As the power of karma increases and blazes, it becomes a mass of fierce flames.
Question: Water results from greed, and fire arises from a mind of anger. Why, then, is excessive lust compared to a fierce fire? Answer: The metaphors for dharmas are not fixed.

When the lustful mind gradually seeps in and moistens the root of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it is likened to water. When the lustful mind blazes up and withers the seeds of purity, it is likened to fire.
A mind of anger is violent and its flames are difficult to extinguish; thus it may be likened to fire. Furthermore, the surging of a mind of anger...
It surges forth, flowing so profusely it is difficult to restrain; this may be compared to water. Within the human body, there are both cold and warm vital energies (*prāṇa*).
When one harbors a mind of excessive lust, these various cold and warm energies are fermented and steamed until they all become hot. By observing with right mindfulness, one asks:

from where do these energies arise, and by what cause do they become fire? Through the application of the power of contemplation, these energies are transformed into divine light, whereas what was previously the fire of desire—
Now the fire of wisdom has been formed; it now burns the treasury of merit. It now consumes the fuel of afflictions; therefore, it is called the Fire-Light Samādhi.

"Mighty One" (Balavīra) is the original name for Vajra; he personally subdues the enmity of Māra. This is the actual manifestation of great vows, for by protecting the Dharma, he subdues the enmity of Māra.
"The Buddha asked," and so forth, concludes the meaning of the present inquiry. First, because of the careful contemplation within his own body...
The sensation of warmth is non-dual and indistinguishable from the fire element of the external world;

they do not obstruct one another. "The exhaustion of all outflows" refers to the destruction of ignorance. "Jewel-flame" is spoken of as a metaphor: the "jewel" is the jewel of the mind, and the "flame" is *prajñā*.
This points to the true wisdom of the perfect mind, for it is through this that one realizes unsurpassed enlightenment. Thus, the fruit is described within the context of the cause.
The Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa appeared in the world, I was a bhikṣu who constantly stood at all major highways and ferry crossings."

Where fields and roads were rugged and narrow, or where conditions were improper and obstructed or damaged carts and horses, I leveled and filled them all, or constructed bridges, or carried sand and earth myself.
I underwent such diligent hardships through the appearance of immeasurable Buddhas in the world.

Furthermore, if there were sentient beings in marketplaces who required someone to carry their goods, I would first carry them for them until they reached their destination; having set down the goods, I would then depart.
I did not take their payment. During the time when Vipaśyin Buddha was present in the world, there was widespread famine;

I worked as a porter and, regardless of whether the distance was far or near, I accepted only a single coin. Or, if a cart or ox became mired in the mud, I possessed supernatural power [to extricate them].
He turned the wheel for them and uprooted their suffering and affliction. At that time, the Great King of the country invited the Buddha to a vegetarian feast.
I leveled the ground at that moment to await the Buddha. Viśvabhū Tathāgata touched my head and said to me, "You must level the ground of the mind; then the ground of the world will all become level.
My mind was immediately opened, and I saw that the subtle particles of my own body were identical to all the subtle particles that constitute the world.
They are equal and without distinction. The self-nature of atoms does not touch one another; even by weapons of war, they are not touched.

Regarding this nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), I realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained arhatship. Now, having turned my mind back, I enter the stage of a bodhisattva.
I have heard the Tathāgatas proclaim the wondrous Lotus Sūtra, the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. I was formerly a witness to this and served as their leader.
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I observed that the two objects—the body and the sensory realm—are equal and without distinction; they are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.
Delusive falsehoods give rise to dust; when the dust is cleared away, wisdom becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way—this is the foremost.

This is the stage of entering through the Great Ground (mahābhūmi). The Bodhisattva Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Earth-Holding) was named according to his practice: he leveled the ground of the world and accumulated practices with profound sincerity.
Yet, he had not yet realized that the nature of dust is fundamentally empty. Upon hearing the teaching of Viśvabhū, his mind immediately opened; he contemplated...
The atoms of the body-realm are equal and without distinction. Through realizing that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are one body, one empties oneself of all atoms.
When emptiness merges with emptiness, how could they touch or rub against one another? Weapons are also but atoms; therefore, there is likewise nothing to be touched.

One who awakens to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) realizes that there is no self within the aggregates (skandhas), thereby attaining the realization of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā). Although...
Having realized non-arising, one extensively cultivates the myriad practices and fulfills the path of a bodhisattva;

therefore, whenever the ground of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is proclaimed, I shall surely join that assembly to serve as a witness. The two types of dust—the body and the world—are fundamentally the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Fundamentally, there is no distinction. It is due to the single movement of ignorance that false cognition and vision arise; thus, the distinctions between sense organs and objects exist.
Now that the organs and objects have dissolved and mirror-like wisdom is perfected, how could one not achieve unsurpassed enlightenment?
The youth Candraprabha immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Jaladeva. He taught all the bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water."

Entering into samādhi, he contemplates within his body that the nature of water is indestructible. Beginning with mucus and saliva, he traces it through all the way to the lymphatic fluids, semen, blood, feces, and urine;
as these circulate and revolve within the body, the nature of water remains identical throughout. Thus, he perceives water within his own body.
It was indistinguishable from the oceans of fragrant water in the Floating Banner King world-system beyond this world.
At that time, I first achieved this contemplation; I saw only the water and had not yet attained the bodiless state. I was then a bhikṣu, practicing dhyāna within my chamber.
I had a disciple who peered through the window to observe the room; he saw nothing at all, for there was only clear water filling the entire space.
Being a young child without understanding, he picked up a piece of tile or rubble and threw it into the water; the water splashed and made a sound, after which he looked back and departed.
After I emerged from samādhi, I suddenly felt a pain in my heart, like that experienced by Śāriputra when he was struck by a malevolent spirit. I reflected to myself:
"I have now attained the path of Arhatship and have long been free from the conditions for illness; why has this heart-pain suddenly arisen today?"
"Lest you should lose [this opportunity]. At that time, the youth came quickly before me and reported the matter as described above. I then told him:
'If you see water again, you may immediately open the door and enter this water to remove the tiles and debris. The youth followed my instructions."
Later, when I entered meditative concentration, I again saw the water; the tiles and rubble were exactly as before. I opened the door and emerged.

After I emerged from concentration, my physical body was as it had been at first. I encountered immeasurable Buddhas, continuing in this manner until I reached the Tathāgata King of Sovereign Penetrations of Mountains and Seas.

Only then did I attain the dissolution of the self-body. My nature became one with the true emptiness of all the fragrant water-oceans throughout the worlds of the ten directions—non-dual and without distinction.
Now, from the Tathāgata, I have received the name "Childlike Purity" (Kumārabhūta) and am included in the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

When the Buddha asks about the perfect penetration [of the faculties], I say that through the single flavor of the flowing nature of water, I attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and perfected Bodhi; this is the foremost.
This [Buddha] enters through the water element (*āpas-mahābhūta*). The moon is a water-crystal; because the nature of water is round and luminous, he is named Moonlight (*Candraprabha*).
As for "Water Heaven" (*Jaladeva*), it signifies realizing the water element and penetrating to the fundamental nature-Heaven (*dharmatā-gagana*).

This Buddha may have entered perfection through this element, or he may have manifested this name according to the occasion and time, in resonance with his contemplation. "Without being superseded" means not being discordant or divergent. This accords with the Flower Garland Sutra (*Avataṃsaka-sūtra*).
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, within the Flower Treasury Ocean, there is a great lotus flower. Within that lotus flower, there are various fragrant water seas;
each of these fragrant water seas has a single flower, which serves as the seed for the worlds of the Buddha-fields.
The Flower Treasury World is situated within these fragrant water seas and consists of twenty tiers stacked high like a banner; therefore, it is called the "Floating Banner."
The royal lands and the oceans of fragrant water are immeasurable and boundless. Now, observing the water within one’s own body, it is identical to those oceans;
the water pervades the entire chamber—this is the sign of successful meditative accomplishment. Question: From where does the water within the chamber come? Answer:

It is matter produced as the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*), manifested by the concentrated mind. It exists when one enters meditative absorption and ceases to exist when one emerges from it; it is not like matter produced as the fruit of karma (*karma-phala-rūpa*).

Karma shared by all is experienced collectively; yet that which is perceived only by oneself can nevertheless cause others to see it, for the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is exceptionally sublime—an inconceivable realm.

It is like when the World-Honored One subdued the dragon-fire, causing the stone cave to blaze forth, or when Master Sengcong entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi*, making the mountains and valleys appear as if on fire.
Even for those who have not yet discarded their bodies, the body and water appear as two distinct things, as if there were still a self-body present.
That is water. One who has lost their body becomes one with the water; if one seeks it within my body, it cannot be found.

While the body exists, there is minor suffering due to its causes; yet when contemplation is perfected, there is forever no great harm. Śāriputra entered meditative absorption on the bank of the Ganges.

He was struck by a ghost of former enmity and suffered a headache upon emerging from meditative concentration. The Buddha said, "If you did not possess meditative concentration, this body would have been shattered and destroyed.
Since this body is empty, the contemplation of water is also empty. It is thus identical to the true water of intrinsic emptiness, which pervades the entire Dharma-realm."
He has attained mastery. One who bears the name "Childlike Purity" (Kumārabhūta) is one who possesses the true virtues of a youth.

One who joins the assembly of Bodhisattvas has realized the dharma-emptiness of the Bodhisattva. That the nature of water flows freely means that he attained perfect penetration through the contemplation of water.
The Dharma Prince Vairocanaraśmiprabha rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I recall that in the past, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, a Buddha appeared in the world named Amitaghoṣa.

He revealed to the bodhisattvas the wondrous clarity of fundamental enlightenment, teaching them to contemplate this world and the bodies of sentient beings as all being driven by the power of the winds of delusive conditions. At that time, I...
At that time, I observed the establishment of the realms, the movement of the world, the motion and stillness of the body, and the stirring thoughts of the mind.
All these movements were non-dual and without distinction. I then realized the nature of this multitude of movements: they come from nowhere and go nowhere;
the motes of dust in the ten directions and the deluded sentient beings are all equally false. Thus it extends even to the three thousand [great thousandfold worlds].

Within this great trichiliocosm, all sentient beings were like hundreds of mosquitoes and gnats contained in a single vessel, chirping and clamoring in a chaotic din, creating a frantic tumult within a mere fraction of space.
Not long after encountering the Buddha, they attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

At that moment, their minds opened and they beheld the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya in the eastern direction; there they became Dharma-princes, serving the Buddhas of the ten directions with both body and mind.
"Radiant and penetrating, unimpeded. When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I realized the Bodhicitta by observing that the power of wind has no basis, thereby entering samādhi.
I unite with the Buddhas of the ten directions and transmit this one wondrous mind; this is the foremost."
This enters through the wind element (*vāyu-mahābhūta*). Because of his thorough and penetrating realization of this, he attained the name Vaidūrya (Lapis Lazuli).

The Buddha Immeasurable Sound (*Amitaghosa*) likewise harmonized with the wind element to reveal that fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is immovable, and that all movements within the realm of the body are driven by the power of the wind.
For this reason, Vaidūrya contemplated the realms and the world, contemplating the body and the mind; he saw that their flux, movement, and stillness are one and the same.
All the myriad movements within the great trichiliocosm are but empty delusions and frantic toil; they are like a hundred mosquitoes buzzing within the space of a single square inch.
Once one realizes this frantic toil, one beholds the Buddha of Immovability (*Aksobhya*).

The East is the head of all movement, yet the Buddha’s name is "Immovable"—this is stillness within movement. Because one can realize stillness within movement, body and mind are unimpeded. (From the *Chuan Yi*)
“Wondrous Mind” refers to the realization of unmoving original enlightenment (*amala-jñāna*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I and the Tathāgata attained the ‘Boundless Body’ at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the ten [directions].”

The Buddha-lands, as numerous as atoms, were transformed into empty space. Furthermore, within his own mind, he manifested a great circular mirror, from which ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights were emitted, flowing and permeating the ten directions to the very limits of empty space.

All the various sovereign lands of the banners entered into the mirror, merging into his body; his body became identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction, and was able to skillfully enter into lands as numerous as atoms.

I extensively performed Buddha-works and attained great accordance. This great supernormal power arose because I contemplated that the four elements have no basis, that conceptualization arises and ceases, that space is non-dual, and that Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same.
By illuminating this sameness, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied: "By contemplating the boundlessness of space, I entered *samādhi*. My wondrous power is perfect."
This is the first clarity.
It enters from the great element of space; its name is established according to its virtue, and thus it is called the "Space Treasury" (*Gaganagañja*). However, it is not a nihilistic void.
It can accommodate all skillful means for benefiting sentient beings; thus, the character "store" (zàng) is added. Dīpaṃkara Buddha is none other than Ratnārcis Buddha.
Because the essence of emptiness is boundless, one attains a boundless body. Within the ocean of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, there are four precious jewels.
It can exhaust the waters of the ocean; this is a metaphor for the Bodhisattva’s four wisdom-jewels, which can exhaust the waves within the ocean of nature.
To illuminate dust-like lands and transform empty space means that nature merges with phenomena.

When the mind and its objects emit light, drawing in all lands into one's own body without the body being obstructed, it is empty yet not empty—this is the Dharmakāya, whose body is identical to empty space.
The body enters into minute particles; this is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). To preach the Dharma of the Three Vehicles constitutes a Buddha-activity (*buddhakārya*).

To accord with the four *siddhāntas* is called "conformity. *Siddha* means "universal" (*vyāpta*); *anta* means "giving" (*dāna*). First, the *loka-siddhānta*: teaching according to different regions to produce the benefit of joy.
Second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*: producing the benefit of generating wholesome roots. Third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*... [text continues]

"Dāna" (giving) means the benefit of destroying evil. The four *paramārtha-siddhāntas* mean the benefit of entering into principle. From "This great [earth]" below, it concludes by returning to the fundamental cause.

This means that by contemplating the four elements, body and mind, and empty space and the Buddha-land as being equally illusory, one awakens to the fact that within this common manifestation, the nature is awakening which is true emptiness, and the nature is emptiness which is true awakening; therefore, it is as described above.
This is the Great Function. Its wondrous power is perfectly luminous; it points to the non-obstruction between emptiness and form, such that bodies and lands interpenetrate.
Bodhisattva Maitreya then rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "I recall the past."
After the passage of as many eons as there are atoms in a microdust, a Buddha appeared in the world named Candrasūryapradīpa. From that Buddha, I went forth into homelessness;

yet, my mind was heavy with worldly fame, and I delighted in frequenting the households of the noble clans. At that time, the World-Honored One instructed me to practice the samādhi of consciousness-only and enter into samāpatti.
Since those kalpas have passed, I have served Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges through this samādhi, seeking only worldly renown.
The mind ceased and vanished into non-existence. Upon the appearance of Dīpaṃkara Buddha in the world, I then attained the supreme, wondrous, and perfect samādhi of the conscious mind.
Even throughout the entirety of empty space, whether the lands of the Tathāgatas be pure or defiled, existent or non-existent, all are manifestations produced by the transformations of my own mind.
