World-Honored One, because I have realized that these are solely the consciousness of the mind, from the nature of this consciousness flows forth all things.
"Venerable Tathāgata, I have now received this prediction that I shall next succeed you in the Buddha’s place. When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I said:

'I have contemplated with clarity that the ten directions are nothing but consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*). The nature of consciousness is perfectly luminous, entering the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), far removed from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Thus I have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); this is the foremost.'"

This enters through the great element of consciousness. Maitreya—here called "The Compassionate One"—those whose minds value worldly fame are those who strive for empty reputation rather than earnest cultivation.
Those who delight in visiting noble families are those who do not turn inward but rush outward in pursuit.
Those who practice the concentration on mind-only consciousness are led to examine closely that all phenomena arise from mind-consciousness.

That which is transformed is not substantially real. "Seeking the mind of worldly names, it ceases and becomes non-existent" means that one knows the illusory objects of perception are unreal and the mind of names suddenly becomes empty;
this is single-minded internal contemplation. "Then lighting a lamp" refers to entering through awakening based on the perfection of contemplation.

The wondrous, perfect consciousness-mind is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. From "down to" [the following], it clarifies that one awakens to the fact that the purity and impurity of the vessel-world all arise from the transformations of consciousness, and thus should not be sought externally.
From "World-Honored One" [onward], it clarifies that all Buddhas flow forth from the nature of consciousness.

It does not arise through transformation by another. Regarding "next to fill the Buddha's place": this means that having attained the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), one is adjacent in rank to the Ultimate Sage.
After the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha has ceased, Maitreya shall immediately succeed Śākyamuni in this realm to perform his transformative work.

If one does not realize Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*), the mind turns away from itself and pursues external objects; if one understands Consciousness-Only, then objects are subsumed back into the mind. [Thus it is stated in] the Sūtras and Śāstras.
It carries the three natures: the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

"Perfected" means that the *dharmakāya* pervades all places; "perfected" (in the sense of realization) means that *prajñā* awakens to the untainted; and "real" refers to the virtue of liberation, which is unimpeded.
The "dependent" arises from conditions and refers to the phenomena that serve as objects of cognition. The "imagined" refers to pervasive conceptualization.

The mind that is capable of cognition is said to have the characteristic of dependent origination (paratantra) and to lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva). The imagined nature (parikalpita) exists in name only but lacks reality. One enters into the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna).
This is spoken of in terms of the qualities of the fruit; one attains the patience regarding non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), which is spoken of in terms of the stage of fruition.
The Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his same rank, rose from their seats, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I recall that in the past, during kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared a buddha in the world named Amitābha.
Twelve Tathāgatas succeeded one another for the duration of that kalpa; the last of these buddhas was named Sūryavairocanaprabhāsa.”

That Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha. It is like this: suppose there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another person who is single-mindedly forgetful.
Between these two people, they may meet and yet not meet, or see and yet not see. Because the two people remember each other, their mutual mindfulness is profound.
In this way, from birth to birth, they are like a form and its shadow, never at variance. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child.
If the child has fled and wandered away, though the mother remembers him, what can she do? But if the child remembers his mother...

Just as when a mother remembers her child, the mother and child do not remain estranged throughout their successive lives; so too, if sentient beings with sincere hearts remember the Buddha and recite his name, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and the future.
They will not be far from the Buddha, and without relying on expedient means, their own minds will naturally open.
Just as a person who has been perfumed with incense carries the fragrance on their body, this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light.

In my original stage of practice, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha; now, within this world, I gather those who mindfully recite the Buddha's name and lead them back to the Pure Land.

When the Buddha asked about the perfect penetration of the Way, I made no selection; I simply gathered all six sense faculties and maintained a continuous stream of pure mindfulness, thereby attaining samādhi—this is the foremost method.
This Bodhisattva entered [the womb] by means of seeing the Great; he is Mahāsthāmaprāpta, also known as Amitābha.

Because his light of wisdom universally illuminates all things, causing them to leave the three evil realms and attain supreme power, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. This is the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nien-fo san-mei*).
If we rely on the perspective of principle (*li*), "mindfulness" (*nian*) refers to initial enlightenment (*shijue*), while "Buddha" refers to original enlightenment (*benjue*).

If we rely on the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), "mindfulness" refers to the act of darkly recording and not forgetting, while "Buddha" refers to emitting light to guide and receive others; thus, that which is mindful belongs to oneself, while that which is the object of mindfulness belongs to the Buddha.
One person who exclusively remembers is a metaphor for the Buddha mindful of sentient beings; one person who exclusively forgets is a metaphor for sentient beings.
Sentient beings do not mindfully recollect the Buddha, whereas the Buddha constantly and exclusively minds sentient beings; thus, he is never absent from before them.

Therefore, whether they encounter him or see him, it is because sentient beings do not mindfully recollect the Buddha that, although the Buddha is indeed before them, they neither encounter nor see him.
If it is like the mutual remembrance between mother and child, then they shall never be separated. The three phrases concerning the ten directions correspond to one person who remembers exclusively;

the two phrases concerning the child correspond to one person who forgets exclusively. If the child [remembers] according to the four phrases, it corresponds to two people remembering so that they are not parted.
"One who is not far from the Buddha" means constantly drawing near to the Buddha; "one who has personally attained the opening of the mind" means seeing the Buddha within one's own body.
This means that once one has attained the vision of Amitābha, there is no longer any worry about failing to achieve awakening. By drawing near to fragrance, the body likewise becomes fragrant;

by drawing near to the Buddha, the mind likewise becomes a Buddha. Regarding "adorned with fragrant light," it means that through the fragrant light of the Buddha’s body, one adorns the Buddha of one's own nature (*svabhāva-buddha*).
Regarding "completely gathering the six sense faculties," it means that when one recollects the Buddha with single-mindedness, all six faculties [are likewise gathered].

Mindfulness of the Buddha: when the eye does not grasp at forms, this is mindfulness of the Buddha through the eye; and so on, until when the mind does not grasp at dharmas, this is mindfulness of the Buddha through the mind.
Because all six sense faculties are thus fully gathered, pure mindfulness is attained in uninterrupted succession. Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta are both assistants to Amitābha;
one welcomes beings through mindfulness of the Buddha, while the other instructs the multitude through the practice of Chan meditation. Both follow this very path.

The realms, faculties, and capacities each have their own distinct openings. When questioning those who practice Chan, one must not only allow for the arising of views regarding a self, persons, sentient beings, or a life-span;
even views of a Buddha or views of the Dharma are not permitted to arise. This sutra denounces the arousal of the mind based on characteristics of views as being birth-and-death;
the *Vajracchedikā* rebukes seeking form through sound and viewing through sight as a deviant path. As for those who practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, their resolve lies in...
Pure mindfulness succeeds one another; in the present and in the future, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. The two gates of Emptiness and Existence are utterly distinct.
To those who practice Chan meditation, their resolve lies in the obliteration of all marks; therefore, they cannot allow a thought to arise, and both good and evil are completely swept away.
For those who practice Buddha-recitation, their resolve lies in being received and guided by the Buddha; they must maintain pure mindfulness succeeding one another at every turn.
To see the Buddha, one must first be able to sweep away all [defilements]; only then can one realize one’s nature. Once one has realized one’s nature, what difficulty is there in seeing the Buddha?
Furthermore, by maintaining pure mindfulness in uninterrupted succession, one will certainly be able to see the Buddha; once one has seen the Buddha, it is likewise easy to realize one’s nature.

Only those who realize the wondrous existence [of phenomena] are those who truly understand emptiness; only those who perceive true emptiness are those who truly understand the wondrous existence of phenomena.
Although there are two gates, their ultimate convergence is one. Generally speaking, among the twenty-five gates, the six sense objects should begin with form (*rūpa*);
yet here they begin with sound (*śabda*). As for why the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*) is placed last, it is because within this True Dharma-body, purity resides in sound.
This reveals the essential framework of the teaching’s substance. Although the seven elements (mahābhūta) should begin with the earth element, fire is placed first because lust invites fire;
thus, this scripture begins its teaching by addressing the downfall of lust, warning those of great learning to first eliminate the outflow of desire.
Although the seven elements should end with the consciousness element, they conclude with the seeing element, because [of the power of] Śrīmatī...
The *Nianfo* (Buddha-remembrance) method of perfect penetration ranks slightly below that of Avalokiteśvara.

What is called "gathering those who recite the Buddha’s name and returning them to the Pure Land" is a vow and a fundamental practice of saving oneself and others; it is originally the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*).
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Five. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the sixth fascicle:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, I recall that in the past, incalculable kalpas ago as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there appeared in the world a Buddha named..."
Avalokiteśvara, I awakened the bodhicitta under that Buddha. That Buddha taught me to enter samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation.
This dharma-gate of the ear-faculty extensively sets forth its merits, manifesting its supreme and perfect penetration. Thus is Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding the title "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World), which signifies perfect awakening and perfect response: the term "observes" (*avalokita*) refers to illuminating [reality] with the wisdom of observation.
It reveals the principle that the six sense faculties function interchangeably. The Buddha whom he takes as his teacher is likewise named Avalokiteśvara.

Cause and effect correspond; this is the single path throughout antiquity and the present. The word "hearing" refers to the nature of hearing that is neither born nor extinguished, as verified by the striking of a bell.
"Contemplation" does not mean thinking of good or evil; it is the correct contemplation of non-thinking.
Focus intently on the nature of hearing and investigate from where this faculty originates, thereby rectifying that inverted auditory mechanism.
Detaching from external attachments and turning inward to rest is the sharp tool for uprooting the source and the vanguard in severing the knots.

From the initial entry into the flow until its manifestation before one, all progress toward deep penetration relies upon this contemplation. For the practitioner, this is not a cultivation consisting of contrived effort or ritual action.

However, when one realizes that all phenomena are like illusions and understands them to be without foundation, such that no grasping or attachment arises, then all subtle defilements will naturally dissolve away and the nature of awakening will manifest before one;
this is called "right cultivation. To "enter" means to have already arrived at this state.
As for *samādhi*, it is precisely the aforementioned Great Dharani-gate; that is to say, by extracting this single root, one immediately gains entry into the Great Dharani-gate.
Question: In the first fascicle, you already refuted that thought (*cintā*) is false.
Why, then, do you employ this thought here again? Answer: The reason it was refuted previously was because Ānanda took this thought to be real. It was not...
To be willing to let it go is to mistake a thief for one’s own son; therefore, it must be refuted and destroyed so that one may recognize the thief and seek out the true son.
To employ this very thought again is to know it to be a thief, yet to borrow the thief in order to kill the thief.

This is to transform calamity into merit. Furthermore, although the gates through which the twenty-four sages practiced were different, when one examines their application of mind, they all employed this very contemplation.
Without this contemplation, there would be no place to begin.
Therefore, the foundational practice of all twenty-four sages is manifested within the single gate of Avalokiteśvara.

At the beginning, within the realm of hearing, one enters the stream and causes the object of hearing to vanish. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise.

As this gradually increases, both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted. When hearing is exhausted, one does not dwell therein; when the awareness of what is perceived is empty, the emptiness of that awareness becomes perfectly complete.
"Emptiness and that which is emptied both cease; when arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests.
This describes the beginning and end of entering contemplation. "Initially, within hearing" refers to the very nature of hearing. It means:
"I initially took the nature of hearing as the object of contemplation, and finally took the nature of hearing as the gateway through which I enter."
The character "flow" (liú) refers to the flow of desire. The character "enter" (rù) refers to the character "reverse. To follow [the flow] is to establish an object based on clarity;
to enter [the reverse] is for the object to naturally vanish. The effort of making the object vanish is simply like an illusion.

To be oblivious to this illusion and flow outward toward the dust of the world is to establish an object. To recognize this as an illusion and still the mechanism of the mind to return to quiescence is to let the object vanish.

The "object entered" is precisely the flow. "Quiescence" means the absence of an object. Because the faculty that enters [the object] flows against the current, the dust (objects) that is entered becomes quiescent.
Not only do the marks of movement not arise, but even the marks of stillness do not arise.
This is to separate the nature of hearing from the dust, so that they do not weave together to form delusion. This is what is called "wondrous within clarity."

Thus it gradually increases until that which is heard and the hearing itself are exhausted; this faculty is like an illusion. This gradual increase is precisely the Illusion-like Samādhi, becoming even more refined and lucid.
"Hearing" refers to the faculty of hearing, and "that which is heard" refers to the two characteristics of movement and stillness.
Because the preceding faculties and objects were intertwined, one now turns the inverted faculty of hearing back toward its own nature so as not to interact with external objects.
Now, although external objects have been relinquished and the auditory faculty has been stilled, one has not yet attained ultimate purity; therefore, next, one exhausts the internal faculties.

This means that when this faculty first resolves, one first attains the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). When the hearing is exhausted and does not abide, the perceived and the perceiver are both empty; this perception is like an illusion.
When the sphere of hearing is exhausted, it may be called the profound stillness of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); yet, one merely abides in this awakening.
These marks are still attachments to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Now, by not abiding in this wisdom, both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are both empty.

This is what is called the perfect clarity of emptiness-nature, which constitutes liberation from phenomena. When the awareness of emptiness is utterly perfected, the emptiness of that which was emptied is extinguished;
this emptiness is like an illusion. The awareness of emptiness is precisely the awareness that the object perceived is empty. This state has already severed the views and activities of phenomena.
[The practitioner] maintains this focus; however, as they have not yet reached the stage of ultimate perfection, the mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*) still remains.

From this point, one cultivates until reaching the state of supreme fulfillment, where both the subject that empowers emptiness (*śūnyatā-vidhāyaka*) and the object that is emptied (*śūnya-vastu*) are entirely extinguished. This is what is called the "Dharma of liberation": when both are empty, nothing arises.
Since birth and cessation have been extinguished, quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) manifests before one. There is no further effort to be made; thus it is said at the beginning.
Entering the stream causes the objects to vanish; the objects are empty. Yet the sense-faculties still remain. The faculties are themselves objects; the faculties are empty.

Yet the wisdom that perceives the emptiness of the faculties remains. This wisdom is itself an object; the wisdom is empty. Yet the emptiness that perceives the emptiness of wisdom remains. This emptiness is itself an object.
All of these do not transcend the evolving consciousness of birth and death. Only when even the emptiness of objects is extinguished does one reach the cessation of birth and death.
All is extinguished. As all delusions vanish, what need is there for anything that is not true? The great ocean of quiescent extinction naturally manifests before one.
This quiescence is not a quiescence opposed to movement; this extinction is not an extinction opposed to arising. It is the quiescence of immobility and the extinction of non-arising;
it is the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, the reality-limit of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is primordially pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm.
It is named the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction. When this principle manifests, the mountains, rivers, and great earth before one transform in an instant into supreme enlightened awareness.
All the various sublime functions below are issued forth from this.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one attains universal clarity throughout the ten directions and achieves two kinds of extraordinary excellence:
first, above, one harmonizes with the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind of all Buddhas of the ten directions, sharing the same compassionate power as the Buddha-Tathāgatas;
second, below, one harmonizes with all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions, sharing the same sorrowful longing.
Not being bound by that which exists within the realms is to transcend the mundane world; not being bound by the emptiness beyond the realms is to transcend the supramundane.

That the ten directions are perfectly luminous is the meaning of stillness and illumination encompassing all space. These "ten directions" do not stop at the trichiliocosm; they may also be understood as the ten dharma-realms.
Because this is something the followers of the two vehicles cannot attain, it is called "extraordinary and supreme. Mind and Buddha...
Sentient beings [and Buddhas] are non-different in three respects; therefore, when one realizes one's own mind, one immediately merges with the birth of a Buddha.

Because compassion can transform those below, it is called the "power of compassion. Below the phrase "sentient beings of the six realms," there should be the four characters "original wondrous enlightened mind" (*ben miao jue xin*).

This is not merely for the sake of emphasis. Both compassion (*karuṇā*) and reliance (*āśraya*) pertain to sentient beings. As for "compassion," it is to feel pity for one's own immersion in saṃsāra; as for "reliance," it is to look up to the Buddha for deliverance.
When sentient beings feel compassion, the Bodhisattva shares that same compassion with them; when sentient beings rely [on the Buddha], the Bodhisattva shares that same reliance with them.
The thirty-two manifestations demonstrate the shared power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), while the fourteen fearlessnesses demonstrate the shared compassion and reliance.
World-Honored One, because I made offerings to the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara,
I was granted by that Tathāgata the Vajra Samādhi of the Illusory-like Cultivation of Hearing through Hearing. Since I share the same power of compassion as the Buddhas and Tathāgatas,
my body has become capable of thirty-two manifestations to enter all lands.
All phenomena are illusory; they are but this single mind. The object of sound is fundamentally empty, yet the nature of hearing is eternally present.
Within this eternal presence, all sounds and all phenomena are entirely like illusions. By means of this dharma-gate of illusion-like reality, [one realizes the truth].
It begins with permeation through hearing and culminates in cultivation and realization through hearing. Functioning in accordance with conditions, its fundamental substance is suchness (*tathatā*):
unmoving, unshakable, undiminished, and indestructible. This samādhi is called the "Illusion-like Samādhi of Hearing and Cultivating through Hearing";
it is the Vajra Samādhi and the very foundation of the thirty-two manifestations.

“World-Honored One, if there are bodhisattvas who have entered samādhi, are progressing in the cultivation of the untainted (anāsrava), and whose resolute understanding (adhimukti) is fully manifested, I manifest the body of a Buddha before them and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training (śaikṣa) whose tranquil, wondrous clarity and sublime excellence are fully manifested, I appear before them in the form of a Pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation. If there are...”
As for those in training (*śaikṣa*) who sever the twelve links of dependent origination, through the excellence of the severance of conditions, their supreme nature manifests in perfection.
Before them, I manifest in the body of a pratyekabuddha and preach the Dharma to cause them to attain liberation.

If there are those in training who realize the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths and enter cessation through the path of cultivation, such that their supreme nature manifests in perfection, before them I manifest in the body of a śrāvaka and preach the Dharma to cause them to attain liberation.
This is the wisdom of realization that arises when ordinary bodhisattvas who aspire to the excellence of the Buddha-body have reached the ultimate limit of their practice.
Question: Why would a Bodhisattva on the level of Equal Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi) temporarily manifest as a Buddha in the first stage (Prathamā-bhūmi) to preach the Dharma?
Answer: By hearing the Dharma, one attains understanding as if not seeking it from another; furthermore, by assuming this superior body, one further increases internal wisdom.
Moreover, as for Avalokiteśvara, he harmonizes upward with all Buddhas; his realization is not shallow. How could it be limited to merely the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*)?

Appearing in worlds where no Buddha exists, he observes the transformation of phenomena and personally realizes non-arising, thus being called a Pratyekabuddha. Delighting in solitary, sublime tranquility, he seeks natural wisdom;
hence he is described as "sublime clarity within tranquil stillness. Having been perfumed by the Buddha’s minor teachings over many lifetimes, he shall pass through seven...

Upon birth, they realize the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). They manifest bodies of their own kind; first, they follow their original habitual tendencies, and later, they cause them to draw near to the Buddha.

[The following is] the same as below. Receiving the Buddha’s teaching, they contemplate conditions and awaken to the Way; thus they are called *pratyekabuddhas*. Knowing that delusion regarding the supreme nature arises from the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), they awaken.

When all [conditioned things] are severed, the supreme nature (*paramārtha*) manifests; hence it is said that "the supreme nature is realized through the severance of conditions. This supreme nature is the very nature of the non-arising of causes and conditions;

it is merely the *nirvāṇa* of the "transformed city" (*pariṇāmika-nirvāṇa*). By severing the delusions regarding the Four Noble Truths, one realizes the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

This is called attaining the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths, severing the innate afflictions, and realizing the principle of the Truth of Cessation; it is called entering cessation through the Path of Cultivation.
If there are sentient beings who desire clear and enlightened understanding, who do not transgress against the dust of desire, and whose bodies and desires are pure, before them I [manifest].
I manifest in the form of Brahmā King and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to attain liberation.

If there are sentient beings who wish to become lords of heaven and exercise authority over the celestial realms, I manifest before them in the form of Śakra and preach the Dharma, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to travel throughout the ten directions, I appear before them in the form of Īśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal.

If there are sentient beings who desire bodily mastery to fly through the void, I appear before them in the form of Maheśvara and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve their goal. If...

To those sentient beings who love to preside over spirits and deities and protect their lands, I appear before them in the form of a Great Heavenly General and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.

To those sentient beings who love to govern the world and protect all living beings, I appear before them in the form of one of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment. If there are... [and so forth].
There are sentient beings who, out of craving, seek rebirth in celestial palaces and command spirits and deities.
Before them, I manifest the body of a prince in the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
It corresponds to the Way of Heaven. The two characters for "desire" (欲) refer to the desire of the mind and the desire of the body; this is the explanation of the character for "joy" (樂).

That is to say, the joy of the mind is clear awakening, and the body is pure. Because the dust of desire exists, it obstructs the gate of awakening; the mind is not clear, and the body is likewise defiled.
Therefore, one should take joy in not transgressing the dust of desire. Brahmā, the Lord of the Form Realm, preached the Dharma as if explaining the transcendence of desire.

This is the treatise. Liberation (*vimukti*) refers to being born in the Brahma realms through the abandonment of desire. Śakra is the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), who horizontally presides over the thirty-two heavens; he is the sovereign of these.

His preaching of the Dharma is, for example, like the teaching of the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*). The heavens of the Desire Realm belong entirely to the category of scattered goodness (*vicitra-kuśala*);
Bodhisattvas, in accordance with this, achieve the bliss of birth in the heavens. The same applies below. Maheśvara is... [text ends]... that is to say:

Regarding those who, at the summit of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), cultivate the meditative absorption of the desire realm: this refers to Maheśvara. Regarding those who, at the summit of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), cultivate untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*):
they travel throughout the ten directions; these ten directions refer to the ten directions of the six heavens of the desire realm and the four continents.

Flying through the void, they are able to reach other realms, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "They can pass through five hundred million *koṭi* of lands" while seeking out Buddhas to make offerings. These are the devas.
The Great General is the supreme commander of Śakra, who leads the ghosts and spirits; "Protector" means one who subdues demons and protects living beings.
The Four Heavenly Kings govern the four continents, the world, and all lands on the four sides of Mount Sumeru on behalf of Śakra.
The Princes of the Four Heavens are of the same class as Nāṭa; they are capable of driving away ghosts and spirits.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being rulers of men, I manifest before them in the form of a human king and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve their goal.
If there are sentient beings who love to be leaders of clans, esteemed and honored by the world, I manifest before them...
I manifest in the body of an elder and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who delight in discussing names and phrases and dwell in purity, I manifest before them in the body of a layman and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.

If there are sentient beings who love to govern territories and adjudicate the affairs of states and districts, I manifest before them in the body of a high official and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
If there are sentient beings who love various arts and techniques to protect and maintain themselves, [I likewise manifest before them].
Before them, I manifest in the body of a brāhmaṇa and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

If there is a man who delights in study and leaves the household life, upholding the various precepts and rules, before him I manifest in the body of a bhikṣu and preach the Dharma for him, causing him to achieve success.
If there is a woman who delights in study and leaves the household life, upholding the various prohibitions and precepts, before her I—
Before some, I manifest in the body of a bhikṣuṇī and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are men who delight in upholding the five precepts, I manifest before them in the body of an upāsaka and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are women who abide by the five precepts, I manifest before them in the body of an upāsikā and preach the Dharma for them.

To cause them to achieve success: if there are women who manage internal affairs and establish themselves through the cultivation of their households and states, I shall appear before them in the form of a queen, a state lady, a titled consort, or a great matron, and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.
If there are sentient beings whose male organs are not impaired, I manifest before them in the form of a young boy and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve accomplishment.
If there are virgins who delight in remaining chaste and do not seek sexual assault, I manifest before them.
He manifests in the form of a young maiden and preaches the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.

Regarding those who correspond to the human realm, from the Wheel-Turning Kings down to the Minor Kings, all are rulers of men. As for "Minor Kings," these are the sovereigns of individual states and nations.
They were scattered throughout the world as numerous as grains of millet. Possessing these ten virtues, he became an elder (*śreṣṭhin*):

his lineage was noble, his rank was high, he was immensely wealthy, majestic and powerful, possessed profound wisdom, advanced in years, pure in conduct, complete in ritual propriety, praised by those above and venerated by those below; thus, even those who had been submerged in worldly life were led to refrain from serving in office.

They are called lay devotees (*gṛhapati*). Some discourse on the Way and discuss virtue, serving as teachers and models for others; some compose books and establish teachings to bequeath to future generations.

They love governing their territories as if establishing the fundamental social constants; they rectify customs and transformations. In adjudicating matters within their districts, they are like those who settle lawsuits with a single phrase or resolve disputes with a single word.
Ministers of the Three Dukes, high officials, governors of provinces, and magistrates of counties are all termed "officials" (*zhāiguān*).

"Brahmin" (婆羅門) is here translated as "Pure Conduct" (淨行); it is one of the four castes. "Arithmetic and Arts" (數術) refers to the categories of harmonizing, divination, physiognomy, and calendrical calculation.

"Preservation and Regulation" (攝衛) means the nurturing and protection of the body and life, referring specifically to physicians. All these ranks are brought about by the Five Precepts and the Five Constant Virtues.
Depending on the breadth or narrowness of one's mind, retribution divides them into the roles of ruler and subject. When benevolence covers a single family, one becomes a "One" (a leader).
Householder, you cover the entire nation with benevolence and serve as its leader; you delight in being a sovereign, possessing virtue and embracing humanity, and cannot bear the chaos of the world.
You have made a vow to be a ruler of the Way in every lifetime to govern the state through principle.

When a Bodhisattva manifests in such a form, he explains to you the causes for birth into noble status and the virtuous achievements of emperors and kings—just as practicing the ten wholesome deeds leads to becoming a Wheel-Turning King.
It is for this reason. If an ordinary person were to harbor deluded ambitions for the imperial throne, would he ever achieve it? Other cases are to be understood by analogy.

The *bhikṣu* precepts number two hundred and fifty; those of the *bhikṣuṇī* are double that. What the *bhikṣu* maintains consists merely of the constant rules (*dharmas*), whereas the prohibitions for the *bhikṣuṇī* are more stringent.
As for the *upāsaka* and *upāsikā*, these are the five precepts for laypeople who serve the Buddha-dharma closely.
The Son of Heaven, the high dukes, and the ministers manage external affairs; the Queen, the consorts, and the palace ladies manage internal affairs.
Thus they cultivate and govern the state. The "Female Ruler" refers to the Queen and the consorts. The "State Lady" (*guó fūrén*) is the wife of a regional lord.

The "Ennobled Ladies" (*mìng fù*) are those who received titles and gifts based on the honor of their husbands. The "Great Ladies" (*dà jiā*) are the teachers among the inner nobility, such as the Consorts of King Huì of Han, each [holding her respective office].
To those who possess the virtues of benevolence, filial piety, gentleness, and kindness,

if there are among them those from the celestial realms who wish to descend from their heavenly status, I manifest a celestial body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve fulfillment.
If there are nāgas who wish to leave their nāga status, I manifest in a nāga body and preach the Dharma for them, enabling them to achieve success.
If there are yakṣas who wish to transcend their own kind, I appear before them in a yakṣa body and preach the Dharma for them.

I cause them to achieve success. If there are gandharvas who wish to be liberated from their class, I manifest before them in the body of a gandharva and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success.

If there are asuras who wish to be liberated from their class, I manifest before them in the body of an asura and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve success. If there are kinnaras who wish to be liberated...
For those of that class, I manifest before them in the form of a kinnara and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve success.
If there are mahoragas who wish to be liberated from their class, I manifest before them in the form of a mahoraga and preach the Dharma to them, causing them to achieve success.
If there are sentient beings who delight in being humans or in practicing as humans, I manifest in human form for them and...

I preach the Dharma to cause them to achieve accomplishment. If there are non-human beings—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—who delight in delivering their own kind, I manifest my body before them all and preach the Dharma for them, causing them to achieve accomplishment.

This refers to the eight classes of beings. As for the "heaven," it is the first heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Since the retribution of this heaven consists solely of pleasure, why would one seek to depart from it?

Because of being addicted to and immersed in desire, when that retribution ends, one returns to suffering. While the former heavens seek to obtain [pleasure], this heaven seeks to attain liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
Regarding those who manifest as dragon bodies, they are like Nāgārjuna, who transformed five hundred dragons so that they all received the full precepts (*upasaṃpadā*), and other such instances.
Yakṣa: translated here as "light and swift. There are three kinds: those on the earth, those in the void, and those in heaven.
Gandharva: translated here as "fragrance-seeking aggregates," the musical deities of Śakra. Asura: translated here as "non-gods."
Because they lack the practice of the heavens (*deva-caryā*). The *kiṃnara* have forms resembling humans but with horns on their heads;

they are called "doubtful deities" (*saṃśaya-deva*) and are the musical deities of Śakra. The *mahoraga* are great serpent deities (*mahā-bhujaga*), such as the Venerable Kapi, who received the Three Refuges while in the form of a serpent.
Having finished listening, [the deity] manifested the body of an old man, dressed in plain white robes, and departed. The *yakṣas* and others of the seven realms of existence are all...
Those who possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), merit, and authority each have their own sufferings; thus, they are all equally termed "evil destinies" (*durgati*).

Therefore, one desires to escape from them. A sutra says: "The various devas often think to themselves: 'May we obtain a human body and be born within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Tathāgata to receive the bhikṣu precepts.
The previous statement regarding "escaping" did not specify where one would joyfully be reborn. Now it is said:

Regarding "delighting people": this refers to those born in the human realm who wish to cultivate [the Way]. As for the various non-humans (*amanuṣya*), there are those with form, such as those possessing the clarity of auspicious or inauspicious portents;
those without form, such as those that are dispersed or dissolved in space; those with thought, such as ghosts, spirits, and numinous essences;
and those without thought, such as when the spirit transforms into earth, gold, or stone. These six classes of ordinary beings are not enumerated here under the category of "ground."

Regarding those in the hells: they are currently submerged in profound darkness and have not yet been able to hear the Dharma. Therefore, one must specifically rescue them by employing the power of bestowing fearlessness.
In preaching the Dharma, first, one teaches the transcendent and excellent dharmas, enabling them to practice so that they may immediately transcend their current state.

Second, one explains their past karmic actions, enabling them to sever these so that they do not enter such states again. For devas, this means severing the mind that seeks existence; for nāgas, it means severing anger. [This applies to] medicinal herbs...
The *Artha* spirits eliminate killing; the *Gandharvas* eliminate frivolous play; the *Asuras* eliminate contention; the *Kiṃnaras* eliminate flattery;
the *Mahoragas* eliminate delusion; and the *Vicitracārin* spirits eliminate false views.

This is called the thirty-two kinds of wondrously pure bodies that enter various lands. All are accomplished through mastery by means of samādhi, the power of non-action, and the cultivation of hearing and the permeation of hearing.
The mind is like the ocean; all bodies are like the patterns on the ocean’s surface. They appear when conditions arrive, yet they come from nowhere;
they vanish when conditions cease, yet they go nowhere. Unobstructed and unhindered, they are called the response of wondrous purity.
Relying on non-action, they give rise to great spiritual efficacy, which is named the Wondrous Power of Non-Action.
World-Honored One, by means of this power of the non-conditioned wondrous efficacy of the Vajra Samādhi— perfumed and cultivated through hearing—
I share in the same compassionate longing with all sentient beings of the ten directions, the three periods of time, and the six realms. Thus,
I cause all sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of meritorious qualities of fearlessness within my body and mind.
The fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are based on the previously mentioned samādhis such as the permeation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*); therefore, the word "furthermore" (*fu*) is used.

To speak of them exclusively in relation to the six classes of ordinary beings (*ṣaḍ-gati*) and not including the four types of noble ones (*ārya*) is because those of superior goodness do not share in the hardships of evil.
As for "fearlessness," it refers to encountering hardship and dread, yet receiving rescue and attaining liberation from it.
First, because I do not observe myself by means of an observing subject, I cause those suffering sentient beings of the ten directions to observe my voice and thereby attain liberation.

Regarding the contemplation of the Bodhisattva’s voice: when one is pressed by manifold sufferings and urgently invokes the Bodhisattva’s name, this single utterance is produced in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
When the whole reality manifests before one, suffering is liberated of its own accord without being sought.

The "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭau durgatayaḥ*) constitute the general category, while the following seven are the specific instances. The word "self" (*zi*) here means "alone. When ordinary people listen to a sound, they merely contemplate the sound itself.
Now, it is not only Avalokiteśvara who is observed; one further observes the one capable of observing him.

Thus, by reversing the auditory faculty that is prone to inversion and turning back to contemplate one's own nature (*svabhāva*), one realizes that all delusions are non-existent and there is only this single truth. Since even pleasure cannot be found, what suffering or affliction could there be?
This is what is meant by "perceiving that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, and thereby crossing over all suffering and calamity. By means of this—
Through the empowerment of their supernormal powers, sentient beings hear the sound of the Bodhisattvas' holy names;

they contemplate them with a single mind, focusing intently without distraction, and thereby attain liberation from suffering and affliction. "Contemplation" refers to the practice of recitation and possesses two meanings:
first, contemplating through the phenomenal aspect by single-mindedly holding the name, whereby one attains liberation from worldly suffering and affliction.

Thus one attains peace and stability. Furthermore, through contemplation based on principle (*li*), one turns the hearing back toward one's own nature (*xing*), thereby liberating oneself from the suffering and afflictions of the triple world and attaining *nirvāṇa*.
This differs from the *Lotus Sūtra*; the latter belongs to the contemplation of bodhisattvas, while this belongs to the contemplation of sentient beings.

For sentient beings to be liberated from suffering, there must be both causes and conditions. The sentient being’s own willingness (*ken*) serves as the cause, while the great compassion of the bodhisattva [serves as the condition].
It serves as a condition. Where causes and conditions converge, one is immediately able to be liberated from suffering.

The Bodhisattva’s great compassion is equal and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, constantly acting as a sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings. If sentient beings can achieve even a single moment of resonance with this, they will directly transcend suffering.
As for those who now recite the name yet do not receive liberation, it is simply because they have not attained that single moment of resonance.
Second, by reversing and returning the faculty of seeing, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter a great fire, the fire cannot burn them.
Third, by reversing and returning the faculties of hearing and listening, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they are swept away by a great flood, the water cannot drown them.

Fourth, by severing and extinguishing deluded thoughts so that the mind is free from killing or harming, one causes all sentient beings such that even if they enter the realms of ghosts, the ghosts cannot harm them. Fifth...
Through the perfuming of hearing, one achieves true hearing; the six faculties are dissolved and restored, becoming identical to the act of listening to sound.

This can cause sentient beings who are about to be harmed to have their weapons broken into pieces as they strike them, so that their arms and spears are like cutting through water or blowing across light—their nature remains unshakable.
Sixth: When the brilliance of hearing-perfuming becomes clear and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, then all dark obscurations are inherently unable to prevail.
This enables sentient beings such as yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and pūtanas to be unable to look even when they draw near its side.
Seventh: When the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of seeing and hearing turn back into themselves, one departs from all sensory dusts and delusions.
Eighth: By extinguishing sound and perfecting hearing, one universally generates the power of compassion, enabling sentient beings to pass through perilous paths without being plundered by bandits.
This causes sentient beings to be unable to be bound by shackles or fetters.
The four great elements of the internal and external are constantly interacting and responding with one another. Vision and cognition belong to fire; hearing and listening belong to water.

When the activity of vision interacts, one perceives fierce flames; when the activity of hearing interacts, one perceives surging waves. Now, if one knows that vision has revolved and returned to its source, there is no longer the karma of seeing;
if one contemplates that hearing has revolved and returned to its source, there is no longer the karma of hearing. Therefore, water and fire cannot burn or drown you. Regarding hearing—

The term "guān" (觀) is pronounced as "yánguān" (音言觀). Originally, it arose from the four great elements being divided; now that they have been rotated back into a single unity, there is no longer any appearance of sensory objects (*dharmas*).

Therefore, water and fire cannot cause harm. Question: Regarding the rotation of seeing and the rotation of hearing, how does a Bodhisattva assist sentient beings so as to enable them to escape the calamities of water and fire?
Answer: By means of the surplus power remaining after their own self-benefit, [the Bodhisattva] adds [this grace].
The compassionate vows and majestic spiritual power [of the Bodhisattvas] are inconceivable; yet, one must invoke their names with earnest mindfulness, reform one’s errors, and turn toward the good.

Only then will the Bodhisattvas seek out the sound [of the invocation] and deliver one from suffering. The same applies to the following cases. Delusory thoughts arise and perish; they can destroy the Dharma-body and harm the life of wisdom.
Since these [delusions] can be severed and extinguished, the true nature remains unharmed; therefore, sentient beings cannot be harmed by ghosts.
To slay it is to possess a body. By perfuming false hearing until it becomes true hearing, the physical form dissolves and merges with sound;
there is no dust to confront, and nothing at all can be touched. Thus, it is like cutting water where the water leaves no trace, or blowing upon light where the light remains unmoved.

When the practice of "returning the hearing" reaches its ultimate, the original radiance is revealed. This radiance is capable of destroying darkness; even the subtle, hidden vapors of ghosts and spirits [are likewise dispelled].

How could they possibly cause harm? Rākṣasas, fearsome ghosts, kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, piśācas, spirits that devour vital energy, pūtanas, and spirits of fever—all these are entangled by the dust of worldly defilements as if bound in confinement; their six sense-faculties are obstructed by materiality.
Like shackles and chains, when both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are eliminated, one is internally unburdened and externally unbound.
"The sound ceases" means liberation from the dust of auditory objects; "perfect hearing" (*yuanwen*) signifies the realization of the nature of the faculty.

When the internal and external are harmoniously integrated into a single essence, one gives rise to the power of compassion throughout all places, such that no one again harbors malicious intent toward another. Thus, one attains fearlessness regarding the aforementioned eight difficulties.
Ninth: When the cultivation of hearing leaves behind sensory objects, it cannot be plundered by forms; this can cause all beings with excessive lust to distance themselves from greedy desire. Tenth:
When pure sound is free from dust, the faculties and their objects are perfectly integrated, such that there is neither subject nor object;
this can cause all beings filled with anger and resentment to abandon all hatred. Eleventh: When dust is dissolved and clarity turns back, the dharma-realm, body, and mind are as...

Like lapis lazuli, it is luminous, penetrating, and unobstructed; it enables all those of dull and obtuse nature, all those with the obstruction of ignorance (*ātyantika*), to forever leave behind the darkness of delusion.
Greed arises from the favorability of sensory objects, anger and resentment from their unfavorability, and delusion from their obscuration. [Through this wisdom, one] becomes free from them.

When the dust of sensory objects is without opposition, and both compliance and resistance are forgotten, the dust dissolves and clarity turns inward; body and mind become luminously transparent, and the three poisons are forever dispelled.

*Adīnaka*—translated here as "lacking a virtuous mind"—refers to those for whom delusion is most heavy. The ten karmic paths are all destroyed within the Dharma-body, yet lust, anger, and delusion are the most severe.
These three are cited to encompass the rest. One fears the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), for they manifest as the bitter fruits of suffering.
The three poisons fear that they will inevitably become the cause of suffering; therefore, they all seek liberation.

Twelfth: Merging his form, he further hears that from the Immovable Bodhimanda, he enters into the mundane world without destroying the worlds, able to pervade the ten directions and make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust in every Buddha-field, becoming a Dharma Prince at the side of each and every Buddha. He is able to...
For those beings within the *dharmadhātu* who are childless and desire a son, may they give birth to a son of merit and wisdom. Thirteenth:
the six sense faculties are perfectly penetrating and luminously clear, non-dual, and encompassing the worlds of the ten directions.

Establishing the Great Perfect Mirror, the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, one receives and upholds without loss the secret *dharmaparyāyas* of the Buddhas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, and is able to cause—

Within the Dharma-realm there are no children; yet for those who desire a daughter—one who is upright and beautiful, endowed with merit and gentleness, beloved and respected by all, and possessed of auspicious marks—[she shall be born].

This enables sentient beings to attain fearlessness regarding their two kinds of seeking. When form is melted away, obstruction ceases; when one further hears [the Dharma], the nature is revealed as true.
Thus, one engages with the mundane world without movement or decay, able to make offerings to Buddhas as numerous as atoms throughout the ten directions.
Having received and inherited his Dharma, each becomes a son of the Dharma. By making offerings to the Buddha, they possess sufficient merit; by inheriting the Dharma, they possess sufficient wisdom.

Being endowed with the virtues of a man, they are thus able to respond to the request as men of merit and wisdom. Because it is perfect, it is luminously radiant; because it is pervasive, it encompasses all realms.
Luminous radiance is the substance of great perfect wisdom; encompassing all realms is the essence of the empty Tathāgatagarbha. Therefore...

She was able to uphold and follow the Dharma-gate, receiving and retaining it without error. "Upholding and following" refers to the gentle virtue of the earth (the Kun trigram), while "receiving and retaining" refers to the duties within the inner chambers.
Thus, she was able to respond to his request as a woman of such gentleness and compliance.
Fourteenth: Within this trichiliocosm, where ten billion suns and moons currently abide in the world, there are Bodhisattvas—sons of the Dharma—as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges Rivers.
They cultivate the Dharma and establish models to teach and transform sentient beings;

their skillful means and wisdom, which accord with the capacities of sentient beings, each differ. Through the fundamental root of perfect penetration that I have attained, I have given rise to the wondrous...
The Gate of the Ear. Thereafter, one's body and mind become subtle and wondrously all-encompassing, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This enables sentient beings to uphold my name together with sixty-two Ganges-sands of Dharma-princes; the merit of these two individuals—[the practitioner and the Dharma-son]—is [immeasurable].
"It is truly equal and without difference, World-Honored One. My single name is no different from those many names.
Because I have cultivated this and attained true perfect penetration, it is called the fourteenth power of bestowing fearlessness, which provides all beings with complete merit."
This causes sentient beings to invoke the Name and attain fearlessness. In this region, the faculty of hearing is sharp; therefore, Avalokiteśvara’s transformation surpasses that of other sages.

Although their stages and positions are equal, they differ in terms of responding to specific capacities. Taken together, those [sages] as numerous as the sands of the Ganges can only match the single person that is Avalokiteśvara.
To uphold the Name with these two forms of merit is precisely equal; thus, the perfect and penetrating [method] has been subtly selected.

World-Honored One, I have also attained this perfect penetration; because I have cultivated and realized the unsurpassed Way, I am further able to skillfully attain the four inconceivable, effortless, and wondrous virtues.
He manifests a multitude of forms and recites each of the mantras to gather and transform sentient beings, perfectly responding to their needs.

This principle arises from the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and his spiritual responses are unfathomable; thus it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Regarding the wondrous virtue of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*):
although he previously manifested forms to respond to requests, that instance was merely a brief indication, whereas this alone is a profound clarification of the inconceivable.
First, because I initially attained this most wondrous mind of hearing, my mental essence left behind all auditory perception;

seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing could no longer be partitioned, becoming a single, perfectly integrated, pure, and precious awakening. Therefore, I am able to manifest wondrous forms to sentient beings and can preach boundless secret divine mantras.
Within these, I may appear with one head, three heads, five heads, seven heads, or nine heads.
Eleven heads; and so on, up to one hundred and eight heads, a thousand heads, ten thousand heads, eighty-four thousand śakara heads;
with two arms, four arms, six arms, eight arms, ten arms, twelve arms, fourteen, sixteen.
Eighteen, twenty, up to twenty-four; and so on, even to one hundred and eight arms, a thousand arms, ten thousand arms, or eighty-four thousand mudrā-arms.
Two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, nine eyes;
and so on, even to one hundred and eight eyes, a thousand eyes, ten thousand eyes, or eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes. Whether manifesting compassion or majesty.
Whether through meditative concentration or wisdom, one rescues and protects sentient beings and attains great sovereignty.
This clarifies the inconceivability of a single body manifesting as many bodies. "Initially attained" refers to what is first obtained within the state of hearing.
Regarding "the wondrously wondrous hearing-mind": first, when the faculties and their objects perish, the mind is already wondrous;

subsequently, when both object and wisdom perish together, and both subject and object are stilled, it is called "wondrously wondrous. Consequently, the essence of the mind abandons hearing, yet the six faculties are no longer obstructed.

A single awakening is perfectly interfused, manifesting and responding without impediment. The head represents the totality of the six functions; the arms represent lifting and receiving; and the eyes represent illuminating and discerning.

Each follows its original number up to eighty-four thousand, representing the application of the wisdom that relies upon the faculties to universally respond to the afflictions of worldly toil (*kleśa*).
*Śakara* means "firm" (*dṛḍha*); *mudrā* means "seal. The pure jewel-eye is the Vajra Right Eye.

It compassionately protects the roots of goodness and majestically rescues those of evil nature; through concentration it protects against distraction, and through wisdom it rescues those mired in delusion. These are one essence.

Within this, the myriad dharmas are fully present. As for the manifestation of the twenty-four sages who followed, it clarifies that each manifested a single aspect, which is here perfectly integrated.
Question: The eighty-four thousand [teachings] merely represent the Dharma; what can a single body possibly apply? Answer:
This is because one uses a conceptualizing mind to measure the realm of perfect penetration. The body contains the ten voids.
"World-systems appear upon the tips of my hairs; these empty world-systems are no more than my head and arms, which are like the eighty-four thousand pores of a human being.

Second, because I have emerged from the six sense-objects through hearing and reflection, just as sound passes through a wall without obstruction, I am thus able to manifest every single form and recite every single mantra with wondrous skill. These forms and mantras can bestow fearlessness upon all beings."
Sentient beings. For this reason, throughout the dust-mote worlds of the ten directions, all name me the "Bestower of Fearlessness.
This clarifies that each body and each form is inconceivable. Because the capacities of sentient beings differ, the forms manifested to suit those capacities also differ.
Because the habitual tendencies of sentient beings differ, the mantras preached to suit those capacities also differ.

Third: Because I have cultivated my original, wondrous, and perfect penetration—the pure fundamental root—I cause all sentient beings in the worlds where I travel to relinquish their bodies and precious treasures, seeking my compassionate pity.

This clarifies the inconceivable nature of his transformative power. Because I have attained the pure fundamental source, I am entirely free from attachment to the objects of the six sense-fields and am able to relinquish them all. Therefore, in whatever worlds I travel, there is no stinginess;
I am able to give away what is most precious, seeking their compassionate acceptance so that I may perform the Buddha-work of giving.

Fourth: I have attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate. I am able to offer various precious jewels as offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, extending also to all sentient beings within the six realms of the Dharma-realm.
If one seeks a wife, one obtains a wife; if one seeks a son, one obtains a son; if one seeks samādhi, one obtains samādhi;
if one seeks long life, one obtains long life. Thus it continues, even until seeking great nirvāṇa, one obtains great nirvāṇa.
Nirvana. This clarifies the inconceivable nature of making offerings. "Attaining the Buddha-mind" refers to first acquiring the Tathāgatagarbha mind;
"realizing the ultimate" refers to fully acquiring the Tathāgatagarbha mind. From beginning to end, one attains this Tathāgata...

The treasury of the mind—the immeasurable jewel-treasury of the Buddha-dharma—is entirely manifest before one. Thus, one is able to bring forth the jewels of the household and extensively perform the work of a Buddha.
Having already made offerings of various Dharma-jewels to the Buddhas, one further bestows upon sentient beings various gifts of wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness.
This is because, through the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the dharma-realm, all sentient beings are seen to be entirely the very essence of the Buddha. Therefore, [the wife]...
"Long life is the happiness of this world; samādhi and nirvāṇa are the happiness that transcends the world.

When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I attained the Samādhi of Universal Illumination through the gateway of the ear. My mind gained mastery by relying on the state of the flowing-in, thereby entering the stream."
I attained samādhi and accomplished bodhi; this was the foremost. World-Honored One, that Buddha-Tathāgata praised me for having well-attained the dharma-gate of perfect penetration.
In the midst of the great assembly, he conferred upon me the name Avalokiteśvara.
Because my contemplation and hearing of the ten directions are perfectly luminous, the name "Avalokiteśvara" pervades the worlds of the ten directions.

This is the perfection of penetration through the unobstructed way. By entering deeply through the single gateway of the ear-faculty, those six faculties of cognition are accordingly uprooted and liberated in their totality.
Thus, above, one accords with all Buddhas; below, one harmonizes with all sentient beings. In responding to conditions and establishing skillful means, there is nothing that is not sovereign.
Entering the stream of the dharma-nature, one attains samādhi; this refers to the causal mind. Accomplishing bodhi, this refers to the resultant awakening.
From the words "World-Honored One" onwards, it further clarifies that both the receiving of a prediction and the attainment of a name all proceed through this gate.

At that time, from his five limbs, the World-Honored One simultaneously emitted precious light that reached far to drench the crowns of the heads of Tathāgatas as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, as well as the Dharma Princes and all the Bodhisattvas; those Tathāgatas likewise [emitted light] from their five limbs.

They simultaneously emitted precious light from every direction of the subtle dust, which came to drench the crown of the Buddha’s head and to drench all the great Bodhisattvas, Arhats, forests, trees, ponds, and marshes within the assembly.
All these places resounded with the sounds of the Dharma; the interlacing lights entwined like a net of precious threads.
This great assembly attained what they had never experienced before; all of them universally obtained the Vajra-samādhi.

Immediately, there fell from the heavens a rain of lotus flowers of a hundred jewels—blue, yellow, red, and white—intermingling and blending together. The empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures.

In this Sahā world, the great earth, mountains, and rivers all disappeared simultaneously; there was seen only a single realm merging with me, composed of lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions.
Chanting and hymns were spontaneously performed and presented.
The various sages each described their realization of perfect penetration; all the doors of the flowered mansion were opened. The Buddha further responded with auspicious signs:
these sages manifested through words, while the Tathāgata manifested through physical marks, thereby awakening and enlightening sentient beings.
The five limbs simultaneously radiated precious light, manifesting that the entire body is the Great Treasury of Radiance. The Buddhas gathered together to bestow the consecration.
This reveals that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have equally realized the Dharma of the Crown (uṣṇīṣa).
Together, they bestow empowerment upon the Bodhisattvas and Arhats, sealing their cultivation and realization as being without distinction of superior or inferior.

The sounds emanate from the forest trees, and the lights interlace with one another, manifesting that once the sense bases and objects have been extinguished, both the insentient and the sentient all attain the Buddha-way. This is not like the formation of worlds through the mutual weaving of delusory thoughts.
Śāriputra, the great assembly has universally attained the Vajrasamādhi, thereby manifesting the Śūraṅgama King, which is the adamantine precious awakening and the equal Dharma-realm.
The lands of the ten directions merge into a single realm, manifesting that the precious, luminous, and empty awakening spontaneously appears.
The outflows of conditioned existence shall never arise again; all defilements are utterly cleared away.

There is no longer any separation or obstruction. Chanting and hymns arise spontaneously, manifesting that the entire Dharma-realm is forever free from all suffering and constantly attains wondrous bliss.
Such is the wondrous nature of this true and perfect penetration.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata addressed Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince:

"Observe now these twenty-five great Bodhisattvas beyond training and the Arhats, each of whom has spoken of the skillful means by which they first attained the Way, all claiming to have cultivated true and perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In their respective practices, there is truly no distinction of superiority or inferiority, nor of priority or sequence. I now wish—"

To cause Ānanda to attain awakening, twenty-five practices were taught. Which of these corresponds to the faculties of those who, after my parinirvāṇa, enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle within this world-system to seek the unsurpassed path?
By what gate of skillful means can they achieve success with ease?
This decree is Mañjuśrī’s selection of the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*). There is no distinction; this refers to the gates of practice, which are likewise equal for all.

The various sages are dispersed throughout the ten directions; their faculties are sharpened according to their respective regions, and each has long been habituated to a particular practice through many lifetimes.

In accordance with their respective spiritual dispositions (*gotra*), each has many predominant afflictions; the sublime gates of cultivation that serve as their appropriate antidotes are, in reality, without distinction.
These are merely taught according to the faculties [of beings] and to suit the capacities of those in this region. When the teaching accords with the capacity, accomplishment is easily attained.

Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince, receiving the Buddha’s compassionate command, immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, spoke these verses in response to the Buddha:
“The nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; this perfect clarity makes awakening fundamentally subtle and wondrous.

When primordial luminosity shines forth, the objects of perception arise; once those objects are established, the nature of the illuminating subject vanishes. Through delusion and ignorance, empty space comes to be; based upon space, the world is established. As thought becomes settled, it forms [the realm of form].”

The lands and the sentient beings who perceive them arise from within Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. These minute, conditioned realms of existence all depend upon emptiness for their birth.
When the bubble vanishes, the emptiness remains as it was from the beginning; how much more so, then, regarding the various states of the three realms of existence?

The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of expedient means. The sagely nature is all-pervasive; whether following the natural order or acting in reverse, all are expedient means for the beginner to enter.
Samādhi. Their speed—whether slow or fast—is not uniform.
This clarifies that from the True [Nature] arises delusion; therefore, there is the returning from delusion to the True.

Because there are variations in speed along the path of returning from delusion to the True, it is necessary to select according to one's faculties (*indriya*). The ocean of the wondrous enlightened nature is originally clear, tranquil, and perfect. And yet, it is perfect...
The nature of clarity and awakening is fundamentally and inherently wondrous; it does not depend on artificial effort, nor does it have any spatial location.

It is because the essence of the primordial luminosity suddenly gives rise to the function of illumination that it consequently falls into spatial location. Once location has been falsely established, the fundamental nature of that illuminating function is thereby lost.
This is precisely how the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is formed based upon original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Having thus become deluded regarding the awakened nature, it forms...

The karmic consciousness thus becomes deluded regarding the emptiness of nature and gives rise to a stubborn, insentient emptiness. From within this darkness where emptiness is obscured, it binds darkness into form.
Furthermore, it establishes two kinds of worlds—the insentient and the sentient—by grasping at a portion of floating, chaotic thoughts.

That which coagulates and lacks cognition becomes the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). That portion of floating, empty false imagination which coagulates and possesses cognition becomes the root-body (*mūla-kāya*).
This is precisely the arising of the two divisions of appearance and perception based upon the karmic consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā-karma-vijñāna*).
Little do they realize that empty space arises within the nature of Great Enlightenment, no different from a single bubble emerging from the great ocean.
If even space is like this, how much more so are the minute, conditioned lands of dust, all of which are established upon space? Their insignificance is evident.
If one understands that when the bubble ceases, the space it occupied was originally non-existent, how much more so is this true for those things produced from space?
How can one remain alone amidst the three realms of existence? If one attains the return to the source, the enlightened nature is inherently non-dual.
However, if one wishes to enter this non-dual enlightened nature, there are many gates of skillful means (*upāya*).

When a sage fully realizes this nature, all phenomena are perfectly interfused and every event is without obstruction; whether it be hatred or love, suffering or joy, all are entryways into the principle.

This gate requires no discrimination. For those who have first resolved their minds and wish to enter samādhi to attain the perfect faculties, there will certainly be differences in the speed of their progress;
therefore, it is essential to select the faculties. Regarding "speed" and "slowness":

this refers to how, upon hearing the Dharma, some may immediately attain the state of no-mind, while others may not attain no-mind until they reach the tenth stage. The two lines beginning with "The ocean of awakening... refer to this.

"The nature of awareness is wondrously luminous" means that fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous. The two phrases "originally luminous" correspond to "based on luminosity, one establishes the object.
Once the object has been falsely established, your false subjectivity arises. The eight phrases beginning with "deluded and false" correspond to "arousing worldly toil":

from movement, the world arises; from stillness, empty space is formed. The two phrases beginning with "the bubble vanishes" correspond to "because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not..."
Birth occurs; once the nature of madness subsides of itself, that subsiding is itself Bodhi.
When the perception of form congeals into dust, the essential clarity cannot penetrate through it. How could one not attain clear penetration? It is in this way that one attains perfect penetration.
Sounds are mixed with speech; they consist merely of phonemes, names, phrases, and meanings. One does not contain all others—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
Fragrance is known through contact; when separated, it fundamentally does not exist. Its perception is not constant—how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The nature of taste is not inherent; it exists only when there is tasting. Since the perception of it is not constant, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?
Touch is clarified by that which is touched; there is no touch that is not clarified. Since the natures of union and separation are not fixed, how can one attain perfect penetration through it?

The dharmas are called internal objects (*viṣaya*). Since one must rely on objects, there must necessarily be a subject; as subject and object do not pervade all things universally, how can one attain perfect penetration?
This excludes the six objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Objects are insentient things and are thus most remote from the mind. Furthermore, they possess two meanings: obstruction and defilement.
Being remote, they are difficult to transform; being obstructive, they are difficult to perfect; being defiled, they are difficult to penetrate. Therefore, they are all excluded.

To distinguish [one] from the non-saintly is to distinguish [them] by means of the Dharma; yet, to distinguish [them] by means of the Dharma is not to distinguish [them] at all, but rather to distinguish [them] by means of their spiritual capacities (*indriya*).
When it is asked, "How does one attain perfect penetration? this refers specifically to the capacities of Ānanda and the great assembly here in this land.

As for the various sages, each attains perfect penetration by relying upon their respective methods; the Buddha declared that there is no superiority or inferiority among them. Śāṭa, for instance, attained it through the contemplation of impurity.

By analyzing form, one clarifies emptiness; wondrous form is subtle and perfectly round. Now, it is discerned that the dust of form is formed by the binding of false imaginings; its substance is obstructive and hindering.
A beginner, though their faculty of seeing may be clear and distinct, cannot penetrate through it.

How could they fail to understand the dharma thoroughly and thereby attain perfect penetration? Dharmatrāta realized the emptiness of the four truths through sound; wondrous sound is subtle and perfectly round. Now, it is discerned...
Sound does not depart from various mixed languages; it is simply names, phrases, and meanings.
That "one" does not contain all means that while the principle is perfect, the words are partial; a single word cannot universally encompass all principles. Question:
How does this differ from the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara? Answer: Sound is the Buddha’s speech, whereas the faculty is one's own mind. To recognize sensory objects is to become attached to others.
