Regarding speech: by observing the faculties, one realizes the nature of one’s own mind. Xiangyan entered through fragrance;

by observing that fragrance is unborn, the sensory dust and its breath suddenly vanished, and the wondrous fragrance became subtle and pervasive. Now, examining this single method of fragrance: it exists when combined but is absent when separated.
Since the awareness is not constant, it does not yet constitute a perfect observation. Yawang and Yao Shang entered through tasting various flavors; they realized that flavor is unborn.
Through the clarity of the sense of taste, one ascends to the rank of a Bodhisattva. Now, I select this [faculty] because the nature of taste is fundamentally non-existent;

it is only in dependence upon the sense organ that it is perceived. Without the organ, there is no taste; therefore, it is not the perfect penetration. Pūrṇa suddenly awakened to the cause of water and attained the state of "nothingness.

Through the manifestation of wondrous touch, he became established as a Son of the Buddha. Now, I select this [faculty] because the cause of touch is manifested through the body that is touched. Without [the body], there is nothing.

Then it would not be manifest. Since the nature [of the object] is not constant or fixed, it is not universally penetrating (*pariṣphuṭa*). Kāśyapa contemplates how sensory objects (*viṣaya*) change and decay, and cultivates the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*);

through the illumination of the wondrous Dharma, he eliminates all outflows (*āsrava*). Although this selection is called the "wondrous Dharma," it is nonetheless an internal object that must be suppressed.

Is this cultivation not still characterized by subject and object? Therefore, it is not universally penetrating. Furthermore, the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) is not one of the five external [objects].
The substantial nature of these objects is merely the shadow of the five sensory objects. Because they are apprehended solely within the mind, they are called "internal objects.
That which necessarily exists must take one object as its condition and necessarily abandon another; both subject and object are thus restricted and cannot engage with all things universally.
Although the seeing-nature is brilliantly clear, it illuminates what is before but not what is behind; the four directions are deficient by half.

How can such a state attain perfect penetration? The breath of the nose flows in and out; yet there is no mingling of these gases before one's eyes, and they remain fragmented without interpenetration. How can such a state attain perfect penetration?
The tongue is not an entrance without cause; it gives rise to discernment because of flavors. When flavors vanish, discernment ceases to exist. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
The body and its objects of touch are likewise each lacking the contemplation of perfect enlightenment. Their boundaries do not merge in silent accord. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

"The faculty of cognition is confused by discursive thought; though profound and clear, it ultimately lacks true vision. Since conceptualization cannot be escaped, how can one attain perfect penetration?

This passage excludes the five sense-faculties. Although the faculties are capable of turning back—such that when they are reversed, they are the very nature itself—and thus surpass their corresponding objects and consciousnesses, they are nonetheless excluded because they are inconsistent in their completeness or deficiency.
Sudatta, through the practice of the Samādhi of the Radiant Illumination of Delightful Vision, turned his vision toward its source..."

This is the original [text]. From this, one obtains proof. Now, although the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*) is capable of illuminating and cognizing, it is fully bright in the direction in front and fully dark in the direction behind.
It illuminates the two dimensions in front but does not illuminate the two dimensions behind; therefore, it is said to be "deficient by half."

Pāṇṭa regulated the inhalation and exhalation of the breath; by reversing the breath and following it through emptiness, he thereby attained the Way. Now, although the nasal breath passes through both inhalation and exhalation, they do not intersect.
Since the constituent parts are already separated, how could this constitute a complete contemplation?

As for Bhaṭṭikara’s contemplation of the cognition of taste—which is neither the substance nor the object—he returned to the taste and revolved within the cognition, attaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). Why, then, do you now reject this?
The tongue has two functions: preaching the Dharma and tasting flavors. Regarding the preaching of the Dharma, it possesses unimpeded eloquence, which is what is meant by "entering the boundless.
This is closely akin to "perfect penetration" (yuantong). If one cannot enter the boundless, then one speaks only of tasting flavors: when the object meets the sense, there is awareness;
when the object ceases, cognition perishes. How can this be called perfect penetration? Pi Linggan [observed] that awareness arises from awareness.
Pain. One perceives the pure mind; there is no perception of pain within pain, but only the perception of the remaining body, thereby attaining the fruit of No-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Now, distinguishing between the body and the object of touch (*spraṣṭavya*), both are known when in contact, but not known when separated; this is not the contemplation of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*). As for "that which is touched," this refers to the object of touch;
each is not Perfect Enlightenment, because their limited dimensions do not merge in harmony. "Limited dimensions" (*yā-lìang*) is synonymous with "boundaries."
It is known that each has its own boundaries and cannot possess consciousness within the profound stillness, just as the ear relates to sound.
Subhūti, having practiced in emptiness and quiescence for vast eons, his empty nature is perfectly luminous; he enters the ocean of precious clarity and shares in the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Now, discerning that the mind is cluttered and confused, it is difficult to subdue; thus, one can never perceive the nature of profound clarity.
Perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*) is a supreme fruit free from discrimination; if one is not liberated from chaotic thoughts, how could such a fruit ever be attained?

Consciousness arises from the mingling of the three aggregates; when its root is examined, it is called "without marks. Its own essence has no fixed prior existence—how can one attain perfect penetration through this?
The mind-hearing penetrates the ten directions, arising from the power of great causes; yet the beginner cannot enter it—how can one attain perfect penetration through this?

Contemplating the nose is fundamentally a provisional means, intended only to cause the mind to settle. Once settled, it becomes that which the mind dwells upon; how, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

To preach the Dharma by playing with sounds and texts merely awakens those who have already achieved success; names and phrases are not themselves untainted. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

Observing precepts and violating them merely restrain the body; if there were no body, there would be nothing to restrain. Since this fundamentally does not pervade all things, how can one attain perfect penetration?

Spiritual powers are rooted in past causes; what connection have they to the discrimination of dharmas? Since mindfulness depends on conditions and is not separate from objects, how can one attain perfect penetration?
This distinguishes [the practitioner] from the six consciousnesses. At the beginning of the sutra, it refutes the mind of the six bases and their consciousnesses as the root of birth and death;

one must not rely upon them for confused practice. That the various sages personally declare this while nevertheless maintaining these six gates indicates that the nature of the sages is all-pervasive.
If beginners employ these [six gates], there are many who become śrāvakas, māras, or heretics; therefore, they must be distinguished and abandoned.
Rāhula has been pure for kalpas beyond measure; his awakened clarity is perfect and complete, and his light extends to the furthest reaches of knowledge and vision.

Now, to distinguish the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*): it is intermingled within the "threefold conjunction" [of eye, object, and consciousness]. When its fundamental nature is investigated, no characteristic can be found.

Its own substance is not permanent; how, then, could it be perfectly pervasive? "Consciousness-vision" refers precisely to the visual consciousness. It arises therein through the union of the eye and form; therefore, it is said to be "intermingled."
The three [factors] must harmonize; when they are in harmony, there is [perception], and when they are not, there is none. Therefore, it is said that there is no fixed [nature].
Samantabhadra’s mental hearing can know matters outside the sands of worlds and attain great mastery.

Now, this is selected because it arises from practicing the great cause of the Dharma-realm conduct (*dharmadhātu-caryā*), and is not due to the inherent subtlety of the ear-consciousness itself. One cannot achieve this fruit at the very first moment of the initial resolve. —Sundarī.

The mind is constantly distracted and restless. By contemplating the white at the tip of the nose, after a long time, illumination arises; when that illumination becomes perfect, the outflows are extinguished.
Now, selecting this as the primary practice is intended as an antidote to distraction, using it as a provisional means to gather and stabilize the mind. Yet the true mind has no abiding place.
If the mind were truly to have an abiding place, it would become a locus where the mental factors reside, becoming biased toward one spot and failing to be universally pervasive. Pūrṇa.
They assist the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma, preach the unsurpassed teaching, subdue demonic adversaries, and extinguish all outflows.
Now, to select those who can expound the Dharma—awakening others without departing from sounds and letters—requires the power of eloquence cultivated over vast eons.
It was only through maturation over successive lifetimes that he attained such a state; it is not something that can be accomplished by the gustatory consciousness in a single moment.

The names and phrases he speaks are not untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas; how could they constitute perfect penetration? Upāli maintains pure precepts, and his body and mind are in a state of tranquil extinction.
One becomes an Arhat. Now, regarding the method of upholding the precepts, it does not exceed the restraint of this body.

Yet, the primordial luminosity of the ocean of awareness is fundamentally not the measure of the body; what, then, is there to restrain? Since there is something to be restrained, it would not be all-pervasive.

Maudgalyāyana cultivated meditative concentration until the consciousness became still and the light of the mind was proclaimed, whereby he attained great spiritual power. Now, we shall distinguish this from supernatural powers.
This is obtained through past causes. The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the nature of discrimination regarding the objects of the mind (*dharmadhātu*).
This thought exists when it conditions an object and does not exist when separated from an object; therefore, it is not the perfect penetration.
If one contemplates through the nature of earth, it is solid and obstructive, not penetrating; it is conditioned and lacks the nature of the noble ones. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?
If one contemplates through the nature of water, thoughts and perceptions are not real; suchness is beyond both conceptualization and observation. How, then, can one attain perfect penetration?

If you contemplate through the nature of fire, you will come to loathe existence as not being true liberation; this is not the expedient means for a beginner—how then can you attain perfect penetration?
If you contemplate through the nature of wind, motion and stillness are not without opposition; where there is opposition, there is no supreme awakening—how then can you attain perfect penetration?
If you observe through the nature of emptiness, that which is dull and dark was originally not awakening; since non-awakening differs from Bodhi, how can you attain perfect penetration?
If you observe through the nature of consciousness, you find that consciousness is not permanent; to maintain a mind is but a delusion, so how can you attain perfect penetration?

"All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing. Cause and effect now yield such disparate results—how can one attain perfect penetration?

This passage distinguishes the seven elements (*dhātu*): the first five correspond to objects (*viṣaya*), the sixth corresponds to consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the seventh corresponds to the faculties (*indriya*).

However, it adds the characteristic of vastness. By maintaining the ground of evenness and the mind of purity, one perceives that objects lack inherent nature and do not engage in mutual contact or friction, thereby awakening to non-arising.

Kṣānti (Endurance). Now, to distinguish this: the nature of earth is solid and obstructive; even leveling and filling [the ground] still belongs to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and does not constitute the holy mind.

Therefore, it is not the perfect penetration (*paripūrṇa-abhijñā*). When one encounters the Buddha with an impartial mind, one has already returned to the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This distinction is made from the perspective of a beginner.

Regarding Candraprabha’s water-contemplation—where the body becomes fragrant water and its nature accords with true emptiness, thereby attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)—this contemplation is now being distinguished.

As long as one has not yet departed from conceptual thought, it is difficult to accord with suchness (*tathatā*). For suchness is a dharma that is free from thought and immovable; it is a dharma that transcends both vitarka and vicāra.

When the Fire-Head Contemplation takes the mind of excessive lust and transforms it into the fire of wisdom, giving rise to the great jewel-flame, one now discriminates the teaching on the "fire of desire" and gives rise to weary detachment.
This is the weary detachment from existence (*bhava*); body and mind are both severed, and even the nature of severance is non-existent.
Only this constitutes true detachment; weary detachment is not true detachment. It is not the case that those with a beginner’s mind all possess many desires, nor is it a fixed expedient means.
When the Lapis Lazuli Light contemplates the mind, body, and world, one sees that they are all turned by the power of the wind of delusive conditions.

To perceive immobility within movement is to realize the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, to distinguish between movement and stillness as opposites—being in opposition is not true. How could this be the same?
Yuan Guan entered the stream by losing the object of perception; he asked about the method of "listening inwardly," which likewise enters through movement and stillness. [The Master] replied:
"He gradually detached from the two objects of movement and stillness, taking the hearing-nature—which is neither moving nor still—as his point of entry.

This [method] takes the wind-nature—which possesses both movement and stillness—as its point of entry. This is why they differ. In the *Ākāśagarbha* contemplation, one contemplates the four great elements as non-existent."
Based on this, deluded thoughts arise and perish; yet empty space is non-dual, and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same.

Having attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one now distinguishes that empty space is fundamentally characterized by insentient rigidity, which is diametrically opposed to the enlightened nature of Bodhi.

To seek the fruit of luminous intelligence from within dullness and obscurity is certainly difficult to achieve. Maitreya cultivated the contemplation of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*); thus, the nature of consciousness is perfectly luminous and clear.

One enters the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Now, if one merely excludes the nature of consciousness—which arises and ceases moment by moment—its principle is not permanent.
If one only eliminates the objects while failing to eliminate the mind itself, it will still result in delusion; how could this be the perfect penetration?

The Great Power Attainment Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance gathers all six sense faculties and maintains pure mindfulness in succession, thereby entering the patience of the non-arising of phenomena. Now, [this] is excluded.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are in flux and thus fall under impermanence. Since the nature of thought arises and perishes, it is truly impermanent.
How can one obtain the fruit of permanence by means of impermanent causes?

Of the twenty-four dharmas, some are partial rather than complete, some are obstructed rather than pervasive, some are stagnant rather than luminous, some are dull rather than awakened, and some are subject to arising and ceasing rather than being permanent. Or...
That which is false and unreal is not the truth. Some [teachings] are so profound they do not encompass the shallow, making them unsuitable for beginners;

others are so shallow they do not penetrate the deep, making it difficult to reach the sublime realm. This [text] precisely reveals that the nature of hearing within the ear-faculty is free from all defects and fully endowed with all virtues.
I now address the World-Honored One: When a Buddha appears in this Sahā world, the true essence of the teaching in this realm is purity found in sound and hearing.
If one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through hearing. To leave suffering behind and achieve liberation—how excellent is Avalokiteśvara!
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he enters buddha-lands as many as motes of dust, attaining the power of great sovereignty and bestowing fearlessness upon sentient beings.
With wondrous sounds, Avalokiteśvara, with Brahma-sounds and ocean-tide sounds, he brings peace and security to all in the world; transcending the world, he attains eternal abiding.
From this point downward, the ear-faculty alone is selected as the perfect penetration (*āyatana*). The Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings varies according to different regions;
in this region, the ear-faculty is particularly sharp. This is entirely because the nature of hearing universally reaches throughout the immeasurable.

Therefore, the Buddha, in accordance with the specific capacities of those in this region, performs the work of a Buddha through sound, catering to the sharpness of their faculty of hearing. Thus, sound and hearing are joined together.
This constitutes the pure teaching-essence for this region. However, the verbal teaching serves merely as a preliminary lead-in;

the nature of hearing is, in truth, the wondrous mind. Therefore, although both sound and hearing are relied upon for awakening, one should single-mindedly take up the nature of hearing when practicing meditative concentration.
"Free from suffering" and below praises the virtues of self-benefit and benefiting others. "Free from suffering" means being free from the suffering of birth and death, attaining liberation.

"Delivered" means attaining the two kinds of liberation regarding persons and phenomena. As for the statement that "one attains freedom from bondage through the nature of hearing," this capacity belongs solely to Avalokiteśvara.
To mention "sands of kalpas" indicates that time is at its most extensive; to mention "dust-motes of lands" indicates that space is at its most vast.
"Attaining great mastery in every direction" praises his thirty-two manifestations, which preach the Dharma in accordance with conditions.
Furthermore, he bestows fearlessness upon sentient beings; thus he is praised as the Fourteen Fearlessnesses, for he seeks out their voices to rescue them from suffering.

He manifests thirty-two responses, preaching the Dharma according to the various types of beings; thus he is called "Wondrous Sound" (Sudhana-svara). He regards the three evil paths and the eight difficulties with impartiality and rescues them all;

thus he is called "Avalokiteśvara. His fundamental source is pure and free from defilement or attachment; thus he is called "Brahma-Sound" (Brahma-svara). He responds everywhere to those who seek him, yet...

Regarding the timing [of his voice], it is called the "Ocean Tide Sound. Possessing these four sounds, he rescues those in the world who are in distress and suffering, causing them all to attain peace and security;
furthermore, he enables those who transcend the world to attain the fruit of eternal abiding.
I now address the Tathāgata as Avalokiteśvara has taught: "Suppose a person is dwelling in stillness, and drums are struck simultaneously in all ten directions;
they hear them all at once in those ten locations. This is the perfection of reality. The eyes do not perceive what is beyond obstructions; the same is true for the mouth and nose."
The body knows through contact; mental thoughts are chaotic and without order. Hearing sounds across a wall, one can perceive them both from afar and nearby.
That which is not uniform for the five sense organs is what penetrates reality. The nature of sound is movement and stillness; within hearing, it exists or does not exist.

There is no sound to call out and no hearing to perceive; it is not that there is truly no nature of hearing. Since sound is absent, it is neither extinguished; since sound is present, it is neither born.
Being perfectly free from both arising and ceasing, this is the eternal reality. Even if one is in a dream, it does not become non-existent through the absence of thought.
It transcends discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and is beyond the reach of body and mind;
this reveals the excellence of the faculty of hearing. That it hears simultaneously with every strike reveals its perfection (*pūrṇa*).

That it is utterly distinct from the other five faculties reveals its penetration (*vyāpti*). That it remains constant whether awake or asleep reveals its permanence (*nityatā*). This is because the nature of hearing is all-pervasive.
In every location, the sounds of the ten directions arise according to their time, without sequence, simultaneously pervading all.

When dwelling in stillness, it is not a time when the mind is disturbed by many affairs; yet if one were in a state of distraction, although the hearing would remain constantly complete, one would fail to perceive it at all.
One desires to verify the sharpness of the ear-faculty within this stillness. As for the eyes, they cannot see what lies beyond obstructions.
It is like being unable to see what is outside when separated by paper or film, or being unable to see the five viscera when separated by skin.
It is like food within a vessel or incense within a burner; if covered with an object, the mouth and nose cannot perceive them. Therefore it is said, "The mouth and nose are likewise.
Although the faculty of the mind (*manas*) is pervasive, it is distracted and not constant. As for the faculty of the ear (*śrotra*), it is even [capable of perceiving] through obstructions.

Huan listened to it; it was heard both far and near. Thus, the function of the ear-faculty does not depend on whether there is obstruction or no obstruction, union or separation, mindfulness or lack of mindfulness;
the nature of hearing is always pervasive, differing from the other five faculties.
Sound has movement and stillness, and within the nature of hearing, it may exist or not exist. Those who are inverted perceive it as being silent and non-existent.
Regarding sound: although it is deludedly perceived as non-hearing, the nature of hearing is not actually nonexistent.

Because this nature of hearing does not arise with the sound nor perish with the sound, even within dreams one still hears the sound of pounding and threshing. This [nature] consists of discernment and contemplation that transcend conceptual thought;
it is superior to the other sense faculties. These three kinds of reality are currently possessed by ordinary beings and do not depend upon realization.
Only after that does it exist. If one cultivates further along these lines, it is like sailing a boat with the wind; what difficulty could there be?

Now, in this Sahā world, the science of phonology (*śabdavidyā*) has been proclaimed and clarified. Yet sentient beings are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; because they follow sounds, they wander in saṃsāra.

"Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, he cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts. Is this not because he follows where he sinks? By reversing the flow, one attains freedom from delusion.
Ānanda, listen attentively! Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic strength, I shall proclaim the Vajra King—illusory and inconceivable."
This is the true samādhi of the Buddha-mother. You have heard from as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust regarding all the gates of secrecy;

yet, if you do not first eliminate the outflows of desire, your accumulation of learning will become a source of error. If you intend to maintain the Buddhas through hearing, why do you not hear that which hears itself?
This clarifies that the faculty of hearing is most conducive for beginners. Regarding the spiritual capacities of those in this land, their faculty of hearing is clear and sharp;

they must rely on verbal expression to attain clarity and understanding. Therefore, in accordance with these faculties which are particularly acute in this region, all the sutras and treatises have been extensively proclaimed.
Yet, what these sutras and treatises elucidate is nothing other than the revelation of the perfect, tranquil, and wondrous nature. One should thus rely upon the discourse of sound.
Instead, one should turn back to hear one’s own nature, just as one looks for the moon by following a pointing finger.

Sentient beings fail to grasp the Tathāgata’s original intent; instead, they become deluded regarding their own inherently existing faculty of hearing. Chasing after sounds and pursuing echoes, they neglect their fundamental capacity to hear.

How is this any different from mistaking the finger for the moon? It is not only with worldly sounds that following them inevitably leads to the cycle of transmigration; even if one were able to forcibly [restrain oneself]...
Even those who record the twelve divisions of the sutras of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cannot avoid falling into perverse thoughts and drowning in brothels;
is this not because they follow the dust of sound, unable to turn back themselves, and thus are submerged? "Following" means following sounds;
"submerged" means transmigrating. If one knows that transmigration follows sounds, then one will know that by turning back the flow, one will surely attain liberation.
"There is no delusion. Below this, Ānanda is specifically instructed that he must certainly practice according to this gate.
He says, "My selection of faculties today is entirely due to the Buddha’s majestic power. This refers to the previously mentioned "Vajra-King Jewel-Awakening" and the "Illusory-like Samādhi";
one can see that these are the actual names of the "Illusory-like Real Samādhi. By means of this samādhi, one is able to emerge [from delusion].
Because they give birth to all Buddhas, she is called the "Mother of Buddhas. From hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, one merely contemplates this and cultivates this.

From the fifth fascicle’s explanation of "untying the knots" onward, all have been clarifying this meaning. This fascicle specifically points to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*), taking Avalokiteśvara as the primary exemplar.
"Vajra King" corresponds with the "Śūraṅgama King" at the beginning of the first fascicle; both are...
This is the ultimate, steadfast intention; it is nothing other than the illusory-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*).

From the passage "As for what you have heard," etc., the faults of following after sounds and circulating in transmigration are exposed. It says: "What you have retained and upheld of the Buddha-dharma is already extremely vast.

Yet, because you delight only in much hearing (*bahuśruta*) and do not eliminate the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the more you accumulate, the deeper the root of craving becomes; thus, it is of no benefit."
This path merely increases errors and will not spare you from the hardships of Māraṇa. When you hear these two lines, they are intended to stimulate your faculty of "hearing back.
It says: "You use this faculty of hearing to remember and uphold the Buddha's teachings; why do you not turn this very faculty of hearing back upon itself?"
Yet, does one hear the nature of hearing itself? Hearing upward refers to the wisdom that is capable of hearing; hearing downward refers to the principle that is heard.
To "hear hearing" oneself is simply to reflect back upon one's own fundamental nature; it is not truly focused upon the faculty of the ear.
Hearing is not born of itself; it exists because of sound. When hearing turns back and detaches from sound, who can name that which is capable of such detachment?
Once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky.
Upon hearing this, the obscuring faculties were removed; as the dust of delusion vanished, awareness became perfectly pure. When purity reached its ultimate limit, light penetrated everywhere;
in silent illumination, it encompassed the void. Returning to observe the world, it was like a dream; Māraṅgaka was but a dream—whence could he have retained your form?
This is the essential practice of the "illusion-like" method. Hearing has no intrinsic nature; it exists only because it corresponds with sound, thereby receiving the name "the hearing-leaf.
Thus, not only are objects illusory, but the sense organ itself is also illusory. If one regards it as real, the characteristics will entangle one in an inextricable web.
If one realizes that illusion has no inherent nature, then the faculty of hearing returns to its source and does not adhere to sound.

At this moment, both subject and object are simultaneously liberated. In the preceding passage, it was stated that "seeing is not seeing," which refers to the fundamental substance reaching the state of ultimate truth;
therefore, the name "seeing" no longer exists. Here, it refers to the practice reaching the state of ultimate truth; thus, even the name "hearing" is not established.
If this single faculty is thus liberated, then all six faculties will be perfectly liberated at that very moment. This is because there is a cataract [obscuring the vision].
There are flowers in the sky; because there is the faculty of hearing, there are the three realms. When the cataracts of the eyes are removed, the flowers vanish and the pure eye appears.
When the faculty of hearing is restored, sensory objects dissolve and awakening becomes perfectly pure. When the pure eye manifests, the various objects before the eyes can no longer obstruct it.
When pure awakening emits its light, the various objects of the world can no longer obstruct it. Awakening is perfectly pure—thus it should be.

The preceding "the nature of the ocean of awakening is clear and perfect; its light penetrates everywhere" corresponds to "the fundamental subtlety of the originally perfect, clear, and awakened state," and "quiescent illumination" corresponds to "the nature of illumination being lost.
"Containing empty space" corresponds to "space arising within great awakening" and "when the bubble perishes, space was originally non-existent.
From "returning" onwards, it corresponds to "how much more so for all the three realms of existence. This "constant quiescent light" penetrates [all].
One penetrates the world-system; thus, although space is vast, it is like a single bubble upon the great ocean, let alone the physical world and the sensory bodies established within that space.
If one can reach such a state, one may then turn back to reflect upon the various phenomena of the mundane world.
True Suchness is like a dream; because during the time of delusion one has never realized this illusory realm, one perceives it as real, and only upon awakening does one know it was a dream.
Just as Mātanga used an evil incantation to draw a person into a bed of lust.
This, too, is within a dream. How could a dream-event bind your body?
It is because your seeing and hearing have not yet eliminated the cataracts of illusion that you are dazzled by empty flowers; thus, you merely wander through them.
Just as a skilled illusionist conjures various men and women, and though their faculties are seen to move, they are all drawn by a single mechanism;
when that mechanism ceases and returns to stillness, all illusions lose their inherent nature. The six sense-faculties are likewise: they originally depend upon a single brilliant spirit.

It is divided into six harmonious aggregates; when one aggregate ceases, the others return to stillness. When the functions of all six are no longer active, defilements dissolve at the mere thought of them.
Thus, perfect clarity, brightness, purity, and wondrousness are achieved. While residual traces remain, one is still a learner; when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.
This statement means that while one faculty is understood, all six faculties are uprooted. The first six lines cite a metaphor to clarify that the six faculties are illusorily formed.

The six lines concerning the faculties apply the Dharma to the preceding metaphor; the "six faculties" correspond to the various men and women, while the "one refined spirit" corresponds to the single essence.
When the mechanism of unification is joined, there is rest and renewal in one place; when the mechanism of respiration is joined, it returns to stillness, and the six functions cease to operate.

When all illusions are joined, they are found to have no inherent nature. This "one brilliant clarity" is precisely the fundamental essence of the clarity of consciousness—the subtle *nāḍa* consciousness.

The six sense organs serve as the support, while this one brilliant clarity serves as that which is supported. From this one brilliant clarity, one grasps at sensory objects to form knots, each of which...
They are distinct; thus they are divided into six. When located in the eye, it is called "seeing"; when in the ear, it is called "hearing," and so forth. Therefore it is said:

"Originally based on one luminous intelligence, it is divided into six harmonious unions. "Harmonious union" (he-ho) refers to the character previously mentioned as "adhesion" (nian); it is the opposite of the character "liberation" (tuo).
"Resting" means the cessation of mental activity (*jī*). "Returning" means returning to quiescence. "Dust and grime": "dust" refers to the preceding conceptual appearances;

"grime" refers to the afflictions of consciousness and emotion. These are the subtle ignorance within the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*). After the six stages of liberation, when both the hearing and that which is heard are exhausted, one has already realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
If one proceeds from this point and suddenly empties the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), then dust and grime will vanish in an instant.
All these are dissolved, and the essence of consciousness transforms into the perfectly interfused, pure, and precious awakening.
If there remains a residue of defilement that has not yet been exhausted, one still dwells in the stage of training and has not yet completed the task.

When the clarity of the signs becomes pure and reaches the ultimate limit, this is precisely the perfect fruition realized by the Tathāgata. Thus, since this dharma-gate is so wondrous, attaining Buddhahood is not difficult.
One should take this single faculty as the path of entry.
O Great Assembly and Ānanda: turn back the mechanism of inverted hearing; by turning back the hearing to hear one's own nature, that nature will perfect the Unsurpassed Way.
Perfect penetration is truly thus. This is the single path to nirvana for all subtle-dust Buddhas.
All Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this door; all Bodhisattvas of the present are now each entering perfect clarity; and those who practice and study in the future—
"You should rely upon this Dharma; I too have realized it through it, not only Avalokiteśvara.
This further extensively cites what has been realized to inspire a heart of admiration and universally urge you toward cultivation.
Such is the efficacy of the practice of 'hearing back' (praty-śravaṇa) and the swiftness of its results. You all should turn back your inverted faculty of hearing."
Following outward and following inward, you will truly be able to turn back your hearing from the secret hearing of the Tathāgata and hear the nature of hearing that is inherently yours.
Taking this nature as the mind of the causal ground, you may achieve the path of unsurpassed enlightenment.

Therefore, although there are many gates to perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-yoga*), if one seeks a true and perfect penetration that accords with the faculties of those in this land to cure the disease of excessive learning, there is only this single gate.
This is because this single gate is the path of all the Buddha-microdusts.
It is the single great highway leading to the home of Bodhi; it is the primary gate for entering the ocean of Nirvana.
Thus, the Buddhas of the past entered by this way, and the Bodhisattvas of the present likewise enter by this way.
Since there are so many precedents before us, future students should enter by means of this Dharma-gate. Not only [the Buddhas]...
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas enter through this gate; I, too, enter through this very gate. How could it be that only Avalokiteśvara does so?

Ānanda previously asked by what cause one establishes the foundation to seek unexcelled enlightenment; therefore, [the Buddha] specifically pointed to the nature of hearing to clarify that it is not in error.
When he asked about the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha—which universally benefits those of the three faculties—why did [the Buddha] also exclude [others]?

Question: Regarding this, although the capacity for reciting the Buddha’s name may vary according to whether it is shallow or deep, one must nonetheless have the name of Amitābha Buddha flow into the faculty of the ear;
thereafter, the faculty of the mind must maintain it without forgetting. This is the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha.
This must also depend upon the faculty of hearing; therefore, even the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha is subject to this selection.
Truly, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, inquired after me regarding various skillful means to rescue those of the final age and to seek those who would transcend the world.
To achieve the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteśvara is supreme. All other skillful means are due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
By engaging with phenomena as they are, one abandons worldly toil; this is not a matter of long-term cultivation and study. Whether at a shallow or deep level, the teaching of the Dharma is the same.
This is my reply to Your Majesty’s decree. It is indeed as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has asked me regarding various skillful means.
As for the twenty-four sages previously mentioned, who among them possesses the capacity to save sentient beings during the final kalpa?
Regarding those previously mentioned, as well as the sentient beings of this realm after my parinirvāṇa, they seek those who transcend the world; thus, they enter the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
Furthermore, "accomplishing the mind of nirvana" refers back to the previous point of accomplishing the Unsurpassed Way.
"Avalokiteśvara is supreme" means that the single gate of Avalokiteśvara’s "turning the hearing inward" alone is the foremost.

As for the gates entered by the remaining twenty-four sages, they all rely on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and grace; they merely encounter a single matter and thereby abandon worldly toil (*saṃsāra*). It is not [independent].
This universal teaching is to be cultivated throughout one's life; it is a dharma taught for both the shallow and the profound, intended that one may practice it with utmost single-mindedness.
I prostrate to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is untainted and inconceivable. I pray that you will bestow your grace upon future generations, so that they may be free from doubt regarding this gateway.
This expedient means is easily accomplished and is fit to be taught to Ānanda, as well as to those sinking in the delusions of the final age.
If one cultivates by means of this faculty alone, its perfect penetration will surpass all others; such is the true mind.

This is a prostration seeking empowerment. It means that this single gateway of the ear-organ (*śrotra-indriya*) is precisely the aforementioned three *tathāgatagarbhas*, the aforementioned untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*), and the aforementioned illusory, inconceivable Buddha-mother’s true *samādhi*.
May the Buddhas, through their spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*), empower all future practitioners so that they may all proceed from this.
Enter directly through this gate, allowing not a single thought of doubt to arise. By taking this Dharma-gate as the primary expedient, one will easily achieve accomplishment;
therefore, it is fit to teach this Dharma to Ānanda and to deliver those submerged in the final kalpa.
As for using only this one gate and no others: by advancing in cultivation according to this one gate, one may transcend twenty [kalpas].
The perfect penetration of the Four Holy Ones consists solely in this one matter through the mind of reality;
there is no other method. Thereupon, Ānanda and the great assembly attained clear understanding in body and mind, receiving a profound revelation.
They perceived that the Buddha’s Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa were like a person who has traveled far on business and has not yet returned, yet clearly knows his home.
On the road where they were heading, there was a vast assembly gathered together:
the eight classes of devas and nāgas, those of the two vehicles still in training, and all the newly resolved bodhisattvas, numbering as many as ten Ganges-sands.

They all attained their original mind, became free from dust and defilement, and obtained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Upon hearing these verses, the bhikṣuṇī Śrī became an arhat. An immeasurable multitude [also attained realization].
All those born [in this state] give rise to the mind of peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This describes awakening.
The fifth fascicle states that "body and mind are luminously clear"; from this, one knows the sequence of the binding and untying of body and mind.
Previously, I did not know through which gate one might enter; now, I have ascertained with certainty that it is through the gate of the ear, and thus I am free from all doubt.
Consequently, my body and mind are clear and lucid. Since both Bodhi and Nirvana refer to the ultimate fruit, they are metaphorically likened to a home.
The faculty of hearing is like a road. For a long time, the impoverished son has fled to another land; now, wishing to return home, he does not know the way.
Today, one path for returning home is pointed out. If he proceeds directly forward along it, [he will reach his destination].
One shall never again encounter diverging paths. What was previously called the "road" and the "gate," is here called the "home";
this signifies that the realization of the faculty of hearing is the path to the home of Bodhi and the gate for entering the home of Bodhi.
The initial expedient means culminates here; those in the assembly below who have obtained benefit all attain their original mind.
This refers to the causal mind attained at the stage of the first faith (*śraddhā*). "Distant from dust and free from defilement" refers to the delusions that have been severed.
"Attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye" refers to the thorough realization of perfect penetration, taking the awakening of the fruition stage as the causal mind;
this is precisely the initial mind of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*). "Arousing the bodhicitta" refers to the very first entry into the stage of faith.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, joined his palms in homage before the great assembly, and prostrated himself with his mind and conduct perfectly clear and bright.
With a heart mingled with both sorrow and joy, and desiring to benefit all sentient beings of the future, he bowed his head to the Buddha and said:

"O Greatly Compassionate World-Honored One, I have now realized the Dharma-door for attaining Buddhahood; practicing within it, I have attained freedom from doubt and confusion. I have often heard the Tathāgata speak thus..."
He said: "To seek to deliver others before one has delivered oneself is the aspiration of a Bodhisattva;

to have perfected one's own awakening and then be able to awaken others is the manifestation of a Tathāgata in the world. Although I have not yet attained liberation myself, I vow to deliver all sentient beings of the final kalpa.

World-Honored One, these sentient beings are gradually moving further away from the Buddha, and false teachers who preach the Dharma are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. I wish to gather their minds and lead them into [the Way]."
Samādhi. How does one cause them to establish the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), remain far removed from all demonic activities, and attain non-retrogression regarding the mind of bodhi?
This request for the establishment of the site of enlightenment serves as the rule for concentrating the mind in the final age. The traces of the mind are perfectly luminous.
First, one awakens to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished; this is the Great Buddha-Crown, the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the perfection of the mind’s luminous clarity.
Furthermore, one awakens to the faculty of hearing as the gateway for entering into that which is neither born nor extinguished; this is the perfection of the traces of that clarity.
Mourning the delusions of vast kalpas and rejoicing in today’s sudden awakening—because of long-standing confusion followed by a sudden realization, sorrow and joy intermingle.
This is the collection. Those who wish to benefit the future remove their own afflictions and further take pity on the afflictions of others.

Regarding "practicing within this so as to attain freedom from doubt": having already awakened to the Dharma-gate of the Buddha's enlightenment, one enters decisively through the faculty of hearing and is thus free from doubt.
From "Constantly hearing" onwards, he cites the Buddha’s words to exhort himself; though not yet liberated himself, he thinks of liberating others.
Those who have already completed their own crossing and are solely intent on delivering sentient beings are Tathāgatas.
Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the deliverance of sentient beings as their task, what I urgently desire is to study to become a Bodhisattva.
[The passage] from "World-Honored One" below states: "I have encountered the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma and already know the path of cultivation; I enter through hearing. However—
Fearing that sentient beings in the末法 (final dharma) age will gradually distance themselves from the Buddha, and that false teachers will propagate many divergent paths through their preaching,
causing those who strive in cultivation to have no direction for their minds; if they wish to gather their minds and enter *samādhi*,
how can one cause them to establish themselves securely on the ground of entering the Way, so that they cannot be shaken by false teachings, and [their] bodhicitta may [only then...]
"Will you not feel discouraged? From this point forward, the discourse gradually proceeds toward the Vinaya.

The World-Honored One, foreseeing that during the Age of Dharma Decline (*mappō*) false teachers would flourish, repudiating the monastic discipline (*vinaya*) and misleading sentient beings, made the precepts the foundation from beginning to end of this sutra.
Ānanda’s display of falling into an error serves as the catalyst; by this time, Ānanda had already attained [the fruit].
Upon attaining enlightenment, [the Buddha] specifically requested, on behalf of future sentient beings, that a site for the establishment of a *bodhimaṇḍa* be designated.

The World-Honored One spoke with earnest and repeated exhortation, foremost proclaiming the precepts as his definitive and clear instruction, saying: "After my parinirvāṇa, there will be many followers of Māra...
and so forth, repeatedly concluding with the warning: "If it is not spoken thus, it is the speech of Pāpīyān. It is like the final testament of an elderly man. Thus it was said.
It is deeply painful and further mutilating; it causes tears to fall and strikes the heart with cold dread.
At that time, the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, praised Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent!
Regarding the establishment of the site of practice as you have asked—to rescue and save sentient beings drowning in the final age—listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you."
"Ānanda and the great assembly replied, 'So be it; we shall respectfully receive these instructions. The Buddha told Ānanda:
'You have often heard me, within the Vinaya, proclaim the three principles of definitive practice for cultivation: namely, to collect the mind as the precept; from the precept arises concentration;
and from concentration issues forth wisdom. These are called the Threefold Training in the Outflow-free (anāsrava). "
*Vinaya* refers to the *Abhidharma-piṭaka*. It is the general designation for the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

In the Hīnayāna, one takes the Dharma as the basis for the precepts, which merely restrains the body. In the Mahāyāna, one takes the mind as the basis for the precepts, thereby purifying its very source.

When the mind can be restrained, concentration arises from this, and wisdom is developed from this. When these three are perfected and luminous, all outflows (*āsrava*) are forever exhausted; thus they are called the "Threefold Emptiness" (*trivimokṣa*).
The training for the outflows. Regarding the three determinations: the determination of precepts is foremost; the determination of concentration arises based on precepts;
and the determination of wisdom arises based on concentration. This meaning is clearly explained in the Vinaya; therefore, it says:

"As for killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—these are the four definitive instructions within the precepts, each distinct and not to be confused with the others. Question: For what reason does the subsequent text...

It speaks only of the four precepts and does not speak of concentration and wisdom. The answer is: the preceding passage’s discussion of "forgetting external objects" and "exhausting the internal faculties," and so forth, all serves to elucidate concentration and wisdom;
it simply had not yet spoken of the precepts, and thus they are specifically clarified here.
Ānanda, what is meant by "restraining the mind"? That which I call "precept" (śīla) is this:

if the beings of the six realms in all worlds do not harbor a lustful mind, they will not follow along with the continuity of birth and death. You practice samādhi to fundamentally escape from worldly toil;

if the lustful mind is not eliminated, you cannot escape the world. Even if you possess great wisdom and meditative concentration manifests before you, if you do not sever lust, you will inevitably fall.
The path of Māra consists of three grades: those of the superior grade are Māra kings; those of the middle grade are Māra subjects; and those of the inferior grade are Māra women.
These various Māras also have their own followers, each of whom claims to have attained the unsurpassed Way.

After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, many such Māra subjects will flourish in the world, widely practicing greed and lust while posing as "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra), causing all sentient beings to fall into the bonds of craving.
Seeing this pitfall, one loses the path to Bodhi. When you teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi*, you must first sever the lust of the mind;
this is called the foremost, definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not sever lust while cultivating meditative concentration, it is like steaming sand and gravel in the hope that it will become rice; even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it shall only be known as such.

Hot sands. Why is this? Because these are not the basis for rice; they are composed of sand and gravel. If you seek the wondrous fruit of Buddhahood with a lustful body, even if you should attain wondrous enlightenment, it will all be rooted in lust.
With lust as its fundamental basis, you will revolve through the three miserable realms and certainly be unable to escape. By what path can you cultivate and realize the Nirvana of the Tathāgata?
You must cause the mechanism of lust to be severed in both body and mind, and the very nature of that severance must also be...
There is none. Regarding the Buddha’s bodhi, such [a person] may still hold hope. What I have spoken in this way is the word of the Buddha;
what is not spoken in this way is the word of Pāpīyān.
If the lustful mind is not eliminated, concentration and wisdom can never be attained. Even if concentration and wisdom should arise, they will be merely perverted concentration and perverted wisdom.

Those with deep power of cultivation are superior; those with shallow power of cultivation are middling or inferior. They may temporarily dwell in the palaces of Māra, but in the end, they must fully experience the three miserable realms.
While the precepts at the head of all sutras forbid killing, this [teaching] takes the severing of lust as primary. It is pure.
Regarding the instruction on "Pure Clarity": True cultivation must first involve the departure from desire. For the vapor of desire is coarse and turbid, defiling the wondrous clarity;

the habituation to desire leads to madness and delusion, making it easy to lose right concentration (*samādhi*). Observe how Ānanda, in initiating the teaching, was shown to have encountered perverse defilement;

yet at the very beginning of his resolve for enlightenment, he first loathed the turbidity of desire. Throughout the three gradual stages of cultivation, he addressed this as the primary object of correction in each instance. Only then...

When body and mind are wondrously perfected, one attains great peace and stability. At the initial stage of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), through the drying up of sensual desire, one ascends from the nature of perfect wisdom to the levels of Equality and Wondrous Enlightenment.
As for ordinary people of the world, because their minds do not flow into dissipation, clarity and brightness arise;

they gradually ascend through the six heavens—this can generally be inferred. As for "mechanism" (*jī*), it is that which is spontaneously emitted from the lustful mind; yet, the nature of cessation is not non-existent. Thus, [the cycle continues].
The full image of desire still remains; it is triggered as soon as it encounters its conditions.
Ānanda, furthermore, among the beings of the six realms in all worlds, if their minds do not kill, they will not follow along with the succession of birth and death.
You practice samādhi in order to fundamentally emerge from worldly toil; yet if the mind of killing is not eliminated, you cannot emerge from the world. Even if you possess...
Possessing great wisdom, they manifest meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). If they do not sever [the root of] killing, they will inevitably fall into the realm of spirits.

Those of the highest grade become powerful ghosts; those of the middle grade become flying *yakṣas*, various ghost generals, and the like; those of the lowest grade shall become earth-walking *rākṣasas*.
These various ghosts and spirits also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have realized the Unsurpassed Way. When I have passed away...
After my passing, during the age of the Dharma’s decay, many such ghosts and spirits will flourish in the world, claiming that by eating meat one attains the path to Bodhi.
Ānanda, when I permitted bhikṣus to eat the five kinds of pure meat, those meats were all produced through my supernatural power.
Originally, there is no life-force. O Brahmin, your land is excessively damp and humid; moreover, it is strewn with sand and gravel, so that grasses and vegetables do not grow.
Through the empowerment of my great compassionate supernatural power, and by virtue of my great kindness and pity, I have provisionally designated this as "flesh," so that you may obtain its flavor.
How can it be that after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, those who eat the flesh of sentient beings yet call themselves disciples of the Śākya?
You should know that such meat-eaters, even if they attain mental clarity resembling *samādhi*, are all great rākṣasas;

when their retribution ends, they will inevitably sink into the bitter sea of birth and death and are not disciples of the Buddha. Such people will continue to kill, devour, and consume one another without end.
"How does such a person escape the three realms? You should teach the people of the world to cultivate *samādhi* by first ceasing the taking of life;
this is called the second definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata and the World-Honored Buddhas of the past. Therefore, Ānanda,"
If one does not cease killing while practicing meditative concentration, it is like a person who covers their own ears and shouts at the top of their voice, seeking not to be heard by others;
such people are said to be "the more they wish to hide, the more they reveal themselves. This applies to pure bhikṣus and all bodhisattvas as well.

When walking on crossroads, one does not tread upon living grass, much less pluck it with one's hands. How could those of great compassion take the flesh and blood of sentient beings to serve as food?

If bhikṣus do not wear silks, cottons, or brocades from the East, nor the boots, furs, woolens, milk, curds, or clarified butter of this land—if such are the bhikṣus, they are truly liberated from the world and have repaid their karmic debts from past lives.

One does not wander through the three realms. Why is this? Because one has consumed their bodily parts, and thus all things become conditions for them. It is like a person who eats the various grains from the earth;

their feet do not leave the ground. If you can ensure that your body and mind do not "consume" or "eat" any sentient beings—whether in terms of the body itself or its constituent parts, across both the physical and mental domains—then I declare such a person to be truly liberated. This teaching of mine is called...
If it is spoken for the sake of the Buddha, it is not as such; rather, it is the speech of Pāpīyān.
Great-power ghosts, such as the various deities of mountains and rivers, ghost generals, and their like, serve as powerful subordinates;

they have not yet escaped the consumption of blood and flesh, and they are easy to fall from but difficult to ascend. When practitioners enter into them, this is called "falling away. They claim for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way.

They recognize their own views as correct while remaining unaware of their errors. They claim that eating meat provides the path to *bodhi*, similar to the assertion that alcohol and meat do not obstruct *bodhi*.

According to the Vinaya, three types of "pure" meat are permitted: meat not seen to have been killed for one's sake, not heard to have been killed for one's sake, and [not suspected to have been killed for one's sake].

Not doubting that [the meat] was killed for one's sake, combined with what has died of itself and what is left over from a bird's feeding, these are collectively termed the "five pure meats. These are merely provisional concessions of the Hīnayāna.
If it were true compassion and true liberation, such things would all be abandoned. Throughout the five regions of the Western Regions, they are generally called the Kingdom of the Brāhmaṇas.
Created through supernatural power, they originally possess no life-force (*jīvitendriya*). In the final age when no Buddha is present, there is no basis for such transformations to appear.

This leads to the eating of the flesh of sentient beings. As for "the opening of the mind," it refers to gaining power through meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). However, the obstacle of eating meat is profound; it appears real but is not so in truth.
Regarding "parts of the body," this refers to skins, furs, and the like, which are also parts of that [sentient being's] body;

wearing them creates a karmic connection with the creature. At the beginning of the kalpa, human bodies emitted flying light and their feet moved as if riding upon clouds; later, they ate the "earth-fat" (*pṛthivī-maṇḍa*).
When they eat fragrant rice, it immediately becomes a condition for the earth; its substance becomes solid and heavy, and they can no longer leave the earth.

Ānanda, furthermore, regarding the sentient beings of the six realms within the world: if their minds do not harbor theft, they will not follow along with the continuous succession of birth and death.
You cultivate samādhi fundamentally to emerge from worldly toil; if the mind of theft is not eliminated, you cannot escape the dust of the world. Even if you possess...
Though they possess much knowledge and manifest states of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), if they do not sever [their attachments], they will inevitably fall into deviant paths.
They will be possessed by superior spirits, middling demons, inferior malevolent persons, and various māras;

these various evil beings also have their own followers, each claiming for themselves that they have attained the Unsurpassed Way. After my parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Final Dharma, such demonic and heterodox beings will be numerous and flourish intensely.
In this world, there are those who harbor deceit and fraud while pretending to be spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Each claims for themselves the attainment of the states of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), deluding the ignorant and causing them to lose their minds. Wherever they go, the households they visit suffer depletion and dissipation.
I teach my bhikṣus to wander for alms according to the directions, so that they may abandon greed and perfect the path to Bodhi. These bhikṣus do not cook food for themselves; they rely upon...

With this wretched life, I am a traveler adrift in the three realms, demonstrating a single coming and going; once departed, there is no returning. How can these thieves, wearing my robes, peddle themselves as representatives of the Tathāgata?

They commit all manner of karmic deeds while claiming them to be the Buddha-dharma, yet they slander those who have left the household life and possess the precepts, calling them followers of the Hīnayāna path.
Because of this, they delude and mislead immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to fall into the Avīci Hell. If I...
After my parinirvāṇa, if there be a bhikṣu who resolves his mind to cultivate samādhi and, before an image of the Tathāgata,
burns a single lamp with his own body, sears a finger-joint, or applies a single incense stick to his flesh— I declare that such a person shall, at once,
repay all karmic debts from beginningless time, bid a final farewell to the world, and forever be liberated from all outflows (āsravas). Although they have not yet...
This clearly elucidates the path to unsurpassed enlightenment. Such a person has already attained a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma;

yet, if they do not undergo this slight cause for the sacrifice of their body, even if they were to achieve the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they would inevitably be reborn as a human being to repay their past debts, just as it was with my own "horse-barley" [period], exactly so and no different.
You shall teach the people of the world to practice *samādhi* first, and only thereafter renounce theft; this is called the Tathāgata’s method following the Buddhas of the past.
“World-Honored One, these three equal determinations are the clear instructions for purification.

Therefore, Ānanda, if one who practices dhyāna-concentration does not cease stealing, it is like a person pouring water into a leaking cup; though they seek to fill it, even after passing through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, it will never be full.
If bhikṣus do not store even a fraction of what remains from their robes and alms bowls, and give away the surplus of their begged food to the hungry...”
When sentient beings gather in a great assembly and join their palms to pay homage to the multitude, if someone strikes or reviles them, they should regard it as identical to praise.
They must ensure that both body and mind are completely relinquished; their flesh, bones, and blood are shared with all sentient beings.

They shall not take the Tathāgata’s teachings of provisional meaning and twist them into their own interpretations to mislead beginners. The Buddha certifies such a person as having attained true samādhi, just as I have.
What is thus spoken is called the Buddha’s teaching; if it is not spoken in this way, it is the teaching of Pāpīyān.
"The mind does not steal" means that thoughts of profit and desire do not arise. Only by wearying of the mundane dust can one transcend the dust;

how could one who craves the world ever be able to go beyond the world? This applies not only to taking another's wealth, but even to assuming a formal appearance to solicit the respect, profit, and gain of others.
To nurture [such things] is entirely theft. A thieving mind turns toward depravity; therefore, one falls into the ranks of the heterodox.

With demonic speech they terrify people, causing them to alter their hearts and change their wills so that they revere [the false teacher] as a divine spirit and exhaust their wealth to serve him. "Vending" means selling. "Assisting" means aiding. It refers to assisting the thieving mind by vending the Buddha-dharma.
To claim that the creation of karma is the Buddha-dharma is to preach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma. It is not...
To possess the precepts for the sake of the Lesser Vehicle is to preach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma. A thief takes another’s *parigraha* (possessions) to support his own body;
now, by sacrificing one’s own *upabhoga* (primary retribution) to provide for the Supreme Sages, one is able to overturn and destroy the karma of theft from beginningless time.

Furthermore, among all things difficult to relinquish, nothing exceeds one’s own body. If one can relinquish that which is most difficult to relinquish, then all other attachments and cravings will certainly be cast aside.
Therefore, it is said that for such a person regarding the Dharma, the mind has already reached a state of certainty.

If one were able to renounce the body while the mind did not reach a definitive renunciation, it would merely increase the suffering of karma and provide no benefit to the Path. In a previous life, the Buddha scolded a bhikṣu, saying he should eat horse barley;

yet after realizing the fruits of enlightenment, he ate it at the city of Vairaṇyā. This demonstrates that past debts must inevitably be repaid. If even harsh words must be repaid, how much more so the karmic consequences of one's deeds!
How much more so for those who fail to repay their debts! One does not hoard things for oneself; one regards destruction as praise.

Regarding the two paths of benefit and harm, one relinquishes both body and mind. To share one’s person with the multitude is the ultimate form of renunciation. When one’s conduct can reach this level, it is evident that the mind is free from theft.
The *Āgamas* state that the goods one accumulates should serve to sustain the body and advance the Way. The *Sarvāstivāda*...
To say that one should store a single item of each of many hundreds of things is a provisional teaching; it is all of expedient meaning and not definitive.

To observe this practice makes one feel shame and shed tears. One can see that the patriarchs of the Final Dharma established the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*) out of compassion for the times, adapting themselves to benefit sentient beings;
it was not their only choice. Those who dwell in such places should always feel ashamed that they are unable to realize the fruit of realization themselves.

If one harbors even a single hair’s breadth of ambition for gain and offerings, one will barely escape transgression. Should one encounter someone challenging this scripture, one must truthfully state that it cannot be mastered in the Dharma-ending age;
one must not employ clever words to claim it is beyond obstruction.
Ānanda, it is thus with the sentient beings of the six realms in this world:

although their bodies and minds may be free from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—such that these three practices are already perfected—if they commit a great falsehood, then their *samādhi* will not attain purity; they will become demons of craving and views and lose the seed of the Tathāgata.
This refers to claiming to have attained what one has not attained, or declaring to have realized what one has not realized, or seeking to be the most honored, supreme, and foremost in the world.

One says to the person before them: "I have now attained the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, the path of arhat, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the various stages of the bodhisattvas from the ten bhūmis down to those prior to the bhūmis. One then requests them to perform prostrations and repentance.
Coveting offerings is the first *icchantika* act; it extinguishes the seed of the Buddha. It is like a person cutting down a *tāla* tree with a sword;

the Buddha has prophesied that such a person will forever destroy their roots of goodness, never again attain knowledge or vision, sink into the ocean of the three sufferings, and fail to achieve *samādhi*.
After my parinirvāṇa, I shall command all bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their bodies within that age of the final dharma,
assuming various forms to deliver those wandering in saṃsāra— whether appearing as śramaṇas, laypeople, householders, kings, or government officials.
Whether they be boys or girls, or even courtesans, widows, adulterers, thieves, butchers, or merchants— whenever he associates with them,
he praises the Buddha Vehicle and causes their bodies and minds to enter samādhi, yet he never says of himself, "I am truly a bodhisattva."
A true Arhat would not leak the Buddha’s secret causes, nor would he speak lightly of what has not yet been learned; only at the end of life would there be a hidden entrustment.
How could such a person delude and confuse sentient beings by committing a great falsehood? You teach the people of the world to cultivate samādhi.
Thereafter, he further eliminated all great falsehoods. This is called the fourth definitive, pure, and clear instruction of the Tathāgata, the World-Honored Buddha of former times.
Therefore, Ānanda, if one does not eliminate such great falsehoods, it is like carving into human excrement.
To seek fragrance from a sandalwood statue—such a thing is impossible.

I teach my bhikṣus that at the site of the Way, within the four modes of deportment and all actions, there must be no pretense whatsoever. How then can you claim to have attained the dharmas of a superior person?
It is like a destitute person who falsely claims to be an emperor, only to bring about his own execution; how much more so for one who would falsely usurp the title of Dharma King?
If the ground is not true, the fruit will be crooked. To seek the Bodhi of the Buddha under such conditions is like a man trying to bite his own navel—who can possibly achieve success?
If there are bhikṣus whose minds are as straight as a bowstring, who are entirely truthful, and who enter samādhi, they will forever be free from the deeds of Māra.
I certify that such persons shall achieve the unsurpassed awakening of a bodhisattva. What I have thus spoken is called the word of the Buddha.
It is not as you say; it is the speech of Pāpīyān.

To claim one has attained the four fruits and ten stages when one has not yet attained them is called great false speech. To crave offerings and seek one’s own preeminence is called the demon of craving (tṛṣṇāmāra).
To falsely give rise to wrong views and claim one is equal to the sages is called the demon of views (dṛṣṭimāra). All of these constitute great falsehoods.
*Tīrthika* refers to the *icchantika*, which here means "one who lacks faith. *Tāla* means "the shape of a shore"; it is the name of a tree.
If its root is severed by a sword, it will never sprout again. One who severs the seed of the Buddha through false speech is like a sword cutting through wood.
He manifests identical forms and activities to make it easy for others to believe and accept. Alternatively, he employs four propositions: these are propositions that accord with worldly practice;

these are propositions that oppose worldly practice; and the praise of two propositions applies to both the preceding categories of accord and opposition, extolling the Buddha’s propagation of the Dharma.

This enables people to enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). Although he manifests his form and engages in activities alongside others, he never speaks of his own sacred traces (*ārya-caryā*) before beginners, lest he leak the secrets of the profound mechanism.

If one abides [in truth], there is no leakage. The four modes of deportment are walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. To result in a circuitous path means to receive retribution in the three miserable realms.

Branches and leaves. Three in the mind and four in the mouth; birth must be without cause.

That the mind and speech are now both termed "branches and leaves" is because, in terms of their arising, internal mental action (manas-karman) first arises, which then externally manifests as bodily and vocal actions.

therefore, he was made to look back within himself. Now that the practitioner has likewise looked back within, he desires to seek empowerment.

The Upādhyāya [prepared] sandalwood, aloeswood, *suhaka*, *turushka*, *urukuru*, *śrīveṣṭaka*, *sāriva*, *agaru*, *jātī*, and *kakkola*.

It is the crown of the myriad practices. Its foundation is level ground, symbolizing the Middle Way and faith.

Because the surface of the earth was not yet pure, it was excavated. Among the five numbers, yellow is selected; among the colors, it represents the pure faith of the "middle of the middle. The ten incenses symbolize the Dharma-fragrance of the ten *pāramitās*.
The fine silk woven into powder symbolizes the subtle and wondrous myriad practices. The altar symbolizes tranquility.

It extinguishes the substance of falsehood; since its substance possesses the Eightfold Noble Path, it has eight corners. Because it can subdue the eight heterodoxies, it measures sixteen feet square.

This represents the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Each is placed in the eight directions.

They correctly encompass one another; their virtuous conduct mutually perfumes one another until, over time, both are transformed. Thus, both the heterodox and the orthodox are forgotten.

Purely burning aloeswood incense, ensuring that no one sees the fire, symbolizes the reversal of the treasury of virtue’s function and the extinction of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), thereby entering into accord with the field of quiescence.

One must necessarily attain the wisdom that dwells detached from objects and without support, so that these two may function in mutual interplay. Only then can the Buddha and the self illuminate one another, and mind and object be simultaneously fused.
The bodies and lands of all Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate one another; all phenomena are universally pervasive, and all things are without obstruction.

Ānanda, this *Buddhōṣṇīṣa-raśmi-samuccaya-sitātapatra* secret verse, these subtle and wondrous phrases, give birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions.
By means of this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, holding this mantra-heart, subdue all Māras and restrain all external [obstructors].
The Way: The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, mounting this mantra-heart, sit upon precious lotus flowers and respond to lands as numerous as motes of dust.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, containing this mantra-heart, turn the Great Dharma Wheel in lands as numerous as motes of dust.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions, upholding this mantra-heart, are able to bestow the prediction of enlightenment by touching their heads in the ten directions; even when their own fruition is not yet complete, they likewise receive the Buddha’s prediction throughout the ten directions.

Record. The Tathāgatas of the ten directions rely upon this mantra-heart to be able to rescue and deliver sentient beings from the various sufferings throughout the ten directions—namely, those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals;
those who are blind, deaf, or mute; the suffering of encountering the hated; the suffering of being separated from the beloved; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks;

the blazing intensity of the five aggregates; and all manner of great and small calamities. They are simultaneously liberated from the perils of bandits, the perils of war, the perils of kings, and the perils of imprisonment.
Difficulties—calamities of wind, fire, and water, as well as hunger, thirst, and poverty—shall dissolve and vanish upon mere recollection.

Following this mantra-heart, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are able to serve spiritual friends throughout the ten directions; within the four modes of deportment, they make offerings according to their wishes.
