Among the assemblies of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are promoted as Great Dharma Princes. When the Tathāgatas of the ten directions practice this mantra-heart, they are able, within the ten [directions]...
This is precisely to gather in the immediate causes [of enlightenment] so that those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), upon hearing this Secret Treasury, shall not give rise to fear or alarm.
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions recite this mantra-heart; thereby they achieve unsurpassed awakening, sit beneath the Bodhi tree, and enter Great Nirvāṇa.

The Tathāgatas of the ten directions transmit this mantra-heart so that, after their parinirvāṇa, the affairs of the Buddha-dharma may be entrusted to them for ultimate maintenance and upholding, and the precepts may be strictly purified.

The Vinaya is entirely purified. If I were to speak this Buddha-Crown Radiance Gathita Mantra from dawn until dusk, with its sounds linked together and its syllables and phrases neither overlapping nor redundant, even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one could never reach the end.
This mantra is also called the Tathāgata’s Crown. You who are still in training and have not yet exhausted the cycle of saṃsāra, should arouse the mind [to seek it].

Truly, if one seeks arhatship but does not maintain this mantra while sitting in the place of enlightenment, it is impossible for their body and mind to remain far removed from all demonic activities.
This mantra can give birth to all Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, because of this, repay [their debt].
This [mantra], by mounting upon this and even transmitting this, accomplishes various wondrous functions. If it is so for a Buddha, how much more so for an ordinary person?
For this mantra-heart is the mother of all Buddhas; it is the true seed from which the Tathāgatas are born.
Thus, a Buddha must necessarily rely upon it to attain Bodhi. Possessing great majestic power, it is the vajra that cuts through evil delusions.
The King’s precious sword; therefore, the Buddha must wield it to subdue Māra and externalists, and to transport sentient beings across to liberation from birth and death.
It is the great white ox-cart that emerges from the burning house; therefore, the Buddha must mount it to respond to the realms of the dust.
Encompassing myriad virtues, it is the true treasure-trove of the complete wealth of the Dharma; therefore, the Buddha necessarily contains it to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
"To contain" (*han*) means to store. It universally sustains (*dhāraṇī*) all phenomena, both wholesome and unwholesome;

it is the authentic seal of the Unsurpassed Sovereign of Awakening. Therefore, the Buddha necessarily maintains it to bestow predictions of enlightenment upon others, serving as the merit for their peace and security.
The place where he dwells is the supreme banner that transcends all fear; therefore, the Buddha necessarily relies upon it to rescue others from suffering and deliver them from distress.
"Relies" (*yi*) means to depend upon. It accords with the nature of awakening and is the wish-fulfilling jewel that satisfies the heart's desires.
Therefore, the Buddha necessarily follows this path to universally make offerings to the sages and worthies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. "Follows" means to accord with;
it is the great thoroughfare through which a thousand sages and ten thousand worthies pass without obstruction.

Thus, the Buddha necessarily practices this to gather in those with whom he has a karmic affinity and to reveal the secrets, reaching ultimate perfection. This is the solemn edict of the Dharma King summoning the myriad nations. Therefore—
The Buddha certainly recited it to achieve perfect enlightenment and enter *nirvāṇa*, remaining forever without extinction.
It is the great lamp of wisdom that universally illuminates both the mundane and supramundane worlds; therefore, the Buddha certainly transmitted it to endure for ten thousand generations.
Among all dharmic practices, the precepts (*śīla*) are the precursor. Once the precepts are pure, all dharmic practices will attain ultimate fulfillment.

Regarding the statement that these ten kinds are spoken of as the *dhāraṇī-mantra-heart*: since the *mantra-heart* is the *tathāgatagarbha-citta*, the first is the general [principle] and the remaining nine are the particulars.

This is still but a brief explanation; therefore, it is further said that even this cannot exhaustively describe it. The above constitutes the realm of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, to speak of the lower [levels]:
this correctly answers [the question of] how the *dhāraṇī* at the site of enlightenment (*dojō*) gathers the mind and keeps one far from demons.
Ānanda, if in any world, in whatever land, among all sentient beings born in that country, one were to write this dhāraṇī on birch bark,
palm leaves, paper, silk, or white woolen cloth, and store it in a fragrant pouch; or if, because the person’s mind is dull and they are unable to recite or memorize it,
they wear it upon their body or inscribe it within their home— it should be known that throughout the entirety of that person’s life, all [obstacles shall be removed].
One cannot be harmed by any poisons.
One should teach others to transcribe and carry [this mantra]. This briefly cites one section of its merit—namely, that poisons cannot cause harm; the details are explained in the text below.

When reciting the mantra, one must necessarily empty the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*) and realize the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*); only then will efficacy be attained. As for transcribing and carrying it, [the same applies].
It relies solely upon faith. If one’s faith is weak or superficial, the efficacy may not be immediately realized; this is not because the mantra lacks power.
Ānanda, I shall now further explain this mantra for you, which protects and rescues the world, grants great fearlessness, and brings about the supramundane wisdom of all beings.
After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sentient beings in the final age who can recite it themselves, or if they teach it to others...

He recited it. It should be known that for sentient beings who maintain this recitation in this manner, fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, and they cannot be harmed by great or small poisons.
Furthermore, no evil spells—whether from devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits, or from *piśācas*, *bhūtas*, or *mārakṣas*—can take hold of them.
Their minds attain right concentration (*samādhi*), and all curses, sorcery, malevolent poisons, and metallic poisons [are rendered powerless].
If the poisons of silver, the venom of plants, trees, insects, and snakes, or the toxic vapors of the myriad things enter the mouth of such a person, they will turn into the taste of nectar.
All malevolent stars, as well as various ghosts and spirits and those who harbor cruel hearts and poison others, cannot give rise to evil thoughts toward such a person.
Even Vināyakas and all the evil kings of ghosts, together with their retinues, will all acknowledge this profound kindness and constantly provide protection. Ānanda!
It should be known that this mantra is constantly attended by eighty-four thousand nayutas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, of koṭis of Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas and their clans;
each one has a retinue of vajra-beings who serve them day and night.

Should there be sentient beings who, with a distracted mind and not in samādhi, remember it in their hearts and maintain it with their mouths, this [Vajragarbha-rāja]— (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the input.)
O Vajra King, [the power of this] constantly follows those sons of good family; how much more so for one who has resolved upon the bodhicitta!
These Vajra Bodhisattvas, Kings of the Treasury, with their refined minds acting swiftly in secret, awaken that divine consciousness.
Such a person, at that moment, will be able to remember eighty-four thousand *Ganges-sand* eons, knowing them all thoroughly and without any doubt.
This is a general statement regarding the merits of reciting and upholding [the mantra], such as "fire cannot burn" and so forth;
that is to say, it provides protection for the world and attains great fearlessness. "With a refined mind, secretly and swiftly, one awakens that divine consciousness" and so forth;

that is to say, it accomplishes the supramundane wisdom of sentient beings. The various specific explanations below do not go beyond these two categories: reciting the mantra for the benefit of others.
Therefore, all the evil ghost-kings shall receive this profound grace. As for the Vajra Attendant, this mantra is itself the Vajra Jewel-Awakening;
thus, they resonate with one another like kindred voices. "Darkness" (*yin*) refers to a shadowy place.

One who has resolved upon the Bodhicitta not only has [the deity] constantly follow them, but can further, within the midst of obscurity, bestow empowerment through spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) to swiftly cause [them] to awaken.
They shall develop spiritual consciousness and be rendered free from doubt; for with adamantine wisdom one is able to sever the doubts of others.
From the first kalpa until their final body, in every successive birth they shall not be born as yakṣas, rākṣasas, or pūtanas.
Kakavīṭas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, and all other hungry ghosts— whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception—
in such evil places, this son of good family, whether reading or reciting, or copying or transcribing [this], [will find no harm].
Whether one wears it or keeps it hidden, by making offerings of various forms, one will not be born into poverty, lowliness, or unpleasant states throughout kalpa after kalpa;
this clarifies that one does not follow the evil destinies. Because this mantra-heart is a pure and white dharma and is the most supreme goodness.
The first kalpa refers to the moment one first generates the bodhicitta; the final body refers to the time of attaining Buddhahood at the very end.
The practice in between is forever free from any signs of deviousness. Yakṣas and the like all possess such devious characteristics.
The passage beginning with "good man" clarifies that one will not be born into a lowly station, because this mantra-heart is the most supreme and noble of dharmas.
Those who read, recite, copy, or transcribe [this scripture] are all like a crown prince dwelling in the womb, their noble status surpassing that of all ministers.
Even if these sentient beings do not personally perform meritorious deeds themselves, they shall partake in all the merits and virtues of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

He gives all of this to this person. By means of this, for *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—indeed, for unspeakably unspeakable kalpas—they shall always be born in the same place as the Buddhas.
Their immeasurable merits will be like clusters of akṣa fruit, cultivated together in one place so that they are never dispersed.
Therefore, it can cause those who have broken the precepts to purify the root of their morality, and enable those who have not yet attained the precepts to attain them.
It causes those who have not yet received the precepts to obtain them; it causes those who are not diligent to attain diligence; it causes those who lack wisdom to attain wisdom;
it causes those who are not pure to quickly attain purity; and it causes those who do not observe the fast and precepts to spontaneously fulfill them.
This clarifies the merit obtained in the present. Regarding the statement that "the Tathāgata’s merits are all bestowed upon this person":

because of this *dhāraṇī*-heart, it is the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Crown; and the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s Crown is precisely the practitioner’s own inherently possessed *garbha-citta* (store-consciousness-heart).
One who can maintain the mantra maintains their own *garbha-citta*. Since the *garbha-citta* is fully endowed with the myriad practices (*sāhasra-pratipatti*), what blessings would not be complete?
Those Buddhas who are born in the same place share a connection with the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of all Buddhas;

their minds are in perfect harmony, for the Buddha does not depart from the mind, and the mind does not depart from the Buddha. Thus, the *akṣa*-berry cluster is a metaphor for precept, concentration, and wisdom.

Those who practice together without distraction do so because that which the practitioner cultivates is precisely that which the Buddhas have realized, having been forged into a single whole. This breaks [the duality].
For those who have not yet observed the precepts, the purity of the roots of morality is like a single grain of elixir that transforms iron into gold;

thus, those who have not yet attained the precepts shall attain them because they possess the root of morality. Those who have not yet attained progress shall attain it because they possess the root of energy.
Those who lack wisdom shall attain it because they possess the root of wisdom. Those who are impure shall become pure by themselves because they possess the root of purity.
Ānanda, when these sons of good family uphold this mantra, even if they have violated the prohibitive precepts prior to receiving them,

all offenses of breaking the precepts— whether light or heavy— are instantly extinguished after upholding the mantra. Even if they should drink alcohol or consume the five pungent roots and various kinds of impurities,
all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajras, celestial immortals, spirits, and deities will not [reject them].
This would be a transgression. Even if one wears impure and tattered clothing, whether walking or standing still, it is entirely the same as being pure.

Even if one does not construct an altar, does not enter a *maṇḍala*, and does not practice the Way, yet recites and upholds this mantra, it is identical in merit to entering the altar and practicing the Way;
there is no difference whatsoever. Even if one has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) or [if] various bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs...
Nuns, having recited this mantra, even such grave karmic offenses as the four *pārājika* and eight *saṃghāvaśeṣa* will be completely eradicated—
just as a fierce wind scatters a heap of sand— leaving not even a hair’s breadth behind. Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas,
have accumulated all manner of light and heavy karmic obstructions from previous lives that they have not yet had the opportunity to repent— if they can [recite this mantra]...

If one recites, chants, copies, or wears this dhāraṇī upon the body, or establishes it in one’s dwelling, house, garden, or villa, then such accumulated karma will be dissolved like snow melting in hot water;
before long, all shall attain the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
This can extinguish present karma before it has been experienced—that is, before the mantra has been recited. Once the mantra has been recited, one must not commit further transgressions.
Wearing impure clothing refers to being destitute and lacking the necessary provisions. The ritual requirements for the mandala are extremely difficult to fulfill completely.
Therefore, it is permitted to recite mantras even without a consecrated altar; do not doubt that there is a difference in their merit.

For a bhikṣu, there are four *pārājika* offenses—namely, the four root transgressions of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. One who commits these four is forever cast out from the Buddha-Dharma as if to the far seas;

they are not allowed to sit together with others, nor are they included in the ranks of the Saṃgha. For a bhikṣuṇī, there are an additional four *pārājika* offenses; the fifth is called "contact," which refers to [sexual contact] with a male.
The sixth is called the eighth because it consists of eight matters:

namely, taking a man’s hand, grasping his robe, entering a secluded place together, sitting together in a secluded place, speaking together, walking together, leaning against one another, and making appointments.
The seventh is called concealment (*paticchādanā*): this refers to when a nun, upon hearing the Great Sangha preach the Dharma, conceals the offenses of others and refuses to acknowledge them.

To confess before the assembly. The eighth is called "following" (*anuvartana*); this refers to a nun who, while the formal rite of co-residence (*sahavāsa*) has not yet been performed for her by the assembly, nonetheless follows those in co-residence.
Together with the four aforementioned *pārājika* offenses, these are thus called the eight *pārājikas*. From the passage beginning with "Ānanda," one is able to exhaust past karma;

just as a single lamp can dispel the darkness of a thousand-year-old room, so too does one awaken to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which constitutes the second gradual stage.
Next is the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*),
which still lies prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is a woman who has not yet given birth to children and desires to conceive,
if she can recollect this mantra with a sincere heart, or if she can wear this *Siddhārthapāṇḍarā* [mantra] upon her person, she will immediately give rise to merit.
Virtuous men and women who seek long life shall immediately obtain long life; those who wish for their karmic rewards to be swiftly fulfilled shall quickly attain fulfillment.
It is likewise so for their physical vitality and strength. After the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the lands of the ten directions according to their vows;
they will certainly not be born in remote regions or among the lowly, much less in mixed forms.

This is able to fulfill all wishes. Among the thousand kinds of treasures of the ocean, one first seeks that which accords with one's intent; this mantra-heart is the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
Taking from it is inexhaustible, and using it is never depleted. Therefore, while alive, one acts with sovereign freedom according to the mind; yet at the time of death—
One shall also attain rebirth according to one's vows and never be born into a lowly station.
Because this mantra-heart is an incomparable dharma and a most precious treasure, one shall go alone and come alone, being honored everywhere.
Ānanda, if there are kingdoms, prefectures, counties, or villages where famine and pestilence prevail,
or where there are calamities of war, bandits, and strife, as well as all other lands of misfortune— copy this divine mantra and place it at the four gates of the city,
as well as at various caityas or atop gate-towers, so that all sentient beings within those territories may welcome and pay homage to this mantra.
With reverence and single-minded devotion, they shall make offerings and cause each of their people to wear it upon their bodies or place it within their respective dwellings;
thus, all calamities and misfortunes shall be entirely extinguished. Ānanda, in every location and throughout the lands, for all sentient beings—
Wherever this mantra exists, devas and nāgas will rejoice; wind and rain will follow their proper seasons; the five grains will be abundant; and the myriad people will be peaceful and happy.
Furthermore, it can subdue all malevolent stars and regional portents, ensuring that calamities and obstacles do not arise, and that no one suffers untimely death.
Manacles, fetters, cangues, and shackles shall not touch their bodies; they shall sleep peacefully day and night, and always be free from evil dreams.

Ānanda, in this Sahā world, there are eighty-four thousand calamitous and malevolent stars, with twenty-eight great malevolent stars as their leaders, and furthermore eight great malevolent stars that act as their sovereigns. When they manifest in the world in various forms, they are able to—
The various calamities and anomalies that arise among sentient beings will all be completely extinguished where this dhāraṇī-ground exists.
Within an area of twelve yojanas, it shall become a consecrated boundary (sīmābandha) where no evil omens or disasters can ever enter.

This can eliminate calamities. Various calamities arise from acting contrary to principle; now, by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one is forever free from all faults, so that nothing can enter.
*Cetiya* (支提) means a place worthy of offerings, a general term for a pure land (*śuddhakṣetra*).
*Dvāra* (脫闍) refers to a city gate-tower. "Single-mindedly making offerings" means to pay homage with undivided attention; only then may one attain [the result].
Regarding these spiritual manifestations: the eighty-four thousand malevolent stars are induced by the eighty-four thousand afflictions of sentient beings.
Each of the twenty-eight lunar mansions governs specific matters, which transform according to the goodness or evil of the human heart.
When there is goodness, blessings respond; when there is evil, calamities respond. The eight great malevolent stars are the five elements (wuxing) along with Rāhu, Ketu, and Piṅgalā. Now...
These are cited as examples of adverse locations; thus, they are collectively termed "malefic stars. *Yojana*—here translated as "limitation"—equals forty *li*.
"Auspicious" (*xiang*) refers to a favorable omen. How does one ward these off? The intention is that tranquility and harmony constitute blessings.
For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaims this mantra to protect all beginners and practitioners in future ages as they enter samādhi,
so that their bodies and minds may be at ease and attain great peace and security, free from all demons, ghosts, and spirits.
As well as the karmic calamities and宿殃 (past misfortunes) from beginningless time, and the long-standing debts of past karma that come to cause harm and affliction:
you, along with all those among the assembly who are still in training, and all practitioners of future ages, shall rely upon my maṇḍala and maintain the precepts according to the Dharma.
If the preceptor from whom one received the precepts encounters a pure monk, and this son of good family does not give rise to doubt or regret regarding this mantra-heart,
then the Tathāgatas of the ten directions would be speaking falsehoods if he were unable to attain mental penetration within this body born of his parents.
One returns to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to practice. Regarding the "body of the parents": it means that the present body is itself the realization.
When the mind penetrates [this], as before, without rising from one's seat, one attains the stage of *srotāpanna*. One knows with certainty that one will attain Buddhahood without error.
At that time, the mind is able to remember [events] across eighty-four thousand *Ganges-sand* eons.

Having spoken these words, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of vajras in the assembly simultaneously joined their palms before the Buddha, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall protect with sincere hearts those who thus cultivate bodhi."
At that time, Brahmā King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Great Kings also simultaneously prostrated before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"If there are indeed such virtuous persons who practice and study in this way, we shall protect them with our whole hearts and utmost sincerity."
May all that they have done throughout their lives be fulfilled according to their wishes.
Furthermore, there are immeasurable yakṣa generals, rākṣasa kings, pūtana kings, kumbhāṇḍa kings, piśāca kings, and the great ghost-kings of the vināyakas.

The various leaders of the spirits likewise joined their palms before the Buddha and prostrated themselves. I, too, vow to protect and sustain these people, causing their bodhicitta to be swiftly brought to full perfection.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable sons of the gods of the sun and moon, as well as the masters of wind and rain.

The Master of Clouds, the Master of Thunder, the Earl of Lightning, and others—the annual circuit officials and the retinues of all the stars—also prostrated at the Buddha’s feet within the assembly and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We, too, shall protect these practitioners and establish their sites of practice.”

They attained fearlessness. Furthermore, immeasurable mountain deities and ocean deities, all the spirits of the earth, waters, lands, and those that travel through air and space, along with the essence-spirits of the myriad things and the Wind Deity Kings, as well as the gods of the Formless Realm, simultaneously bowed their heads before the Tathāgata.
And he addressed the Buddha, saying: "I, too, shall protect these practitioners so that they may attain Bodhi, forever free from demonic interference.
This is the mantra for protection by the assembly of deities: the assembly of Vajra-mighty ones; the assembly of devas from the Brahma realm downward;

the Formless Heavens shall be present here; the assembly of the Eight Divisions from the Yakṣas downward; the assembly of celestial spirits from the Sun and Moon downward; and the mountain spirits from below."
O assembly of terrestrial deities, this mantra is the heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of the Tathāgata; therefore, wherever it may be, it shall be guarded by a hundred spirits.
At that time, there were eighty-four thousand *nayuta* of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* *koṭi* Vajragarbha-rāja Bodhisattvas.
In the great assembly, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, as for the meritorious deeds we have cultivated, we shall long ago attain Bodhi and not enter Nirvana, but shall constantly follow this mantra to protect and deliver those who cultivate *samādhi* and practice correctly during the final age.
World-Honored One, for those who thus cultivate the mind and seek right concentration...”
Whether they are at a place of practice, walking in meditation, or even wandering through villages with a distracted mind, we and our followers shall always follow and protect this person;
even if Māra or Maheśvara should seek an opportunity against them.
It can never be obtained. All minor spirits and deities shall remain ten yojanas away from these virtuous people, except for those who have resolved their minds to joyfully cultivate dhyāna.

World-Honored One, if such evil Māras or their retinues should wish to come and harass these virtuous people, I shall shatter their heads with my precious mallet until they are like fine dust, so that the deeds of these people may always proceed unimpeded.
"May it be as you wish.
This is the protective mantra of the Bodhisattva. In the 'Ten Stages' chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Dharma King [Vajrapāṇi] acts as the master of the teaching;
abiding in the higher stages, he manifests a vajra body and constantly protects this mantra. Below the words of the World-Honored One, the urgency of protecting the mind is clarified, even though..."
Let it descend! Drive away the external māras. Maheśvara, who rules over the world with a mind of deep attachment and stubborn clinging, has become a god of great pride;
even he shall find no opportunity. As for the other minor spirits and ghosts, they shall depart of their own accord.
Those who have resolved to cultivate dhyāna shall personally dwell beneath the seat of the Tathāgata and may draw near to him. Protect!

Regarding the practitioner who says that the precious vajra shatters his head: this is the simultaneous application of both subduing and gathering, wherein killing is practiced as an act of compassion.

In cultivation, there is the primary practice and the auxiliary practice. For those of sharp faculties, it is sufficient to engage in the primary cultivation through the single gateway of the ear-faculty.
However, for those whose capacities are somewhat inferior, they must employ the recitation of mantras as an auxiliary practice before they can achieve accomplishment. (Volume Four)
"Please enter this magnificent hall; this is called the Section on the Factors of the Path to Cultivation. Below this begins the Section on the Realization of the Fruits.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "We are dull-witted and fond of mere erudition;
regarding our minds of outflows, we had not yet sought liberation. Having received the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, we have attained correct cultivation of body and mind."

How joyful! We have gained great benefit. World-Honored One, when one thus cultivates and realizes the Buddha’s samādhi, yet has not yet reached nirvāṇa, why is it called the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuklavipaśyanā)?
Regarding the forty-four minds, at what gradual sequence does one obtain the eye of cultivation?

"To what destination does one go to be called 'having entered the stages' (bhūmi)? What is meant by being a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment? Having spoken these words, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground.
The great assembly, with single-minded devotion, awaited the Buddha’s compassionate instruction, gazing up at him with fixed and longing eyes.
This is a request concerning the stages of cultivation and realization. "Nirvana" refers to the ultimate fruit; "dry wisdom" refers to the causal mind.

The stages of faith, abiding, practice, and penetration, along with the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*), are termed the forty-four minds. The three gradual sequences are the headings for the practice.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is termed "realization and entry. Ānanda asked only about the stages of cultivation and realization; the Tathāgata first clarified [the following].

First is the enlightened nature; next, delusion is distinguished; finally, the gradual stages are shown. The wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, fundamentally transcending both the holy and the ordinary, and is likewise devoid of cultivation or realization.
Because of the existence of delusion, one extinguishes the false to reveal the true; it is only then that the stages of cultivation and realization begin to exist.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent!

You are indeed able to universally act for the sake of the great assembly and all sentient beings of the future age who cultivate *samādhi* and seek the Mahāyāna, beginning from the stage of ordinary persons."
In the Great Parinirvāṇa, he has distantly revealed the path of unsurpassed, correct practice. Listen attentively now; I shall speak for you.
Ānanda and the great assembly joined their palms, hollowed out their hearts, and silently received the teaching.

Previously it was said that [this teaching] is far in accord with the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity; here it is said that it reveals from afar the Tathāgata’s path of correct cultivation.

From the three gradual stages up to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment, one passes through fifty-five positions before finally arriving at the home of the Dharma-nature of Bodhi—is this not indeed far?
You have not yet attained entry; therefore, I now lift the curtain for you in advance.
When this is shown to them, they proceed directly from beginning to end toward the place of treasure, without any further detours. "To hollow out" means to carve away;
it signifies emptying the mind to receive the teaching.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda, you should know that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous and free from all names and marks. Originally, there were no worlds or sentient beings;
it is due to delusion that there is birth, and due to birth that there is extinction. Birth and extinction are called delusion; the cessation of delusion is called the True.
This is termed the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed Bodhi and Great Nirvāṇa—the two designations for the transformation of the basis. Ānanda, if you now wish to practice...”
Regarding the true samādhi that leads directly to the Great Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata: one must first recognize these two causes of perversion within the world of sentient beings.
When perversion does not arise, this is the true samādhi of the Tathāgata.
First, it clarifies that the *tathatā* (suchness), which serves as the basis, is free from all marks. "Sublime nature" (*miaoxing*) is a direct pointer to the essence of *tathatā*.

It is called "perfect" (*yuan*) because it universally encompasses and fully possesses all virtues; it is called "luminous" (*ming*) because it brilliantly illuminates the masses of darkness while shining alone.
Regarding that which is free from all names and signs: within the realm of true thusness (tathatā), the provisional designations of "sentient being" and "Buddha" are cut off;
within the state of equality, there are no forms of self and other. Not only are there no worlds or sentient beings, but there is also no bodhi or nirvāṇa.

Regarding the three phrases on the cause of delusion: it is because of defiled conditions that there arise the names "sentient beings" and "the world. The wondrous nature is free from names and transcends all marks; fundamentally, there are no delusions.
It is due to the initial single thought of non-awakening and its deluded movement that the mark of birth and ignorance subsequently arise.
Because of the mark of birth, the marks of abiding, change, and extinction further arise. It is precisely because there is birth and extinction [that these distinctions exist].
Therefore, it is termed "delusion. Consequently, there are two kinds of inversion: namely, that because of fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), there is non-awakening (*a-bodhi*).
Regarding the five phrases on the extinction of delusion: through pure conditions, there arise the designations of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
One transforms the inversion of the world by relying on *bodhi*; one transforms the inversion of sentient beings by relying on *nirvāṇa*. That is to say:

Based on non-awakening (*abodha*), there is awakening (*abhisambodhi*). From "Ānanda" onwards, [the text] directly indicates that the two kinds of fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) should be sought within the two kinds of causes of inversion (*viparyāsa*).
This is because it is at the place where these two kinds of inversions do not arise.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s true samādhi; it is what was previously stated: "The deluded mind ceases of its own accord; this cessation is itself bodhi.
Thus we know that the two paths of the sage and the ordinary person are both established based on birth-and-death versus delusion-and-awakening. Within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā),...
"In truth, such a thing does not exist. Below this, the two types of inversion are elucidated. Sentient beings dwell in dependence upon the world, and the world arises because of sentient beings;
the two are inseparable, as is seen from their mutual relationship in the text.

Ānanda, what is meant by the "inversion" of sentient beings? Ānanda, because the nature of the luminous mind is inherently bright and perfect, one takes that luminosity as a basis to give rise to a "nature.
From this, deluded vision arises. What was ultimately non-existent becomes ultimately existent. This existence and its objects—this is what is called inversion.

It is not a cause for a cause, nor is it the characteristic of that which abides or that in which it abides; it is understood to be utterly without foundation. Taking this non-abiding as its basis, it establishes the world and all sentient beings.
This is a general indication that ignorance perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness) to produce its defiled function, serving as the cause for the two kinds of inversion.

The two characters "zhòngshēng" (sentient beings) are a corruption of the two characters "èrzhǒng" (two kinds). "Xìngmíngxīn" (nature-bright-mind) refers to the essence of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*).
"Yuán" (perfect/round) means it penetrates both the delusory and the true. Regarding "due to brightness, the nature is manifested": "brightness" here refers to ignorance (*avidyā*);

"manifesting the nature" means the nature manifested by ignorance, which is the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*). "Delusory vision" refers to the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*). "Ultimately existent" refers to the aspect of appearance (*nimitta-bhāga*).

From the essence of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*), there arises a single moment of deluded movement, whereby ignorance (*avidyā*) comes into being. Due to ignorance, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is formed;

due to the karmic consciousness, the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arises; and due to the subjective aspect, the sense organs, the physical body, and the objective world (*bhājana-loka*) come into existence.

This is what is meant by: "Within that which is devoid of identity or difference, there blazes forth the formation of difference. Thus, the ignorance that possesses the capacity for manifestation and all sentient beings [are one].
The world is fundamentally without cause; it is not a cause from which anything is produced. It is also without abode;
it is not a place wherein anything dwells. Like flowers in the sky, like dreams during sleep, when interrogated it has no root, and when sought it has no basis.
Taking this very non-abiding ignorance as the basis, one establishes the two kinds of perversion regarding the world and sentient beings.

Being deluded regarding the fundamental perfect luminosity gives rise to what is false and illusory. This illusory nature has no substance and does not have anything upon which it depends. Now, wishing to return to the truth, [one proceeds].

Desire, being truly unreal, is not the true nature of suchness. Seeking to restore what is unreal results in the manifestation of unreal characteristics. It is neither arising nor abiding; it is neither mind nor phenomena.
Through successive occurrences, the power of arising brings forth illumination, which perfumes the seeds to form karma. Thus, through the mutual resonance of similar karma, [the cycle continues].
Due to the existence of karmic conditions through perception, one characteristic ceases while another arises. For this reason, sentient beings undergo perversion.

This clarifies that the perversion of sentient beings arises from views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The wondrous nature is luminously perfect; when deluded regarding it, false and illusory phenomena arise.
Delusion of the truth gives rise to falsehood, yet the nature of falsehood is fundamentally empty and lacks any substantial essence. Such is the perversion of ordinary beings.
This being so, let it be. To proceed: this refers to the inverted views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

Since the nature of delusion is empty and one realizes that delusion has no substance, and since delusion itself has no basis, they nonetheless pointlessly seek to return to the True. They claim that apart from delusion there exists a separate True Reality.
Yet this very single thought of desiring the True is already not the true Suchness-nature (tathatā). True Suchness...
Because its nature does not depart from delusion, once one knows it is not real, one still seeks to restore it—just as knowing something is an illusion, yet one still seeks that very illusion;
ultimately, nothing exists. Therefore, it is called "non-characteristic" (*alakṣaṇa*). The two phrases "not arising" (*anutpāda*) and so forth precisely clarify non-characteristic and non-arising.
"Not arising" means not taking what is not a cause to be a cause—that is, falsely calculating and practicing erroneously as the cause for producing a fruit. "Not abiding" (*asthiti*) means not...
To calculate effects as effects and falsely calculate all impermanent states as permanent effects is a mind that is itself deviant wisdom;
it encompasses all deviant and deluded views and understandings, each claiming to clarify the original mind.

To take what is not the Dharma as a deviant object is to encompass all deviant and deluded cultivation and realization, each claiming to have attained the unsurpassed Dharma, thus causing them to revolve and proliferate.

The "six categories of those born" all refer to non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). This class of people claims that they do not create manifest karma and will not undergo future existence, thus distinguishing themselves from ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Yet how could they know that false causes and false effects, false wisdom and false objects mutually induce one another, giving rise to the power of delusion?
Through their actions and intellectual fabrications, they perfume karmic seeds in the present, which will inevitably bring about karmic retribution in the future.
Birth and cessation have no end; when will there be deliverance? Ordinary people derive existence from non-existence, while those of external paths seek the true within the non-true.
Though ordinary people and those of external paths differ, their delusions are one and the same.
Ānanda, what is meant by the inversion of the world? It is that which exists as something possessed; through the false arising of fragmented divisions, this realm is established.
It is not caused by a cause, nor does it abide in an abode; it flows on without staying still, and thus the world is formed.
The three periods of time and the four directions intermingle and interact, transforming sentient beings into twelve categories. Therefore, the world arises from movement.
There is sound; from sound comes form; from form comes fragrance; from fragrance comes touch; from touch comes flavor; from flavor one perceives mental objects (*dharma*).
These six deluded false conceptions constitute the nature of karma. Through these twelve divisions, one revolves in saṃsāra.
Therefore, the world’s sounds, fragrances, tastes, and touches undergo twelve transformations, forming a single cycle. Driven by this revolving cycle, one falls into inversion.
By way of characteristics, there are worlds of egg-birth, womb-birth, moisture-birth, and transformation-birth; those with form and those without form;
those with perception and those without perception; those that are neither with form nor without form, and those that are neither with perception nor without perception.
This explains that the inversion of the world arises from the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). The world is fundamentally pure; how could there be inversion?
It is entirely due to the inversions of sentient beings, whereby consciousness falsely manifests forms. These form twelve categories;
thus, the world also becomes inverted. The phrase "those who possess existence" refers to sentient beings arising from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because there are segmented physical bodies with sense faculties, the boundaries of sentient beings are established; this is the origin of the designation "realm" (*dhātu*).
Fundamentally, there is no cause that serves as the cause for their production, nor is there any location that serves as the place where they abide.
It is solely through the moment-to-moment flux of mental states that the three periods of time are formed; this is the origin of the designation "world" (*loka*).
Thus, by applying the world to the directions and the directions to the world, both result in twelve. This is how sentient beings are transformed;

accordingly, they are formed into twelve categories based on that number. Therefore, below, it is shown that within a single moment of deluded movement, the internal faculties and external objects are simultaneously complete.
When sensory objects come to meet the mind, sound must arrive first, for sound is the most...
It penetrates thoroughly; the ear is likewise pervasive and beneficial. Following a sound, it inevitably seeks form; encountering form, it inevitably perceives fragrance;
perceiving fragrance, it inevitably experiences touch; experiencing touch, it inevitably tastes flavor; tasting flavor, it inevitably cognizes phenomena (*dharma*).

Once phenomena are cognized, the conditions for conceptualization are not relinquished. From the distant to the intimate, it gradually forms the characteristics of grasping and attachment. All things...
Sentient beings wander through birth and existence due to these very things. "Karma" (karmā) means habituation (*vāsanā*). "Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to that which cannot be altered;
this is what is meant by the saying, "habituation forms one's nature. These karmic natures expand to eighty-four thousand, yet they are collectively categorized into twelve divisions.
By citing the four—sound, fragrance, taste, and touch—one encompasses all twelve; the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) exhaustively comprise ten.

The second transformation constitutes one cycle of circulation and return. "Riding upon this downward" means that since the primary elements—the faculties and their objects—already comprise twelve categories, the sentient beings produced from them likewise possess twelve classes.
Ānanda, due to the world’s false transmigration and its fluctuating inversions, the combination of vital energies produces eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts of flying and sinking.
Because of this, there are egg-born beings such as the *kalala* stage, which circulate through the lands;
fish, birds, turtles, and snakes—these kinds fill the world.
The first three phrases refer to the causes that produce [existence]. The final several phrases refer to the results received.

From "harmonious union" (*saṃnipāta*) up to "confused thought" (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*), these point to the interval between cause and effect—the time when one takes rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The same applies below. Regarding the egg-born, they are born solely through confused thought.
"Falsehood" refers to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). "Falsehood and saṃsāra" refers to those who delight in grandiosity and loftiness, refusing to abide in their natural station;

they create their own karma and must undergo its retribution. Because causes inevitably summon their effects, it is called "saṃsāra. "Moving in inversion" means that the true mind does not remain still, as the whole being is agitated.
"Conjunction" refers to the conjunction of the intermediate state body (*antarābhava*) with the conditions for rebirth.
"Qi" refers to the intersection of vital energies; it is the condition for taking birth.

Because one was fond of loftiness and the exertion of vital energy during the causal stage, one takes qi as the condition for birth, thereby giving rise to chaotic thoughts. One will receive the body of a bird due to the thought of levitation;
one will receive the body of a fish due to the thought of swimming. Following these deluded thoughts, life is then transmitted. *Kalala*—this is translated as "congealed."
The world revolves and transforms sentient beings; thus, the twelve classes of birth are all said to arise from the world as their cause.
That each class consists of eighty-four thousand types is because they have each been transformed by eighty-four thousand afflictions.
Due to the causes of the world’s defiled saṃsāra and the perversions of desire, eighty-four thousand horizontal and vertical disordered thoughts are formed through their conjunction and development.
Thus, there is the *kalala*, the *arbuda*, and so forth, as they transmigrate through various lands among humans, animals, nāgas, and ṛṣis.
Their species fill [the world].
The womb is caused by emotion (*kleśa*), which is precisely defilement. Emotion arises from desire; this is called the perversion of desire.

"Nourishment" (*tsi*) refers to the conditions of the parents' sexual union. Sexual intercourse between husband and wife is considered "right lust," while sexual contact with external objects is "perverse lust. Emotion exists...

Because there are the deviant and the correct, the fruits they induce likewise have horizontal and vertical aspects. When one is to receive a human body, one should form the thought of a vertical progression;
when one is to receive an animal body, one should form the thought of a horizontal progression. *Ātapatana* (遏蒲曇) is translated here as "blister."
Due to the world as a cause, through attachment to saṃsāra and the pursuit of perversions, eighty-four thousand inverted and chaotic thoughts are formed by the conjunction of warmth.
Thus, there arise moist-phase *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through lands, containing wriggling and crawling creatures.
Their species fill [the world]. Through moisture they experience union;
this attachment is precisely "union. Union arises from the stagnation of craving; as they touch objects and rush toward them, it is called the "inversion of the realms of rebirth.
Moisture gives rise through yang-energy; this is called "formation through the warmth of conjunction. That which is sought has no fixed destination; this is called "reversal and confusion."
*Xiāng* (thought/imagination) and *bìshī* (embryo/ovum)—the latter being translated here as "soft flesh"—are the initial signs of moisture-born beings. Their state of mind is dull and insentient;

their form is weak and supple, such that one perceives only movement without being able to distinguish its specific features. This is called *ruǎn* (crawling), like the class of insects known as *xījī* (vinegar flies).
Because throughout their lives they have not conformed to the Way and righteousness and lack the spirit of a man, they receive this retribution of ignorance.
Due to the world as cause, through the false inversion of the cycle of change and rebirth, the conjunction of contact gives rise to eighty-four thousand discursive thoughts of new and old.
Because of this, there are transformed forms (*kalala*) that flow through lands, undergoing metamorphosis and flying about.
These types fill [the world]. Transformation occurs through the response to detachment;

this change is precisely detachment. To leave this and rely upon that is called "false inversion. To touch various categories and undergo transformation is called "accomplishment through harmonious contact.

To loathe the old and pursue the new is called "confused thoughts of the new and the old. *Kalala* (this...)* *Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "羯南。此" (kalala. this...), which refers to the embryonic stage of *kalala*. The translation reflects the available fragment.*
It is called "hard flesh. The term *kalala* used below is a general designation for all such categories. To cast off the old and move toward the new is called "molting" (*tuì*).
It is like a worm becoming a butterfly, where movement transforms into flight; or like a sparrow becoming a clam, where flight transforms into submergence.

Whenever different forms successively replace one another, it is all "transformation through molting. This is what is meant by the characteristic of transformation (*huàxiàng*). Only that which, throughout its life, possesses no...
Regarding integrity: wherever one encounters change, one receives this indeterminate retribution.
Because of the world of causes, one remains obstructed in saṃsāra; due to the hindrance of inversion, one combines and clings to form eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of radiant energy.
Thus, there arise material forms and *kalala* (embryonic stages), which circulate through various lands as auspicious or inauspicious spiritual intelligences.
Such types abound.

There are those among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who take the sun and moon as their parents; they recognize the power of water to remove impurities and understand the nature of fire to produce heat.

They serve the sun, moon, water, and fire, seeking to harmonize their radiance, clinging to these practices with stubborn persistence and refusing to abandon them, thereby creating barriers and obstructions.
Because it penetrates, it is called "obstructive"; because it obstructs and is inverted, it is called "hindrance. It is clear, brilliant, and manifest;

because one takes birth based upon this, it is called "form-characteristic" (*rūpa-nimitta*). Such things as the sun, moon, and stars—wherein the auspicious are termed "rest" (*xiū*) and the inauspicious are termed "calamity" (*jiù*)—down even to the light of a torch or the luster of a pearl oyster, are all instances of brilliant radiance.
This person abandons the great wisdom-light of their own self and instead recognizes [the external].
The "Manifest" (zhāo) refers to the ultimate principle of affairs. Thus, whenever one encounters a manifest state, it is immediately taken as the condition for birth.
Because the world dissolves and revolves through the delusions of inversion, these combine with darkness to form eighty-four thousand obscure and chaotic conceptions.
Consequently, there exists the formless *kalala*, which flows and transmigrates through various lands, dispersing, dissolving, and sinking into emptiness.
These types are so numerous that they fill [the realms].

Disgusted with existence, they cling to emptiness; by extinguishing the body, they return to non-existence—this is called the cycle of dissolution. Deluded, leaking, and lacking hearing, this is called the confusion of inversion.

Relying on the dark and obscure emptiness, it is called the formation through the union with darkness. The hidden and chaotic perceptions of the aggregates constitute the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As for those of the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) class who possess perception yet lack form, they do not establish a karmic body; these are also termed *kalala*.
One interpretation holds that this refers to a state of bondage. Such individuals do not know that within the body possessing characteristics there exists a body devoid of characteristics;

consequently, they cause this mind and body to dissolve, sink, and disperse into space. Having already become obscured within the causal state, upon encountering a dark environment, they immediately take it as their support.
Conditions. The two types mentioned above are transformations of sentient emotion.

Because they revolve through the world due to causes, like insubstantial phantoms, and because their reflections are inverted, their harmonious conjunctions and recollections form eighty-four thousand latent knots of chaotic thoughts.
Thus, there exist the *kalala* (embryonic stage) with its characteristics of perception, which flows and transmigrates through various lands as gods, ghosts, and spirits.

These types are so abundant that they seem to exist yet are as if non-existent; appearing only vaguely and not truly real, they are called *wangxiang* (the phantom-like). "Shadow" (*ying*) refers to a shadow—that is, having a shadow but no form.
When non-Buddhists and ordinary people offer sacrifices and prayers to deities, these all arise from recollective conceptualization (*smṛti-vikalpa*); therefore, it is said: "Harmony."
It is formed through recollection. The forms of spirits and ghosts cannot be seen; sentient beings, out of perverse longing for spiritual powers, pursue shadows and recollect their appearances.

In a state of dizziness, they see them, and after a long time, these recollections form a perceptual realm. Furthermore, they take this illusory mind and conjoin it with the objects thus recollected, using them as the conditions for rebirth.
Through a process of subtle emergence and agitation, distinct features are formed. Therefore, it is said that "chaotic thoughts are secretly formed."
Upon rebirth, one will fall into their own kind. Whether it be spirits, ghosts, or numinous beings—such as celestial Māras or strange monsters—all arise from erroneous cultivation;
they obtain their shadows but not the reality. Thus, while they may possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they have not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Due to the world of causes, through dullness, cyclic existence, and the delusions of inverted views, they combine with stubbornness to form eighty-four thousand parched and chaotic thoughts.
Consequently, there arise non-perceptive *kalala* (embryonic stages) that circulate through various lands;
their spirits transform into earth, wood, metal, and stone, such that these types fill the world.
The heterodox practitioners do not realize that the nature [of mind] is fundamentally round and active; they instead strive to suppress it.

Consequently, their minds shift according to external conditions and take form upon encountering objects—much like the "essence" produced from a flower-pillar or the yellow-headed man turned into stone. When asked about such withered and parched states, they claim there is no thought;
yet how can you say there is "chaotic thought" in what is withered? If the spirit is transformed into earth, wood, metal, or stone, does it still undergo saṃsāra, or does it not?
Regarding saṃsāra: the answer is that it is like withered grass; though it has recently withered, its root is not yet severed, and when the time comes, it grows again.
By means of the power of stubborn concentration, one becomes a stubborn object; yet upon encountering conditions, emotions arise, and one continues to flow through the cycle as before.
These two aforementioned types are transformations of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Taken together, there are four types, all of which are practitioners who have failed to attain the truth.

Due to the world of causes, through the false inversions of mutual dependence and cyclic existence, they combine with defilement to form eighty-four thousand disordered thoughts based on causal conditions.
Thus, these exist; yet they do not possess the characteristics of material form, nor do they become the *kalala* (embryonic stage) of matter as it flows through the lands.
The various jellyfish and similar creatures take shrimp for their eyes; such beings fill the world.
Those who rely on others depend upon Mount Tai, seeking support through fame and power. The "false" refers to those who mistake external things for themselves.
Not knowing that one’s own nature stands preeminent before all things, yet relying on others as one's own strength—is this not a perversion?

Within the causal state, there is originally no core essence; one follows whatever defilements arise from others. Thus, through the conjunction of defiled conditions, one regards them as objects upon which to rely.
Unaware, one’s body falls into the category of creatures such as the *śiśumāra* (water-mother). The *śiśumāra* takes water foam as its [sustenance].
Its body uses shrimp as eyes; fundamentally it has no color, yet it acquires color in dependence upon objects, and is therefore said to have "no color.

Because it is drawn along by the world through causes and conditions, its nature is inverted; thus, through the conjunction of incantations, it forms eighty-four thousand chaotic thoughts of summoning.
For this reason, there exists that which is neither formless nor possessing the characteristics of form—the *kalala* of the formless—which wanders through the lands.
Curses and incantations arise; their like fills the world.

"Those who lead one another" refers to those who, through perverse speech and perverse karma, entice and draw others in. "Those whose nature is inverted" cause things to go awry and manipulate them with craftiness;
this is entirely the functioning of their karmic nature at work. Suddenly, by riding upon the power of curses and incantations, they provoke the seeds of past karma.
One might think that by invoking others, one is unaware that one's own body has fallen into the power of curses and malevolent incantations, and is instead being coerced and employed by another.
As for "invoking," this refers to such things as writing talismans and forming mudras.

In the world, there are malevolent spirits and ghosts who listen to and are employed by humans, such as the *zhāngliǔ* spirit and those who form armies from scattered beans; these do not follow the laws of natural life, and thus their very essence is... [incomplete].
It is not formless; since it has already been induced to form a substantial entity, it is not without form. The two types mentioned above are transformations through conjunction.
Because they arise from the world’s conjunction with delusion and revolve in samsara due to inverted views, various combinations produce eighty-four thousand chaotic and confused thoughts.
Thus, there are the characteristics of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," forming the *kalala* (embryo) stage of perception, as beings transmigrate through the lands.
Those such as the *pulu* (parasites) and others form their substance through mutual transformation; their kind fills the world.
Those who unite through delusion do not fundamentally join with the true mind; rather, they falsely conjoin for the sake of wealth and power.
Because they deceive others during their lifetimes and misappropriate the property of others, claiming it as their own, the conditions for rebirth as these creatures arrive.
At that time, when substances of different natures are combined, one also forms the perception of their mutual transformation;

unaware that one's own body has fallen among things such as the *pulu* (a term rendered as *guoluo* in the *Shijing*, referring to the earth-bee), one instead allows oneself to be transformed by those other things into their own offspring. The *pulu*—the *guoluo* mentioned in the *Shijing*—is the earth-bee.
It captures a silkworm and carries it into a hollow in wood; after seven days, it transforms into its own offspring. Because the natures are different, [this occurs].
It is not characterized by the mark of having perception, for it is established through marks; thus it forms the *kalala* of perception.

Due to the world’s causes of mutual enmity and cyclic existence, and because of the perversity of killing, they combine to form the eighty-four thousand "monsters" who harbor the thought of devouring their own parents.
For this reason, there exists that which is neither the mark of non-perception nor the *kalala* of non-perception, as these continue to flow through the realms of existence.

For example, there are creatures such as the earth-owl that take clods of earth for their offspring, and the mirror-breaking bird that takes the fruit of poisonous trees and embraces them as its young;
once the offspring have matured, both parents meet their end at the hands of those very children. Such species abound.
"Enmity and harm" does not refer to ordinary resentment; rather, it refers to ingratitude for bestowed kindness, a hatred that penetrates to the very marrow of one's bones.

"Killing those who have been inverted" means that the causal conditions of past acts of kindness have, by this point, entirely transformed into the mechanism of killing. "Monstrous" refers to strange and extraordinary circumstances.
Because the grievance is so deep-seated, upon encountering such a monstrous situation, one takes it as a condition for rebirth and consequently gives rise to [the perception of] parents.

With the thought that it was edible, he did not realize his body had entered the fruit. Because he originally harbored the thought of eating his parents, it is said that this is not a state of non-perception (*asaṃjñika*).
Because he was conceived and born within the fruit, it is called "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*). What kind of phenomenon is this?
Yet such perceptions arise. If one traces their origin, they are caused solely by resentment and harm.
We must be careful not to resent others, and we must also be careful not to cause others to resent us. These two points constitute the transformation of detachment.
These are called the twelve types of sentient beings.
Because they all fail to understand the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind, they become deluded and ensnared by emotional desires.

Through the accumulation of delusions, they give rise to further delusions and follow them in cyclic transmigration. Without correct cultivation, none can escape. Therefore, the lower fascicle demonstrates the method for eliminating delusion and cultivating the correct path.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas:
The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, Fascicle Seven.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas: The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
As it was said to Ānanda in the eighth fascicle:
"In this way, within each and every class of sentient beings, there are likewise twelve types of inversions.
These are like flowers appearing when one rubs the eyes; they invert the wondrous, perfect, truly pure, and luminous mind, resulting in such empty delusions."
"Confused thoughts.
This concludes the preceding section and introduces what follows. "Each possesses [them]" means that within each individual inversion, there are twelve inversions;
one is manifest at any given time, while the others lie dormant. Upon investigating the reason for this, they are all fundamentally inverted subtleties.
The Perfect True Mind exists, yet it possesses no substantial reality whatsoever.

Above, it was explained how the True Suchness (*tathatā*) is permeated by ignorance (*avidyā*) to produce defiled functions, thereby serving as the cause for the twelve classes of sentient beings; this section is now complete.
Below, it is explained how the True Suchness permeates ignorance to produce pure functions, thereby serving as the cause for the fifty-five stages of Bodhi.
As you now cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi, you must establish three gradual stages to eliminate the fundamental deluded thoughts that originally caused your confusion.
It is like removing poisonous honey from a clean vessel by using various hot decoctions, along with ashes and incense.
One cleanses the vessel so that it may later store the nectar of immortality. What are called the three gradual stages?

First, through cultivation, one eliminates their auxiliary causes. Second, through true cultivation, one hollows out their fundamental nature. Third, through further advancement, one opposes their manifest karma.

The "fundamental cause" refers precisely to the cause of perversion. Regarding the establishment of the three gradual stages based on this fundamental cause of deluded thought, the teaching is that one must turn defilement into purity by necessarily taking action at the very point where defilement resides.
The "pure vessel" refers to the illusory and empty body, which is the Dharma-body;
it points to the six sense faculties. If these were not the ground of non-arising and non-ceasing, how could they contain poison and honey? How could they possibly be washed clean?

"Ya. The removal of the poisonous honey is a metaphor for eliminating auxiliary causes and excising the fundamental nature. Washing the vessel with hot water is a metaphor for counteracting present karma.
Storing ambrosia within it later is a metaphor for attaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) and being established in the stages of the sages.
"How" and so forth below state the names of the gradual stages; that is to say, if one wishes to practice the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, one should first...
Only by establishing these three kinds of gradual stages can one attain realization and entry. The auxiliary causes serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*);
the fundamental nature of birth and death serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); and present karma serves as the root-condition and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

When these three kinds of conditions are removed, the nectar-like Dharma of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) will manifest. Cultivation, true cultivation, and progressive advancement are all forms of cultivation. [Remove...]

The auxiliary causes—the carving away of the true nature and the contravening of manifest karma—are both severed. That which is cultivated is the auditory nature; that which is severed consists of the faculties and their objects.
The rushing of the faculties toward their objects is called manifest karma; the forgetting of objects and the exhaustion of the faculties is called contravention.

The previously mentioned precepts, concentration, and wisdom constitute the three definitive meanings of cultivation; these three gradual stages do not transcend the intent of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
"What is the auxiliary cause? Ānanda, these twelve classes of beings in this world cannot sustain themselves by their own power;
they abide by means of the four kinds of nutriment, namely: edible food, contact-food, volition-food, and consciousness-food. For this reason, the Buddha said that all sentient beings..."
All exist by depending on food. Ānanda, all sentient beings live because they consume what is sweet and die because they consume poison.
Therefore, those who seek *samādhi* among sentient beings should sever the five kinds of pungent vegetables of the world. These five pungent vegetables, when eaten cooked, arouse lust;
when eaten raw, they increase anger. Thus, in this world, those who eat pungent vegetables, even if they can proclaim the twelve [dhātus],...
The celestial seers (*ṛṣi*) of the ten directions loathe its foul stench and all avoid it.

When hungry ghosts (*preta*) lick the lips and mouths of those who eat such pungent foods during their meals, they dwell constantly with them; their merit (*puṇya*) diminishes daily, and they find no long-term benefit.
When those who eat pungent foods practice *samādhi*, the Bodhisattvas, celestial seers, and virtuous deities of the ten directions will not come to protect them, nor will the great powers.
The Māra King, seizing an opportunity, manifested in the form of a Buddha and came to preach the Dharma to them. He reviled the prohibitions and precepts, and praised lust, anger, and ignorance.
At the end of their lives, they became members of the Māra King’s retinue. Once their demonic blessings were exhausted, they fell into the Avīci Hell. Ānanda!
Those who cultivate Bodhi must forever sever the five pungent roots. This is called the first stage of progressive cultivation and advancement.
This explains the elimination of auxiliary causes. Food and drink are the most essential of all daily human functions; yet, without food and drink, [life cannot be sustained].

Life cannot sustain itself on its own; therefore, it abides by means of the four kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*). To speak of these four nutriments in general terms, there are those that are complete and those that are incomplete.

Among humans, there is the nutriment of physical food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*); whatever is consumed must necessarily be in distinct portions. Ghosts and spirits are satiated by inhaling contact (*sparśa-āhāra*); they have the nutriment of contact.

In the heavens of dhyāna, there is the nutriment of volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā-āhāra*); in the heavens of consciousness (*vijñāna-āhāra*), there is the nutriment of consciousness. Since these latter realms lack form and color, they subsist solely upon consciousness.
Because of these thoughts. As for the "five pungent roots" (*pañca-garaka*): they are leek, garlic, chives, scallion, and *hingukhu*.
The *hingukhu* is not found in this region. The five pungent roots arouse lust and increase anger; therefore, they must be abandoned. Such are the faults that follow:
celestial seers loathe their foul stench; hungry ghosts lick their lips; Bodhisattvas do not come to provide protection; and the Māra gains an opportunity.
Transgressions and evils abound while merit and virtue diminish; defilements draw near while purity and emptiness recede.

If one does not sever and eliminate them, then day by day and month by month, one will gradually become an associate of Māra. Those who have newly resolved to enter the Way must first eliminate these.

"What is right nature (*samyaktva*), Ānanda? Such sentient beings who enter *samādhi* must first strictly maintain pure precepts, forever severing lustful thoughts, abstaining from wine and meat, eating food purified by fire, and never consuming raw, living breath. Ānanda..."
For such a practitioner, if they do not cease sexual desire and the taking of life, it is impossible for them to transcend the three realms.
One should regard sexual desire as being like a venomous snake or as seeing a hostile enemy; first, one must uphold the four parājikas and eight śaikṣa-dharmas of the Śrāvaka.
Holding the body motionless, one subsequently practices the pure discipline of a bodhisattva; holding the mind without arising, one achieves the fulfillment of the prohibitive precepts.
Thus, within the world, there will forever be no karma of mutual birth or mutual killing; theft and robbery will not occur, and there will be no mutual burdens or debts.
Furthermore, they shall not remain in the world to repay past debts. These pure persons cultivate samādhi;
without needing the divine eye, their physical bodies naturally perceive the worlds of the ten directions, behold the Buddhas, hear the Dharma, and personally receive the holy instructions.
Attaining great supernormal powers, they travel through the worlds of the ten directions; their past lives are purified, and they encounter no difficulties or perils.
This is called the second stage of progressive advancement in cultivation.

This explains the excision of the "correct nature" (*zhèngxìng*). It is called "correct" in contrast to the "auxiliary. Sexual desire and killing arise together with the body and exist together with its nature;
they are, in truth, the correct nature of birth and death, and therefore they must be excised. One must not consume the vital energy of life.
This means that one would not even bear to harm insentient things that possess the appearance of life, let alone sentient beings who possess actual life.
This is the ultimate way of preventing evil at its inception and stopping it before it grows. Sexual desire harms the Dharma-body and damages the life of wisdom;

if one views it as a venomous snake or a hostile thief, one will not dare to approach or become intimate with it. To "hold the body motionless" means not to transgress the seven limbs of conduct. To "hold the mind" [steadfast].
"Non-arising" means that not a single thought arises. By severing lust, one does not give rise to mutual birth;
by severing killing, one does not engage in mutual slaughter; by severing theft, one does not repay past debts. When the three karmas are thus eliminated, one is called a pure person.

For those who cultivate *samādhi*, they do so by means of the precepts to develop concentration. As stated in the subsequent text, wisdom is brought forth through concentration. With the physical eye, one perceives the ten directions.

The "world" refers to the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). "Beholding the Buddha" in four phrases refers to the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

The two phrases concerning "past lives" mean the removal of dust and defilement, and the eternal departure from the perilous difficulties of birth and death and the evil destinies; this refers to the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*).

What is manifest karma? Ānanda, when a person thus purely upholds the prohibitive precepts, their mind is free from lustful desire and does not wander excessively among the six external sense objects.
Because they do not wander, they return to the source of the fundamental element. When the sense objects are no longer engaged, the faculties have nothing with which to pair.
The flow is reversed and the one essence is perfected; the six functions cease to operate. The lands of the ten directions are brilliantly pure, just like—
Within the lapis lazuli, a bright moon hangs; body and mind are blissful and at ease. Wondrous, perfect, impartial, and secure, one attains great peace and stability.
All the secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [realms] of all Tathāgatas manifest therein. This person immediately attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
From this point on, they gradually practice, establishing themselves in the stages of sagehood according to their initial resolve. This is called the third stage of progressive cultivation.
"Gradually.
This explanation contradicts the manifest activity [of the senses]. Such a person who maintains pure prohibitory precepts reiterates the aforementioned cause:

that meditative concentration and wisdom are generated through the observance of the precepts. Because the nine grades of afflictions of thought within the desire realm have been exhausted, the mind is free from lustful craving.
Regarding the six external sense objects, one does not allow them to flow forth excessively; yet, it is not permitted for them to be entirely absent.

This is because the beginningless, empty habitual tendencies within the sense faculties have not yet been completely purified, the objects they encounter still persist, and current karmic activities have not yet ceased.

Only when these causes do not descend can the forgetting of objects and the exhaustion of the faculties be manifested, at which point one first contravenes current karma. Since one no longer flows outwardly toward external objects, then...
Not following after the cognitions and views arising from external objects, one returns once more to the original source. There is nothing entering from without and nothing emerging from within;
the faculties and their objects do not meet, and the two no longer pair together. Only then does one turn back from the flow of desire and realize the entirety of the single brilliant clarity.
At this point, when the six faculties encounter their objects, no discrimination arises—like a mirror reflecting an image—and thus the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted.
[This is] the characteristic. Herein, what was heard through correct hearing is exhausted; the afflictions of thought have already been severed, and concentration is attained by means of precepts.

"In the ten directions," and so forth, further reveals the state realized after the objects of perception have been forgotten and the sense faculties have been exhausted. Because the faculties no longer contact objects, the world is pure;
thus one sees the lands of the ten directions, transparent throughout from both inside and out, like lapis lazuli, with [a light] suspended within.
The bright moon. Thus, these aforementioned floating dusts and the vessel-world should, upon thought, transform into supreme awareness.
Because the dusts no longer interact with the sense organs, there is nothing to bind them; thus, body and mind are blissful.
