Since the measure of the body and the measure of the mind are equal and unmoving, it is called "wondrous, perfect, and impartial," attaining great peace and stability. What was previously called "perfect" (yuan) [is now fully realized].

"Transparency, awakening, origin, and subtlety. Herein, the two characters "subtle" (miao) and "perfect" (yuan) specifically refer to the aspect of awakening. In the Tathāgata, this constitutes ultimate awakening;
therefore, the two characters "dense" (ji) and "pure" (jing) are added. "All manifest therein" means that these fruits of merit are all manifested within the mind of this person.

Regarding the ten kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the third is called the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), which means not seeing...

There is not the slightest dharma that arises, nor does one perceive the slightest dharma that ceases. Free from all defilements of the senses, without action and without aspiration, to dwell securely in this Way is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).
This person attains the realization of the stage of fruition—which is neither arising nor ceasing—as the mind of the causal stage;
thus, wisdom is brought forth from meditative concentration. When the Bodhisattva first enters the stream, they immediately employ the Illusion-like Samādhi.
One contemplates the principle of universal emptiness and non-arising. This so-called principle must be realized suddenly; once awakened, all delusions are simultaneously extinguished.

Therefore, one immediately attains this patience (*kṣānti*). While other sutras state that one realizes the patience of non-arising only upon entering the [Bodhisattva] stages, and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states it is realized only after the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samāyikajñāna*), the fact that one attains it prior to these stages here is because this sutra concerns the arousal of the mind on the causal ground, as opposed to the fruition.

The realization of the stages (*bhūmi*) corresponds to their designations; thus, there is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas on the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*), and the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas on the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*).
There is the dry wisdom on the causal stage, and the dry wisdom on the resultant stage. These are not different in essence at all, like the new moon and the full moon.
From this point, one gradually cultivates, taking this non-arising and non-ceasing as the mind of the causal stage, and thereafter...

The cultivation and realization that perfects the stage of fruition are as follows: in the subsequent text, "abiding" (住) establishes virtue; "practice" (行) establishes conduct; "orientation" (向) establishes vows;
and "stages" (地) establish the severance of delusions and the realization of truth—all of which take this present position as their foundation.
Ānanda, these sons of good family have the craving of desire dried up; their faculties and objects no longer meet. Their remaining physical form before them will not continue to be reborn.
Their grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is bright and perfect, polishing the ten directions.

Possessing this wisdom alone, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*khaṇḍa-jñāna-bhūmi*). Although the habits of desire are initially dried up, they have not yet connected with the flowing water of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Rebirth takes the sense faculties and their objects as its cause and craving for desire as its condition. When one is withered and solitary, both cause and condition are severed;
there is no basis for karmic retribution, and one does not undergo further existence, being free from the fetters within the realms. This is what is called "emptiness" by the Unattached One.
Non-obscuration is called clarity (*prabhāsvara*). When desire is dried up, wisdom (*prajñā*) arises; because one abides and maintains oneself by means of this wisdom, it is named "ground" (*bhūmi*).

There are two meanings of "drying": first, the exhaustion of desire, which refers to the withering of the craving for desire; second, mere drying, which refers to not yet having connected with the flowing stream of the Dharma.
The flow of the Dharma takes vitality and moisture as its meaning, and does not favor dryness or stagnation. The nature of wisdom is luminous and perfect.

Having already perfected the adamantine body, yet being unable yet to exercise sovereign mastery as one desires, they give rise to the function of the essence and characteristics of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

The following ranks of sages are established, beginning with the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) as the initial cause, followed by the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
The Equal and the Wondrous follow one another in succession. The practitioner enters by means of faith and dwells upon the ground of Buddha-wisdom.

Relying on wisdom, they give rise to practice; they sustain their practice with vows. Thus they transcend the Three Levels of Worthiness and enter the Ten Holy Stages, ascending to the Equal and the Wondrous. This is the sequence of cultivation and realization.
With this very mind, one flows into the center of the center; it unfolds with perfect subtlety. From the truly wonderful perfection, the truly wonderful again emerges.
Wondrous faith abides eternally, and all delusive thoughts are extinguished without remainder. This state of pure truth in the Middle Way is called the Abode of Faith.

"This very mind" refers to the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing. "Center within the center" (zhōngzhōng) refers to the ultimate true nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) mentioned previously.
"Perfectly wondrous" (yuánmiào) refers to the essence of the mind. The previous statement regarding "wondrous perfection and equality" merely referred to the initial attainment of this mind;
[now it is said that] the Tathāgata’s secret, perfect, pure, and wondrous [qualities] all manifest within it—this simply means they are reflected within the Buddha-mind.
Now, the wondrously perfect essence of one's own mind is like a flower in full bloom.

Although it has not yet attained the secret purity of a Buddha, the true arises from within the true, becoming increasingly vast and expansive. Relying on this opening of the mind, one should advance further;
thus it becomes ever more wondrous and perfect. As it blooms repeatedly, one gradually enters the realm of the living, which is different from possessing wisdom that is merely dry and insubstantial.

Profound endurance without movement is called "constant abiding" (*nitya*). Delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) are precisely the various extreme views; when delusive thoughts are exhausted, the Middle Way becomes pure.

At this time, the characteristics of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*) are extinguished, which is termed "abiding in the mind of faith. This refers to being able to dwell securely in the mind of faith.
Faith is defined as being truly pure and free from delusion; it is defined as being in accord with reality. By means of the mind of the Middle Way, one is purely true and without delusion.
The causal mind corresponds with the resultant awakening. With faith as the foremost among these ten minds, they are collectively termed the "Stage of the Ten Faiths.
When true faith becomes clear and lucid, all things are perfectly penetrating; the three categories of aggregates, bases, and elements can no longer act as obstructions.
In this way, even throughout countless eons of the past and future, as one discards and receives bodies, all habitual tendencies manifest before one.
These good sons are all able to recollect and maintain it without forgetfulness; this is called "abiding in the mind of mindfulness.
"True faith" refers to the preceding stage. "Clarity" points to the fundamental stage. "All-encompassing penetration" generally refers to what follows in the text:

the aggregates (*skandhas*) cannot cover it, the sense bases (*āyatanas*) cannot confine it, and the elements (*dhātus*) cannot separate it. As for the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, they are not merely—
Cultivation and abandonment are difficult; even the ability to see [the truth] is not easy. When it manifests before one today, delusion has nowhere to escape.
By seeing delusion, one can eliminate delusion; by being without forgetfulness, one maintains mindfulness. Therefore, it is called the "application of mindfulness" (smṛtyupasthāna).
Sublime, perfect, and purely true, the essence of truth gives rise to transformation. The habitual tendencies from beginningless time merge into a single, brilliant lucidity.
By means of this alone—this brilliant lucidity—one advances toward ultimate purity; this is called the mind of diligence.
"Wondrous, perfect, and purely true" refers to the first stage. "True essence" refers to the subsequent stage.

From "giving rise to transformations" onwards, it means that the pure essence of the luminous signs described in the fourth fascicle manifests all transformations without being subject to afflictions; whereas in the preceding stages, habitual tendencies still manifest.
If one has still not yet achieved transformation, this is because the true essence has emerged through the void, transforming beginningless habits and penetrating the single luminous clarity;

thus, the delusory immediately returns to the real. This "true purity" is the wondrous, perfect body of the mind, but it must reach the state of being extremely subtle, pervasive, pure, and wondrous before it can be called truly pure.
Because one advances by means of this luminous clarity, it is named "vigor" (vīrya).
When the essence of mind manifests before one, consisting purely of wisdom, it is called "the abiding of the mind of wisdom.
Although the refined clarity of the higher stages still pertains to the realm of the mind with outflows (*sāsrava*), this is precisely the substance of spontaneous wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*).

One progresses through the refined clarity of the former stage, whereas here, by means of the substance of wisdom and bodhi, there is no further admixture of delusion; this is called the "mind of wisdom. As for the preceding...
"Purely wisdom" refers to the wisdom that cuts off delusions, like the night approaching dawn.
"Purely by means of wisdom" refers to the wisdom that realizes the truth, like the sun rising at dawn.
Maintaining the clarity of wisdom, it is pervasive, tranquil, and profound; this tranquility is wondrous and eternally coagulated—this is called the abiding of the concentrated mind.
The wisdom of the distracted mind has boundaries and is not pervasive; it comes and goes and is not eternal. Therefore, wisdom must rely upon concentration.
When wisdom arises from concentration as described above, it is a concentration that reverses the flow [of consciousness], like a vessel clarifying turbid water. This...
Wisdom first, concentration later: this is the wisdom of constant radiance. Like a lamp placed within a sealed chamber, it is universally quiescent and eternally still;
these are all the characteristics of Great Samādhi. Therefore, it is called "the dwelling of the concentrated mind."
The light of Samantaprabha shines forth; its luminous nature penetrates deeply, proceeding only forward without retreat—this is called the "non-retrogressive mind.

The simultaneous operation of concentration and wisdom is like the two wheels of a chariot, proceeding only forward without retreat. Diligence still involves conscious effort, like a horse being spurred with a whip;
non-retrogression is effortless, like a sail driven by a favorable wind.

The mind advances with serenity, maintaining its state without loss. When the vital energy (*prāṇa*) of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions intersects with one’s own, it is called the "mind that protects the Dharma.
Although previously there was no regression, diligent effort remained uninterrupted and still involved deliberate exertion;
now, although one is vigorous, no sign of toil is perceived. Hence, it is called "serene. When the maintenance of the mind reaches this state of serenity, it becomes far-reaching...
"Ut-tang! You shall forever be preserved without peril. What is it that you maintain so as not to lose? It is the life-vein of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas.
Because I maintain this life-vein of the Dharmakāya without loss, my vital energy naturally becomes one with and perfectly harmonized with that of all Buddhas;
therefore, I am named 'Protector of the Dharma' (Hufa)."
Awakened clarity maintains this state; it is able, through its wondrous power, to turn back the Buddha’s compassionate light and direct it toward the Buddha’s own abiding presence.
This is like two mirrors facing each other with their radiance, wherein wondrous reflections interpenetrate one another in infinite layers. This is called the mind of dedication.

"Sublime Power" refers to the power of meditative concentration and wisdom. It is described as "power" because it sustains and maintains; it is described as "sublime power" because it sustains enlightened awareness and clarity.
Previously, when one’s own constituent essence interfaced with that of the Tathāgata and was sustained by the Buddha’s compassionate light, there still remained a distinction between self and other.
This means that by means of one's own sublime power, one abides within the Buddha of one’s own mind. In reality, there are not two distinct entities;

the mind is not separate from the Buddha, and the Buddha is not separate from the mind. Like two mirrors reflecting one another, their radiance is transmitted without end; therefore, it is called *pariṇāmanā* (dedication).
The light of the mind secretly returns, whereby one attains the Buddha’s eternally concentrated, unsurpassed, wondrous purity and dwells securely in the unconditioned, achieving non-forgetfulness;
this is called the "abiding of the mind in precepts.
Because one suddenly attains the essence of the tranquil, pure mind through subtle and secret contemplation, it is said that "the light of the mind secretly returns."

"Constantly concentrated" (*cháng níng*) refers to the eternally abiding true mind (*zhǔ zhān xīn*). "Sublime purity" (*miào jìng*) refers to the pure, sublime, and luminous mind. In the preceding stages, these qualities were still relative;
here, one has attained the Buddha-mind. "Constant concentration" and "sublime purity" together constitute the mark of the unconditioned (*wéi*), which is the precept-mind of all Buddhas.
If for even a single thought-moment there is a lapse into the conditioned (*yǒu wéi*), this is precisely breaking the precepts.

Abiding in the mastery of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*), one is able to travel throughout the ten directions; wherever one goes is according to one’s vow, which is called the "abiding of the aspirational mind" (*praṇidhāna-citta-vihāra*).

Maintaining ethical discipline is still associated with the exertion of effort, whereas abiding in ethical discipline is mastery itself. To act in accordance with one’s vow is precisely the meaning of mastery.

Wandering arises from abiding; wandering has its foundation. Therefore, one can act according to one's wishes—namely, being able to universally make offerings to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
In the preceding stage, there was a silent resonance; in this stage, there is direct reception.

At the beginning of cultivation, one must first wither and sever craving and desire, causing the nature of the mind to become empty and luminous; only then can one enter the wondrous, perfect, true nature. This true nature is luminous.
When it becomes perfectly round, subtle habits will manifest. Because they manifest, they subsequently transform, causing pure wisdom to be free of habituation.

Furthermore, maintain this through meditative concentration so that stillness and clarity emit light, penetrating deeply into the luminous nature and guarding it without loss. This is to turn back the compassionate light of the Buddha.
He attains the pure precepts of the Buddha and traverses the mundane world without being defiled; his movements accord with his vows. This is the sequence of the Ten Faiths.

Ānanda, this good man, through true skillful means, gives rise to these ten minds. As the essence of mind radiates brilliance, the ten functions interpenetrate one another, perfectly accomplishing the One Mind;
this is called the Abode of Resolving the Mind.
The wondrous, perfect, true mind is neither one nor ten; yet, due to the distinctions in its functions, it possesses ten aspects.
If these ten aspects are not manifested, it cannot be called the arousal of the bodhicitta; if the ten aspects are not integrated, it likewise cannot be called the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Therefore, the three gradual stages serve as the true expedient means for developing the ten minds. It is like ten pieces of lapis lazuli, each suspending a lamp, shining brilliantly.

They appear simultaneously; this is the realm of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). After a long time, their refined radiance becomes all-pervasive, interpenetrating and merging with one another until they are entirely the One Mind, such that the ten characteristics (*daśa-nimitta*) are utterly absent.
It is like placing ten flames together within a single piece of lapis lazuli; the ten lights fuse into one another.
The radiance and signs grow ever greater; only upon reaching this stage is it called the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*).
Within the mind, illumination is revealed like pure lapis lazuli, with refined gold appearing within. By means of this previously marvelous mind, one treads upon it to form the ground.
This is called the Stage of Cultivating the Ground (*bhūmi-karman*).
Among the three gradual stages, one takes non-arising and non-extinction as the mind of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi-citta*). Although the true mind has been attained, ignorance still persists;
it must be dismantled layer by layer so that one may attain layer-by-layer intimacy. The preceding stage involved the destruction of the characteristic of difference (*visama-lakṣaṇa*).

Because of ignorance, it is like a bright moon suspended in lapis lazuli; since entering and abiding [in the stages], one has shattered the ignorance of abiding marks, and thus it is like lapis lazuli manifesting refined gold.
Lapis lazuli is a metaphor for wisdom (*jñāna*), and refined gold is a metaphor for principle (*tattva*). At the first stage, the wondrous mind first arises;
now, one treads upon it to complete the grounds. All objective realms are the cultivation and refinement of the mind-ground; therefore, it is said:
Regarding the Stage of Cultivating the Ground: what preceded was the principle that must be realized suddenly; this present stage involves the gradual elimination of phenomena.
When the mind-ground and its cognitive activities are both clearly understood, one traverses the ten directions without obstruction; this is called the Dwelling of Cultivated Practice.
"Mind-ground" (*cittabhūmi*) means that the supreme and wondrous mind constitutes the ground. "Engaging in cognition" (*saṃjñāna*) means engaging with objects without confusion;

it refers precisely to the meaning of clearly understanding both [the mind and its objects]. Second, "clarity through faith" is the clarity of mindfulness; this stage is characterized by such clarity.
This is the illumination of right knowledge; the two types of faith cannot obstruct it. It is like the eyes seeing at a distance;
herein one attains freedom from hindrance, like the body entering empty space. The Four Great Vows and the Six Perfections proceed spontaneously, unimpeded by external objects.

In the preceding stage, the mind and its objects correspond; in this stage, the mind and its objects are of one suchness. Therefore, it is called the Dwelling of Cultivation and Practice (*bhāvanā-vihāra*).
Their conduct is identical to that of the Buddha, and they receive the Buddha’s spiritual influence, like a being in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) who seeks its own parents;
through the subtle communion of their latent faith, they enter the lineage of the Tathāgata—this is called the Stage of Noble Birth.
"Buddha" means "awakened. Now that one has attained clarity and unimpededness, this is precisely to accord with the nature of awakening;
thus, one is directly identical to a Buddha and receives the Buddha’s vital essence (*buddha-gandha*). Seeking one's own parents is a metaphor for the mind being unimpeded;

the subtle correspondence of hidden faith refers to the time when those of similar karma meet during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which is a metaphor for receiving the Buddha’s vital essence. Entering the Tathāgata...
The category is as follows: that which I call "neither arising nor ceasing" is conjoined with the Tathāgatagarbha. When a crown prince dwells in the womb, his nobility surpasses all ministers;
hence he is called "born noble. What was previously described as the "connection of the vital breaths" (qi-fen) is like a close attendant gaining entry into the royal palace;
what is here called "receiving the Buddha’s vital breaths" is like a crown prince personally inheriting the sovereign's body.

Having already entered the womb of the Way and personally inherited the lineage of the Awakened One, one is like a fetus that has fully formed with all human features complete; this is called the stage of "Abiding in the Perfection of Expedient Means.

"Personally inheriting the lineage of the Awakened One" refers to personally receiving the direct transmission of the orthodox pulse. "Human features" is a metaphor for the function of skillful expedient means.
This refers to the perfect and wondrous functioning of hearing, seeing, and so forth, which is fully endowed with all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

Just as the six sense faculties are perfected in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and resemble those of one's parents, the roots of goodness thus cultivated are entirely for the purpose of rescuing and protecting all sentient beings and benefiting all sentient beings; therefore, it is called "perfection of skillful means."
Their physical appearance is like that of a Buddha, and their mental characteristics are likewise identical;

this is called the "Abiding in the Right Mind. Regarding these mental characteristics: the mind of a Buddha is characterized by immovability. Although it employs skillful means, its essence remains eternally unmoving.

"Right mind" is synonymous with a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*). Having attained the Buddha’s precept-mind during the preceding nine stages of faith, one now attains the Buddha’s concentration-mind at this stage.
Body and mind are synthesized and grow day by day; this is called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avinivartanīya-vihāra*).
"Body and mind are synthesized" reiterates the aforementioned virtue of being equal to the Buddha. "Growing day by day" means that the scope of objective realm and wisdom becomes ever more expansive.
Within this state of growth, one perceives non-retrogression.
The ten spiritual marks of the body are fully perfected at once; this is called the Dwelling of the Youthful (Kumārabhūmi).
Because there is progress and no regression, and because the form is complete though minute, it is designated as "youthful. As for the ten bodies:
the Bodhi-body, the Vow-body, the Transformation-body, the Sustaining-power-body, the Adornment-body, the Majestic-potency-body, the Mind-born-body, the Merit-body, and the Dharma-body.
The Wisdom Body (jñānakāya). Although its function has not yet been manifested, its essence is already fully perfected.
Having formed and emerged from the womb, one becomes a true son of the Buddha; this is called the Abiding of the Dharma Prince (dharmarājaputrabhūmi).

"Emerging from the womb" is a metaphor for breaking through obstructions and giving rise to functional activity. From the initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the stage of "Noble Birth" (*janmakula*), it is called "entering the noble womb.

From the stage of "Perfection of Skillful Means" (*upāyaparipūri*) up to "Youthful Purity" (*kumārabhūta*), it is called "nurturing the noble womb. Having reached this point, the work of nurturing is perfected;
therefore, it is metaphorically described as "emerging from the womb. Being worthy to succeed to the position of the Buddha, one is called a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmaputra*).

Through these manifestations, one becomes a full person. Just as a great king of a nation delegates various state affairs to his crown prince, when that son of a Kṣatriya king has reached maturity and the rites of consecration have been performed for him, it is called "abiding in consecration."

The outer form constitutes the person; it is capable of performing the Buddha-work. When all virtues are fully perfected, one is capable of transforming and instructing the ten directions while performing the Buddha-work.

Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King takes the waters of the four great oceans, places them within a golden vase, and pours them over the crown of the prince’s head—thereby receiving the royal position—so too is the Bodhisattva’s reception of office. This is the wisdom of all Buddhas.
Because water is poured over their crowns, Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are called "Consecrated" (Abhiṣikta). This is also partially attained at each of the ten dwellings (vihāra).

One must first resolve the mind to cultivate the stages; having cultivated the stages, one then practices. Only thereafter is one born into the family of the Tathāgata and endowed with the marks of enlightenment.
They share the Buddha-mind, extend the essence of the Way, perfect the ten bodies, become sons of the Buddha, and undertake the Buddha’s work. Regarding the sequence of the Ten Abodes:
Ānanda, once these good men have become sons of the Buddha, they are endowed with the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of the Tathāgatas and act in accordance with the ten directions;
this is called the Practice of Joy.

Possessing perfect and wondrous virtue, he follows the preceding to initiate the succeeding, serving as the general heading for the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). Regarding the "ten directions": it means manifesting bodies within the ten realms to benefit sentient beings.
Since the faculties and practices of sentient beings differ, the Bodhisattva accords with them through both form and teaching; this is the accord of the capacity to transform.
The Bodhisattva manifests various transformations, and sentient beings accord with them, each receiving transformation accordingly. As for... [text continues]
Transformation is compliance. Since both the subject and the object are compliant, the capacity and the response both give rise to joy; this is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Being well able to benefit all sentient beings is called the practice of benefiting others (*anugrahacaryā*).

"Abundant" means that there is nothing that does not benefit [others]; this is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). There are three types of ethical discipline, among which that which benefits sentient beings is supreme.
Through the ninefold faith, one attains the mind of the Buddha’s ethical discipline; reaching this stage, one takes the Buddha’s ethical discipline as one's practice.
To awaken oneself and awaken others, thereby attaining freedom from opposition and rejection, is called the practice of being without anger or resentment.

To awaken oneself and awaken others, one perceives that among all sentient beings there is not a single one who does not accord with the awakened nature; hence it is said that one attains freedom from opposition and rejection.

This does not merely mean being able to endure insults and humiliation. The practice of being without anger or resentment is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). Within this, there are six... [end of fragment]
This is not like ordinary paths. If one does not accept the joy of the Dharma, that is stinginess in giving.
If for a single thought-moment one fails to protect sentient beings, that is breaking the precepts. If for a single thought-moment one discriminates among sentient beings, that is hatred.
Born of various types, extending to the limits of the future, equal throughout the three periods of time, and penetrating the ten directions—this is called inexhaustible conduct.

According to the capacities and responses of beings, it manifests bodies of various types, benefiting sentient beings immeasurably until the end of the future. [The phrase] "throughout the three periods of time" follows below.
This explains the reason. Because he knows that the three periods of time are empty and quiescent, he is able to reach the furthest limits of the future.

Because he has attained unimpeded penetration throughout the ten directions, he can manifest bodies of various kinds; at whatever time and in whatever place, his manifestations and transformations are uninterrupted, hence they are called "inexhaustible.
This is the perfection of vigor. In the sixth stage, one attains the Buddha’s concentrated mind; reaching this stage, one takes the Buddha’s concentration as one's practice.
All are unified; various dharma-gates are attained without error, which is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.
If a concentrated mind cannot maintain the various dharma-gates, this is "deluded concentration. Regarding these dharma-gates, one has not yet escaped error and remains a distracted mind.
Now, when a single moment of concentrated mind can maintain various dharmas, there are then various [realizations].
Each and every sound is distinct and clear, without deviation even by a hair’s breadth; this is called the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā) that is free from both delusion and distraction.
Thus, within the midst of sameness, a multitude of differences is manifested, yet each and every distinct characteristic is seen as identical; this is called the skillful manifestation of practice.
When sameness and difference manifest separately, it is not called "Excellent Manifestation" (Sudṛśa). When sameness and difference manifest reciprocally, this is indeed "Excellent Manifestation.

Because the ultimate does not contradict the conventional, difference is revealed within sameness. Because the conventional does not contradict the ultimate, sameness again manifests within difference.

This is Prajñāpāramitā. In the preceding stage, stillness while being alert constitutes *samādhi*; in this stage, alertness while being still constitutes *prajñā*. At the tenth dwelling (*daśabhūmi*), one attains Buddhahood.
Wisdom-mind. Reaching this point, one takes wisdom as the practice.
In this manner, it extends even to the empty space of the ten directions, filling it with atoms; within each and every atom, the worlds of the ten directions are manifested.
Manifesting the objects (*viṣaya*) and manifesting the realms (*dhātu*) without mutual obstruction or hindrance is called "unattached practice.

This generally subsumes the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Manifesting lands within the objects is called "manifesting the realms. Not destroying the characteristics of the objects is called "manifesting the objects.

Regarding "without mutual obstruction or hindrance": when the realms enter into the objects, the realms do not become small; this is because the small does not obstruct the large. As for the objects...

When boundaries are joined, the boundary does not become larger; yet the large does not obstruct the small because, through the practice of skillful means (*kuśala-pratipatti*), they are expanded and harmoniously integrated.
Attachment is precisely the meaning of obstruction; where there is no obstruction, there is no attachment. By abiding in the third stage, one attains non-obstruction.
These objects do not obstruct the mind; these do not mutually hinder one another; and these objects do not obstruct other objects.
As they manifest in various ways, they are all the foremost *pāramitā*, called the "Practice of Reverence."
Among the six perfections, prajñā is the foremost. When they are integrated by the perfection of wisdom (jñānapāramitā), all five perfections tend toward the perfection of wisdom;
therefore, they are all prajñā. Because prajñā is most venerable, it is called the "practice of veneration."
Thus, through such perfect integration, one is able to fulfill the norms of the Buddhas of the ten directions; this is called "skillful practice of the Dharma.

The former [stage] was for one's own fulfillment, while this is for the fulfillment of sentient beings. Although the former also involved benefiting others, it was generally established as one's own door of practice;
this, however, ensures that both walking and staying fulfill the norms, thereby relying upon the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
Each and every one is pure and untainted (*anāsrava*), a single true unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) state; because its nature is thus from the beginning, it is called "True Practice.

This refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*) of the preceding preparatory stages (*pūrvaprayoga*). There is no inequality between the untainted and the unconditioned. Previously, morality gave rise to concentration and wisdom, which were termed the "Three Untainted Trainings" (*trīṇy anāsrava-śikṣāṇi*);
it is only upon reaching this point that they truly attain purity. The former were conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); [the latter are not].

It is able to accord with the nature. This is the wondrous functioning of the true nature as it originally is. Although its manifestations are myriad and diverse, its essence is solely the one true reality;
therefore, it is called "true and real. From the preceding section up to this point, the character for "nature" (xìng) has finally been revealed.

While both the defiled and the pure are the Tathāgata-garbha, it is only when it is purely clean and free from defilement that it constitutes the wondrous True Suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.
Ānanda, when these good men have perfected their supernormal powers and completed the work of Buddhahood, they will be pure, refined, and true, far removed from all lingering afflictions.
They shall deliver sentient beings while extinguishing all marks of deliverance; turning their minds toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they proceed upon the path to Nirvāṇa.
This is called the Dedication of Protecting and Saving All Sentient Beings While Remaining Free from the Mark of Sentient Beings.
From "fulfilling" up to "removing afflictions," these preceding practices have been fulfilled; one should now cultivate the practice of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

The practice of dedication is characterized by the deepest compassion and vow; therefore, its function lies in the liberation of sentient beings. However, if one perceives that there are beings to be liberated, one immediately becomes involved in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because this turns one's back on the path to Nirvana, it is necessary to extinguish the characteristics of the various *pāramitās* and turn the unconditioned mind toward the path to Nirvana.
This unconditioned mind is precisely the mind that is neither arising nor ceasing. Within the three gradual stages, one takes this very mind as the fundamental cause for cultivation.

The ninth stage, the Stage of Faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*): one first attains stable dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). From this unconditioned realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*), one establishes the myriad practices;
reaching this point, one returns to the source and reverts to the origin, once again abiding within the unconditioned realm. There is no Buddha to be sought, and no birth to be saved.
Looking back at the non-active Buddha-mind attained on the previous day, it remains unchanged and non-dual. From this point, one gradually advances toward the Buddha-vehicle.
Within the stage of the Ten Abidings (*daśavihāra*), although the Middle Way is exclusively employed, there has never been an explicit mention of saving sentient beings;

thus, the wisdom that inclines toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*) predominates. Within the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), there is an explicit mention of saving sentient beings; this is the "Emergence into the Provisional" (*niṣkramaṇa-prajñapti*).

This [practice of] compassion is most supreme. These ten dedications clearly demonstrate the simultaneous operation of compassion and wisdom, the mutual integration of the ultimate and conventional truths, and the perfection of the Middle Way.
"Dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) means "to transform"; "direction" (*nāman*) means "to proceed toward. It refers to transforming one's myriad practices and proceeding toward the three destinations.
The three objects are sentient beings, bodhi, and true suchness (*tathatā*). Sentient beings and bodhi are characterized by appearances; true suchness is free from appearances.
This and the subsequent stages constitute the dedication for the sake of sentient beings. According to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, dedication is precisely the making of vows.
For if there is practice without vows, the practice will surely be aimless; if there are vows without practice, the vows remain merely [aspirations].
Since these are established in vain, one must rely on both practice and vows to enter the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
Destroying that which is destructible and remaining far removed from all forms of detachment is called the "Non-destructive Dedication."
"To destroy that which is destructible" refers to the aforementioned eradication of the marks of deliverance (*tāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*).

"To distance oneself from all distances" means that one distances oneself even from the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*). One is called "indestructible" because one does not destroy the activity of delivering sentient beings.
Generally, the existence of a deliverer and a delivered constitutes that which is destructible; now, by eradicating the marks of deliverance, one destroys that which is destructible. If one can...
The mind that is subject to destruction is not empty, and it too can be destroyed; therefore, one must distance oneself from all such states of separation before it can be called indestructible.
When fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) is serene and still, its awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas; this is called the dedication equal to all Buddhas.
The following four stages constitute the dedication toward the Buddha-way. Fundamental awakening (benjue) is profoundly still; it is the manifestation of one's own original Buddhahood.
"Awakening equal to the awakening of the Buddhas" means that one’s mind-essence is in perfect, seamless accord with the mind-essence of all Tathāgatas.
"Dedicating oneself equally to all Buddhas" means that I and the Tathāgata’s precious, true, awakened mind are non-dual and perfectly complete.
The essence of purity and truth is brilliantly manifested; this stage is like the Buddha-ground and is named the Dedication Reaching All Places.
"Essence of purity and truth" refers to the substance of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). "Brilliantly manifested" refers to the unfolding of its wondrous function.

"This stage is like the Buddha-ground" signifies that the boundless realms contained within the causal ground are identical to the immeasurable lands manifested on the resultant ground of Buddhahood. The character "ground" (*bhūmi*)—
This refers to the state of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*). Since its virtuous functions are all-pervasive, it is called "reaching all places.
In this world, Tathāgatas mutually interpenetrate without obstruction; this is termed the "Dedication of the Treasury of Inexhaustible Merit."
This refers to contemplating all virtues within the stage (*bhūmi*). "World" (*loka*) means reaching all places; "Tathāgata" means being equal to all Buddhas.
Previously, there was still a distinction between self-awakening and Buddha-awakening, or between one's own stage and the Buddha-stage;
here, these are fused into one without division. Regarding their mutual interpenetration: when the world interpenetrates the Tathāgata, then within every single pore, there are immeasurable...
The jewel-adorned lands are exquisitely embellished and subtle.
When the Tathāgata traverses the worlds, within every single atom there are immeasurable Tathāgatas turning the Great Wheel of Dharma without obstruction.

When the world traverses the Tathāgata, it does not obstruct the Tathāgata, yet enters directly into him. When the Tathāgata traverses the world, he does not obstruct the world, yet enters directly into it.
Come. As for those with the inexhaustible treasury of merit, each Buddha possesses immeasurable adornments, which manifest immeasurable virtues.

The seven non-attached practices manifest within both the sensory realms and the objective worlds; this is spoken of solely in terms of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environmental retribution). Thus, the environment and the primary retribution (the body) are non-obstructive.
Equal to all Buddhas, they are like the moon emerging from the clouds, reaching every place; like the moon illuminating the sky, they are without [obstruction].

Exhausting the treasury of merit, like the reflections of mountains, rivers, and the great earth appearing within the moon, they each give rise to causes of purity within the ground of the same Buddha-ground; relying upon these causes, they manifest them and take up the path to nirvana.
This is called the dedication of roots of goodness that accords with equality.
Thereafter, from the treasury of merit, one gives rise to the unconditioned activity. This is the Buddha-ground; it steps upon the aforementioned treasury of merit.
When a Bodhisattva realizes this, they are identical to the stage of fruition of a Tathāgata. Regarding "each within the stages":
because the merits within this *tathāgatagarbha* are inexhaustible, such as the six perfections and myriad practices, all are inherently present.

As for "producing the cause of purity," based upon that inherent presence, each [practice] follows conditions to give rise to a cultivation that is not cultivated, just as one fashions vessels from gold. The vessels...

The vessels are all made of gold; how could they not be purely and uniformly pure? Relying upon and manifesting through causes, those who take up the path to nirvana ride upon causes to attain the fruit.
Cause and effect penetrate one another: the myriad virtues serve as the cause for the myriad practices, and the myriad practices serve as the cause for nirvana.
Practice arises from principle; therefore, it is called "conformity with equality. It can produce sublime fruits; therefore, it is called "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).
Once the true roots are established, all sentient beings of the ten directions are my own original nature. When this nature is perfectly accomplished, one does not lose sight of sentient beings.
This is called the dedication that accords with the equal contemplation of all sentient beings.
Because these roots of goodness are the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they are termed "True Roots. They accord with the equality of all Buddhas as mentioned previously.
This is conformity with the equality of sentient beings. If there were even one sentient being who could not be saved, it would not be equality.
If one were to abandon a single sentient being and fail to save them, it would not be equality. In terms of realization, every person is fundamentally perfected;
in terms of salvation, one does not lose this moment by moment. Only then is it called "conformity that accords with the nature. At this stage, one further dedicates [the merit] to sentient beings.
That is, all phenomena are free from all marks; being both "identical" and "free," there is non-attachment to either. This is called the dedication of the mark of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
The three stages below this constitute the dedication to True Suchness. The two phrases "identical with all" and so forth share a single meaning. That is to say:

The characteristic of separation is not the characteristic of being separated from extinction. There is no birth to be delivered, and there is no Buddha to be realized. One does not cling to identity.
One delivers the birth that is inherently undeliverable, and realizes the Buddha that is inherently unrealizable.
One does not cling to separation. What was previously called "remaining far removed from all characteristics" refers to the ultimate state of detachment; here, even detachment itself is not clung to.

Regarding the statement that the seventh stage is "non-attachment": it means not being attached to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This implies, moreover, that one is not attached even to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Previously, the mind focused on the unconditioned was entirely directed toward True Suchness (*tathatā*); now, for the first time, its characteristics are clearly perceived.
Truly attaining that which is as-it-is (*tathatā*), one is unimpeded throughout the ten directions; this is called the dedication of liberation without bondage.
"Truly attaining" has the meaning of direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). "That which is as-it-is" is precisely *tathatā*. If one can directly realize *tathatā*, then everywhere is *tathatā*;
the two obstacles of karma and retribution cannot bind one, and thus one is able to sport throughout the ten directions and manifest [various forms].
The body is unimpeded and unbound; this is the cause of liberation. Liberation is the fruit of being unbound.
When the qualities of intrinsic nature are perfectly fulfilled and the limits of the *dharmadhātu* are extinguished, it is called the "Infinite Dedication of the *Dharmadhātu*."

"Nature" (*xing*) refers to the nature of *tathatā* (suchness). "Virtue" (*de*) refers to the attributes of the characteristics of *tathatā*. Whatever possesses limitations is not the perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*).
When a Bodhisattva dwells within this stage, they penetrate and perceive the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is perfectly accomplished and does not fall into numerical categories;
how could it have any limits? Therefore, the lands within atoms and the atoms within lands appear in successive layers.
They accord with the nature of reality; they mutually encompass and mutually integrate one another. Therefore, it is said that the Dharma-realm is immeasurable.
Ānanda, these good sons have fully perfected the forty-one pure minds and subsequently accomplished the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*).
Regarding the forty-one minds: there is one stage of Dry Wisdom; then ten each for the stages of Faith, Abiding, Practice, and Direction.

As for the addition of the "stages of practice" (prāyogika), because the noble stages of a Bodhisattva are difficult to enter, one must apply diligent effort and cultivation. These are specifically designated as "wondrous and perfect" to distinguish them from the four stages of application in the Hīnayāna.
The third gradual stage says: "Body and mind are blissful; wondrous, perfect, and impartial, like gold extracted from ore, lacking only final purification.
From the entry into the stage of faith onward, it speaks of the "wondrous and perfect blossoming" and "advancing toward true purity.
Only upon reaching the ten practices does it say "each and every thing is pure," and only upon reaching the stage of dedication does it say "producing the cause of purity."

The forty-one stages can thus be seen; in total, nothing is added beyond the preceding mind. It is merely a matter of skillful means to refine and polish it, causing the realm of the Buddha to manifest.
It is like repeatedly smelting and refining pure gold, whereby the pure characteristics become increasingly evident.
As long as there is a mind and a Buddha, and subject and object remain distinct, it is still not the state of ultimate purity. Therefore, one further employs the wondrously perfect mind.
When the practice of wondrous perfection is accomplished, the preceding characteristics of subject and object vanish utterly;
only then can one proceed from the cause of differentiation to realize the cause of equality on the stages (*bhūmi*). It is like gold undergoing the "nine refinements" before it can become an elixir.
One immediately takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind. Whether it has emerged or not yet emerged, it is like drilling wood to produce fire;
the desire to ignite the wood is called the stage of "warmth" (uṣmagata).

Therefore, it is called the internal division (*antar-bhāga*). When perception (*saṃjñā*) excels and separates from the body, it is called the external division (*bahirdhā-bhāga*). Both love and hatred are states of emotion (*bhāva*);

since emotion necessarily transforms into water, and one clings to one's fundamental destination without seeking liberation, both are considered the internal division. To hear of sublime matters and to feel thirsty for them with longing is "empty perception" (*śūnya-saṃjñā*).

When such perception is sustained and perfected through contemplation, it can generate a sublime vital energy (*vīrya*). If the perception is defiled, it is simply emotion; thus, emotion and perception [are interconnected].
Ascent and descent are distinguished by the light-and-clear versus the heavy-and-turbid; though they differ in superiority or inferiority, both are merely empty and false.
Ānanda, throughout all worlds, birth and death continue in succession: birth follows from habitual tendencies, and death follows from the flow of transformation.

At the moment of the end of life, before warmth and tactile sensation have been abandoned, the good and evil of one’s entire life manifest simultaneously. Death is contrary to the flow of birth, yet both follow their respective two habits.
When thought and emotion intersect, if one consists purely of thought, one will immediately ascend and be born in the heavens.

If within the mind of flight there is both merit and wisdom, as well as pure vows, the mind will naturally open and one will see the Buddhas of the ten directions and all the Pure Lands, being reborn therein according to one’s vows.

If emotion is slight while thought is predominant, one will ascend lightly but not to a great distance, becoming a flying immortal (*fei-xian*), a powerful ghost king (*guai-wang*), a flying *yakṣa*, or a terrestrial spirit.
The rākṣasas roam throughout the four continents, moving without obstruction.

Among them, if there are those with virtuous vows and virtuous minds who protect and uphold my Dharma, or who guard the prohibitive precepts following those who observe the precepts; or who protect divine mantras following those who recite them;

or who protect meditative concentration and maintain the patience of the Dharma—such as these dwell personally beneath the seat of the Tathāgata. Their thoughts and intentions are impartial and equal, and they do not fly away.
They do not fall [into the hells], but are born among humans. When their thoughts are clear, they are intelligent; when their emotions are deep, they are dull-witted.

When emotion predominates and thought is scarce, they flow into the realm of horizontal birth, becoming heavy as fur-bearing beasts or light as winged creatures. With seven parts emotion and three parts thought, they sink below the water wheel and are born at the boundary of fire, receiving the breath of fierce flames.
Their bodies become hungry ghosts, constantly consumed by burning; even water can harm them, and they have no food.
They shall have no drink for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. With nine thoughts of passion and one thought of goodness, they look down into the wheel of fire;

their bodies enter the ground where wind and fire intersect. They are reborn lightly in the *sāntara* hells and heavily in the *avīci* hells—these two types of hell. Those of pure passion sink directly into the *Avīci* hell.
If, while sinking into the mind, they have slandered the Mahāyāna, violated the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, spoken deceptive and false teachings, or greedily craved in vain—
Having received offerings of faith and unworthily accepted their veneration, one is reborn in the Avīci Hell throughout the ten directions for the five heinous crimes and the ten grave offenses.
Although such evil karma is self-invited through one's own actions, within the commonality of sentient beings, there is also a primordial ground.

All sentient beings love life and hate death. Life proceeds from existence and abiding, which accords with their habitual tendencies; death proceeds from transformation and flux, which opposes those habitual tendencies.

The scriptural passages are mutually abbreviated. To flow outward and rush toward the dust of sensory objects is called "accordance"; for the light of life to shift and pass away is called "transformation.
When life follows favorable conditions and becomes defiled by habituation, there is no karma that is not created; when death follows the condition of transformation...
As for this process of transition and flux, there is no karma that can be newly created. At the moment between being alive and dying, the various karmas of good and evil manifest vividly before one;
thus, those who were subject to transformation depart, while those to whom one is habituated approach. As these two meet, one receives retribution according to one's karma.
If the body of thought becomes light and buoyant, one will purely ascend by flight. If one has cultivated only goodness, one will certainly be reborn in the heavens. If...
If one combines merit and wisdom with pure vows, the mind will surely open, one will behold the Buddha, and be born in the Pure Land.

Thus, it can be seen that rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha (nienfo) all arises from visualization (xiang), though it merely combines merit and wisdom. Because such visualization is not yet pure and is slightly hindered by deviant sentiments, it results in rebirth among the class of immortals (xianlei).
Their light flight is not far-reaching; vertically, they do not transcend the four heavens, and horizontally, they do not go beyond the Cakravāḍa mountains. They wander...
These beings arrive for a brief moment; they do not dwell long. The scriptural text refers to them collectively. If we discuss them according to their relative status:

those with one emotion and nine perceptions become flying immortals (*vidyādhara*); those with two emotions and eight perceptions become powerful ghosts (*mahābala-piśāca*); those with three emotions and seven perceptions become flying *yakṣas*;
and those with four emotions and six perceptions become earth-walking *rākṣasas*. Those who dwell beneath the Buddha’s seat are the devas and nāgas.
The eight classes of beings, though mired in perverse emotions, possess virtuous aspirations; thus they evoke favorable conditions. Their emotional conceptions are equal to those of humans.
Among humans there are those who are sharp and those who are dull; while their conceptions are equal to their emotions, the clarity of their conceptions possesses greater power.
This constitutes being "acute. Although emotion (*qing*) is equal to perception (*xiang*) in its nature, when the hidden power of emotion is strong, it becomes "dull.

Among the six emotions and four perceptions, those with many emotions and few perceptions—such as the fur-bearing land-dwellers—are heavy; those of the feathered species who travel through the air are light.
The wheels of water, fire, and wind. The hungry ghosts receive retributions such as the eight cold and eight hot hells;
they do not reside beneath the earth upon the gold, water, or wind wheels. Because they take up the heat of fire as their bodies, they are constantly being burned.

Even if they obtain water to drink, it transforms into fire; thus, water can harm them. "Mutual transgression" (*jiaoguo*) refers to mutual overcoming (*jiaosheng*). Furthermore, while they are within the wheel of fire...
Near the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), as recorded in the sūtras, there are eight missing [types of] feelings and two missing types of perception; one is born into the *sāntara* hells.
*Sāntara* refers to the eighteen hells, while *anantara* refers to the eight *avīci* hells. *Avīci* is translated here as "Great Uninterrupted" (*mahā-anantara*).

This means that regarding five factors—the nature of the offense, the instruments of suffering, the physical size of the body, the duration in kalpas, and the lifespan—there is no interval or interruption whatsoever. One remains there until the kalpa is destroyed before finally emerging. If...
Furthermore, those who slander the Mahāyāna and so forth will, even when this kalpa is destroyed, enter the Avīci hell throughout the ten directions with no prospect of escape.
This is because such slanders of the Dharma cause infinite beings to give rise to false views. Those who violate the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts are like the bhikṣuṇī Ratnapadmagandhā;
those who deceive others by preaching false doctrines are like the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra; and those who covet wealth without merit...
To give alms out of faith while being empty-handed is called "vain. To receive the respect and offerings of others while lacking virtue is called "unmerited.

Regarding the "original ground" (*yuandi*): each follows its own original cause as the ground for its experience. The previous question asked whether hell has a fixed location or whether each individual experiences it privately.
This answer clarifies that although the acts were committed privately, the retribution has a fixed location; thus, though each acts individually, they experience the result together.

Ānanda, all these are what those sentient beings have experienced as the result of their own karma. Having created the ten causes of habitual practice, they undergo the sixfold intersecting retributions.

Above, the internal and external conditions of feeling and perception have already been bound together; below this, the seven realms of rebirth should arise separately, yet the text appears to be interconnected.

"Continuing from the previous discussion on emotions and perceptions, which proceeded from the superior toward the inferior, we now examine cause and effect in detail, proceeding from the inferior toward the superior.
These two inferior states connect with one another; this phrasing follows the natural flow of the argument rather than continuing the subject matter of the preceding text.

The preceding section discussed how emotions and perceptions induce transformations, briefly clarifying the seven realms of existence (*sapta-gati*). The following section details how faculties and objects encounter and create karma, precisely investigating the seven realms. As for 'mutual retribution,' there are six [types]."

When the faculties interact, they give rise to evil retribution. For example, when the eye faculty creates karma, the other five act as its assistants; thus, at the time of receiving retribution, it extends to all of them. What are the ten causes?
Ānanda, the first is the habit of sexual intercourse, which arises from mutual friction; this grinding continues without ceasing.
For this reason, there arises within it a great, fierce blaze of fire.
Just as when two hands rub against each other, the phenomenon of heat manifests, so too do these two habits ignite one another; thus there exist such things as iron beds and copper pillars.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate sexual misconduct by the same name: "the fire of desire. When Bodhisattvas behold desire, they avoid it as they would a pit of fire.

Second, the habit-energy of greed intermingles with mental calculations, giving rise to mutual attraction. As this attraction and grasping ceaselessly continue, there thus come to be accumulated cold and solid ice, within which one freezes and shivers.
It is like a person drawing in cold air through the mouth, whereby a sensation of chill arises.
Because these two habits mutually assail one another, there exist the phenomena of the *ṭaṭa*, *papa*, and *lala* hells, as well as the blue, red, and white lotus-like ice. Therefore—
All Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate excessive seeking with the same name: the Water of Greed. When Bodhisattvas perceive greed, they avoid it as one would a miasmic sea.
Third, the habit of pride intermingles and overcomes others, arising from mutual reliance; it flows on without ceasing.
For this reason, there is surging and rushing, and the accumulation of waves forms water. It is like when people’s mouths and tongues taste each other’s flavors, whereby water is produced.

Second, because the two habits strike against one another, there are rivers of blood and rivers of ash, hot sands, poisonous seas, and the various occurrences of being drenched and swallowed by molten copper.
For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize pride as "drinking the water of delusion. When Bodhisattvas perceive pride, they see it thus.

It is like avoiding a great flood. Fourth, the habitual tendencies of anger clash; arising from mutual opposition, this opposition knots together without ceasing, heating the mind until it emits fire and forging the vital energy (*qi*) into metal.
For this reason, there exist mountains of knives, iron spikes, sword-trees, and sword-wheels, as well as axes, halberds, spears, and saws.

Like a person harboring a grievance, the murderous energy flies and stirs; as these two habitual tendencies strike one another, there are punishments of imprisonment, dismemberment, beheading, and hacking.
Chopping, stabbing, beating, and so forth—therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate anger as the "sharp sword.
When Bodhisattvas see anger, they avoid it as they would an execution. Fifth is the habit of practicing deception through mutual enticement, which arises from flirtatious banter.
This gives rise to instability. Because of this, there are ropes, wooden stocks, and the binding of limbs, just as when water saturates a field, grasses and trees grow.
As these two habits perpetuate one another, there are cuffs, shackles, pillories, and fetters, as well as various matters involving whips, staves, clubs, and maces.

For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize the deceitful and the false as being identical to slanderers and thieves; Bodhisattvas view such fraudulence with the same dread as they would a jackal or a wolf.
Sixth, the habit-energy of deception involves mutual cheating. It originates from the intent to mislead; as this false deception does not cease, the mind flies toward the commission of villainy.
Thus, there arise dust, soil, excrement, urine, filth, and impurities, like dust carried by the wind, such that each can see nothing.

As these two habit-energies combine, there result various events such as drowning, being submerged, leaping up, being cast down, flying, falling, drifting, and sinking. Therefore, throughout the ten directions, all...
The Tathāgata designates deception as being identical in name to killing. When a Bodhisattva encounters such deception, he views it as treading upon a venomous snake.

Seventh is the habit-energy of enmity and mutual resentment, which arises from harboring hatred; because of this, there are flying stones and hurled rocks, as well as [traps such as] boxes and carriage-traps.
Like one who keeps a venomous snake in a jar or harbors a malicious beast in their bosom, these two habits devour one another;
thus there arise acts such as hurling, seizing, striking, shooting, throwing, and snatching. For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize the enemy as such.
They are called the "Harmful Ghosts. When Bodhisattvas see their enemies, it is like drinking poisoned wine.

Eighth, the mutual illumination of the two habits is like the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and various karmas born of false awakening; these give rise to opposition and produce contradictions.
For this reason, there are kings, messengers, and chief clerks who testify to and uphold written records, like travelers on a road who meet one another as they come and go—this is the second habit.
They intersect; thus there is the interrogation of deception, the examination and cross-examination, the investigation and thorough inquiry for illumination.

The boys of good and evil hold registers in their hands to adjudicate all matters. For this reason, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions designate this evil view with the same name: "The Pit of Views.
When Bodhisattvas see these pervasive attachments to falsehood, they regard them as if facing a precipice of poison. Ninth.

The habits of perversion and falsehood intermingle, giving rise to slander and calumny. For this reason, there are mountains and stones that press together, grinding, crushing, plowing, and rubbing, just as slanderous thieves oppress and wrongfully persecute the virtuous.
Because these two habits clash with one another, there are matters such as being crushed, pressed down, beaten, and squeezed, or measured out by scales.
Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions characterize resentment and slander as being of one name: the "Slanderous Tiger."
When the Bodhisattva sees such injustice, it is as if he were struck by a thunderbolt. Tenth, the habit of litigation leads to mutual clamor, which arises from the concealment of faults.

For this reason, there is the mirror of discernment that illuminates all things, like one who cannot hide their shadow in the midst of the sun. As these two habits confront one another, there arise evil associates;
the karmic mirror and the fire-pearl reveal past deeds and verify all matters. Therefore, throughout the ten directions, all Tathāgatas...

"Come. The term for concealment (*mrakṣa*) is also called 'hidden thieves' (*chāyā-taskara*). When a Bodhisattva contemplates concealment, it is like carrying a high mountain while treading upon a vast ocean.
First, he speaks of the objects that evoke [the affliction]; next, he speaks of the matters that result as retribution. These two practices consist of the subject and the object. They join together.
They grind against one another and ignite one another; these are both the subjective and objective realms, as is the case below.

As for the habit of lust, it consumes one's own essence, causing the fire-element to blaze intensely, giving rise to ailments such as consumption and internal heat while alive, and making it fitting that one sees fierce fires upon death.
Because the Tathāgata is the Teacher, he designates this with a specific term to warn [beings]; because the Bodhisattva is a practitioner, they feel deep terror and avoid it.
"Color-designations" (*śe-mu*) refer to names given based on physical appearance. "The habit of greed" (*t'an-hsi*) refers to calculating and seizing, as if sucking and grasping;
it is like inhaling cold and raw sensations. *T'a-p'o-lo* is the sound of enduring cold; "blue, red, and white lotuses" are the colors of freezing frost—these are the Eight Cold Hells.
"Greed-water" refers to the Spring of Greed; drinking from it engenders greed. "Miasmic Sea" refers to the pestilential miasmas of the south.
As for the element of air (*vāyu*): touching it causes immediate death. The habitual tendency of pride (*māna*) and arrogance arise from looking down upon others and relying on oneself;

consequently, one experiences realms of surging, rushing, and turbulent motion, as well as the retribution of being drenched and swallowed by rivers of blood. In the Western lands there is a water which, if drunk, causes delusion.
Pride belongs to ignorance; it is a state of turbid, dull energy. Hatred is a habit that causes heat and affliction within body and mind. The mind belongs to fire, while energy belongs to metal.

When the fire of the mind produces energy, it is cast and transformed into metal. Therefore, one experiences the realm of mountains of knives and trees of swords, where killing others results in returning to kill oneself.
One does not realize that to accord with sentient beings is precisely to accord with the nature of awakening. If the fire of hatred...
It is removed. Just as metal cannot be cast by breath, there is no room for its blade to enter.
Those who practice deception and use flattering words to entice others are like binding wood with ropes or confining it with shackles and collars; they ensure there is no escape.

Thus, one experiences realms of ropes, wood, shackles, and collars because of long-standing, gradual infiltration that causes the heart to find pleasure, after which one is drawn into their snare, just as water soaks into wood.
In a field, grass and trees grow tall. A *jiao* belongs to the category of shackles; a *zhua* belongs to the category of mallets. The habit of deception consists of speaking wildly to cheat others;
their intent is fraudulent and their mind is flighty, like wind blowing dust so that people cannot see.

Therefore, they experience the retribution of encountering realms of dust, filth, and evil, as well as being submerged, drowned, tossed about, or falling. The habit of resentment consists of harboring a heart of hatred; therefore, they experience...

Scenarios such as flying stones and hurling rocks devour one another; this refers to those who harbor resentment and desire only to bite and devour the flesh of others, unaware that they should view their enemies as kin.
To harbor gratitude rather than resentment is the primary cause for transcending the world.
"Violating and harming ghosts" refers to evil ghosts who violate principle and harm people; "views of habitual practice" refers to evil views; and "mutual illumination" refers to each [of these].

There is the manifestation of one's own views. There are five types of evil views: first, the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to the body as having a self and involves various forms of conceptual attachment;

second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), which, regarding all phenomena, clings to either annihilationism or eternalism; third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which consists of erroneous awakening and mistaken understanding.
1. Denying cause and effect. 2. Adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): regarding what is not a fruit as a fruit, such as taking the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) to be *nirvāṇa*.
3. Adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): regarding what is not a cause as a cause, such as observing the precepts of cattle or dogs as a means for rebirth in heaven.
4. *Satkāya-dṛṣṭi*: translated here as "view of a self" (*shen-jian*). Those who oppose and contradict [the truth] each cling to their own position as being correct.
Because they violate [the Dharma] and refuse to submit to what is correct, they are made to encounter royal messengers who testify to and determine right from wrong.
This is like travelers meeting one another on a road; when they meet on a narrow path, there is no place to escape.

As for "illuminating," it means being placed before the Mirror of Karma (karmādarśa-maṇḍala) to be illuminated, with nothing left unconfessed or concealed. That which can drown the *dharmakāya* is called the "pit of views. It can...

It brings about the suffering of karma; it is called a "poisonous ravine. Through perverse habituation, one is falsely accused of crimes one has not committed, and though one is not crooked, one is forcibly called crooked.
With a haughty air, one is coerced by others. Two mountains close in from both sides, leaving no place for escape.

It is like being caught between two stones. To "push" (*pai*) means to shove, squeeze, and crush; it constricts the body and drains away the blood. Furthermore, one must pass through a narrow opening sideways.
Its body is like the state of pulling silk; it can harm people and is called the "slanderous tiger. It is terrifying and is called "thunder.
The habit of litigation exposes the hidden faults of others; when one covers up their own faults while litigating against another, this is called "mutual clamor.

To present and expose [one’s own purity] while harboring secret malice is to conceal evil. Once exposed, one incurs punishment; this is sufficient only to oppress and cast oneself down, as if carrying a mountain upon one's head.
Treading upon the sea, one does not guard against litigation but guards against submersion; the intention is to uproot the very foundation of litigation.
What are the six retributions? Ānanda, all sentient beings create karma through the six consciousnesses, and the evil retributions they attract emerge from the six sense organs.
How do evil retributions emerge from the six sense organs? First, the retribution of seeing invites and draws forth evil fruits. This seeing—
When karma intersects, at the time of death, one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions.

The deceased’s consciousness flies and falls, riding upon the smoke to enter the Avīci Hell. Two manifestations arise: first, the vision of light, wherein one can see all manner of evil things and give rise to immeasurable fear;
second, the vision of darkness, wherein one sees nothing in the profound stillness and gives rise to immeasurable terror. Thus it is.
It burns the sight, becoming cauldrons of boiling brine and molten copper; it burns the hearing, becoming black smoke and purple flames; it burns the taste, becoming scorched pellets and iron gruel;
it burns the touch, becoming hot ashes, furnaces, and charcoal; it burns the mind, producing sparks that scatter and fly, fanning and swelling throughout the void.
Second, the retribution for hearing invites and draws forth evil fruits; when these karmic conditions of hearing intersect, then at the moment of death—
At the time of death, one first sees waves that submerge heaven and earth. The deceased’s consciousness descends and flows along with them, entering the Avīci Hell.
Two signs then manifest: first, "opening the hearing," where one hears various clamors and the spirit becomes confused;
second, "closing the hearing," where it is silent and nothing is heard, and the dark soul sinks away. Thus, when hearing these waves and this descent, they can bring about retribution.
When directed toward sound (*śabda*), it can become thunder or a roar; when directed toward odor (*gandha*), it can become a noxious vapor that settles upon one's breath;
when directed toward taste (*rasa*), it can become pus, blood, and various kinds of filth;
when directed toward touch (*spraṣṭavya*), it can become animals, ghosts, excrement, or urine; when directed toward mental objects (*dharma*), it can become lightning.
It acts like hail, shattering the heart and soul. Third, the retribution of smelling invites evil fruits.

When this karma of smelling intersects, at the moment of death, one first sees poisonous vapors filling the near and far surroundings. The deceased’s consciousness leaps up from the ground and enters the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs:
first, the pervasive hearing, wherein one is suffocated by various foul vapors, causing extreme mental agitation; second, [the pervasive seeing].
When the ears hear [the sound], the breath is stifled and blocked; one faints upon the ground. Thus, when the inhalation is struck by the sense of smell, it can become solid matter or footwear;
when struck by sight, it can become fire or a torch; when struck by hearing, it can become submerged or drowning, or boiling and bubbling;
when struck by taste, it can become hunger or refreshment; when struck by touch, it can become tearing, rotting, or great swelling.

The Mountain of Flesh: possessing hundreds of thousands of eyes and immeasurable mouths for devouring, when one’s thoughts collide with it, it can turn into ash, pestilence, or flying sand and gravel, shattering the body.
Fourth, the retribution of flavors invites evil fruits;
when this karma of flavor intersects, at the moment of death, one first sees iron nets and fierce, blazing flames enveloping the world, through which the deceased’s consciousness passes downward.
They are cast into nets and suspended upside down, entering the Avīci Hell. Two manifestations arise: first, their inhalation forms freezing ice that cracks and splits their flesh;
second, their exhalation flies forth as fierce fire that scorches and rots their marrow and bones. Thus they experience flavors:
through repeated tasting, they become capable of enduring and bearing [suffering]; through repeated seeing, they can cause metal and stone to burn; through repeated hearing...
Then it can become sharp weapons; passing through the breath, it can become a great iron cage covering the entire land;
passing through contact, it can become bows and arrows, crossbows and projectiles; passing through thought, it can become flying red-hot iron raining down from the sky.
These five are the retributions of contact that summon evil fruits. When this contact and karma intersect, at the time of death, one first sees:
Great mountains close in from all four sides, leaving no further way out.

The deceased’s consciousness perceives a great iron city, where fire-snakes, fire-dogs, tigers, wolves, and lions, along with ox-headed hell-wardens and horse-headed rākṣasas, brandishing spears and lances, drive them through the city gates toward the Avīci Hell.
Two manifestations then appear: first, the manifestation of contact, wherein closing mountains press against the body, crushing the flesh and bones.
The blood will burst forth. Secondly, there is contact through separation: when swords and blades touch the body, the heart and liver are butchered and torn asunder.

Such contact through union and contact through succession can serve as the path and the contemplation, as the hall and the tribunal. Contact through succession through seeing can serve as burning and incineration; contact through succession through hearing likewise serves as such.
Thus, one can strike and hit; one can stab and shoot. Passing through the breath, one can form a bowstring and a quiver;
one can examine and bind. Passing through the sense of taste, one can plow and use tongs; one can cut and sever. Passing through thought, one can cause things to fall or fly;
one can fry and roast. These six types of thought bring about and attract evil fruits. When these thoughts and karmas intersect, then at the moment of death—

At the time of death, one first sees an evil wind blowing away and destroying the land. The deceased’s consciousness is blown upward into the air, then whirled down by the wind and falls into the Avīci Hell.
This gives rise to two manifestations: first, non-awakening; when delusion reaches its extreme, one becomes desolate and runs about without ceasing. Second, awakening;
