through awareness, one realizes the suffering, undergoing immeasurable burning and scorching, with such deep pain that it is difficult to endure. Thus it is.
When wrong thoughts are bound, they can become directions and locations; when views are bound, they can become mirrors and proofs;
when hearing is bound, it can become great congealing stones, ice, frost, earth, and mist;
when breath is bound, it can become great fire-carts, fire-boats, and fire-traps; when tasting is bound, it can become great wailing, regret, and weeping; and when touch is bound...
Thus, one can manifest as large or small; undergo ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day; and assume various postures, such as lying face down or face up.

In the creation of karma and the summoning of retribution, the faculties (*indriya*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) necessarily coexist. Now, while karma is produced by consciousness, retribution follows from the faculties.

Since karma arises entirely from the mind, whereas retribution mostly concerns the functions of form (*rūpa*), the two are diametrically opposed within their respective domains; therefore, the various faculties are distinct from one another, yet they are mutually integrated within their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Know this: therefore, the source of receiving retribution is universally pervasive. At the time of awakening, one sense-faculty returns to its origin, and all six faculties are liberated.
At the time of delusion, one sense-faculty creates karma, and all six faculties receive retribution. Within the state of ultimate awakening, a single faculty pervades the entire Dharma-realm;

within the realm of ultimate suffering, a single body pervades the entirety of hell. What is first seen at the moment of death is the retribution of the present life. As for the spirit of the deceased...

Consciousness is the retribution of hell. In these six modes of interaction, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*); one enters directly into the Avīci Hell. This is based on the discourse regarding extreme evil.
The eye presides over the mind, and the mind belongs to the element of fire; the eye is the external aperture of the mind, and thus it perceives fire.

What is perceived is that which is grasped by karma, never departing from light and darkness. When the ears interact [with this], water and fire strike one another; hence there are cauldrons of boiling water and molten copper. Interaction...
Smell. Smell is the sense of air; thus it becomes black smoke and purple flames. Taste. Taste is manifested through food; thus it becomes scorched balls and molten iron dross.
Touch. Touch involves proximity to objects of desire; thus it becomes a hot ash pit and glowing coals. Mind. The mind belongs to fire;
when the internal and external fires ignite one another, it becomes sparks scattering and spraying. All this arises from being unable to turn back and see.
Following the primordial flow, it rushes forth to receive the retribution of form. The ear presides over the kidneys; the kidneys belong to water, and the ear is the external orifice of the kidneys.
Thus, when seeing water, one hears the basis of karma, which does not depart from movement and stillness. This mutual hearing issues forth from the fundamental root.

Reproach and interrogation belong to the category of the sound-object (*śabda-viṣaya*). When [the breaths] meet and see one another, they strike like water and fire, manifesting as the roar of thunder and transforming into poisonous vapors.
When they meet and rest, the breath carries the water, dispersing it as rain and mist and transforming it into venomous insects.

When they meet and taste one another, they transform into things such as pus and blood. When they meet and touch, touching that which has form and substance, the Yin and Yang breaths combine to become domestic animals and ghosts.

Excrement and urine; sexual intent; and likewise the mutual clashing of water and fire—these arise and cease according to the movement of the mental consciousness, resulting in being shattered by lightning and hail.
This is the retribution for failing to turn the hearing back toward one's own nature, instead allowing it to flow outward and rush toward sounds. Smelling belongs to the element of air (*vāyu*).
Therefore, at the moment of death, one first perceives the vital breath (*prāṇa*). When the nasal breath is inhaled, it descends; when exhaled, it ascends.

Thus, the consciousness (*vijñāna*) moves from the earth upward, and then falls back down from above. It follows the odors upon which karma depends, never departing from their penetration or obstruction.

"Substance" (*zhì*) refers to obstruction; "treading" (*lǐ*) refers to penetration. In the causal state, one relied on the empty breath to strike others; now, it strikes its own fundamental root and cannot escape.
Arrogant, he relied on his vision of fire to harm others; now his breath strikes that vision of fire, and it becomes a torch that burns him from within.

Relying on his keen hearing to damage others, he now relies on his breath to strike the water of hearing; if his ears are blocked, he is submerged and drowned; if they are open, they become a vast ocean of boiling seas.
Taking flavors as his satiety, his breath now strikes those flavors, causing them all to rot and decay. That which is spoiled by fish is called "putrid."

When soup is spoiled, it is called "sour" (*shuǎng*). When one uses a sharp blade to contact the flesh of sentient beings, now that the vital energy (*qì*) surges and contacts [the object], it results in tearing, cracking, and rotting, or being gnawed and eaten by sentient beings.
When clever schemes injure people, now that the vital energy surges through those schemes, it results in ashes, miasmas, sand, and gravel.
The body is shattered and crushed; this is the retribution for being unable to reverse the breath to follow the primal source, instead allowing it to flow errantly toward fragrances.

Transforming the sense of touch into taste, one receives its name from that which is tasted. Through greed for flavors, one sets nets and burns the wilds; hence, one perceives such signs as nets and flames.
The tongue is the support for the karma of tasting; it is inseparable from inhalation and exhalation. Inhalation constitutes cold, while exhalation constitutes heat. Because of these...
The middle of the tongue devours living beings, causing them to experience and endure suffering; thus, as it repeatedly tastes and gives rise to pain, one also experiences and endures it oneself.
Relying on the sense of smell, one indulges in greed and captures various flavors within a cage; therefore, there is the great iron cage.

Because the taste of contact harms living beings, one is reborn with bows and arrows to wound oneself. Because of craving for flavors, one thinks of objects; therefore, flying iron [spikes] are produced to satisfy that craving. Although this is merely...

It is said to be the retribution for [craving] flavor. To examine the place of this retribution in detail, it is also mostly summoned by the four types of speech. This arises from being unable to turn back from the pursuit of flavors and following the flow of the senses, instead rushing headlong toward them;
as a result, one encounters mountains of swords and blades, and through greedily clinging to the physical forms of men and women, one undergoes this retribution.
These signs are doubly numerous and doubly evil. Through the habitual defilement of sexual misconduct, they bring about ruin and corruption, violating the social order.

They give rise to killing and theft, accumulating even more extensive sins. These are the bases for karmic actions that lead to no liberation. "Slaughter" and "tearing apart" refer to the characteristics of separation. The "path" is the road leading to hell.
"Observing" refers to the palace of the King of Hell, the hall, and the desk—the places where punishments are administered. When a blade is thrust into flesh, it is said:

"Stabbing" refers to piercing [the body]. "Binding in a sack" means tying the mouth so that one cannot breathe out. "Torture and binding" means fettering the body so that it cannot move. "Plowing" refers to plowing while pulling out the tongue.
"Tongs" are a type of gripping tool. "Slicing" refers to dismemberment. "Thinking" refers to either descending or ascending, or experiencing feverish distress;

thus, one undergoes falling, flying, boiling, and roasting. This arises from being unable to turn back toward oneself to practice cultivation, instead allowing the mind to flow away and rush toward distractions.
Regarding the retribution for contact (*sparśa*): because thought (*cetanā*) belongs to the earth element yet is subject to drifting and tossing, one sees evil winds blowing and destroying the land.
This is summoned by the karma of thought; it does not go beyond delusion and awakening. Wandering aimlessly in desolation is deluded thought; knowing suffering is awakened thought.

Since thought must have an object, thought is bound to form the location where retribution is experienced. Since seeing (*darśana*) has the capacity to reflect and verify, seeing is bound to constitute the proof of the offense.

The "Matter" refers to things such as molten rock, which result from the interaction of water and earth. The "Flaming Chariots" and so forth are all vehicles for carrying beings, produced by the transformation of the vital energy (*vāyu*).

The "Crying Out," "Lamenting," and "Weeping" represent sufferings that are difficult to endure. The "Large" and "Small" [hells] and so forth are transformations resulting from karma of contact driven by distracted thoughts.
These are the retributions for being unable to reflect upon oneself to acknowledge one's own faults, and instead allowing the mind to flow outward and rush toward external phenomena.
Ānanda, these are called the ten causes and six effects of the hells; all are created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings.
If sentient beings collectively create evil karma, they enter the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering for immeasurable kalpas.
If the six sense organs each create [evil], and if those actions involve both objects and organs, such persons enter the Eight Uninterrupted Hells. Body and mouth...
Regarding the three mental [actions]: if one commits killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, such a person enters the eighteen hells.
If the three karmas are not all committed together, but one performs either one instance of killing or one instance of stealing in the interim, such a person enters the thirty-six hells.

If one perceives each sense-faculty individually and violates only a single karma, such a person enters the one hundred and eight hells. It is because sentient beings act and create their karma separately that they experience these various destinies.
Within the world, one enters the stage of homogeneity (*sabhāga-bhūmi*), where deluded conceptualization arises;
these do not exist from the beginning but are created by confusion and delusion. These are the false manifestations of the delusive karma of one's own mind and are not external objects.

All things do not transcend the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) and the two polarities (*yīn-yáng*); this is what is known by worldly wisdom. All transformations do not transcend the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*); this is what worldly wisdom does not know.
The World-Honored One’s discourse on reaching the source states: Regarding "joint commission," the six faculties and ten causes are fully present and act together.
Regarding "individual commission," although they are fully present, there is a sequence and interruption;

one has the intention but does not transgress because the objects are not combined, or one acts unintentionally and commits an error because the faculties are not combined. Thus, intentional transgression occurs when both objects and faculties are combined; these aforementioned cases are all extreme.
Evil. If one ceases from committing only the three evils of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, rather than all six, it is lighter;

if one does not commit all ten, it is even lighter. Among these three evils, if one commits only two, it is again lighter. As for "seeing" and "that which is seen," these refer to the faculty of vision and its corresponding object.
If a single faculty alone commits them, constituting a solitary violation of two karmas, it is still lighter. The hells likewise decrease in severity according to the gravity of the offense. Eight.
The "Uninterrupted" (Avīci) hells consist of the eight cold and eight hot great hells; these are slightly lighter than the Avīci hell itself. The eighteen hells are subdivisions of the great hells.
The thirty-six hells are subdivisions of the eighteen hells. The one hundred and eight hells are subdivisions of the thirty-six.
As for the distribution of the hells' power, the suffering experienced therein becomes lighter. The perpetrator begins with the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), from which it is initiated.
Regarding evil karma and its agent: subsequently, within the six sense objects, one accomplishes evil karma. Since these evil karmas differ, they are individually performed and individually created.
As for the retribution of hell that is experienced, upon entering the *sabhāga-bhūmi* (the common ground), there is a fixed location; it is not something received in private.
What is called the "common ground" can be seen as having clearly manifest objective realms. What is called "not inherently existent" can be seen as the total emptiness of the very substance itself.

Furthermore, Ānanda, these sentient beings—having neither violated the codes of discipline, nor transgressed the bodhisattva precepts, nor subverted the Buddha’s nirvāṇa, yet having performed various other miscellaneous karmas—are scorched by them throughout successive kalpas.
Only after their retribution is exhausted do they receive the forms of various hungry ghosts, based on their original causes.

To covet material objects is a transgression. When such a person’s retribution for this sin is exhausted, they encounter matter and take form; these are called *guǐkuài* (strange ghosts). To covet sensual forms is a transgression.

When such a person’s retribution for this sin is exhausted, they encounter wind and take form; these are called *póguǐ* (drought ghosts). To covet delusions is a transgression. When such a person’s retribution for this sin is exhausted...
When they encounter livestock and take form, they are called *mei* ghosts; their transgression was greed and resentment.

When these people have exhausted their retribution, they encounter insects and take form, becoming *gu-du* ghosts; their transgression was greedy recollection. When these people have exhausted their retribution, they encounter decay and take form, becoming *li* ghosts.

Greed and arrogance constitute an offense. When this person’s retribution for the offense is exhausted, they encounter the vital breath (*qi*) to form a body; this is called a hungry ghost (*preta*). Greed and deception constitute an offense.

When this person’s retribution for the offense is exhausted, they encounter the darkness of the unseen to form a body; this is called a nightmare ghost (*yamadeva*). Greed for brightness constitutes an offense. When this person’s retribution for the offense is exhausted—
When encountering essence, they take form; these are called *wangliang* ghosts. Their crime was greed for achievement. When this person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter light and take form;
these are called *yishi* ghosts. Their crime was greed for factions. When this person’s retribution is exhausted, they encounter humans and take form; these are called *chuan-song* ghosts.
Ānanda, these people all fall because of their pure delusion; when the fires of karma have burned them dry, they emerge above as ghosts.
All such beings are summoned by the karma of their own false imaginings. If one awakens to Bodhi, then it is wondrous, perfect, and luminous—fundamentally nothing at all.
It is not that one enters the realm of hungry ghosts after completing the retribution for hellish offenses. It is [the result of] slandering, destroying, and violating all precepts;

specifically, it is to violate while simultaneously slandering the Bodhisattva precepts—there being only violation without slander—or to disparage the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, which constitutes both slandering the Buddha and slandering the Dharma.
The precepts are the instrument for delivering sentient beings from suffering, and the Buddha is the teacher who extracts sentient beings from suffering.
The Dharma is the ground for sentient beings to exhaust suffering. To slander these three [vehicles] is called severing the Buddha-nature;
there is no sin more grave than this. Regarding the various sins, light and heavy, I have briefly cited the causes for rebirth in hell.

As for those who suffer in hell, it is the body of the sentient being’s karmic consciousness that manifests according to that consciousness. Only when the body of karmic consciousness is exhausted will they receive the body of a hungry ghost. (10)

Greed is the first of the ten habitual practices. To give rise to greed for objects results in rebirth among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), who remain attached to material things as spirits of gold, silver, grass, or wood.
Greed for beauty harms the proper harmony of the vital energy (*prāṇa*), and its residual habituation manifests as wind-demons and drought-spirits (*bhūta*) capable of causing severe droughts.

Delusion is the practice of deception; through illusory transformations and bewilderment, it attaches itself to animals to become a monster, such as a *cāṅ* spirit attaching itself to a tiger, or a rat.

Those belonging to the class of *jing* (spirits) and *mei* (demons) manifest forms to delude people; these are the residual habits of anger and hatred. Those who harbor resentment attach themselves to venomous insects to bewitch people;

these are those with grievances who, recollecting past enmities, wait for a moment of decline to seek retribution, thus becoming the ghosts of pestilence, such as those who spread epidemics and cause malaria.
Those who are arrogant and rely on their own vital energy become hungry ghosts by riding upon the empty breath. Furthermore, arrogance inevitably turns into stinginess.

Stinginess leads to rebirth as a hungry ghost (*preta*); deception results in being falsely accused. By oppressing the virtuous, one becomes a ghost that relies on the dark and dwells in obscurity, haunting those who sleep to cause nightmares;
habitual perceptions are mistaken for clarity, leading to a semblance of cleverness devoid of true wisdom.

*Wangliang* (sprites) are the strange transformations of wood and stone—this is merely one example. When crookedness and fraud become private interests, it is called the perfection of greed. "Ming" (明) refers to incantations; thus, within the causal state...

Because they used deceptive arts to manipulate and drive others, they become ghosts who are compelled by the incantations of others. As for litigants, they form factions and alliances to provide testimony;
this is called being "greedy for a faction. Therefore, their retribution lies among the class of ghosts, where they attach themselves to humans to vent their grievances and transmit messages.

It is like the divinations of shamans and priests that transmit the arrival of good or bad fortune; it is pure emotion (*qing*). When "heavy" is raised, it encompasses the nine emotions and the eight emotions, etc.
"Burning dry" means that causes are exhausted and effects are ended. "Awakening to Bodhi" is like waking from a dream—what dharma can be obtained?
"Sublime" means not being bound by karma; "perfect" means allowing no other things to enter; "luminous" means there is absolutely no darkness or obscurity.
All realms of existence are empty; how much more so the realm of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the karma of a ghost is exhausted, both emotion and thought become empty, and only then does one exist within the world.

If one encounters a person with whom they have a long-standing enmity from a previous life, and having been reborn as an animal, repays that karmic debt, then once the object of their resentment is exhausted and the retribution is finished, they will be born into the human world, mostly as a species of owl.
As for ghosts of wind-drought spirits, once the wind has subsided and the retribution is exhausted, [they likewise attain birth].

Those born into the world as omens of many calamities are ghosts who bewitch all manner of different species; when their animal existence ends and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world as foxes.
Those born into the world as ghosts of insects and vermin are those whose insect forms have perished and whose retribution is exhausted. Thus they are born into the world.
Those who were mostly of the poisonous class, as spirits of decay and pestilence, when their retribution for decay and poverty is exhausted, are born into the world, mostly as the class of worms;

as spirits that received vital breath, when their breath is dissipated and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as the class of food; as spirits of long-term obscurity...
When their retribution for the "dark" (you) is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as the class of "clothing" ghosts (fu-lei), which are ghosts of refined harmony (he-jing).

When their retribution for the "harmonious" (he) is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as the class of "correspondence" ghosts (ying-lei), which are ghosts of luminous spirit (ming-ling). When their retribution for the "luminous" (ming) is exhausted, they are born into the human world.
Most are auspicious omens for all classes of beings. Those ghosts who depend on humans, when the person dies and their retribution is exhausted, are born into the human world;
most become compliant types.
When their karmic influence as ghosts is exhausted, they enter the realm of animals. Within the animal realm, there are likewise higher destinies and downward degradations. And...

Regarding those who practice killing while harboring hatred, such as the Dragon Kings (*nāgarāja*) and the Garuḍa Kings (*garuḍarāja*), these are for the most part those who originate from the realm of ghosts (*preta*).
This is stated in terms of the majority; it is not the case that all are so. Their categories are manifold and not limited to one. They cause the objects they possess to be destroyed.
When ghosts follow the end of their lifespan, this is called the exhaustion of retribution. The earth-owl (*tǔxiāo*) attaching itself to clods of earth resembles a strange ghost possessing an object;

its greed for seizing and plundering through pits and killings is merely the repayment of such debts. As for omens of calamity, they are like the *shāngyáng* bird dancing over water or the flying squirrel (*wúshǔ*) calling out to people;
the drought-demon (*hànbié*) causes disaster, and the transformation of livestock likewise serves as a portent of misfortune. The origin of *mèi* ghosts lies in madness and delusion.
They transform into seductive foxes, poisonous species such as snakes and scorpions, or malevolent ghosts that enter the human body to cause illness;

they further transform into *rāji* and *krimi* (threadworms and intestinal worms) to take refuge within the body. Due to habits of arrogance, pride, and stinginess, they will inevitably have many debts;

thus, as ghosts they suffer hunger, and as animals they serve as food—this is how they repay their karmic obligations. "Mian" means to be attached; "you" means dark obscurity. It refers to being oppressed by nightmares in the darkness.

These ghosts wear the likeness of their former forms—belonging to the category of camels, donkeys, oxen, horses, and the like—which serve as the attire and implements for human use, thereby repaying the debts incurred through oppression.
When they manifest clearly as ghosts, they harmonize with various spirits to become animals according to their kind; such as the swallows of spring and the wild geese of autumn.
"Being able to respond to the proper seasons" means that "harmony" (*he*) implies a mixture. Mantras produce spiritual efficacy through the power of their retention;

when that power is exhausted, no further results are seen, and the ghost likewise reaches the end of its retribution. It is then reborn among those with auspicious signs, such as the *phoenix* or the *qilin*, or it attaches itself to the ghosts of shamans.

When the sorcerers attached to them die, the ghosts likewise meet their end. Following this principle, those such as cats and dogs who depend upon and follow humans—Ānanda, all these are dried up by the fire of karma;
having repaid their past debts, they become animals as their secondary retribution.
These too are all summoned and drawn forth by their own deluded karma. If one awakens to Bodhi, then these delusive conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
All such things as you have mentioned—Bao-lian-xiang and the others, as well as King Vaidūrya and the bhikṣu Śunakṣatra—these evil karmas were originally produced from within themselves;
they did not descend from heaven, nor emerge from the earth, nor were they bestowed by others.
They were summoned by one's own delusions and must be received back by oneself. Within the mind of Bodhi, they are all merely the solidification of floating, empty, and false imaginings.
This summarizes the three miserable realms (*durgati*). Each of these three realms arises from the false and deluded creation of karma;

it is not bestowed by Heaven, nor produced by the Earth, nor granted by humans. One falsely creates and falsely receives. Within the nature of awakening (*bodhātman*), they are all like flowers in the sky.
If they were conferred by another, there might be some who escape the net; but since one creates for oneself and receives for oneself, there is truly no place of escape.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when these animals repay their prior debts, if the debtor repays more than what was owed, these beings will again become human and demand the excess back.
This occurs if the debtor possesses both power and merit.
Thus, among human beings, they do not relinquish their human form to repay that labor. If they lack merit, they return as animals to discharge the remaining balance.
Ānanda, you should know that whether it be through the use of money and goods or the employment of one's labor, once the debt is fully repaid, the obligation ceases.
Just as they might kill one another’s lives or eat their flesh in the interim, so it continues for as long as an atom-dust number of eons;
devouring one another and slaughtering one another like a turning wheel, alternating between high and low status without rest, except through *śamatha*.
Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world, they cannot remain in a state of sleep;
animals will surely come to repay their debts. If the creditor takes an excessive amount in repayment, these beings will subsequently be reborn as humans.
They demand payment for the remaining balance. It is commonly seen that when virtuous people have children, their families are ruined;
or they are robbed, or fall into debt, or are unjustly subjected to forced labor, or are falsely beaten.

All of these are instances where, due to prior karma, one must relinquish this body to repay the surplus as an animal. By cultivating merit, one may partially compensate for it among humans. Below, Ānanda further clarifies this.
Debts are easy to repay, but a life-debt is difficult to repay. *Śamatha* is the power of one's own right concentration;
the appearance of a Buddha in the world and his releasing of one from enmity is reliance upon the power of another. Only through these two means can repayment be brought to rest.
You should now know that those of the owl species, once their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical form, are born among human beings as members of the dull-witted class.

Those of the ill-omened species, once their retribution is exhausted and they restore their physical form, are born among human beings as members of the foolish class. As for those of the fox species...
When their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical forms, they are born among the human race, yet they are integrated among the common and mediocre.

Those of the worm-like class, when their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical forms, are born among the human race, yet they are integrated among the cruel and violent. Those of the intestinal parasite-like class, when their retribution is exhausted and they regain their physical forms, are born among the human race.
Those who combined with the subtle class, having their retribution fulfilled and their forms restored, were born among the human race as those of a gentle nature.

Those who combined with the compliant class, having their retribution fulfilled and their forms restored, were born among the human race as those of a laborious nature. Those who combined with the responsive class...
Having fulfilled their retribution and returned to form, they are born among the human realm and integrated into the category of literary refinement.

Those who possessed auspicious omens, having fulfilled their retribution and returned to form, are born among the human realm and integrated into the category of clarity. Those who followed the various social norms, having fulfilled their retribution and returned to form, are born among the human realm.
Ānanda, these beings have all settled their karmic debts from former lives and have returned once more to the human realm.

Yet, from time immemorial, their karmic calculations have been inverted; they have alternately given birth to and killed one another. Having never encountered the Tathāgata nor heard the True Dharma, they naturally revolve within the midst of worldly afflictions.
Such people as these are called "those who are to be pitied."
When the karma of the animal realm is exhausted, one returns to human form. This is a reward for the wholesome deeds of the human path;

yet, having come from the animal state, one is mixed among the common masses. Thus it is called "intermingled. Among the ten classes of beings, misfortune is frequent and auspiciousness rare; suffering is abundant and joy scarce. Their karmic calculations are inverted:
those who seek to collect debts exact life, and those who claim their dues give rise to mutual slaughter. These are not favorable conditions for meeting.

This is an accumulation. Had they not encountered the Tathāgata and heard the explanations of the Dharma, their births and deaths would have continued without end; thus, they are to be pitied. These ten classes are all the retributions of past habitual tendencies.
As for those whose cause was arrogance and whose retribution is gentleness: in the past they looked down upon others, and now as humans they are looked down upon by others.
This is merely a response to their opposition; it is superficial understanding, a mere cleverness in various arts.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are followers who do not rely on Perfect Enlightenment to cultivate *samādhi*, but instead cultivate deluded thoughts, seeking to preserve and solidify their physical forms.
They roam in mountain forests and remote places inaccessible to ordinary people; these are the ten kinds of *ṛṣis*. Ānanda, those sentient beings—
If one is steadfast in ingesting medicinal elixirs without ceasing, and the path of the elixir is perfected, one is called a terrestrial immortal (dixingxian).

If one is steadfast in [consuming] plants and trees without ceasing, and the path of medicine is perfected, one is called a flying immortal (feixingshan). If one is steadfast in [consuming] metal and stone without ceasing...
When the transformation of the Way is perfected, one is called a "Wandering Immortal" (*cāraṇa-ṛṣi*); they solidify their movements and stillness without ceasing.

When the vital essence (*ojas*) is perfected, one is called a "Sky-Walking Immortal" (*khe-cara-ṛṣi*); they solidify their fluids without ceasing. When the virtue of moisture is perfected, one is called a "Heaven-Walking Immortal" (*divya-cara-ṛṣi*).
Firmly maintaining the essence of their vital energy (*ojas*) without ceasing, they achieve perfection through absorption; these are called *karmadeva* (Heavenly Beings of Action).

Firmly maintaining the power of incantations and prohibitions without ceasing, they achieve perfection through ritual arts; these are called *ṛṣideva* (Heavenly Beings of the Sages). Firmly maintaining their contemplation without ceasing...
The perfection of recollection is called the Immortal of Illuminating Conduct; it is the firm and uninterrupted union [of mindfulness].

The perfection of responsive resonance is called the Immortal of Refining Conduct; it is the firm and uninterrupted transformation. The perfection of awakening is called the Immortal of Transcendent Conduct.
Ānanda, these individuals all refine their minds among human beings, yet they do not cultivate true awakening.

Instead, they attain a distinct mode of existence, living for ten million years, dwelling in deep mountains or on remote ocean islands far from the realm of men. This, too, is the wandering and revolving of deluded thoughts;
failing to cultivate samādhi, when their retribution is exhausted, they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

This is to advance from the human path to enter the path of the immortals (*ṛṣi*). To rely on perfect enlightenment and cultivate *samādhi* means to take the mind that is neither born nor extinguished as the fundamental cause of cultivation.
To harbor thoughts of longevity, desiring the physical form to be firm and indestructible, is merely a deluded thought;
such a state ultimately ends in decay and ruin. Compared to the heavens it is inferior, yet compared to humans it is superior. [It belongs to those in] mountain forests...
In places beyond the reach of ordinary men—such as famous mountains, caves, and sacred precincts, the hidden abodes of immortals—one practices the "ten acts," which refers to meritorious cultivation.
As for "ingestion," this refers to substances such as sesame, lotus seeds, and water chestnuts, which are commonly used in diet; hence it is called the "path of food.

Through this, one attains robust health and longevity, yet has not yet attained the power of levitation. As for "plants," this refers to substances such as *zhī* fungus, achillea, pine, and cypress, which are commonly used as medicine; hence...

It is called the Way of Medicines (*yàodào*). [These involve] lightness of body and flying steps; ascending heights and leaping over ravines; and substances such as metal and stone, lead, mercury, and cinnabar. There are two types of transformative practices (*huàdào*):

first, those that can transform the bones, resulting in longevity and a firm physique; second, those that can transform matter, enabling one to turn the base into the noble, to roam among humanity, and to extensively practice acts of benefit.
[This also includes] matters concerning movement and stillness, the circulation of *qì*, the regulation of life, and the refinement of the essence (*jīng*).

Returning the Qi; refining the Qi to return it to the Spirit; refining the Spirit to return it to the Void. To undergo feather-transformation and ascend, to roam through the void—this involves the vital fluids.
Stirring the Celestial Pond and swallowing the Jade Elixir can cause water to rise and fire to descend, thereby forming the Inner Elixir;
hence it is called "moistening virtue. Transcending the void to travel to the heavens, its essence and color are like gathering the solar essence at dawn and gathering [the lunar essence] at night.

Yuehua (Moon Flower). Tongxing (Pervasive Practice): The spirit and vital essence communicate with the creative transformation (*zaohua*). By upholding mantras, one spontaneously attains the Way of the Immortals;
it also concurrently cures illnesses and expels malevolent spirits to benefit all living beings. Hence, it is called Tongxing. Sinsan (Meditative Recollection):

One may visualize the spirit emerging from the fontanelle, or fix the mind upon the navel wheel to refine the elixir. Purifying the spirit and concentrating the thoughts, after a long time, they will respond with illumination.

Therefore, it is called "Illuminating Practice" (zhàoxíng). By taking from the *kan* trigram and filling the *li* trigram, one extracts and adds lead and mercury (*qián-hóng*) to form the immortal embryo (*xiāntāi*).

This is what is meant by "intercourse" (*jiāogòu*). By governing and protecting the essence and vital energy (*jīngqì*), it is called "Essence Practice" (jìngxíng). Do not be confused by heterodox teachings;

through thorough awakening to the principles of transformation, one can achieve great illusory manifestations (*huànhuà*) that are wondrous beyond this world, and is thus termed an "Ultimate Practice Immortal" (juéxíng xiān). Refining the mind does not consist merely of ingesting elixirs and the like; it is even more so.
They take conduct as their foundation. Thus, they maintain the precepts, accumulate merit, and perform deeds of rescue and relief.

Yet, those who do not cultivate right awakening fail to reach the true and eternal nature of their own minds—the self-substance of all myriad forms—and consequently fear death while clinging to life, using "longevity" as their designation.

To speak of "longevity" is merely to surpass the short; to speak of "birth" is ultimately to await extinction. How could one who seeks a separate principle for the process of birth fail to recognize the wondrous essence of non-arising?
To seek a separate, deluded principle for prolonging life outside of perfect enlightenment is a false path.
Ānanda, there are those among the people of the world who do not seek permanence and have not yet been able to abandon their affection for wives and concubines;
yet, regarding sexual misconduct, their minds do not wander into excess, and they polish themselves until clarity arises. After the end of their lives, they dwell in proximity to the sun and moon.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*). In their own quarters with their wives, their lustful attachment is slight, and when they dwell in purity, they do not... [engage in such acts].
They obtain the full flavor [of existence]. After their lives end, they transcend the brilliance of the sun and moon and dwell at the summit of the human realm.

This class of beings is called the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (the Heaven of the Thirty-three). When encountering desire, they engage briefly; once it has passed, they have no lingering thoughts. In the world of humans, they are active for little and tranquil for much.
After their lives end, they abide serenely and radiantly in the midst of space, such that the light of the sun and moon cannot reach them from above. This is...
O people, there is a class of beings who possess their own radiance; they are called the Suyāma devas.

They are tranquil at all times, and when any sensory contact arises, they are unable to be disturbed by it. After their lives end, they ascend to a subtle and refined state, no longer descending to the realms of humans or devas in the lower worlds.
Even until the kalpa is destroyed, the three calamities cannot reach them. This class of beings is called Tuṣita.
"O Celestial One, I am free from desire. I engage in your practice only because it is your way; when we lie together, the flavor is like chewing wax.
After my life ends, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations. Such a class of beings is called the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations.

Without worldly thoughts, they engage in worldly affairs; yet in their engagement in these affairs, they clearly transcend them. After their lives end, they are able to universally transcend and emerge from the realm of transformations."
The realm of transformation. This class of beings is called the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).
Ānanda, these six heavens, although their physical forms move about, the traces of their minds still intermingle; from this point downward, they are known as the Realm of Desire (Kāmadhātu).

The following clarifies the heavenly realms. Those who do not seek the permanent are those who do not seek the supramundane cultivation of the fundamental eternal principle, but merely hope for the fruits of worldly pleasure that are subject to exhaustion.
Taking one’s own wife or concubine constitutes right sexual conduct, while taking the wives of others constitutes wrong sexual conduct.

Not only does such a person refrain from committing wrong sexual conduct with the body, but their mind is also free from even a single thought of transgression. When the waters of craving no longer flow, the mind becomes serene and still.

Their nature is refined and polished; thus they are born on the mid-slope of Mount Sumeru as the gods of the Four Great Kings—Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Vaiśravaṇa—who each occupy one side.
Their purity and flavor are not yet complete because they still possess a slight attachment; compared to the former [gods], they have already surpassed them by a factor of two.
Therefore, one is born upon the summit of Mount Sumeru in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—this is translated as "The Thirty-three," the realm governed by Śakra.
These two heavens above are called the Earth-Dwelling Devas (*bhūmi-vāsin*). As they gradually incline toward stillness, it is said that "movement is slight and stillness is abundant.

They are able to evoke birth in the Luminous Abodes of the Sky-Dwelling Devas (*antarīkṣa-vāsin*), which are twice as high as Mount Sumeru. The light of the sun and moon cannot reach upward to illuminate them; they exist only...
They possess bodily radiance that illuminates one another. As for Suyāma (translated here as "Time-Span"), they take the opening and closing of lotus flowers as their day and night.
Constantly dwelling in stillness, they are naturally free from desire; yet if some sensory contact should arise, they may not yet be able to resist it.
He merely responded briefly. [The deceased] was reborn in the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven. This heaven consists of an inner court and an outer court;

the inner court is where Bodhisattvas in their final birth (abhisambodhi-bodhisattvas) reside as temporary dwellings. Even those in the outer court may not peer into its inner sanctum, let alone the various devas of the lower realms.
Therefore, it is called "subtle and refined. The Lord Maitreya, having made great vows, was born in that place;

by the power of his outflow-free (*anāsrava*) merit, he is not affected by the three calamities. Outside the second enclosure, there are further heavens of karmic retribution, which are produced by outflowing (*sāsrava*) karma.

The three calamities can destroy [the lower realms]. In the sutras, sometimes the outer heavens are mentioned first, followed by the inclusion of the inner court; this is a case of the translator omitting redundant text. Tuṣita is translated here as "Contentment.
When objects appear before one without intentional thought, it is called "laid out crosswise" (horizontal presentation).

As with the previous case of responding to objects without intention, here one is superior in being free from craving. Those born beyond the Realm of Transformation (Nirmāṇarati) are able to transform objects of desire themselves according to their will.

They enjoy [the realm], transcending the non-transformative states of the lower heavens and dwelling in the Land of Transformation (*nirmāṇarati*). Those who possess no worldly mind aspire to the higher realms;
being devoid of worldly passion, they merely assume the roles of husband and wife as a conventional worldly expedient.

Not only is there a complete absence of sensual flavor, but they are clearly and fully transcendent, surpassing the spheres of both transformation and non-transformation. "Transformation" refers to the fifth [heaven].

"Devas. Regarding "the non-transformative," these are the aforementioned four heavens. As for the Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations), they do not labor to transform objects themselves;
rather, all objects of sensual pleasure are transformed by others, which they then enjoy with mastery. The four heavens above these are called the "Sky-Dwelling Devas.
To restrain movement and turn toward stillness is called "Emerging from Movement. As for the two heavens that dwell upon the earth, there is physical union, and men and women marry. Furthermore—
Just as among humans, the outflow of desire is eliminated by a single encounter of the vital energies (*vāyu*); it is not like among humans where impurities flow forth.
In Yāma, they embrace; in Tuṣita, they hold hands; in Nirmāṇarati, they smile at one another;

in Paranirmita-vaśavartin, they gaze at each other. They share food, drink, sleep, and sexual desire; therefore, they are called the Desire Heavens (*kāmadeva*). This is the merit of the six heavens of the desire realm.
The five precepts and the ten wholesome actions lead to this state. Now, we shall briefly discuss how to slightly increase one's excellence within the realm of desire. Desire is the root of saṃsāra;
it was previously explained that the beginning of one’s sinking into ruin starts here, and now it is explained that the beginning of one’s transcendence and soaring upward also starts here.
Since a beginner cannot yet achieve meditative concentration and wisdom, they should first swiftly sever the root; then, escape from saṃsāra will be possible.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas, Volume Eight.
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Cultivation and Realization of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
As it was said to Ānanda in the ninth fascicle:

"Among all those in the world who cultivate the mind, there may be those who do not rely on *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) and possess no wisdom, yet they are able to restrain their bodies and refrain from sexual desire.
Whether walking or sitting, they are free from such thoughts; no defilement of attachment arises, and they leave nothing behind."
In the desire realm, those who should regard themselves as companions of Brahmā form one class known as the *Brahmapārṣadya* Heaven.

Once the habits of desire are removed and the mind of detachment manifests, they delight in and accord with all forms of discipline; these individuals are able to practice the virtues of Brahmā at that time, forming another class known as the *Brahmapurohita* Heaven.
Their bodies and minds are wondrously perfect, their dignified deportment is flawless, and they are pure.
Observing the precepts and further adding clear awakening, such a person is able, at that time, to lead the assembly of Brahmās and become a Great Brahma King.
This class of beings is called the Mahābrahmā Heaven. Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any suffering or affliction.
Although it is not the true, correct samādhi, when the various outflows (āsrava) do not move within a pure mind, it is called the first dhyāna.

While the heavens of the desire realm are produced solely through the influence of the ten wholesome actions, the heavens of the form realm are produced by both the ten wholesome actions and meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).

Nevertheless, these are merely the six practices of tainted (sāsrava) dhyāna-contemplation. As for the six practices: one feels aversion toward the desire realm as being suffering, coarse, and an obstruction, while taking delight in the form realm.
The realm is pure, sublime, and detached. Coarse afflictions do not defile it; the retribution of purity manifests before one.

By recollecting [this], one is born in the Brahma-world through the power of precepts alone. When the mind of detachment manifests and affection accords with the discipline, then concentration and precepts are in harmony.
One who practices the virtue of Brahma propagates the Brahma-transformation. The Brahma-purohitas are the ministers of heaven. Body and mind—

He is encompassed by both [the two gates]. Wondrous, perfect, and pure, he is further endowed with clear awakening; his wisdom transcends the Brahma hosts, and thus he is able to preside over them as the Great Brahma King.

Turning his back on defilement and inclining toward purity, he is called a "Superior Stream-winner" (*śrotāpanna*). Holding his body and subduing desire, he is said to be "unoppressed by suffering and affliction.
With the mind free from distraction, he is said to have "all outflows (*āsrava*) unmoved. *Dhyāna* refers to the meditative concentration of *dhyāna*. From the beginning—
Fourth: All these are impure dhyānas. Dhyāna is named after samādhi, yet this is not true samādhi.
Why is it called the first dhyāna? It is because one has already abandoned the defiled mind of desire and has already abandoned the habitual tendencies of agitated desire;
thus, it receives the name "first dhyāna. From this point upward, there are no women at all; both mind and conduct are entirely detached, and there is nothing [to disturb them].
He passed the time without food or sleep; whenever he felt even slightly hungry or fatigued, he would immediately enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Upon emerging from concentration, he was satiated and his spirit was lucid and vigorous. Thus, he took the joy of meditation alone as his sustenance and rest.

Ānanda, next there is the Brahmā Heaven. Those who govern the Brahmā people, perfect the Brahmā conduct, and whose minds are clarified and unmoving, producing light from their profound stillness—this class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*).
Their lights shine upon one another, illuminating without end; they reflect throughout the ten directions, pervading them so that everything becomes like lapis lazuli.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Infinite Light (*Apramāṇābha*). They absorb and sustain this perfect light, forming...
Regarding the substance of the teaching: its transformative power is pure, and its application is inexhaustible. This class of beings is called the Ābhāsvara Heaven (Light-Sound Heaven).
Ānanda, these three superior streams cannot be oppressed by any anxiety or distress.
Although they have not yet attained the true Samādhi of correct cultivation, within their pure minds, coarse outflows have already been suppressed; this is termed the Second Dhyāna.
The mind becomes clear and unmoving; this is how concentration arises from ethical discipline. Tranquility and depth give rise to radiance; this is how wisdom is manifested from concentration.

This refers to the luminosity of the physical body and not to the illumination of wisdom. Because that light is still inferior, it is called "Limited Light" (Parīttābha). When the power of concentration becomes further clarified, [it is called "Immeasurable Light"].
Sublime light flashes forth in alternation; as the objects follow this initial manifestation, they universally become composed of lapis lazuli, which is named "Immeasurable Light.
To take these objects into the mind is called "absorbing" (*xi*). Following the prior perfection, one absorbs, retains, and maintains them so that they do not disperse.

This causes people to contemplate the light and cultivate the Brahma-conduct; therefore, it is called the "accomplishment of the teaching-body" (*jiaoti*). Being independent of words, it is called "pure," whereby beings receive benefit according to their capacities.
It is called "Inexhaustible" (*akṣaya*). Because light replaces sound, it is named "Light-Sound" (*ābhāsvara*).

While the power of concentration in the first dhyāna still requires the support of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the gods of this heaven do not require the support of ethical discipline and are naturally unmoving. Their concentration is so superior that it emits light, and they are ranked according to the excellence or inferiority of that light.

In the first dhyāna, the mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*) is unmoving, yet it has not yet been subdued; in this heaven, the coarse outflows have already been subdued. [The text here appears to be truncated.]
It is peace. Anxiety and apprehension are lighter than suffering and affliction. Suffering belongs to the body; anxiety belongs to the mind.

Ānanda, when such devas and humans have perfected their radiant halos and voices, revealing the subtle through their voices, and having brought forth refined practice, they attain the bliss of tranquil extinction.
This class of beings is called the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha). With the pure void manifest before them, it induces boundlessness, and their bodies and minds—

Through pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), they achieve the bliss of cessation (*nirvāṇa*). Such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (*Apramāṇaśubha*). Their worlds, bodies, and minds are all perfectly pure;
having accomplished pure virtues, they manifest supreme reliance and return to the bliss of cessation. Such a class [of beings] is called the Heaven of Universal Purity (*Śubhakṛtsna*).
Ānanda, these three superior streams possess great conformity; their bodies and minds are peaceful and secure, and they attain the immeasurable.
Joy (*sukha*). Although one has not yet truly attained genuine *samādhi*, within a mind of tranquility, joy is fully present; this is called the Third Dhyāna.
Because the essence of the teaching is revealed through the circular light, one is able to give rise to and perfect refined practice, thereby generating pure joy.
This bliss is not an external object; it arises from the pure nature. Being tranquil, serene, and still, it is called the "bliss of cessation.

When it is merely pervasive but not yet fully realized, it is called "limited purity" (*parītta-śubha*). As this purity persists, emptiness emerges, gradually becoming vast and open until it reaches the infinite. Initially, there is only mental pervasion;

subsequently, both body and mind become expansive and empty, resulting in a state of vast and sublime peace. Therefore, it is called "perfected" (*abhinirvṛtta*). This immeasurability pertains to both body and mind.
[The merit] is immeasurable. First, it concerns only body and mind; subsequently, the world is added, such that all together achieve emptiness and stillness.
Therefore, it is called "perfectly pure" and "the accomplishment of pure virtues. The wondrous bliss within the heavens reaches its ultimate limit here;

thus, one recognizes this as the land of the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, the place of lifelong refuge and entrustment. Hence, it is called "entrusted" (*tuo*) and "returned to" (*gui*). [This applies to] body, mind, and the world.

When both the primary and secondary environments are entirely pure, it is only then called "Universal Purity" (Subhakṛtsna). The first dhyāna accords with the code of discipline (*vinaya*); this [third dhyāna] accords with pure karma.
When it reaches the state of being immeasurable and all-pervasive, it is "Great Accordance. "Peaceful and secure" means enjoying mastery and freedom.
Within this realm, the third dhyāna is considered the place of ultimate bliss; therefore, it is called "Immeasurable Bliss. This is termed "sublime bliss free from joy" (*prīti-virahita-sukha*). Joy—

This [state] is what is stirred by the moving mind; bliss is what is fused by the pure mind. In the mind of the second dhyāna, there is the sensation of joy (*prīti*), which involves conceptualization and distraction;
it is not yet tranquil. Only upon reaching this [third dhyāna] does one first attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and stable composure.

Ānanda, furthermore, there are devas and humans whose bodies and minds are no longer oppressed; the causes of suffering have been exhausted, yet pleasure is not permanent, for it must inevitably decay after a long time.

They simultaneously and instantaneously relinquish both the mind of suffering and the mind of pleasure. The characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are extinguished, and the nature of pure merit arises.

This class of beings is called the Heaven of Merit-Born (Puṇyaprasava). Their minds of equanimity are perfectly integrated, their resolute understanding is pure, and within the unobstructed state of merit, they attain the sublime.
Following this, until the end of the future, such a class of beings is named the Heaven of Meritorious Affection (*Puṇyapriya*).
Ānanda, from within this heaven, there are two diverging paths: if one dwells in the cultivation and realization of that former mind of immeasurable pure light and perfectly luminous merit;

This class of beings is called the Bṛhatphala Heaven (Gods of Vast Results). If, from their previous state of mind, they simultaneously grow weary of both suffering and pleasure, and cultivate a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*) with continuous, uninterrupted application until they fully master the path of equanimity, then body and mind both cease;
their mental deliberations become ashen and solidified, and they remain thus for five hundred kalpas.
Since these people take arising and ceasing as their cause, they are unable to manifest the nature that is neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
For the first half-eon they cease, and for the latter half-eon they arise; such a class is called the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Ānanda, these four superior streams cannot be moved by any worldly states of suffering or pleasure. Although they do not constitute the truly immovable stage of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they possess...
When the mind attains mastery and its functions become fully refined, it is called the Four Dhyānas.

The first dhyāna is collectively termed "Brahma" because one maintains precepts with such purity. The second dhyāna is collectively termed "Light" because light is generated and transformative power is manifested.
The third dhyāna is collectively termed "Pure" because one is able to subdue the defilements of the six consciousnesses. The fourth dhyāna is [free from] suffering...
When joy and equanimity are both relinquished, one attains spontaneous mastery; this is the true merit of the world, hence it is called "the arising of merit" and "the love of merit.
This pure merit differs from the turbid merit of the lower realms, hence it is called "pure merit. At the very moment of initial relinquishment—
The characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*) still remains. After a long time, it becomes fully matured and perfectly integrated, gradually approaching spontaneity.

Initially, one takes equanimity as a resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), which merely achieves the purification of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*). Upon reaching this stage, by no longer forming thoughts of resolute conviction, even the thought of resolute conviction itself becomes purified.
At the beginning, the mind of equanimity was hindered; therefore, merit was also hindered. Now that the mind of equanimity—
Having already been melted away, merit is thus without obstruction; until the end of the future, it accords with the mind and fulfills one’s intentions.

From the branch of "merit-love," two divergent paths arise: the path leading to the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) is the direct route; the path leading to the Realm of Non-conception (*Āsaṃjñika*) is the circuitous and deviant route.
One is progressive advancement; the other is cessation. One does not grasp at suffering or pleasure, nor does one loathe the medicine of suffering; one simply relies on the four [immeasurables].
Measuring the mind, one cultivates merit and realizes vast fruits.

If one regards suffering and pleasure as objects of aversion and adheres to a mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), investigating them without interruption, one relinquishes everything of body and mind and attains the fruit of the "extinguished-heart" (*huīxīn*).

This is precisely the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). It is characterized by the cessation of the minds of suffering and pleasure and the arising of a mind of weary detachment.

Nevertheless, it remains a cause for birth and cessation. Only at the eighth stage is a Bodhisattva truly in the "Immovable Stage" (*acalā-bhūmi*). This [stage] merely means not being moved by suffering and pleasure;
it is not yet the unconditioned true realm (*anabhisaṃskṛta-bhūtaviṣaya*), but conditioned functional mastery (*saṃskṛta-prayoga*) has become fully matured.
Ānanda, herein there are further five classes of non-returning devas (*anāgāmin*). Within the lower realm, they simultaneously extinguish the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*);
both suffering and pleasure have vanished, and since there is no longer a place to dwell below, they establish their abodes within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) of equanimity.
Ānanda, because both suffering and pleasure are extinguished and contentious minds do not interact, this one class is called the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Avṛha*).
The mechanisms of their faculties function independently; they have no ground for cultivating social bonds. Such a class of beings is named the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa).

Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, their wondrous vision is perfectly clear and serene; there are no further sensory images or any defilements whatsoever. Such a class of beings is named the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa).
Their refined vision manifests before them, and they mold all things without obstruction. Such a class is named the Sudṛśa Heaven (Good-Vision Heaven).
Having reached the ultimate limit of all phenomena and exhausted the nature of form, they enter the boundless. Such a class is named the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (Ultimate Form Heaven).
Ānanda, as for these Non-Returner heavens, even the various kings of the four levels of the fourth dhyāna can only hear of them with admiration; they cannot know or see them. As it is said:
In this world, the wildernesses, deep mountains, and sites of the sacred path are all sustained by Arhats;
therefore, they cannot be seen by coarse worldly people. Ānanda, these eighteen heavens are solitary and without social intercourse, yet they have not yet exhausted the burden of form.
From here downward, it is called the Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).

No longer taking birth in the desire realm is called "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin). It is also termed the "Five Pure Abodes. When both habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) are extinguished, it is called "the exhaustion of both.
Since suffering has perished, one does not dwell in the five destinies; since pleasure has perished, one does not dwell in the three dhyānas.

It is not the same as the state of non-participation (*asabhāga*). Only when the ground of pure equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*) is attained can one predict that it is the same as the state of participation (*sabhāga*), suitable for entering the summer retreat (*varṣā*) with the aspiration for the fruit of Arhatship. "Striving mind" refers to a mind where suffering and pleasure are in combat;

at this stage, while there is no internal mind capable of engaging [in such conflict], one still perceives an external ground with which to engage. When the mechanism functions in solitude, then one comes and goes.

Freedom. When one investigates the locus where [subject and object] intersect, it is utterly unfindable. The former [verse] speaks exclusively of the mind; this [verse] refers to both the object and the subject.
In these two cases, as the objects are no longer perceived, the sense organs have nothing with which to pair. "Dust-phenomena" (*rajas-pratibimba*) refers to objective realms;
"sinking defilements" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*). Reaching this point, the lands of the ten directions appear vividly.
It is pure. One who is unimpeded in forging and smelting melts and refines all delusions so that they do not form obstacles;
such a person can give rise to the fourteen transformations of sovereign mastery, just as a potter molds clay or a smith refines gold, transforming them according to their will.
Reaching this point, all manifestations appear as if in a faint haze; they no longer constitute afflictions. "The manifold *jī* (群幾)" refers to the various subtle particles (*paramāṇu*).
In the Hīnayāna, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) are held to be composed of the aggregation of these subtle particles.

Now, by investigating these subtle particles and exhausting the nature of all matter, everything returns to emptiness. Thus, one proceeds from the limit of form (*rūpa-koṭi*) into the limit of the formless (*arūpa-koṭi*). Regarding that which...

This refers to distinguishing between form (*rūpa*), light (*āloka*), and space (*ākāśa*). The former heaven cultivates the mundane, out-flowing concentrations (*sāsrava-vaipākika-samādhi*) of ordinary beings; this heaven cultivates the supramundane, outflow-free concentrations (*anāsrava-ārya-samādhi*) of noble ones.
Because their coarseness and subtlety are as vastly different as heaven and earth, one can only look up to admire its name but cannot see it. The five subsequent phrases serve as metaphors for this:
there are three heavens each in the first, second, and third dhyānas, four heavens in the fourth dhyāna, and furthermore, there are five non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

The heavens consist of eighteen celestial realms. These are produced solely by the influence of meditative concentration and wholesome perceptions; as they are devoid of sensual desire, they are said to be "solitary and without union.
Yet, because they still possess material form and obstruction, they are said to be "not yet free from the burdens of the physical body. Collectively, these are termed the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, from within this limit of form at the Peak of Existence, there are again two divergent paths.
If one brings forth wisdom through a mind of equanimity, and the light of that wisdom becomes perfectly penetrating, one will then transcend the realm of dust and become an Arhat.
They enter the Bodhisattva vehicle. This class of individuals is called "Great Arhats who have turned their minds.

This designation marks them as noble beings who stand alone. Because they ultimately dwell at the summit of the realm of form, it is called the "Peak of Existence" (bhavāgra); it is adjacent to the formless realm.

Therefore, it is called the "limit of form" (*rūpānta*). Regarding the three fruits, there are those with sharp and dull faculties; thus, within the state of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), two further paths are distinguished.
Those of sharp faculties investigate the nature of form until they penetrate and perceive true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

They give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), and with the perfect penetration of the light of wisdom, they transcend the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and head toward the Mahāyāna, no longer being restricted to the celestial realms.
If one abides in a mind of equanimity, having accomplished the relinquishing of aversion, they perceive the body as an obstruction; by dissolving this obstruction, they enter into emptiness.

This class of practitioners is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Once all obstructions have been dissolved, there is neither obstruction nor cessation; within that state, only the *ālaya-vijñāna* remains.
Throughout the manas, there remains only half of its subtle activity; such a class is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).

When both emptiness and form have vanished and the consciousness-mind has utterly ceased, the ten directions are tranquil and there is nowhere for it to go; such a class is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
In this station, the nature of consciousness is unmoving. By exhausting their investigation through cessation, they proclaim the nature of exhaustion within the inexhaustible.
It is as if existing yet not existing; as if exhausted yet not exhausted. This class of beings is called the Station of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

These individuals exhaust emptiness, yet do not fully exhaust the principle of emptiness. Those who have reached the end of the holy path from the Heaven of No-Retreat (*anāgāmin*)—this class of beings is called "Non-returning" (*anāvartin*).

An Arhat of dull faculties, if from among the non-Buddhist heavens of the Non-conceptualizers (asaṃjñisattva), having exhausted the state of emptiness without returning, remains deluded, leaking, and without hearing [the Dharma],
shall then enter the cycle of rebirth.

The four heavens below this do not realize that the nature of form is empty and true, yet they diligently strive to dissolve obstructions. Loathing form as if it were a prison, their minds desire to escape;

perceiving the physical body to be a substantial hindrance that lacks autonomy, they cultivate the contemplation of emptiness to extinguish the body and return to non-existence—this is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
They then suffer from the thought that infinite space is too vast and have many mental objects to attend to.
Then it disperses. Being able to break through meditative concentration, all obstructions immediately dissolve and vanish; thus, one does not rely on form (*rūpa*).
When even the non-obstruction of non-existence ceases, one does not rely on emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Ālaya refers to the eighth consciousness; Manas refers to the seventh consciousness.
"Entirely within Manas" means that the seventh consciousness is fully present. Within this entirety, there is a half.
The divisions gradually become subtle. The *manas* consciousness is termed "constant and deliberative," giving rise to the two types of grasping: toward self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).

Because this deity possesses the power to suppress the afflictions (*kleśa*), although the *manas* is fully present, the aspect of its deliberation within the subjective division (*darśana-bhāga*) becomes spontaneously light and subtle;

this is called the "Sphere of Infinite Consciousness" (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*). As for the "consciousness-mind" being entirely extinguished, this refers to the partial extinction of the *manas*, which relies upon deep meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
By means of this power, one subdues their active manifestations so that they no longer function;
that which is utterly non-existent is the objective realm realized within the meditative absorption of the cessation of consciousness, known as the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*.

When the nature of consciousness becomes unmoving—referring to the eighth stage which is profoundly still and unshakable—one perceives this realm and, with the thought of cessation, applies deep investigation, thereby extinguishing even the perception of "nothingness."
One seeks to reach the state of profound stillness and merge with that realm of stillness. Within the inexhaustible, one brings forth the full realization of one's nature;

that is, within a fundamental realm that is not itself quiescent extinction, one perceives it as the true nature of quiescent extinction. The first seven [stages] have already been dissolved, yet ignorance remains unbroken;
therefore, it is said that "as if existing, yet not existing. If exhausted, it is not truly exhausted; thus one transcends the dualistic notions of existence and non-existence. This...

"Et cetera" refers to the first four classes of devas. The first class exhausts form (*rūpa*) and returns to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the second class exhausts emptiness and returns to consciousness (*vijñāna*);
the third class exhausts consciousness and returns to nothingness (*akiṃcanya*); the fourth class exhausts nothingness and returns to cessation (*nirodha*). Such is the exhaustion of emptiness.

Not only do they fail to comprehend the principle that the nature of form is true emptiness according to the Perfect and Sudden teaching, but they also fail to understand the truth of the twofold emptiness of person and phenomena.
They falsely desire to dissolve, empty, extinguish, and exhaust them, yet they do not realize that in the end they can never dissolve, empty, extinguish, or exhaust them.
Therefore, those who have reached this heaven from the five heavens of non-returning, having exhausted emptiness to enter this realm, possess faculties...
This person fundamentally cherishes what is correct. They await the completion of eighty thousand kalpas, exhausting all afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) to emerge from the three realms;
they are called Arhats of dull faculties. Compared to those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment] from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), they are thus termed "dull.

Those who proceed from the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) to the limit of emptiness and enter this heaven are fundamentally and originally heterodox, for they mistake the tainted heavens for the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, after eighty thousand kalpas of retribution have been fully exhausted, having no place to turn for refuge, they fall into ruin.
Ānanda, those various devas among the heavens are all ordinary beings receiving the fruits of their karma; when that retribution is exhausted, they enter into ruin.
Those heavenly kings, however, are bodhisattvas who dwell in samādhi, gradually advancing and turning their merit toward enlightenment.

The path practiced by the Noble Ones connects with the lords of devas and humans throughout the three realms; yet ordinary beings and sages remain distinct. "Devas and humans" refers to the subjects of heaven, who are categorized as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Regarding the "retribution of karmic fruits," this refers to having cultivated the ten wholesome actions and the eight dhyānas during the causal stage. By means of...
The six heavens of the desire realm and the four dhyānas serve as their retribution; therefore, when this retribution is exhausted, they enter the cycle of saṃsāra.

As for the statement that "the heavenly kings are bodhisattvas," this refers to those who advance through their respective stages and do not fall into saṃsāra. This section should follow below the section on the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).
Although the various heavens are not themselves the primary site of cultivation, by gradually progressing therein, one is a bodhisattva traversing samādhi.
This is to move from the inferior toward the superior. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have already attained the correct fruit;

yet, being satisfied with what they have gained as a small measure, they eventually fall into the ten kinds of false views within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), moving from the superior toward the inferior.
Ānanda, in these four heavens of the formless realm, body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of stability manifests before them; there is no matter resulting from karmic fruit.
From this point until the end, it is called the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
This bond belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). In the first two heavens, both form and space are absent; thus, the body is extinguished.

In the latter two heavens, the active manifestations of consciousness (*vijñāna*) are suppressed; thus, the mind is extinguished. Because both body and mind are extinguished, the state of fixed nature (*niyata-dharmatā*) manifests.

Regarding the absence of "karmic-resultant form" (*vipākaja-rūpa*): it is not like the physical sense-faculties and the environment (*bhājana-loka*) produced by the karmic retribution of the desire and form realms.

The realm [of formlessness] exists because of superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*); thus, one freely enjoys the transformed environments and inhabitants, which are what are known as "matter produced by the fruit of concentration" (*samādhiphala-rūpa*).
From the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, these are collectively termed the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
All of these arise from failing to comprehend the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind; through the accumulation of delusions, the three realms of existence are produced.
Within them, beings wander delusively, submerged in the seven destinies, with each *pudgala* following their own kind.

This summarizes the three realms. From the six heavens of desire up to the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, all arise because one fails to fully comprehend the wondrously enlightened and luminous mind that is inherently present.
Through the accumulation of delusion upon delusion, one falsely gives rise to the three realms.
When the karmic retributions of the various devas and humans are exhausted, they cannot avoid sinking further into the seven destinies, finding no rest. *Pudgala* translates as:

The *saṃkhyeya-gati* (beings who repeatedly take rebirth) refers precisely to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body, because it is able to repeatedly undergo birth and take up various realms of existence (*gati*).
Furthermore, Ānanda, within these three realms, there are four further classes of *asura*. If they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*),...
By the power of protecting the Dharma, they ride upon their supernatural faculties and enter the void. These asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the realm of hungry ghosts.
If they have descended from the heavens due to a loss of merit, their dwelling place is adjacent to the sun and moon. These asuras—
Born from a womb and categorized among the human realm, there is an asura king who maintains the world. His power is profound and he is fearless;
he can contend for authority with the Brahma King, Śakra Devendra, and the Four Heavenly Kings. This asura exists through transformation.
"Ānanda, there is another class of inferior asuras included within the realm of the devas. They are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns;
they roam through the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras exist due to moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals."

This clarifies the four types of asuras. Regarding the mention of the "realm of hungry ghosts" (*preta*), this reveals their prior causes—that is, they have generated the aspiration for enlightenment from within the realm of hungry ghosts.
Just as one guards the precepts, guards meditative concentration, guards the sūtras, or guards mantras, all such practices are termed "guarding the Dharma.
