This means that from the realm of hungry ghosts, by relying on the power of guarding the Dharma, they are born into this destiny and are able to employ supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) to enter and dwell within the empty realms.
Judging by their manifest fruit, they are egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), because the egg arises from thought.

Judging by their cause, they may be three yakṣas who were reborn after personally approaching the seat of the Tathāgata; they should be categorized as belonging to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

When it says "among the devas," this refers to their prior cause. Regarding the phrase "decreased virtue," it means that while they were among the devas, their merit was diminished and they were subsequently demoted.
Those who dwell adjacent to the sun and moon do not remain apart from the human realm; they are certainly of placental birth and are thus subsumed within the human destiny (*manuṣyagati*).
Those who uphold the world are said to be able to command spirits and deities, bringing about both calamity and fortune.
Those whose power penetrates all and who are fearless refer to those whose strength is vast and pervasive, reaching through both humans and devas, such that their minds are free from dread. Śakra...

The Four Heavenly Kings constantly engage in battle. When it is now said that even the Brahma King contends, it may be that when Śakra is not victorious, the Brahma King and those below him all provide assistance.
If they still cannot prevail by force, he enters the pores of a lotus fiber;
being able to contract and expand at will, one knows he is a transformation-born being. His power is equal to that of the gods, and thus he is included within the celestial realm (*devagati*).
Regarding those born from the heart and mouth of the ocean waters, the sūtras refer to them as the asura king Vemacitra;
because he dwells at the bottom of the sea, he is moisture-born. Due to his inferiority, he is categorized among the animals.

Ānanda, these hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, seers and gods, devas, and asuras—having closely examined these seven realms, you will see that they are all the signs of the conditioned states of delusion.
They are births resulting from false imagination and followings of karma through false imagination.

Within the wondrous, perfect, and luminous mind of non-action, they are all like flowers in the sky; fundamentally, there is nothing to which they cling. They are merely a single void fabrication, and nothing more.
Ānanda, these sentient beings do not recognize their fundamental mind and thus undergo this cycle of rebirth for immeasurable kalpas, failing to attain true purity.
This is entirely due to their compliance with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. By reversing these three, they give rise to the absence of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.

Those who possess [these qualities] belong to the class of ghosts; those who lack them belong to the realm of devas. As existence and non-existence contend with one another, the nature of saṃsāra arises.
If one attains the sublime arising of samādhi, then there is sublime, eternal stillness. Both existence and non-existence are absent; even non-duality is extinguished.
Since there is not even "non-killing, non-stealing, and non-lust," how could one further follow after the affairs of killing, stealing, and lust?

Ānanda, if the three karmas are not severed, each has its own private [delusions]. Because of these individual privacies, these private states share a common lot. They are not without a fixed location; they arise from one's own delusions.
Arising occurs; this deluded birth is without cause and cannot be investigated.

Those who study it intently find themselves ascending and descending, wandering back and forth hundreds of thousands of millions of times, yet remain unaware of the essential means of escape. The seven realms of existence all arise from deluded thoughts;
within the perfect and wondrous [nature], they have no root or trace. Thus, they are like flowers in the sky. As you previously asked about the wondrous mind:

It is all-pervasive and perfect. How could there be the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, humans, animals, and so forth? This conclusion demonstrates that the three—killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—are the root.
If one possesses these karmas, one falls into the category of ghosts; if one lacks these karmas, one ascends to the heavenly realm.

By citing two of the seven destinies, they are comprehensively subsumed: one falls because of existence, and one ascends because of non-existence. Thus, existence and non-existence mutually overturn one another, giving rise [to the cycle].
Regarding the nature of saṃsāra: if one attains the sublime arising of true samādhi, then one may escape it.

As for "non-duality," it means that both existence and non-existence are absent. Since both existence and non-existence are absent, there is also no thought of the absence of existence and non-existence; this is called "the extinction of even non-duality.
This not only transcends birth and death, but further transcends the nirvāṇa of the Hīnayāna. It was stated above that all [this] arises from following...
Because [the text] follows upon the discussion of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, it has already exposed the root cause of the afflictions of rebirth.

Fearing that people might doubt this by asking, "If beings in the heavenly realms observe these three precepts, why do they not escape saṃsāra? it states: "This is not the fault of observing the precepts;

rather, it is the fault of observing them with a mind that is still subject to outflows (āsrava). Within the untainted (anāsrava) training, not even a speck of dust arises; therein, there is no longer even 'observing.'"
"Observe the precepts; how much more so, do not violate them. These words represent a strict prohibition against the three types of karma.
The statement that "the retribution for the private creation of karma has a fixed location" means that it is originally summoned and induced by one's own delusions.
Since what is produced is illusory, there is in fact no cause; therefore, its point of origin cannot be investigated.

Exert yourself in your practice. If you wish to attain Bodhi, you must eliminate the three delusions. If these three delusions are not exhausted, even if you should acquire supernatural powers, they will all be merely worldly, conditioned functions;
with habitual tendencies unextinguished, you will fall into the path of Māra. Though you may wish to remove delusion, [you cannot].
To redouble one's falsehoods is what the Tathāgata calls pitiable. You have fabricated this yourself; it is not the fault of Bodhi.
To speak thus is called speaking correctly; if anyone speaks otherwise, they are speaking as Māra does.
The three evils and the three virtues are all karma. Failing to realize this as the root of bondage and the source of the obstruction to wisdom is called the "three delusions.
Not only are the "three existents" eliminated, but the "three non-existents" are also eliminated;

for while one may suppress active manifestations without eradicating the seeds, these will arise again when meeting with conditions, ultimately leading one down the path of Māra and doubling one's hypocrisy. As each person says for themselves:

They have attained the Unsurpassed Way; yet in reality, they all rely on worldly wisdom to engage in false investigation, and by riding upon supernatural powers to create karma, they distance themselves from perfect penetration and turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa.
Therefore, the Tathāgata takes pity on them. Previously, you asked about the true reality of the Buddha-body:
how can there still be the various realms of existence? Thus, he replied: "You have created these delusions yourself; it is not that the Buddha-body possesses any fault. This is Bodhi."
This is precisely the essence of the Buddha. Furthermore, he warns: "If, in the final age, one exhorts others to depart from these three kinds [of things], that is the teaching of the Buddha;
if one praises these three kinds as being unimpeded, that is the teaching of Māra. This reflects the demonic activities regarding the five aggregates below;
for Māra’s affliction of people begins first with the breaking of the precepts.
At that moment, as the Tathāgata was about to conclude his session upon the lion throne, he took up the seven-jeweled armrest, turned toward the Purple Gold Mountain, and leaned against it once more.
He then addressed the great assembly and Ānanda, saying: "You who are still in training—whether pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas—"
Today you have turned your minds toward great bodhi and supreme, wondrous enlightenment. I have now explained the method for true practice;
yet you still do not recognize the subtle demonic activities and the manifestation of demonic realms that arise during the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā.
"You cannot recognize it; your purification of mind is not correct, and you have fallen into false views.

Perhaps you are an *antarābhava-māra*, or perhaps a celestial *māra*, or possessed by a ghost or spirit, or beset by a *chi* or *mei* demon. Your mind is not clear, and you mistake a thief for your own son.

Furthermore, within this state, you consider a small attainment to be sufficient, like the unlearned bhikṣu in the fourth dhyāna who falsely claimed to have realized the holy fruit. Once his heavenly retribution has ended,"
The signs of decay have appeared before him; having slandered an Arhat, he shall undergo future existence and fall into the Avīci Hell. You should listen attentively;
I shall now explain this to you in detail for your sake. Ānanda rose from his seat, as did all those in the assembly who were still in training.
With joyful prostrations, we humbly await your compassionate instruction.
This path of true practice has not yet been personally traversed by Ānanda and others; thus, they do not know the hardships and obstacles along the way.
The World-Honored One, being one who has already passed through it, therefore turned back from his seat to remain, pointing out what is encountered upon the journey.

This causes them to recognize [the truth] for themselves and prepare for unforeseen circumstances; this is the true method of cultivation, which refers specifically to the single gate of "listening inwardly.
Demonic activities are most subtle; they may suddenly manifest before one and accord so perfectly with the human mind that one cannot discern whether they are evil or righteous.
If there is even the slightest impurity within the breast, those demons will immediately seize upon that minute gap to entice [the practitioner].
One has entered into false views. The *skandha-māra* (the demon of the aggregates) manifests from the very first thought within the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); it does not come from without.
The *deva-māra*, ghosts, spirits, and malevolent apparitions all manifest from the two aggregates of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*).

If the eye of the Way is not clear, one will be turned by them and consequently mistake a thief for a son, which will surely cause the family treasure to be plundered until its exhaustion. Both the mental and visual demons are...

Within the aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there is the fault of one’s own mind harboring false views and being satisfied with meager attainment, as described below.

To provide a single example: those who lack learning possess no wisdom born of much hearing; yet, by diligently practicing minor deeds, they manage to attain birth in the four dhyānas and then claim to have realized arhatship.
When their celestial retribution is about to end and they perceive a place of rebirth, they consequently slander the Buddha with falsehoods.
To say that an Arhat does not undergo further existence and to fall away from this [view] is the fault of erroneous delusion.
The Buddha told Ānanda and the great assembly: "You all should know that within the world of outflows, there are twelve categories of living beings."
Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous; this perfected essence of the mind is non-dual and undifferentiated from the Buddhas of the ten directions.

It is due to your deluded thoughts that you mistake the principle for error. From ignorance and craving, birth arises; as this birth and arising lead to pervasive delusion, the nature of space appears. Thus, delusion continues without ceasing.
Since there is the arising of worlds, these lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions are not without outflows;

they are all established through deluded, stubborn, and false conceptualization. You should know that space arises within your own mind, like a fragment of cloud appearing within the vast clarity of the great sky.

How much more so for all worlds that exist within empty space? If even one among you were to give rise to true realization and return to the source, this emptiness of the ten directions would entirely dissolve and vanish;
how then could the lands existing within that emptiness fail to tremble and shatter?

Fundamental enlightenment is profoundly still; not even a speck of dust can be established therein. From deluded ignorance arises stubborn emptiness, and from this stubborn emptiness the tainted realm is formed, serving as the locus for demons.
When deluded ignorance is severed and the true mind is manifested, then empty space dissolves and the world-system shatters;
thus the demons naturally lose their support. Question: Throughout antiquity and the present, there have been many who have manifested the truth, yet the empty realm remains. Why is this?
"Why is this so? [The answer is: "The world is produced by the collective karma of sentient beings. Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, the world is inexhaustible.
When one person awakens to the Truth, they can only dissolve the world of that single individual.

Although the common lot (*sabhāgatā*) of those other beings may momentarily tremble, it soon re-solidifies. If all were able to awaken to the Truth together, then the mountains, rivers, and the physical vessel-world..."
The realms are transformed into unsurpassed awakening, becoming pure and wondrous Buddha-lands.
You all cultivate dhyāna and adorn samādhi; together with the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions and the various untainted Great Arhats, [you shall attain this].
The mind is thoroughly proficient and tranquil in its very place. All Māras, as well as ghosts, spirits, and all ordinary devas [are unable to disturb it].

They saw their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason; the great earth quaked and split open; and all creatures of water, land, and air were struck with such terror that they could not contain themselves.

Ordinary people, shrouded in darkness, did not perceive these transformations. Those beings all attained the five supernormal powers, with the sole exception of the extinction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Because they are attached to these worldly defilements, how can you cause them to be shattered and torn asunder?
For this reason, when you are in samādhi, ghosts and spirits, as well as all celestial Māras, wangsliang, and yingjing demons, will all come together to harass you.
"Adorned" means strictly guarded. Through the power of dhyāna, his mind attained profound resonance with that of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Great Arhats.

As he was about to emerge from the realm of Māra, the great earth shook violently and the palaces of Māra were shattered. Māra, however, clings to worldly toil and has long relied upon the tainted realm;
how could he willingly abandon it? Thus, he came to cause affliction and harm, soaring across water and land, pointing his finger at the host of Māra’s waters.

Regarding those who dwell on land, their perceptions shift and distort; this refers to the sense of trembling and cracking. Ordinary people do not understand that such shifting and distortion are caused by the meditative power (*dhyāna-bala*) of a practitioner, and thus they mistakenly claim it is an earthquake.

This is true for all except those who have exhausted their outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); among the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they have not yet realized the one power of the exhaustion of outflows.
Since they possess the other five powers, they know that this is produced by your meditative power and will certainly not tolerate it.

Yet, although those Māras may be filled with great rage, within their defilements and within your wondrous awakening, they do not interact at all—like wind blowing upon light, or like a blade cutting through water.
You are like boiling water, and they are like solid ice; as the warmth gradually approaches, [the ice will surely melt].
You have not yet extinguished yourself through verbal confession, but merely rely on supernatural powers; thus, you remain but a guest who brings about disruption.

This is because you are the master of the five aggregates within your own mind. If the master is deluded, the guest gains the advantage. You must practice *dhyāna* right where you are and awaken to the truth without confusion.
Then those demonic affairs will be powerless against you. As the five aggregates dissolve and enter into clarity, all those various malevolent spirits will receive only their dark, ethereal breaths.

Since clarity can destroy darkness, they will perish on their own as they draw near; how then would they dare remain to disturb your meditative concentration? This is so unless you have not yet attained clear awakening.
Deluded by the aggregates, you, Ānanda, would surely become a son of Māra and an accomplice of Māra, just like the Matanga woman;
you would be exceedingly inferior. She merely used incantations to subvert your Buddhist precepts; among the eighty thousand practices, she destroyed but a single precept.
Because the mind is pure, it has not yet sunk into ruin; yet this [delusion] shall destroy your entire body of precious awakening.
It is like a high minister’s family suddenly suffering confiscation and seizure, falling into disarray and decay beyond all hope of rescue.

This means that if one awakens to this truth, there is no fault; if one remains deluded, it leads to chaos. The accomplishment of samādhi and the destruction of the confusion of samādhi do not depend on external conditions, but arise entirely from the "host.
The host is the true mind. One who awakens to this and is free from delusion remains unmoving in single-mindedness;
toward those states of good and evil, they feel neither joy nor fear. Thus, even though the power of Māra may be strong, it cannot [overcome them].

"Disturb you? Since your yin-qi has already been dissipated and you have attained the Great Treasury of Radiance (*mahā-ābhāsvara-garbha*), they are all receiving dark vapors and dwelling in a realm of gloom.
If they draw near to this light, their dark vapors will naturally vanish;
how would they dare disturb your meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)? If one is deluded by yin-qi, one instead falls among those very beings. The Minister relied upon...
"Extinct. This is a metaphor for one who has nearly ascended the precious throne, yet sinks back into the evil realms.

Ānanda, you should know that when you sit at the site of enlightenment and cause all thoughts to dissolve and fall away—if those thoughts are exhausted, then all that is pure and brilliant, free from thought, will remain unmoved by motion or stillness, and recollection and forgetfulness will become as one. You should abide in this state and enter samādhi.

It is like a person with clear vision situated in great, profound darkness; though the essential nature is wondrously pure, the mind has not yet emitted light. This is called the domain of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
If the eyes become bright and clear, the ten directions open up completely, and there is no longer any gloom or obscurity; this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of form.
Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the kalpa. Observing its origin, one finds that solidified deluded thoughts constitute its root.
To sit at the site of enlightenment does not necessarily require an earthen altar or a mirror-image; one may sit upright therein at all times, throughout the four modes of deportment.

Turning the hearing back toward itself is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). This is precisely what is meant by "dissolving all thoughts": when the practice is profound, thoughts are exhausted, becoming equal to the realm of empty space.
"All-pervading lucidity" means being constantly unobscured; it is lucid and clear in stillness and does not shift during movement;
it is lucid and clear when forgetting and remains so when recollecting. This is the point where power is gained in *dhyāna*; relying upon this, one advances toward right concentration.
"One may enter. This refers to having clear vision while situated in darkness, describing the state where [the eyes] are about to open but have not yet opened.

The subtle nature is wondrously pure; this describes the manifestation of the concentrated mind. "Clear vision" corresponds to the metaphor of clarity; that the mind has not yet emitted light and wisdom has not yet arisen corresponds to the metaphor of being in darkness.
"Obscuration" (āvaraṇa) takes the meaning of covering and veiling; it restricts the true nature. This describes the state when the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has not yet been shattered.
If the light of the mind is made to radiate forth, all obstructions will be penetrated;

then what is seen by the physical eye will have the ten directions opened wide, such that the preceding darkness is entirely transformed into light, penetrating inwardly through the five viscera and outwardly through the mountains and rivers.
Heaven and earth are as clear to him as the palm of his hand; this is the sign that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been shattered. A *kalpa* refers to time.

The turbidity of the *kalpa* (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) arises because of the aggregate of form. Once the aggregate of form is shattered, the three periods of time are severed; thus, one is able to transcend the deluded attachment to solidity.
Regarding the four external great elements, one stubbornly clings to them as being truly existent entities external to the mind; regarding the four [internal]...
"Great! To firmly grasp [the aggregates] as the dwelling place of the mind is the very root of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
If one does not cling to them, how could form constitute an aggregate? In the previous section on 'Definitive Meaning,' the five turbidities were pointed out in succession;
these are precisely the present five aggregates. Next, it says: 'Like clearing turbid water by storing it in a clean vessel'—this refers to the present elimination of the five aggregates. However..."
I have not yet had the opportunity to show this in detail. Here, by analyzing the works of Māra, one also resolves the previous koan.
Ānanda, you should investigate the wondrous clarity within this state until the four elements no longer entangle you; in a brief moment, your body will be able to pass through obstacles.
This is called the overflowing of refined spirit into the external realm; it is merely a temporary attainment through spiritual practice and is not—

This is the realization of the Sage. If one does not give rise to the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome state. If one interprets it as the realization of a sage, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.
The following ten types are all signs of the color-aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) being on the verge of breaking down but not yet broken. First, the external penetration is clarified;

"within this" refers to the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Subtle clarity" is the nature of hearing. By reversing the hearing and refining it with precision, the four great elements become empty and harmonious. As...
The clouds are like shadows; they no longer weave so densely or solidly that the body can pass through obstacles.

It suddenly penetrates walls and barriers by means of this specific power, which compels the subtle essence to overflow, allowing for a temporary state of vacuity and integration with the environment before one.

This attainment is gained and lost according to circumstances, unlike the realization of a sage who has attained the fruit, which is once-gained and forever retained. If the practitioner lacks discerning insight, [the experience will not endure].
If one immediately gives rise to the realization of sainthood, then Māra will find his opportunity.

Ānanda, if one again uses this mind to investigate the wondrous clarity until it penetrates deeply within the body, that person may suddenly pick out roundworms and maggots from within their own body;
yet the physical form remains intact, without any injury or damage. This is called the overflowing of refined clarity.

As for these physical forms, they are merely temporary attainments resulting from refined practice; they do not constitute holy realization. If you do not conceive of them as being holy, they are called "wholesome states.
If you interpret them as holy realization, you will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

This clarifies internal penetration. The light of the mind suddenly shines forth, and the five viscera open and become luminous, as if lifting a covering lid. One personally sees the *rāhu* and *krimi* worms;
picking them up with the hand, the body suffers no injury or destruction. The overflowing [of fluids] is the same as before, but the internal fusion of the physical form is different.

Furthermore, with this mind, one investigates thoroughly both internally and externally. At that time, the soul (*pō*), spirit (*huó*), will (*yì*), and consciousness (*shén*)—excluding the body which they grasp and sustain—all enter into mutual interpenetration, each acting as both guest and host.
Suddenly, one hears the sound of the Dharma being preached in the midst of space, or hears the profound meanings being expounded simultaneously throughout the ten directions.
This is called the successive separation and union of the refined spirits, whereby wholesome seeds are accomplished; one may temporarily attain such a state.

This is not yet the realization of a sage. If one does not conceive of it as the state of a sage, it is called a "wholesome realm. If one interprets it as the realization of a sage, one will immediately be possessed by various demons.

This clarifies that both the internal and external have been thoroughly penetrated: the *hun* spirit is stored in the liver; the *po* spirit is stored in the lungs; the *yi* (mind) is stored in the spleen; the *zhi* (will) is stored in the gallbladder;
the *jing* (essence) is stored in the kidneys; and the *shen* (spirit) is stored in the heart. Through the refined investigation of meditative power, the four elements are found to be empty.
The primary [consciousness] has no basis and flows outward; only the eighth consciousness maintains the body, remaining tranquil and unmoving.

Those six [consciousnesses] interpenetrate one another, with one acting as the host and the other five as guests. Regarding "separation and union": this refers to departing from one's original position to unite with the positions of others.
Because one has long ago heard that the six sense faculties can function interchangeably, wholesome seeds have been infused [into the mind]; therefore, within meditative concentration—
At times, he would occasionally reveal this; it was not like the holy ones who have realized entry into perfect penetration.
Furthermore, because this mind was clear, revealed, and brilliantly transparent, an inner light shone forth, causing all ten directions to appear everywhere as the color of Jambūnada gold.
All kinds of forms transform into Tathāgatas. Suddenly, one beholds Vairocana seated upon a celestial light-pavilion, surrounded by a thousand Buddhas;
ten billion lands and lotus flowers appear simultaneously. This is called the defilement of the awakening of the soul and spirit;
it is the mind’s radiance becoming refined and clear, illuminating all worlds. To attain such a state momentarily does not constitute a holy realization.
If one does not give rise to the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome realm"; if one forms a conception of being a sage, one immediately succumbs to various delusions.
This clarifies that the realm of the manifest Buddha—both pure and impure—is perceived according to what the mind evokes.

When this mind is limpid and transparent, spiritual awakening wells up; the realm of the Buddha manifests before one, such that the insentient world everywhere becomes a golden land and all sentient beings become Tathāgatas.
That which is permeated by spiritual awakening refers to the seeds of the originally perfumed, perfect, and sudden wisdom-awakening— the fact that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas—
which, stimulated by meditative concentration, temporarily manifests in its excellence.

Furthermore, with this mind, he investigated the wondrous luminosity with intense precision, observing without ceasing, suppressing and subduing it, and restraining it until it transcended [ordinary perception].
At that moment, suddenly the empty space of the ten directions became the color of the seven treasures, or the color of a hundred treasures, filling everything simultaneously.
They do not obstruct one another; blue, yellow, red, and white each appear purely and distinctly. This is called the power of suppression exceeding its limit;

such a state may be attained temporarily, yet it is not a holy realization. If you do not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a wholesome state; if you interpret it as a holy realization, [it will lead to delusion].
One immediately succumbs to the various evils.
This clarifies that emptiness achieves the color of a jewel. "Observation" means investigating the place where the deluded mind arises.
"Suppression" means pressing down upon the place of its arising. "Subjugation" means following and complying with what has been suppressed. "Restraint" means fearing future leaping and clamoring.
Furthermore, as you apply ever-increasing precautions and undergo repeated disciplinary measures, you transcend the ordinary to an extreme degree.

Consequently, the wondrous clarity reaches its ultimate limit, radiating and manifesting so intensely that empty space takes on the hue of jewels. This jewel-colored space is none other than the light of your own mind.
Furthermore, by using this mind to investigate until it becomes transparent and clear, its refined radiance remains undisturbed.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, within a dark room, one sees various objects no different from those seen in broad daylight; yet the objects in the dark room do not vanish.

This is called the mind becoming so subtle and dense that its vision clarifies the profound depths. To attain such a state temporarily does not constitute a realization of sainthood (*ārya*). Do not conceive of it as a state of sainthood.
This is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes this to be a realization of the sacred, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.

This refers to seeing objects in the dark; when the light of the mind is subtly clarified, objects cannot escape it, yet the darkness and the objects themselves are not eliminated—this is said to be the actual realm.
It is the temporary manifestation of the merit of investigating and attaining clarity, not the true attainment of the constant light.
Furthermore, as this mind enters perfectly into a state of voidness and fusion, the four limbs suddenly become like grass and wood;
even when burned by fire or cut by knives, there is no sensation whatsoever. Moreover, the flames cannot burn or scorch them; even if one were to slice their flesh, it would be as if carving wood.

This is called the merging of sensory objects. It displaces the natures of the four great elements and enters exclusively into purity; one may temporarily attain such a state, yet it does not constitute a holy realization.
If you do not conceive of it as a holy attainment, it is called a "wholesome realm. If you interpret it as a holy realization, you will immediately succumb to a multitude of demonic influences.

This body is the same as grass and wood. When the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is empty and harmonious, the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are simultaneously extinguished and the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) are cast aside.

Pure awareness remains while the body is left behind; therefore, there is no injury from contact. This is merely a temporary manifestation, for one has not yet attained the true emptiness of essential form (*prakṛti-rūpa-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, as this mind achieves purity and the power of the pure mind reaches its peak, one suddenly sees the great earth and the mountains and rivers of the ten directions all become Buddha-lands, fully endowed with the seven treasures and pervaded by radiant light;
moreover, one sees the Buddhas and Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

It fills the entire realm of space; the towers and palaces are magnificent and radiant. Looking down, one sees the hells; looking up, one beholds the celestial palaces, perceiving them all without obstruction.

This is called the deepening of focused contemplation through the alternation of joy and revulsion. After long practice, these images manifest as transformations; they are not yet the realization of a sage. One must not mistake them for such realization.
This is called a "wholesome realm. If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences;

this is what is meant by "beholding the Buddhas and beholding the realms. Before entering meditative concentration, one fixates on thoughts of longing for the pure and loathing the defiled, whereby these habits are perfumed and formed into seeds.

Now, as the practice of "returning hearing" reaches its ultimate limit, the mind’s radiance intensely illuminates everything, causing all [past impressions] to manifest within the ears. Although it is said that these are transformations...
It is established, yet it is not a void realm. Although it is a real realm, it remains like an illusion or a transformation.
Furthermore, as he investigated with this mind into the profound and distant, suddenly in the middle of the night, he saw from afar the markets, streets, and alleys of a distant city.
When relatives and kinsmen hear such words, it is called "oppressing the mind. Because the spirit is so intensely pressured that it flies out, one frequently sees things separated from oneself;

this is not a sign of saintly realization. If one does not conceive the thought of being a sage, it is called a "wholesome state"; yet if one interprets it as a sign of sainthood, one will immediately succumb to various demonic influences.
This refers to seeing and hearing at a great distance. By applying the mind to investigate until reaching a profound depth, the light of the mind is eventually forced to its limit and flies forth;
consequently, one is able to see and hear through all obstructed spaces. This occurs during the middle of the night, when both mind and environment are utterly tranquil.
This, too, is but a temporary vision; it is not the actual realization of the boundless ocean of lands that is not separated from the tip of a single hair.

Furthermore, if one pursues this mind with extreme refinement, the physical form of the spiritual teacher may shift and change, undergoing various transformations in an instant without apparent cause.
This is called the mind harboring malevolent spirits or being possessed by celestial Māras who have entered its heart and belly.

To preach the Dharma without cause, while thoroughly understanding its subtle meanings, does not constitute a sign of saintly realization. If you do not give rise to the thought of being a saint, demonic activities will subside;
however, if you take this to be a sign of sainthood, you will immediately fall under the sway of various evils.
The "upper nine" objects are all wholesome objects produced by the extreme intensity of a concentrated mind; they are not the work of Māra.

One must necessarily realize them through direct experience before they become the occasion for inviting Māra. This occurs when, within this great samādhi, one exerts all effort in exhaustive investigation until reaching the most refined and ultimate state, where one’s mind merges perfectly with the minds of the sages, and the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) is about to be shattered; thus, the mind of Māra [arises].
Terror and agitation arise; thus do demonic disturbances begin. "Seeing the virtuous" refers to the emergence of deluded visions.

"Seeing a spiritual friend" means that the practitioner perceives this within stillness. "The transformation of physical form" refers to the manifestation of images such as Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, and nāgas.
"A depraved mind receiving [these]" means that because the practitioner’s guarding of the mind is not rigorous, they accept these delusions.
Because of the sensory objects, ghostly spirits cause delusion and manifest these illusory images; it is not that they truly see the Sage. Or, as stated below, they may trigger their "mad wisdom.
Regarding "the celestial Māra entering the mind": this means the Māra enters the practitioner’s body and seizes their mental faculty.
When they preach the Dharma and penetrate its subtleties, appearing to speak for themselves, it is the power of the Māra sustaining them to act thus; it is not genuine.

This is because the true mind has opened. As the practitioner applies effort, [the process] proceeds from shallow to deep; as demonic influences cause disturbance, they proceed from subtle to manifest.
These stages, along with the ten objects of the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) discussed below, all enter the mind in secret, causing internal confusion to arise spontaneously.
It is only upon reaching the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) that they fly out to attach themselves to others, manifesting their deceptive delusions clearly.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states appearing during *dhyāna* all arise from the mutual interaction of the mind with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

Thus, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering such conditions, they remain lost and fail to recognize them for what they are, claiming instead that they have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, you all should rely [on this teaching] in the final age...
Within the Dharma, I proclaim this meaning so that the celestial Māras may find no opportunity; I shall maintain and protect you, enabling you to achieve the Unsurpassed Way.

As for "interacting," it refers to the mind in meditative contemplation engaging in combat with the deluded thoughts of the various aggregates (*skandhas*), each seeking victory over the other. It is like...
Within the realm of form, whenever each wholesome object momentarily prevails through the power of contemplation, the light of the mind is thus revealed;
yet as soon as it opens, it closes again, for delusive thoughts have once more gained the upper hand. This is precisely how Māra seizes such an opportunity to enter.

Ānanda, when those good men who cultivate samādhi reach the exhaustion of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) within śamatha, they perceive the minds of all Buddhas as images appearing in a clear mirror. Although they have attained something, they are not yet able to employ it;

they are like a person suffering from a nightmare, whose hands and feet are perfectly present and whose sight and hearing are unconfused, yet whose mind is touched by an external malevolent spirit so that he cannot move. This is...
This is called the domain of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). When the affliction of nightmares ceases, the mind detaches from the body;

one can turn back to observe one’s own face, moving or staying at will without further obstruction. This is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*).
Observing its origin, one finds that empty luminosity and false conceptualization constitute its root.

The mind of all Buddhas is precisely my own wondrously enlightened and luminous mind. When the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is exhausted, the four great elements have already dissolved, and there is no longer any obstruction;

thus, the mind opens and one is able to see it. Although one has personally seen the fundamental substance, the fact that one has not yet been able to manifest its sovereign function indicates that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has not yet been shattered.
"Sensation" takes the meaning of receiving and taking in; it receives objects into the mind and is capable of...

The "void and wondrous nature of the skandhas" refers to the two lines concerning the hands and feet, which serve as a metaphor for having something to grasp. The two lines concerning the mind and touch serve as a metaphor for not obtaining their function.

"The fault of the nightmare ceases" serves as a metaphor for the exhaustion of the skandha of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The mind fundamentally does not reside within the body; it is the delusion of the skandha of sensation that falsely acts as a recipient.
When the skandha of sensation is exhausted, the mind is able to transcend obstructions; thus, it can depart from the body to engage in retro-cognition.
Moving and abiding with sovereign ease, this resembles the Yellow-Cap practitioners who produce a yang-spirit; yet they are fundamentally different.

Those practitioners seek it through the mind, whereas this is attained without the mind. When deluded views and perceptions arise, they turbidly disturb the profound nature; this is called the turbidity of views.

This is the very substance of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). When it is exhausted, one transcends it. Due to illusory conditions of opposition and compliance, there arise false sensations of loss and gain.
Since the aggregate of sensation has no substantial body and is merely a void that is clearly manifest, it is called "illusory clarity" (*vymāna-vikalpa*).
Ānanda, that son of good family shall therein attain a great radiance, his mind becoming luminous and penetrating.

Yet, because he suppresses [the mind] excessively within, he suddenly gives rise to boundless compassion toward that very state. Thus, even upon seeing a mosquito or a gadfly, he regards them as an infant, feeling such pity in his heart that he involuntarily sheds tears.
This is called the overstepping of effort through excessive suppression; if one awakens to this, [it is no longer so].
"There is no fault; this is not a sign of saintly realization. Once one awakens and understands, delusion will naturally dissipate over time.

If you mistake this for saintly attainment, the demon of pity will enter your heart and viscera. You will feel compassion upon seeing others and weep without limit, losing your correct meditative absorption and inevitably falling into ruin."
This refers to suppressing oneself and giving rise to compassion. Having already shattered the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), there is no longer any darkness; thus, one attains great radiance.
Knowing that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the source of fault, one suppresses and subdues it within oneself and thereby destroys it.
However, by suppressing and subduing it to excess, one loses gentleness and compassion, resulting in an abundance of pity and sorrow, which causes the demon of sorrow (*śoka-māra*) to attach itself.
Ānanda, furthermore, within that state of concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear.

As superior signs manifest before them, they are moved with excessive intensity; suddenly, within this state, they give rise to boundless courage. Their minds become fierce and sharp, and their resolve becomes equal to that of all Buddhas, thinking:
"The three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* can be transcended in a single thought-moment. This is called the error of overreaching through the forceful application of effort (*prayoga*). If they awaken to it...
There is no fault; this is not the realization of a sage. When one awakens to this and is no longer deluded, [the afflictions] will naturally dissolve and subside after a long time.
If you take this to be the realization of a sage, then a mad demon will enter your heart and viscera. Upon seeing others, you will boast with incomparable arrogance;
your mind will reach such a state that it neither perceives the Buddha above nor perceives other people below. Having lost right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), you shall surely fall into ruin.

This is to exalt oneself as being like a Buddha. As for "the marks of excellence appearing before one": it means that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has been exhausted, and one perceives the minds of all Buddhas.
As for "being moved beyond measure": previously, one had heard that "the mind itself is the Buddha," yet had never personally seen it;
now, for the first time, one beholds the original Buddha-nature, and thus arouses great courage, declaring that one will attain Buddhahood on the spot without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

I do not know whether, though the principle may be realized all at once, its manifestations must be eliminated gradually. These words were spoken out of arrogance and recklessness, overstepping my station and presuming upon myself.
If I reflect upon this and recognize my error, returning to the path, I shall be without fault; but if I remain deluded and do not repent—
Then a mad demon will enter their mind, giving rise to great arrogance. Above, they recognize no Buddhas; below, they recognize no sentient beings.
They claim for themselves that they alone are supreme. Having lost right concentration, they will undoubtedly fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive that the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) has dissolved and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) has become clear.
Having no new realization before them and having lost their former abode, their power of wisdom declines and they fall into a state of desolation.

Seeing nothing at all before them, a great parching thirst suddenly arises in their hearts; at all times, they remain submerged in this recollection without dispersal, taking this to be the mark of diligent vigor.
This is called "cultivating the mind while lacking wisdom and thereby losing oneself. If one awakens to this, there is no fault; it is not a realization of the holy.

If one takes it as a realization of the holy, then the demon of recollection will enter one's heart and viscera, seizing the mind morning and evening and suspending it in one place, causing one to lose right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).
One will then fall into ruin;
this is the sinking of mindfulness due to a lack of wisdom. That there is nothing newly realized means the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) has not yet been shattered.

That one has retreated from their former dwelling means the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) has already been shattered. One should use the power of wisdom to illuminate and shatter that the aggregate of sensation is fundamentally empty; then, one will naturally be able to [proceed].

As for entering [the realization]: if the power of one’s wisdom declines, one falls between the two pillars with nothing to rely upon; having entered the middle and lost one's footing, one becomes utterly disoriented before and behind, seeing nothing at all. Because there is no water of wisdom to irrigate it, a sudden parching thirst arises. Because one is detached from both the preceding and the following, with no ground for advancing or retreating, one sinks into constant recollection, not daring— [The text continues: —to act. Thus, one must diligently cultivate the path of wisdom. If one does not cultivate wisdom, one will surely fall into the pit of ignorance.

If one cultivates wisdom, one will surely ascend to the terrace of enlightenment. Therefore, the wise person constantly maintains mindfulness and vigilance, never allowing the mind to be lax. They take the Dharma as their teacher and the precepts as their guide, ensuring that every thought is directed toward the Way. Only by such means can one escape the cycle of birth and death and attain the fruit of liberation. This is called the "Entrance through the Power of Wisdom.

If one lacks this power, one is like a blind man wandering in a vast wilderness, unable to find the path. Therefore, the sages have said: "Wisdom is the eye of the Dharma; without it, one is lost. One must strive to cultivate it until it is perfected. This is the essential instruction for those who seek the Great Vehicle. May all beings, hearing this, awaken to the truth and enter the gate of the Tathāgata. Thus ends the section on the Entrance through the Power of Wisdom. May all be auspicious.

To move about restlessly, and furthermore to take the state of sunken recollection and non-dissipation as the mark of diligent vigor while desiring to break through the aggregate of sensation—is this not an error?
This is called losing oneself through a lack of wisdom. If one recognizes this is not [the truth] and corrects it swiftly, then one will incur no fault.
If one takes sunken recollection and non-dissipation to be a sign of saintly realization, then the demon of recollection will seize the opportunity to enter day after day.
At night, they fix their minds on a single point; yet, losing their right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*), they fall into ruin.

Furthermore, within that meditative state, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*); the power of their wisdom surpasses the concentration itself.
They lose their vigor because they harbor various notions of excellence within their minds; suspecting their own minds to be Vairocana, they take a little attainment as sufficient.
This is called losing constant discernment through the application of the mind, becoming mired in intellectual views. If one awakens to this, there is no fault.
This is not true realization of the holy state. If you mistake it for such realization, then the demon of inferiority and easy contentment will enter your heart and innermost being.
You will see others and say of yourself, "I have attained the unsurpassed ultimate truth," thereby losing right concentration and falling into ruin.

This wisdom causes one to become excessively deranged. When form is exhausted and sensation is clarified, this is the superior nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it is appropriate to forget one’s own mind.
Yet, one may take a little as sufficient and, suspecting oneself to be a Buddha, allow the demons of inferiority and complacency to take possession.

What was previously called "the Buddha can be quickly accomplished" means that if one contemplates it, there is no difficulty in practicing through many kalpas; this vision is precisely the self-nature. It is not so.

The fault of falsely relying on cultivation and realization is even more severe. Question: In the Zen school, it is said that one is inherently Buddha and does not depend on cultivation or realization;

why is this so? Answer: It is because people cling only to the idea of achieving Buddhahood through cultivation, thereby neglecting their own spiritual nature. I merely used such words of praise and censure to stir them.
When one advances further up the fishing pole, how could they ever rely on their own spiritual nature to dismiss cultivation and realization?

Furthermore, within that samādhi, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear; yet, as they have not yet attained new realization, their former mind has already perished.
As they survey these two boundaries, difficulties arise spontaneously within them, and a sense of inexhaustible anxiety suddenly wells up in their hearts.
It is as if sitting upon an iron bed or drinking poisonous medicine; the mind has no desire to live and constantly seeks someone to end its life so that it may quickly attain liberation.
These are each practices that have lost the correct means (*upāya*). If one awakens to this, there is no fault; however, they do not constitute the realization of a sage.
If one forms a holy understanding [of these states], then a portion of the demon of constant sorrow and anxiety will enter their heart and viscera.

Grasping a sword in hand, they will cut their own flesh, rejoicing in the relinquishing of their life-span; or they will be constantly sorrowful, fleeing into mountain forests, unable to bear the sight of people.
One loses right concentration and shall fall into ruin;
this awakening is the anxiety of perilous thoughts. "Surveying the two limits" means contemplating the two extremes of form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*).
"The mind gives rise to hardship" refers to the concern over encountering decline and loss. This is originally due to excessive vigilance and fear in one's diligent practice, lacking true wisdom.
Using skillful means to liberate themselves, they instead bring about affliction and harm.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons see the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) dissolve and the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha) become clear; they abide in a state of purity.
After the mind has become settled and secure, suddenly an infinite joy arises of its own accord; the heart is filled with such rapture that it cannot be restrained.

This is called "pliancy" (praśrabdhi) without wisdom acting as a self-restraint. To realize this is not an error, yet it is not a realization of the holy ones. If one takes it to be a holy realization, [one will fall into delusion].
Then there is a certain demon of attachment to pleasure who enters one's heart and innermost being. Upon seeing people, he laughs;
by the side of the roads, he sings and dances to himself, claiming that he has already attained unimpeded liberation. Having lost right concentration, he is destined for a downward fall.
This joy is merely a superficial delight. It arises from self-restraint devoid of wisdom. If one observes with the eye of wisdom, what is there to be so deeply rejoiced over?
Then the wind of joy will naturally subside, and one returns to a state free of fault.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear and bright.

Believing themselves to have reached sufficiency, they suddenly experience groundless great conceit (*māna*), extending even to pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*).

Whether it be overweening pride or the pride of inferiority, if these arise simultaneously, one’s mind may even slight the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, let alone those of lower rank such as Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
This is called "viewing oneself as superior. Lacking the wisdom to save oneself, there is no fault once awakening occurs.
This is not a sign of saintly realization. If one takes this to be such a realization, then a portion of the great demon of pride will enter their heart and inner organs.
They will cease to pay homage to stupas and temples and will destroy scriptures and images, saying to donors: "These are merely gold and copper, or perhaps clay and wood."
The sutras are made of tree leaves or *mālā* flowers; the physical body is true and eternal. To fail to show reverence to it while instead venerating wood and earth is truly a perversion.
Those with deep faith should destroy these [sutras], burying them in the ground, lest they mislead and delude sentient beings.
One enters the Avīci Hell and loses right concentration; one shall thus fall into ruin.

This is the pride of considering oneself superior (*abhimāna*). There are seven types of pride: relying on oneself to despise others is called *māna* (pride); being arrogant toward those of equal virtue is called *atimāna* (excessive pride);
contending for superiority among equals is called *mānātimāna* (pride-excessive pride); contending for superiority over those who are already superior is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride).
To claim what has not been attained as having been attained is called *adhimāna* (overweening pride). To settle for what is inferior within oneself is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride).
The sutra omits *mithyāmāna* (false pride). Not paying homage to stupas and shrines is *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am"), which also serves as a general category for the seven types of pride.

Regarding "superiority," this arises from perceiving excellence and being driven by a sense of superiority. When one possesses wisdom, one realizes equality and does not perceive even a single sentient being toward whom one could feel pride.

"How dare one be disrespectful toward the various sages? Question: When Linji did not pay obeisance at the ancestral pagodas, when Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, and when Yantou described the words and phrases of the patriarchs as "tattered straw sandals," was this not an act of great arrogance? Answer:

This was done to rouse those who cling to seeking externally without realizing their own mind, and who cling to words and teachings while refusing to advance in practice. Therefore, he used these examples to provoke them.
This is a single thought of compassion. If one were to harbor even a slight sense of pride, and this were tested against the scriptures, one would surely enter the Avīci Hell.

Furthermore, within that state of meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha), amidst a state of brilliant lucidity.

When Yuanwu refines his principles and attains great compliance, his mind suddenly gives rise to immeasurable pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). He may then claim to have become a sage and attained great mastery (*vaśitā*).
This is called obtaining various states of lightness and purity through wisdom; while there is no fault in such awakening, it does not constitute the realization of a sage.
If one takes this to be a realization of the holy, then a portion of the "light-and-pure" demon will enter their heart and inner organs.
They will consider themselves satisfied and no longer seek further progress. Such individuals mostly become unlearned bhikṣus who mislead sentient beings and fall into the Avīci Hell.
Having lost right concentration, one will surely fall into ruin.

This is what is meant by being "sufficiently settled in wisdom. By dissolving form into brilliant clarity (*jīngmíng*), and taking that brilliant clarity as perfect enlightenment, one then claims to have attained great compliance, light ease, and self-mastery.
To be satisfied with such a small attainment is the mark of those who lack learning. Compared to this—
The aforementioned transgressions may seem slight; they merely result from being content with one's own state and failing to advance, rather than from further disparaging others.

Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those sons of good family perceive the dissolution of the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the clarity of the aggregate of sensation (vedanā-skandha). Within this clear awakening, [they fall into error].
One attains a state of empty luminosity. Within this state, one suddenly turns toward eternal extinction, repudiating cause and effect and entering exclusively into emptiness.

When the mind of emptiness manifests before one, even to the point that a long-standing understanding of annihilation arises in the mind, there is no fault if one awakens to it; however, it does not constitute a holy realization.

If one forms a sacred understanding [of emptiness], then an empty-demon (śūnyatā-māra) will enter their heart and inner organs. Such a person will then slander those who uphold the precepts, calling them followers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Claiming that a Bodhisattva has realized emptiness and thus has neither transgressions nor observances, they will frequently drink wine and eat meat in the presence of faithful donors.
They engage extensively in lewd and impure acts. By means of demonic power, they captivate their victims so that no suspicion or slander arises.

Once the ghost’s mind has long since entered them, they may consume excrement, urine, alcohol, meat, and the like—all of which are equally empty [of inherent nature]. Thus they violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code and lead others into sin.
One loses right concentration and shall fall into ruin;

this is attachment to emptiness that destroys the precepts. The former was "perfect awakening" (yuanwu), while this is "clarifying awakening" (mingwu); it is merely an awakening within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).

Because they have attained a state of empty clarity, they mistakenly cling to nihilistic emptiness (*uccheda-śūnyatā*), thereby incurring various false faults; this is the demon of emptiness (*śūnya-māra*).

Recently, there have been those who claim that the great void is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*) and that all Buddhist activities involve attachment to signs (*nimitta*), while all worldly affairs are unimpeded.
These belong to this same category. They have misled themselves and others beyond measure. One must urgently listen to the sutras and repent to awaken from this error.
Furthermore, within that meditative concentration, those good sons perceive the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) dissolving and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becoming clear.

They savor its empty luminosity, which penetrates deep into their very marrow. Suddenly, an infinite love arises in their hearts; when this love reaches its peak, it gives rise to madness, which then becomes greed and desire.
This is called the state of meditative concentration where the mind enters with ease and compliance; yet, lacking wisdom to sustain itself, one mistakenly falls into various desires.

If one awakens to this, there is no fault, for it is not a realization of the holy. If one mistakes this for a holy attainment, then the demon of desire will enter one’s heart and viscera, constantly claiming that desire is the path to Bodhi, and transforming laypeople to practice desire equally.
Those who engage in sexual misconduct under such influence are called "sons and disciples who uphold the Dharma."
By the power of divine spirits, they gather ordinary and ignorant people during the final age;

their number reaches as many as one hundred, or even two hundred, five, six, or seven hundred, until it fills ten million. When the demons grow weary and their minds become disenchanted, they depart from those bodies.
Deprived of majestic virtue, they fall into royal calamity; misleading sentient beings, they enter the Avīci Hell;
losing right concentration, they shall surely undergo a downward plunge.
This refers to engaging in sexual misconduct. Attachment arises from compliance; when an empty object complies with the mind, perverse attachment incurs fault.

For within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), there naturally exists the realm of sublime touch and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) that accords with and enters the mind. One must employ wisdom (*prajñā*) to observe it and not accept anything at all;
only then is it "right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*). If one is addicted and fails to relinquish it, it will give rise to the demon of lustful desire.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of visionary states that appear during *dhyāna* all arise because the mind is applied in a conflicted manner within the *vedanā-skandha*.

Thus, these phenomena manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. Encountering these conditions, they fail to recognize their own confusion and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You, too, should take the words of the Tathāgata as my [instruction].

After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the Dharma’s decay, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect them so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
These ten types of demonic activities have already been established; they are not the same as the preceding ten, which serve as the initial triggers.
Rather, they secretly enter the human mind, causing one to fall into delusion without even realizing it. This differs from the latter ten, which directly afflict, disturb, and ensnare individuals.

Ānanda, when that son of good family practices *samādhi* and the *vedanā-skandha* (feeling aggregate) is exhausted, although his outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet extinguished, his mind has already detached from its physical form like a bird escaping from a cage.

He is already able to achieve this and, proceeding from this ordinary body, ascend through the sixty holy stages of a bodhisattva to attain the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body), moving everywhere without obstruction.
It is, for example, like a person who, while in deep sleep, speaks in a dream. This person...
Although there is no separate object of cognition, the words he utters already possess rhythmic cadence and sequential order, causing even those who do not sleep to fully comprehend his speech.

This is called the domain of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). If all stirring thoughts are exhausted and floating perceptions are eliminated, so that the mind of awakened clarity is like a heart cleansed of dust and grime, and one perceives the beginning and end of a single cycle of birth and death with complete illumination, this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception. Such a person—
Thus one is able to transcend the turbidity of afflictions. Contemplating its origin, one finds that pervasive delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) constitutes its root.
The true mind is all-pervasive and fundamentally not confined to the body; yet, though unconfined, it appears confined—this is the function of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Once the aggregate of sensation is exhausted, one proceeds from the ordinary body through the various stages of sainthood, manifesting bodies at will. "Conceptualization" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the floating appearances of mental deliberation.
It can obscure the wondrous clarity and obstruct the holy path; hence there is the analogy of deep sleep and talking in one's sleep.

The sequence of the phonemes and rhythms is an analogy for the divisions of the stages of holiness (*āryabhūmi*). Those who do not sleep all understand the words, which is an analogy for those who have realized the holy state.

One knows that there exists the stage of sainthood; yet, because the *saṃjñā-skandha* (the aggregate of perception) still remains, one has not yet been able to realize that stage of sainthood immediately.

The three gradual sequences are: the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*), the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), the ten abidings (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), the ten transferences (*pariṇāmana*), the four levels of added practice (*prakarana*), the ten grounds (*bhūmi*), and the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenment].

This encompasses sixty stages. Although there are both the worthy (*bhadra*) and the noble (*ārya*), these are all merely pathways toward the noble stages; therefore, they are all uniformly designated as "noble stages.
Awakening-clarity is like a mirror, and floating thoughts are like dust. When the dust is cleared away, the mirror is bright; when thoughts are exhausted, the mind is luminous. Thus it is said.
They are of the same category. Although the ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the three realms are divided into twelve types, their birth and death are largely the same;

hence they are called "one class. "Beginning and end" refers to the commencement and conclusion. Birth and death each have their own beginning and end; when ideation (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, there is no more birth and death.

Hence it is said that "beginning and end are perfectly illumined. Afflictions arise because of ideation; when ideation is exhausted, one transcends them. Ideation is capable of melting and transforming.
Causing the mind to follow objects, and causing objects to follow the mind, is therefore called "interfused deluded thinking.

Ānanda, when that good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration brings forth illumination within the samādhi.

At that time, his mind comes to cherish this perfect luminosity; he sharpens his refined contemplation and greedily seeks out skillful illusions. It is then that the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity.

Taking advantage of this opportunity, a flying spirit will possess a person and speak the Dharma and the sutras with their mouth. That person, unaware that they are possessed by a demon, will claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They will come to the place of a son of good family who seeks skillful means, arrange a seat, and preach the Dharma.
For a brief moment, their form may appear as a bhikṣu so that the person may see them; or they may become Śakra, or a woman, or a... [bhikṣuṇī].
A bhikṣuṇī may sleep in a dark room while her body emits light; such a person is deluded and confused, claiming to be a bodhisattva.

People believe in their teachings, which agitate their minds and cause them to violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code, secretly practicing lust. Such individuals delight in speaking of calamities, auspicious signs, and supernatural anomalies;
they may claim that the Tathāgata has appeared in a certain place, or speak of the kalpa-ending fires, or of wars and weapons, thereby instilling fear.
Regarding humans, it causes their family wealth to dissipate without cause; this is called a "strange ghost" (*guǐ*). When old, it becomes a demon (*māra*) that harasses and disturbs the person.
Once its desire is satisfied, it leaves the person's body. Both the disciple and the master will then fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*); if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the skillful mastery of craving. Regarding the "emptiness and subtlety of the aggregate of sensation": it means being able to turn back from the body and observe [the mind], such that its functioning is sovereign and free.
"Not encountering deviant deliberations" means not being disturbed or moved by the ten objects of perception.

"The perfect concentration manifests clarity" means that once the aggregate of sensation is shattered, the delusions of views have already been eliminated; thus, one no longer gives rise to discrimination regarding the various sensory objects before them. This constitutes...

This is the first: the essence of clarity. "The mind cherishes perfect luminosity" means that the mind gives rise to a sense of love and joy, desiring to exhaust all deluded thoughts so that the awakened mind may be perfectly luminous, such that there is nothing it does not know and understand, and no skillful means (*upāya*) that is not accomplished.

Desiring to deliver sentient beings through the practice of teaching and transformation, one thus exerts oneself with sharp resolve and greedily seeks after skillful means; this single instance of greed—

This is precisely the root of stirring up demonic influences. When a celestial demon seizes upon a single moment of mental lapse, it dispatches its essence to possess a person and preach the Dharma to delude them.
One who has exhausted their karmic retribution cannot allow such malevolent spirits to enter their heart or inner organs;

therefore, the demon sends its essence to possess someone nearby to incite and confuse them, causing that person to destroy their own settled mind. This individual does not realize they have been possessed by a demon.
Therefore, by means of preaching the Dharma, he claimed for himself that he had attained realization of *nirvāṇa*.
Before those who sought skillful means, he presented himself according to their preferences, employing various expedient methods to transform his appearance and delude their minds.
Consequently, those seekers of skillful means surrendered their hearts to receive his teachings; thus, their former concentrated minds have now become agitated, and their former discipline...
Now that it has already been destroyed, one has fallen into its arts and cannot emerge. Those who delight in speaking of calamities and auspicious omens refer to those possessed by demons;
their speech is strange and aberrant, deluding and confusing the minds of people. This is called "naming and designating harm.

The "strange ghosts" are those whose habitual tendencies of greed take form upon encountering objects; they only become emissaries of Māra when they reach old age, their minds being weary and satiated.
"Birth. As for "departing from the person's body," it means that after a long time, the demon grows weary and leaves the body of the person he has possessed.
"Disciple" refers to one who seeks out a skilled person; "teacher" refers to a teacher who expounds the Dharma;
and "the awakened ones" refers to those who, whenever someone violates the precepts or entices them toward lust, immediately recognize this as a demon and do not follow its lead.
Ānanda, furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, he is no longer beset by perverse thoughts.
Within the samādhi of perfected concentration, his mind delights in wandering and flightiness; his refined thoughts soar as he greedily seeks out various experiences.

At that time, a celestial demon (*deva-māra*) seizes the opportunity, dispatching its essence to possess a person who then speaks the sutras and the Dharma. This person does not realize they are possessed by a demon, and likewise says:
Having attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, he came to the place of that good son who sought his guidance, spread out his seat, and preached the Dharma.
His own form underwent no change, yet those listening to the Dharma suddenly saw themselves sitting upon precious lotus flowers, their entire bodies transformed into masses of purple-gold light.
Every member of the assembly experienced this; each attained what they had never known before. This person was deluded and confused, taking it to be [something else].
A bodhisattva whose mind is licentious and who violates the Buddha’s code of discipline secretly indulges in lustful desires.

He delights in speaking of various Buddhas appearing in the world, saying that such-and-such a person in such-and-such a place must be the incarnation of a certain Buddha coming here, or that such-and-such a person is a certain bodhisattva and so forth, coming to transform the human realm.
When people see him, their hearts become filled with longing; thus, false views secretly arise, [obscuring] the wisdom of all modes.
It is extinguished. This is called a *pūtana* ghost. Having grown old, it becomes a demon and harasses this person. Once its desire for gratification is satisfied, it leaves the person's body;
then both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth;
if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This is the experience resulting from greedy seeking. The boundless oceans of lands are not separated by even a single hair-tip; when the fruit ripens and the cause is perfected, they manifest spontaneously.
If one greedily seeks [such things], the celestial Māra will dispatch spirits to possess people, who do not transform themselves but change the forms of others.
Those who appear to become Buddhas in this life do so because they have experienced Buddha-lands through that greedy seeking; therefore, they manifest.
The Buddha-land is presented according to their inclinations. "This person" refers to a practitioner whose mind is licentious;
having transformed his settled mind into one that is unrestrained and dissolute, he speaks from the mouth of Māra, claiming that what is currently before him is the Buddha-land.

Because he was fond of wandering about in dissipation, he was enticed by this means. Having seen the various Buddhas and further heard their teachings, his heart became inclined toward them with thirsty longing;
thus, he abandoned himself to follow others. The *póguǐ* (Drought Ghost) is a demonic entity that takes form upon encountering the wind due to the habit of lust;
it now serves as an emissary of Māra.

Furthermore, when the son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (samādhi) gives rise to illumination.

Within this *samādhi*, his mind becomes attached to a lingering, subtle state; he clarifies his refined contemplation and greedily seeks a point of accord. At that time, celestial spirits and ghosts watch for their opportunity.

A flying spirit attaches itself to a person and speaks the sutras and the Dharma with their mouth. That person is truly unaware that they are possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
They come to the place where a son of good family seeks harmony, spread out a seat, and preach the Dharma.

The appearance of the speaker and those listening to the Dharma undergoes no outward change; yet it causes the listeners to experience spontaneous awakening in their minds even before they have heard the Dharma.
From moment to moment their states shifted and changed. Some attained the knowledge of past lives; some possessed the power of knowing others' minds; some beheld the hells;
some knew all manner of good and evil affairs among humans; some spoke verses aloud; and some recited sutras themselves. Each was filled with joy, experiencing things they had never known before.

Such a person is deluded and confused, mistaking themselves for a bodhisattva. Their hearts are permeated with attachment, and they violate the Buddha’s precepts while secretly indulging in greed and desire.
