They are fond of saying that among Buddhas there are great and small; that such-and-such a Buddha is a former Buddha and such-and-such a Buddha is a later Buddha;

and that among them there are both true Buddhas and false Buddhas, as well as male Buddhas and female Buddhas—the same applies to bodhisattvas. Because the person sees this, their original mind is washed away.
It is easy to enter into deviant awakening; this is called a "possessing ghost" (*māyā-ghost*). When it grows old, it becomes a demon (*māra*) that torments and disturbs this person.

Once its desire is satisfied, it leaves the person's body, and both the disciple and the teacher fall into royal calamity. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Deluded and ignorant, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to the greedy pursuit of "conformity" (kiai). "Mian" means "dense"; "yong-hui" means "to join. By means of this mind, one conforms to all Buddhas.

This refers to harmonizing with sentient beings below. When one’s practice reaches the point where quiescent extinction (*śānti*) manifests before them, one naturally harmonizes with those above and unites with those below;
there is no need for deliberate seeking. Because the practitioner harbors a mind that seeks to accord with [the truth], demons likewise manifest matters of silent resonance.
"Moment by moment shifting" means that for one whose mind has opened, each thought-moment is different, as will be explained below.
Furthermore, some may attain the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa-jñāna*), whereby they suddenly come to know what they were previously unaware of as their own ordinary state.
Or some may attain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), whereby they likewise now know the thoughts that others have been constantly harboring.
Even the recitation of verses and the chanting of sutras are all matters of manifesting secret *samādhi* in order to bewilder their minds and cause them to cherish [the teaching] deeply.
As for the mind: when a practitioner is deluded, they also secretly cherish it, desiring to fulfill what their heart seeks.
Yet the mouth of Māra further agitates them with seditious words.

Having seen the person with whom they share a secret pact and having heard these strange and supernatural utterances, the practitioner thereby washes away the mind of right concentration from its former state without remainder, turning instead toward the heterodox.
One knows this to be a false interpretation. As for "demon-ghosts" (*mèiguǐ*): these are ghosts that assume form upon encountering the habit-energy of deception.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination within the state of *samādhi*.

The mind is the root of love. One thoroughly examines the transformation of things and the beginning and end of their nature, refining and clarifying the spirit of the mind while greedily seeking analytical discernment.
At that time, a celestial demon seizes the opportunity; its essence flies to inhabit a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma.

That person was previously unaware of being possessed by a demon, and they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed Nirvana. They come to the place of that good man who seeks the ultimate source.

He spread his seat and preached the Dharma. His body possessed majestic spiritual power that subdued those who came to seek instruction, causing them to submit naturally even before hearing the teaching.
These people [realized] that the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* and *bodhi-dharmakāya* are none other than their own present physical bodies;
that fathers and sons, generation after generation, mutually giving birth to one another, is itself the eternally abiding and uninterrupted *dharmakāya*.
They all claim that the present world itself is the Buddha-land, asserting that there are no separate Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa) nor the golden-hued marks [of a Buddha].

Such people accept this with faith, forgetting their former resolve; they surrender their very lives in devotion and experience what they have never had before. These deluded and confused individuals mistake themselves for Bodhisattvas.
Investigating his mind, one finds that he has violated the Buddha’s code of discipline and secretly practices lustful desires.

He delights in saying that the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are all pure lands, and that the male and female organs are the very locus of Bodhi and Nirvana. Such is the case for those who lack wisdom.

"Believe that these are foul words. These are known as the *gudu* (poisonous charms), *yan* (hypnotic spells), and malevolent ghosts. In their old age, they become demons who harass and disturb this person.
Once they have had their fill, they leave the person's body; then both the disciple and the teacher will fall into royal punishment. You must be aware of this beforehand."
One does not enter saṃsāra; yet, being deluded and ignorant, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to the greedy pursuit of analytical discernment. As for "the root of craving," it is the seeking of the fundamental source of all things.

One desires to cause each and every transformation of phenomena to be thoroughly penetrated to its very core, leaving no room for doubt or obstruction, so that the mind may become expansive and the spirit refreshed; thus, one greedily pursues this.
Analysis: Because of this single thought-moment, it becomes the very beginning of inviting Māra; thus, Māra takes advantage of the interval to enter.
[The practitioner] possesses a physical majesty and spiritual power that subdues those who seek [him], while using the power of Māra to captivate the hearts of people.
These people receive the methods of Māra and successively convert one another, deluding and confusing the minds of men. This arises because the practitioner greedily seeks transformation.
Originally, they pointed to that which is currently subject to annihilation as the eternally abiding essence (*dhruva*), and to that which is defiled as the pure root.
To satisfy their desires, once practitioners have accepted their words, they cast aside their analytical minds one by one;
they then come to believe that the succession of fathers and sons appearing before their eyes, reproducing one another, constitutes the fundamental principle of the transformation of things.
Ri took the mind and speech of Māra and investigated them, regarding them as ultimate truth; he subsequently joined their faction.
That Māra-essence, having already ordered his demonic followers to proclaim foul words to incite and delude others, further uttered foul words himself to provide corroboration.
How could there be anyone who is not deluded? A *gū* ghost is one who, due to the habitual tendencies of resentment, takes form by encountering insects.
Furthermore, when a virtuous man’s *skandhas* are empty and subtle, and he does not encounter perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the state of *samādhi*.

With hearts full of longing and devotion, they circulate widely and investigate with refined diligence, greedily seeking a response from the unseen realm. At that time, a celestial demon (tianma) awaits its opportunity;

it dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person has no prior awareness of being possessed by a demon, and likewise claims to have personally attained supreme nirvana.
Coming to the place of those good men who seek such responses, he spreads out his seat and preaches the Dharma, able to cause the audience—

Upon seeing his body for a brief moment, it was as if they had been together for hundreds of thousands of years; their hearts were filled with affection and attachment, such that they could not bear to part from him.
They served him as slaves, providing the four types of offerings without feeling any weariness, each causing those in his retinue to recognize him as their former teacher.
This original spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) gives rise to a separate attachment to dharmas that is as sticky as glue or lacquer; such a person has attained what was never before experienced.
This individual is deluded and confused, leading others to mistake him for a bodhisattva. Those who draw near to his mind violate the Buddha’s precepts and secretly practice lustful desires.
Such people are fond of saying: "In a previous life, during a certain birth, I first delivered such-and-such a person; at that time, they were my wife, concubine, brother, or sibling."
Now I have come to deliver you; I shall accompany you back to a certain world to make offerings to a certain Buddha.
Or it may be said that there is another realm called the Great Radiant Heaven where a Buddha dwells—the place where all Tathāgatas take their rest—and yet no one knows of it.
Faith is deceptive; it causes one to lose their original mind. This is called a malevolent ghost that becomes a demon in old age, harassing and confusing this person.
Once its desire is satisfied, it leaves the person's body; both disciple and teacher will then fall into royal calamity. You must be aware of this beforehand.
One does not enter saṃsāra; yet, being deluded and ignorant, one falls into the Avīci Hell.
This is the response to greedy seeking. To "suspend love" and seek a response from the unseen is to desire to attain the response of the Buddhas by means of a settled mind.
The way of response and resonance is like the moon appearing when the water is clear; how can it be sought through the intentional mind?
Once this thought arises, demons and malevolent spirits will seize the opportunity to manifest in response.
If one suddenly sees their body as being hundreds or thousands of years old, it is because the demon has manifested in the form of an elderly person.

Because of seeing them as aged, those in the assembly come to recognize them as teachers from previous lives or spiritual friends (*jñātaka*) from former existences; thus, they develop a distinct attachment to the Dharma, like glue and lacquer.
This firm entanglement constitutes instances where demons falsely manifest signs of mystical response. Practitioners, deluded by them, draw near day after day;
unaware and unperceiving, they eventually turn from children of the Buddha into the retinue of Māra.
Since these demons not only falsely manifest signs of mystical response but also falsely utter words of mystical response, how could people not believe them? [These are] fierce ghosts.
This is the manifestation of the habit-energy of anger when encountering adversity.

Furthermore, O son of good family, when the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is empty and subtle, and one is not beset by deviant thoughts, the perfect concentration (*samādhi*) gives rise to illumination within the state of *samādhi*.
Their hearts are deeply attached; they discipline themselves with diligent toil, delighting in secluded stillness and craving tranquility.

At that time, a celestial Mara seizes his opportunity, dispatching an essence to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person originally does not realize they have been possessed by a Mara.
He also declares that he has personally attained unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, and comes to the place of a good man who seeks the aggregates (*skandha*).
There, he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma, causing those who listen to each recognize their own past karma. Or, at that place, he says to one person: "You have not yet died."
Having already been reborn as an animal, he commanded one man to step on his tail from behind; the man was instantly unable to rise.

Thereupon, the entire assembly bowed their hearts in admiration and submission. If anyone conceived an evil thought, the Buddha already knew its inception. This was beyond the scope of the Buddhist Vinaya discipline.
They further increase their ascetic rigor, slandering bhikṣus, reviling their followers, and exposing private matters without avoiding public censure.
They delight in speaking of future calamities and blessings, which, when the time comes, are accurate to the very hair’s breadth. These are the powerful ghosts.

When they grow old, they become demons who harass and disturb these people. Once their desires are satisfied, they leave the person's body; both the disciple and the teacher will then fall into royal calamity.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to craving for past lives. The mind’s attachment to the four lines should be exchanged with the mind’s attachment to the three lines in the following chapter;

then the preceding and succeeding sections will correspond. To love knowledge and views and to crave past lives means desiring to fully know the realms of the three periods of time and desiring to fully see the minds of others.
Once such knowledge and views are established, demons and humans will arise. You, now—
Those who have not yet died but have already manifested as animals do so by craving the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*), and thus falsely display that power.

When someone gives rise to a thought, those who already know its inception do so by craving the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*), and thus falsely display that power.
Those who, outside of the Buddha’s discipline (*vinaya*), subject themselves to further rigorous asceticism do so by falsely displaying diligence (*vīrya*) to delude the minds of people.

Furthermore, the two phrases regarding "slander" refer to accusing upright people of being depraved. The two phrases regarding "exposure" refer to exposing a person's hidden secrets in order to compel their submission and faith.
The four phrases regarding "the mouth" refer to the fraudulent manifestation of the divine eye and divine ear.
These aforementioned five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are those fraudulently manifested by powerful ghosts who practice emptiness.

Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the state of samādhi.

At that time, his mind comes to cherish knowledge and vision; he exerts himself with diligence to investigate and seek, greedily craving knowledge of past lives. It is then that the celestial Māra watches for an opportunity to seize him.

A flying spirit takes possession of a person, who speaks of the sutras and the Dharma. That person is entirely unaware that they are possessed by a demon, and likewise claims to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.
He comes to the place of a seeker of the Way, a son of good family, where he spreads out a seat and establishes the Dharma.
At that place of preaching, this man unexpectedly obtains a great precious jewel. Sometimes that demon transforms himself into an animal, with the jewel held in its mouth.
Furthermore, he first bestowed upon those people various rare treasures, bamboo slips, tally-strips, and all manner of extraordinary objects, which they subsequently wore upon their bodies;

or he enticed the listeners to bury them underground, where a bright moon-jewel (candrakānta-maṇi) would illuminate that spot, causing all who heard of it to experience what they had never known before.
He consumed many medicinal herbs instead of fine delicacies, and at times ate only one sesame seed and one grain of barley a day.
His form is plump and robust because he is sustained by the power of Māra. He slanders bhikṣus and reviles their assemblies, showing no regard for reproach or suspicion.
His mouth is fond of speaking of treasures in other regions and the hidden abodes of sages and worthies from the ten directions; those who follow after him...

One often encounters individuals who appear strange and extraordinary; these are known as the spirits of mountain forests and local lands, the deities of city walls, rivers, and peaks, or ghosts and gods who have grown old and become demons.
Some may propagate lust and violate the Buddha’s precepts, secretly indulging in the five desires with those who serve them.

There may be those who practice asceticism by subsisting solely on grasses and trees, yet their conduct lacks constancy. Such individuals will provoke and disturb these practitioners until they become weary and dissatisfied; once this state of mind arises, the spirits will leave the practitioners' bodies.
Consequently, both the disciples and the masters often fall into royal persecution. You must recognize this beforehand so that you do not enter the cycle of rebirth.
Deluded and unaware, they fall into the Avīci Hell;
this is the consequence of seeking stillness and tranquility. Stillness and tranquility are the ultimate state of dhyāna-samādhi; others do not know them, for only a Buddha can know them.
Yet, as soon as there is a heart of attachment, Māra seizes upon that attachment and manifests the phenomena of the five aggregates in a state of quiescence to delude them.
As for this person who unexpectedly obtains a great precious jewel: it refers to the practitioner obtaining the "jewel" from the place where the Dharma is preached.
Alternatively, they may first hold a jewel in their mouth and cast it upon people to attach to their bodies; or they may first bury a jewel underground to lure people;
or they may consume medicinal herbs, hemp, or wheat to appear nourished and robust. These are all deceptive manifestations of hidden tranquility that cannot be discerned.
This is done to cater to their inclinations. Once Māra has manifested these secret matters to agitate and draw them in, he further preaches on such secret matters to delude the multitude.
These are all spirits and ghosts of the land who, over time, have become Māra’s messengers. Or there are those of lower rank;
the demonic factions form groups and bands to disturb and confuse practitioners.

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within the samādhi.
At that time, his mind comes to love various supernatural transformations and he researches the source of such transformations, greedily seeking spiritual powers.

Then, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatching a refined spirit to possess a person who speaks the sutras and the Dharma. That person truly does not realize they have been possessed by a Māra.

He also declares that he has personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa and comes to the place where that son of good family seeking supernatural powers resides; there he spreads his seat and preaches the Dharma.
This person may then take fire in his hand and, grasping that flame with his hand, distribute it over the heads of the fourfold assembly gathered to listen.
As for these listeners, flames several feet long issued from the crowns of their heads; yet they lacked the quality of heat and never burned them.
Some walked upon water as if treading on level ground; some sat motionless in mid-air; and some entered into jars.
Sometimes he was inside a sack; sometimes he passed through windows and walls without ever encountering any obstruction. Only regarding weapons did he lack mastery.
He claimed to be a Buddha, wore white robes, and accepted the prostrations of bhikṣus. He slandered dhyāna and the Vinaya, and reviled his own followers.
They expose the private affairs of others without avoiding censure or suspicion; they constantly speak of supernatural powers and mastery while in their own mouths;
or they cause people to see Buddha-lands by the side of them. These are delusions produced by demonic forces and lack any reality; they praise sexual misconduct and do not condemn coarse behavior.

To take such vulgar and lewd matters as the transmission of the Dharma—these are known as the mountain spirits, sea spirits, wind spirits, river spirits, and earth spirits of great power within heaven and earth;
or the accumulated karmic enchantments of all plants and trees over many kalpas; or perhaps dragon spirits; or immortals whose lives have come to an end.

They may be revived as *māra* spirits; or, when their celestial lifespan ends and they ought to die according to the reckoning of years, their forms do not decompose and become possessed by other monsters.

As they grow old, they become *māras*, harassing and disturbing these people. Once they have grown satiated, they leave the person’s body. Both the disciple and the master often fall into royal punishment for this.
You should be aware of this beforehand so that you do not enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). If you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This refers to greedily seeking supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). As for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are naturally and fully possessed once the six sense faculties are mutually interchangeable;

how could one possibly crave them? To become attached to such craving immediately invites demonic affairs (*mārakarman*). The passage "this person" and below describes how they falsely manifest eighteen miraculous transformations to delude others.
The fact that they fear only weapons is sufficient proof of their being a malevolent spirit. The passage "in his mouth" and below describes what he says.
Supernatural powers (ṛddhi) are used to delude people. To praise sexual indulgence while failing to condemn coarse conduct is sufficient evidence that these are the teachings of Māra.
These are all instances of various spirits dwelling in water or on land who falsely manifest supernatural powers.
Furthermore, when a good man’s aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by deviant thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination.

Within this *samādhi*, his mind comes to cherish entry into cessation and studies the nature of transformation, greedily seeking the profound emptiness. At that time, a celestial Māra watches for an opportunity and seizes it.

A flying spirit will possess a person, who shall speak of the sutras and the Dharma. That person will never realize they are possessed by a demon, and will also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvana.
They will come to the place of that son of good family who seeks emptiness, arrange a seat, and preach the Dharma within the great assembly.
His form suddenly vanished into emptiness, so that the assembly could see nothing; then, from the void, he emerged abruptly. He exercised mastery over his appearance and disappearance.

At times he manifested his body as transparent as lapis lazuli; at times he extended his hands and feet, which emitted the fragrance of sandalwood; and at times his excrement and urine were like thick rock honey.
He slandered the precepts and held those who have left the household life in contempt, constantly proclaiming with his own mouth that there is neither cause nor effect.
They believe that death brings eternal extinction and no further rebirths for either ordinary beings or sages. Although they attain a state of empty stillness, they secretly harbor lustful desires;
those who indulge in such desire also claim to have attained the empty mind, thereby repudiating cause and effect. This is known as the "essence of solar and lunar eclipses."
Jade, gold, *zhicao* fungi, *qilin*, phoenixes, tortoises, and cranes—though they may live for thousands of myriad years without dying, they become spirits.

When they are born into a land and grow old, they become demons. They vex and disturb these people; once their desires are satisfied, they depart from the person's body. Both the disciples and the teacher often fall into royal punishment.
You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). If you are deluded and unaware, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.
This is the profound seeking of emptiness. True emptiness does not obstruct wondrous existence; though things exist, their nature is eternally empty.

Therefore, one fully cultivates the myriad practices while remaining entirely free from attachment. If one wishes to block off all practices in order to establish what is called "profound emptiness," [one has misunderstood].
This is identical to the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), which immediately invites the interference of Māra.

Regarding the passage "among the great assembly," it refers to manifesting emptiness out of a craving for emptiness to cater to their desires. The two phrases concerning "slander" refer to slandering the Dharma and disparaging the Sangha because of that [craving for] emptiness.
"Explaining 'emptiness as annihilation' below refers to using the doctrine of emptiness to deny cause and effect.

Although one may attain empty stillness, 'secretly practicing lust' means that while discussing emptiness, the mind remains attached to existence. To 'experience desire and yet claim to have attained an empty mind' is to be held fast by the power of Māra, becoming transformed along with him.
This is called 'below'; it causes people to recognize these names so they may guard against them strictly."

Furthermore, when a son of good family’s aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) becomes empty and subtle, and he is not beset by perverse thoughts, his perfect concentration gives rise to illumination within samādhi.

At that time, his mind comes to cherish long life; he labors diligently to investigate the subtle, greedily seeking eternal years. He abandons the coarse process of birth and death, suddenly hoping for the permanence of the subtle signs of the transformation-death (pariṇāma-maraṇa).
Then, a celestial Māra seizes the opportunity, dispatches a refined spirit to possess a person, who speaks the teachings of the sūtras with their own mouth.
That person ultimately does not realize they are possessed by a māra; they also claim to have personally attained unsurpassed nirvāṇa.

They come to the place where that seeker of birth—a son of good family—resides, arrange their seat, and preach the Dharma. They speak favorably of traveling to and from other directions without obstruction, even across ten thousand *li*.
In an instant they returned; in every case, they had obtained the object from that very place.

Or, within a single location, inside a single house, over the span of a few paces, they were made to go from the eastern wall to the western wall; though this person walked with great haste, they would not arrive even after many years.
Therefore, with faith in this mind, one has no doubt that the Buddha is manifest before them. He constantly says: "The sentient beings of the ten directions are all my children.
I give birth to all Buddhas; I bring forth the worlds. I am the primordial Buddha; appearing in the world spontaneously, I did not attain this through cultivation."
This is called the Sovereign Heavenly Demon who dwells in the world.

He causes his retinue—such as Cāmuṇḍā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the Viśākha boys who have not yet resolved their minds—to take advantage of its empty luminosity and consume its vital essence; or else, they do so without relying on a teacher.
The practitioner will personally see one who calls himself Vajradhara, who grants him long life. He manifests in the body of a beautiful woman and indulges extensively in lustful desires;
yet before a year has passed, his liver and brain will wither away, and he will engage in solitary muttering that sounds like the speech of a malevolent spirit.
The fate of those who came before is not well known; many fall into royal peril. Before they even face execution, they have already withered and died.

They torment and disturb others until those others meet their end. You should be aware of this beforehand so as not to enter the cycle of rebirth; if you are deluded and ignorant, you will fall into the Avīci Hell.

This refers to the craving for eternal years. It is only when the delusions of the three realms within the *pariccheda-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death) are exhausted that one finally attains liberation from it.
Those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*) all attain *pariṇāma-maraṇa* (transformational birth).

Since one has not yet abandoned defilement at this stage, one seeks to transform the coarse into the subtle and change the short into the long within the body of segmented birth; therefore, it is said: "Abandoning segmented birth, one suddenly aspires to transformation."
It is easy. To come from ten thousand *li* in an instant; to travel swiftly for many months without arriving.
They feign the ability to prolong or shorten the present moment in order to cater to people's desires. With their mouths, they speak of longevity to rouse the listeners' attention.
Īśvara is the Māra King of the Desire Realm, subsumed under the sixth heaven (*Ṣaṭ-deva*).

As for those who cause him to employ his retinue, it is not the Māra King himself who manifests his body, but rather a flying spirit (*fei-jing*) that possesses a person. Cāmuṇḍā—translated here as "the Envious Woman"—is a ghost employed [by the Māra].
Piśāca—translated here as "the Consumer of Vital Essence"—both belong to the Four Heavenly Kings. Those who have already resolved their minds [to seek awakening]...

Those who have already resolved their minds protect people; those who have not yet resolved their minds devour people. This is because the practitioner’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is empty and luminous, and [the demons] consume its vital essence (*ojas*) to harm them.
Alternatively, for those who do not rely on a teacher, the māras do not merely possess others to preach the Dharma, but manifest their own bodies so that the practitioner sees them directly.
Those who call themselves Vajra-sattvas or appear as beautiful women are those who harm people.

This is a clever ruse. The "solitary woman" refers to a beautiful maiden. One who does not discern her intent and follows her words to engage in lewd and debauched acts will often fall into royal peril;
even before the execution is carried out, their spirit will first wither and they will die.
Ānanda, you should know that these ten kinds of Māras, during the final age, will appear within my Dharma— having left the household life to practice the Way—
either possessing the bodies of others or manifesting their own forms, all claiming to have already attained right and universal enlightenment, and praising sexual desire.

They violate the Buddha’s code of discipline. These former evil demonic masters and their disciples transmit lustful practices from one to another. Such perverse spirits darken the heart and inner organs;
for as few as nine lifetimes, or often for more than a hundred generations, they cause those who truly practice the Way to become entirely part of the demonic retinue.
After the end of your life, you will inevitably become a subject of Māra, lose the knowledge of the Right and Universal, and fall into the Avīci Hell.
You need not seek nirvāṇa first; even if you attain the stage of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa), remain with your vows within that age of the Final Dharma and give rise to great compassion.
I deliver those sentient beings who possess a correct mind and deep faith, causing them not to be attached to demons and enabling them to attain right knowledge and vision.
Now that I have delivered you from birth and death, if you follow the Buddha’s words, this shall be called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.

This is an entrustment to the appropriate recipients, leaving behind the vow to deliver sentient beings. Regarding the ten types of māras mentioned previously, only the tenth manifests its own form; the others all attach themselves to human beings.
In the past, while the Buddha dwelt in the world, various māras sought to destroy the Dharma, yet by the Buddha’s spiritual power, they were all unable to do so.
The māras then made a vow: "After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, we shall leave the household life in accordance with the teachings and destroy the Buddha-Dharma. Thus it is known.

Monks who destroy the Dharma are all companions of Māra. Ānanda previously said, "I vow that I may now attain the fruit and become a Treasure King, and further deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
This was once again a earnest entreaty to remain among humans and cause the teachings to circulate.
He previously said, "To offer this profound mind to every dust-mote world is what is called repaying the Buddha's kindness. Therefore, he spoke again.
He instructed him to follow the Buddha’s words, for to transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings is precisely how one repays the Buddha’s kindness.

Ānanda, these ten kinds of manifest states during *dhyāna* all arise from the interaction between the mind and the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of mental formations); therefore, these phenomena appear.
Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves, and when encountering such conditions, they fail to recognize them within their own confusion, saying:
To claim sainthood is a great falsehood; one will fall into the Avīci Hell.

You must take these words of the Tathāgata and, after my parinirvāṇa, transmit them during the Final Dharma Age, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to this meaning. Do not allow celestial Māras to find any opportunity;
maintain and protect [this teaching] so that they may achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
These ten Māras violate the Buddha’s disciplinary code even more severely than the various Māras of the four aggregates;

therefore, when the Tathāgata reached this point, he entrusted [the teachings] to Ānanda with double the earnestness and urgency. That Ānanda compiled the various sūtras was precisely because he received the Buddha’s entrustment.
That the teachings circulate today—who would say it is not due to his compassionate concern for the world and the power of his sorrowful salvation?
The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas,
Volume Nine. The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of Cultivation and Realization of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the tenth fascicle concerning Ānanda:
"When that son of good family has cultivated *samādhi* and the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, this person’s ordinary dreams and thoughts are extinguished;
whether awake or asleep, he remains constant in one state. His awakened clarity is empty and still, like a cloudless sky, no longer burdened by the coarse objects of the external world."
The Matter of Reflections: Contemplate the great earth, mountains, and rivers of all worlds as being like a bright mirror; they come without attachment and pass away without a trace.
They receive illumination in emptiness, yet are entirely devoid of habitual tendencies. Only this single, refined reality reveals the root-source of birth and death.
One sees all twelve classes of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, exhausting every category; though one has not yet penetrated their individual destinies, [the source is revealed].
The Prologue: One perceives the basis of co-arising as being like a wild horse, shimmering and turbid, serving as the ultimate pivot for the floating sense-faculties and their objects.
This is called the realm of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

If this shimmering and turbid fundamental nature enters its original clarity, and once clarified, its habitual tendencies vanish—like waves subsiding and transforming into still water—it is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*. Such a person...
Thus one can transcend the turbidity of sentient beings. If one examines its origin, one finds that hidden and obscure false imaginings constitute its root.
Floating habitual tendencies manifest as thoughts during the clarity of day and as dreams during the obscurity of night, agitating the true nature.
When the aggregate of thought is exhausted, dreams and fantasies vanish, and the essence of awakened clarity is forever empty and still. These coarse and heavy shadows of sensory dust—
This is precisely the dharma-object (dharmāyatana). It takes conceptualization (saṃjñā) as its substance; when conceptualization is exhausted, the object is exhausted.

By means of this, one contemplates all worlds as being like an object reflected in a mirror—without attachment and without trace. A mirror possesses four kinds of wondrous functions: that which is empty can contain the myriad phenomena.

The recipient does not reject things as they come; the illuminator manifests forms according to the size of the objects; the responder investigates both the beautiful and the ugly without acceptance or rejection.
This singular, refined, and true clarity is thus extreme. Therefore, the hidden *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) is here revealed.
The *saṃskāra-skandha* is the root source of birth and extinction, for it consists of shifting flux and conditioned activity. Thus, the twelve types of sentient beings are encompassed within it.
"Exhausting all that exists in heaven and on earth" means that all beings within these twelve categories of existence emerge from this;

for it is through the performance of this karma that they constitute their essential substance. "Each with its own destiny and lineage" refers to the causal roots and lineages that determine the individual destinies of each category of being, which is precisely consciousness (*vijñāna*).
"A common basis for birth" means that all beings within these categories share a common foundation for their arising, which is—

This is the movement. "Wild horses" refers to a mirage (*marīci*). In spring, when the weather is clear, the drifting vapors take the form of water; their luster is like a flame, shimmering and flickering—this describes their appearance.
"Clear turbulence" refers to the subtle movement [of these vapors], serving as a metaphor for birth and death. "Floating roots and dust" refers to the physical body.

The pivot of a door is called a *shu*, and the socket of the door is called a *xue*; these are the essential points of rotation. Likewise, the arising and ceasing of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and sense-objects (*viṣaya*) are all...

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the pivot-hole; this is the sign that the aggregate of formations has not yet been exhausted. The aggregate of perceptions (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is like a great torrent, while the aggregate of formations is like a fine stream.
When the aggregate of perceptions is exhausted, it is like the cessation of the great torrent; when the aggregate of formations manifests, it is like the arising of the fine stream.
If one takes this nature of the fine stream—the fundamental habituation—and reverses its entry into the fundamentally limpid essence free of waves, then the fundamental habituation becomes limpid.

This is the sign that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted. Birth and cessation ceaselessly continue; karma and destiny are constantly shifting—this is called the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

When the aggregate of formations is exhausted, one transcends it. Because the birth and cessation of the aggregate of formations are subtle and difficult to perceive, they are termed "hidden and obscure."

Ānanda, you should know that among those good men who have attained right awareness within *śamatha*, ten classes of celestial Māras cannot find an opportunity against them, as they concentrate their clarity and fix their minds correctly.
Only then are they able to investigate with refinement and exhaust the root of all living beings.

When the fundamental source of birth is revealed within that fundamental category, they observe that profound, pure, and perfectly agitated source of movement. Within that perfect source, they give rise to conceptual calculations.
This person falls into two types of causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*). First, this person perceives that there is no fundamental cause. Why is this?

Because this person has already attained the complete destruction of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and, by means of the eight hundred merits of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), sees all sentient beings throughout eighty thousand kalpas.
They see the winding currents of karma as they die here and are born there; they see only sentient beings revolving within those very places. Eight...

Beyond ten thousand kalpas, there is nothing observed in the darkness; thus one forms this interpretation: "These sentient beings of the world throughout the ten directions have existed spontaneously without cause for eighty thousand kalpas.
By such conceptualization, they lose the correct universal knowledge and fall into the ways of external paths, deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi.
Second, these people see that the end has no cause. Why is this? Because these people, regarding birth, having already seen...
As for their roots: know that humans are born as humans, and awaken to the fact that birds are born as birds. Crows have been black from the beginning; cranes have been white from the beginning.
Humans and devas are fundamentally upright; animals are fundamentally horizontal. White was not made by washing; black was not created by dyeing.
From eighty thousand kalpas ago, there has been no further change or alteration. Now, at the end of this present form, it is likewise so. Yet I originally did not perceive bodhi—how could it be...?
There is yet another matter regarding the attainment of Bodhi: you should know that all phenomena today are fundamentally without cause.
By such conceptualization, one loses right and universal knowledge and falls into the ranks of the externalists, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the first type of externalist who establishes the doctrine of causelessness.
With correct awareness of *śamatha*, one stabilizes and clarifies the mind, contemplating the sign of total exhaustion. All external māras are summoned by the mind;

when the [mental] conceptions are exhausted, the celestial māras cannot approach. However, there is that which occurs when practicing dhyāna but losing its proper course—mad interpretations and false reckonings, known as the "mind-māra.
The fundamental source of all living beings is precisely the same as the basis of co-arising. Within this fundamental class, that which reveals the primordial element is [the true nature].
Within the common basis of birth, one perceives the fundamental source of one's own activity. This "subtle, pure, and moving source" is precisely the source of activity.
When investigating the root of all living beings, one sees only that the subtle, pure, and pervasive agitation of the aggregate of activity (*saṃskāra-skandha*) constitutes the source of birth;

yet, failing to investigate the beginning and end of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), one consequently falls into the two types of causeless theories (*ahetuvāda*). Among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), there is a class of teachers who propound such causeless theories.
When a practitioner, within the state of śamatha, erroneously gives rise to conceptual constructions, they unconsciously fall into that [view] without realizing it;

this is not a case of independently establishing a theory of causelessness. "Fundamentally causeless" refers to the absence of causes regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). "The mechanism of arising is completely destroyed" means that the process by which things are produced is utterly shattered.
This is the disclosure of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of formations is disclosed, the six faculties do not function [as they normally would].

Thus, by means of the merit of the eye-faculty within meditative concentration, one sees sentient beings over eighty thousand kalpas drifting with the waves of their karma. "Wan" (灣) means revolving; "huan" (環) means circling. Before eighty thousand kalpas, it is dark and nothing is seen.

One falsely calculates that this darkness is a place where nothing can be observed. This is [the state of]... (Note: The final character "為" in the source text appears to be an incomplete or truncated term, likely referring to a specific meditative state or realization, such as *wei* (位, stage/position) or a similar technical term.)

The *mṛṣā-tattva* (the principle of darkness) is considered to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Not knowing that the scope of one's own vision is limited, they claim that all sentient beings originally did not exist but now do.
By calculating that they were originally non-existent, they lose the nature of perfect universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) and fall into wrong views. Regarding "ultimately causeless":

this refers to being causeless at the posterior limit (*paścima-koṭi*). They erroneously cling to the arising of roots [of existence] and fail to comprehend the principle of transformation, [concluding] that humans ultimately...

Regarding human beings: if they are black from beginning to end, they remain black without any change or transition. By this analogy, I originally did not see the Way, and in the end there was no realization;
thus, the end has no cause. The original character for "text" (*ben*) should be combined with the character for "end" (*mo*).

This is because one clings to the idea that the beginning has no cause, and consequently clings to the idea that the end also has no cause. To say that everything has no cause is to mean that everything is the beginning.
That they come about spontaneously is because one has not yet perceived the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and does not understand the life-origins of the twelve classes of beings.
This type is precisely what is called the "Nihilistic Naturalist" (*svabhāvavāda*); they reckon that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is primordial and does not depend on causes and conditions.
This means they claim things exist of themselves without a cause; it does not mean that everything is annihilated.
Ānanda, when these good sons within this *samādhi* concentrate their clarity and align their minds, Māra finds no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who give rise to speculative calculations regarding this perfect and eternal reality fall into the four theories of universal permanence.
The first is when such a person investigates the nature of the mind and its objects and finds no cause for these two states; they then cultivate this [view].
They are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within twenty thousand kalpas;

they see that these all circulate in a cycle, never being lost or scattered, and thus reckon them to be permanent. Second, this person exhausts the source of the four great elements and perceives their four natures as eternally abiding.

Through cultivation, they are able to know all the births and deaths of sentient beings throughout the ten directions within forty thousand kalpas, seeing that their essence is constant and has never [ceased].
Third, this person exhausts the six sense faculties and the *manas* that grasps and sustains them;

because the fundamental source within the mind, intellect, and consciousness is eternally constant by nature, they cultivate the ability to know that throughout eighty thousand kalpas, all sentient beings circulate without losing their essence, remaining fundamentally abiding and never exhausting their inherent nature, thus reckoning it as permanence. Fourth...
Once this person has exhausted the source of perception, the principle of their nature no longer flows, ceases, or revolves.

The mind of birth and death is now forever extinguished, and within this principle, non-arising and non-extinction are spontaneously realized. Yet, because they rely on what is measured by the mind, they reckon this state to be permanent.

Due to this reckoning of permanence, they lose right and universal knowledge and fall into the ways of external paths, becoming deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the second [delusion].
The non-Buddhists establish a doctrine of pervasive permanence (*pariccheda-nityatā*).
This arises from their singular reckoning that that which flows and changes without ceasing is omnipresent and eternal, thereby giving rise to the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

Because the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) continues through the succession of arising and ceasing without being lost, it is called "permanent. Because they reckon these four types as pervading all phenomena, it is called "pervasive" (*pariccheda*).

"Ubiquitous" (*piān*) means "perfect" (*yuán*). Therefore, it is first designated as "ubiquitous and eternal," and finally concluded as "perfect and eternal. As for the four kinds: first, the mind and its objects; second, the four great elements; third, the eight consciousnesses;
and fourth, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). This is because one falsely conceives of the aggregate of formations as the perfect source of birth and extinction.
Consequently, regarding the mind, objects, the four great elements, and so forth, they all reckoned them to be permanent. First, they reckoned the mind and its objects to be permanent.

As their conceptualizations were shattered and their practice manifested, their minds opened accordingly. They investigated the fundamental origin of the internal mind and external objects as to how they came to be.
Not searching far, they saw that twenty thousand kalpas ago, things existed spontaneously without cause; within those twenty thousand kalpas, there was only arising and ceasing.
It is not a case of non-interruption through the cessation of existence beyond kalpas; rather, it is the calculation that within a single kalpa there is continuity, which is taken as permanence.
Second, they calculate that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are permanent. They hold that all phenomena are formed from the combination of these four great elements;

by applying their attention to investigate them, they perceive the nature of the four great elements to be permanent, and thus they calculate that the essence of sentient beings is permanent. Regarding the "four ten-thousand kalpas," the phenomena investigated therein are somewhat more extensive.

Therefore, the number of kalpas is double that of the former. Third, it calculates the eight consciousnesses as being eternal. "Root" refers to the consciousness within the roots, which is the six consciousnesses;
"Manas" is the seventh consciousness; and "Appropriation" (ādāna) is the eighth consciousness. "Collectively arising" is named *citta* (mind); "deliberating" is named *manas* (intellect);
and "discriminating" is named *vijñāna* (consciousness). The "six roots," along with "Manas" and "Appropriation," collectively enumerate all eight consciousnesses. This is *citta*.
The fundamental source within the mental consciousness is the very nature of consciousness itself.
It is said to be eternal; sentient beings rely upon it, dwelling in cyclic existence without ever being lost. This is the deluded conceptualization regarding the *vijñāna* (consciousness).

The dharma-gates investigated therein are profound and vast, doubling those of the four great elements; therefore, the number of kalpas known therein also doubles compared to the former. Fourth, the [deluded] calculation...

The *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) is eternal. Based on the point where the source of perception (*saṃjñā*) is exhausted, one mistakenly believes that all five aggregates have been completely extinguished.

Based on the manifest state of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, one mistakenly identifies it as the perfectly luminous, essential mind. Only when observed with the Buddha-eye does one realize that this is actually the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

The "source of perception" refers to the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception); the "vital process" refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha*. To falsely claim that the flow of transmigration and the cycle of birth and death both belong solely to the perceiving mind is an error.

Now that [the other aggregates] have been eternally extinguished, one perceives the principle of non-arising and non-extinction; naturally, this belongs to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

One does not realize that the aggregate of formations is the very root-source of arising and extinction. Seeing only the principle of the arising of the aggregate of formations, and observing the absence of those coarse and heavy fluctuations, one concludes that arising and extinction have already ceased.
Yet one does not know that the flowing current of arising and extinction remains perfectly intact; it is not because of its pervasive completeness that one reckons it as pervasive.
It is circular. Because they conceive of what is not truly eternal as being truly eternal, they fall into false awakening and lose right awakening.

Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who stabilize and concentrate their correct minds will not be given an opportunity by Māra; they exhaust the root of all classes of living beings.
Contemplating that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source, those who give rise to conceptual calculations regarding self and others fall into four inverted views:
the theory that one part is impermanent and one part is permanent.

First, such a person contemplates the wondrously luminous mind as pervading the ten directions of space, regarding its profound stillness as an ultimate *ātman*; from this, they calculate that the self pervades the ten directions.

Concentrated clarity is unmoving; all sentient beings are born and die within my own mind, yet the nature of my mind is termed "constant," while those who undergo birth and death possess a truly impermanent nature. Second, such people do not contemplate their own minds.
He surveys throughout the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions. Where he sees places where kalpas are destroyed, he calls them the ultimate nature of impermanence;
where he sees places where kalpas are not destroyed, he calls them the ultimate permanence. Third, this person separately contemplates his own mind, which is subtle, refined, and profound.
It is like a minute speck of dust that flows through the ten directions; its nature is unchanging.

It can cause this body to arise and perish in an instant, yet its indestructible nature is called the "eternal nature of the self. All birth and death flow forth from this self, which is termed the "nature of impermanence."

Fourth, this person knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has been exhausted and perceives the flow of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Because the aggregate of mental formations flows constantly, they reckon it to have the nature of permanence.
Since form, sensation, and perception have now ceased and been extinguished, they designate them as impermanent. Based on this deliberation, they conceive of one part as impermanent.
Because they hold that one part is eternal, they fall into the ranks of the externalists and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the third externalist doctrine:
the theory of partial permanence.

Within the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, they perceive the exhaustion of thought and the manifestation of formations; they investigate themselves and others, giving rise to false and delusive discrimination. In the Śūraṅgama Samādhi...
Only when one fully understands all phenomena and reaches ultimate firmness can one be called truly awakened. To differentiate between the permanent and the impermanent constitutes a perversion.
This [view] shares with the four types of "universal permanence" the adherence to the source of movement as being truly permanent;

however, while they reckon that everything is entirely permanent, this [view] reckons that within both self and other, there exists only a single portion of true permanence—namely, that which resides within the self.
Elsewhere, one calculates permanence and impermanence; yet this wondrous clarity, perfect and profound stillness, is free from "I" and "mine.

The practitioner falsely establishes a divine self (*pudgala*) therein, and from this calculation of a self, they conceive of it as pervasive, solid, and unmoving, while all sentient beings undergo birth and death within it.

Consequently, they calculate that their own realm is permanent while other realms are impermanent. Second, they calculate that the three calamities and the places beyond their reach are both permanent and impermanent;
they do not observe their own minds, but only observe the lands. From the third dhyāna downward, these are ultimately destroyed by the three calamities and are thus termed "of an impermanent nature.
From the fourth dhyāna upward, the three calamities cannot destroy them, and are thus termed "ultimate."
Third, one reckons one's own body and mind as being either permanent or impermanent. Because the nature of the mind is subtle and secret, it is difficult to perceive;
thus, it is likened to a minute particle (*paramāṇu*), not because it is small in size. One clings to this subtle mental nature as the "self" (*ātman*).

The term "self" carries the meaning of an independent and sovereign master. Therefore, while the nature itself is capable of transmigrating and remains unchanging, it is that which causes these coarse aggregates to flow.
The physical body (rūpakāya) has arising and ceasing;

because these coarse aggregates all flow forth from my own mind, that which flows forth is called impermanent, while that which is able to flow forth is called the permanent nature. Fourth is the dualistic reckoning based on observing the four aggregates:
one reckons the flow of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) as permanent, and the exhaustion of form, sensation, and perception as [impermanent].
"It is impermanent. From this point downward, he summarizes the errors of the four views.

Furthermore, within samādhi, those sons of good family who stabilize and concentrate their correct minds will not be given an opportunity by Māra; they will exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
Observing that profound, pure, and eternally agitated source, those who engage in conceptual calculations regarding its various states fall into the four theories of finitude.
The first is when a person calculates the origin of birth; as its flowing function never ceases, they calculate the past and the future.
That which is called "having limits" refers to calculating the successive moments of the mind.

That which is called "limitless" refers to when these two types of people observe eighty thousand kalpas and see that before those eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings were quiescent, beyond hearing or seeing. This state of being beyond hearing or seeing is called "limitless."
There is a state of sentient beings called "having limits. Third, there are those who reckon that their self possesses universal knowledge and has attained a boundless nature;

yet all such people appear within the scope of my own knowledge, while I have never known the nature of their knowing—thus they are said not to have attained a boundless mind, but only a limited nature.
Fourth, there are those who exhaustively investigate the emptiness of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), according to what they perceive.
The mind deliberates thus: "Within the single body of every sentient being, it calculates that all are half-born and half-extinguished;
it clarifies that everything within this world is such that one half is finite and one half is infinite.

By means of such calculations regarding the finite and the infinite, they fall into the ways of external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fourth type of externalist.
The thesis establishing the existence of limits (antavāda) has four divisions: namely, the three time periods, seeing and hearing, self and other, and arising and ceasing.

Although it simultaneously calculates both "having limits" and "being limitless," it is designated simply as "having limits" because having limits is not a supreme dharma. "Limit" (anta) means a boundary or extremity. [End of preceding section]
These four types of views reckon [the self] as truly eternal; this view reckons it as vast. "From within the great awakening, emptiness arises, like a single bubble emerging from the sea.
How could there be any distinct stages? Such a person merely knows that the dharma-nature is boundless, yet has never personally perceived the dharma-nature.
Thus, they falsely establish a state of being and cling to one portion as being "unbounded," while regarding all the rest as "bounded";
hence, it is called the "Four Theories of Boundedness. The first of these calculates boundedness and non-boundedness based on the three periods of time.

The fundamental flow of activity is the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). Because of this shifting flow, one calculates the three periods: that which has passed is already extinguished; that which is yet to come is... [not yet arisen].
That which is seen is called "finite. That which is the present continuity is called "infinite.

To falsely establish a limit within this infinite expanse—how could such a person know that the path to Bodhi is devoid of coming and going? Second, there is the calculation of finitude and infinity based on seeing and hearing:
that which has a range of seeing and hearing within a kalpa is finite, being limited by eighty thousand [yojanas].
This refers to the number of kalpas. That which lies beyond the kalpas is "boundless" (*ananta*) because it is a realm beyond seeing or hearing; it is infinite and unfathomable.
Thirdly, they calculate based on self and other as being either finite or infinite, thinking: "I am able to know all sentient beings everywhere."
I reckon that I have attained the nature of boundlessness; yet I see only the person, not the person's nature.

I falsely conceptualize that nature as having limits, failing to realize that it is my own failure to perceive it, rather than the nature itself being finite. Fourth, one calculates finitude and infinitude based on arising and ceasing:
this person investigates this *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and sees that they first exist and subsequently become empty. First...
Arising and subsequently ceasing—based on one’s own perceptions and views, one falsely calculates that half of a sentient being’s body belongs to arising and half belongs to ceasing;
thus, one judges arising to be finite and ceasing to be infinite. Regarding these four types of finitude: the first refers solely to oneself;

the second refers exclusively to others; the third encompasses both self and others; and the fourth involves a further calculation regarding all environments and inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *āśrita*) of others.
This constitutes a sequence that is narrow in the front and broad in the rear.

Furthermore, among those sons of good family within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright; thus, Māras cannot find an opportunity, as they exhaustively investigate the fundamental source of all living beings.

Contemplating that profound clarity as a source of constant agitation, those who give rise to conceptual calculations within their cognition and vision fall into four kinds of inverted, chaotic, and futile discursive theories regarding immortality. The first is when such a person contemplates the source of transformation.
To perceive the locus of transition is called "change. To perceive the locus of continuity is called "permanence. To perceive the locus of what is seen is called "arising.
Not perceiving the locus of seeing is called "cessation. This is the cause of continuity; it is the state wherein the nature is uninterrupted.

That which is called "increase" refers to the state within the correct continuity; that which is called "decrease" refers to the intervals therein that are separated; that which is called "existence" refers to each respective place of arising;
and that which is called "non-existence" refers to each mutual point of cessation. When observing through principle as a whole, one perceives distinct aspects through the application of the mind.
When seekers of the Dharma come to inquire about its meaning, he replies, "I am now both arising and ceasing; both existent and non-existent;
both increasing and decreasing. At all times, he confuses their speech, causing those before him to lose the essential passages.
Second, this person contemplates the mind and perceives that it has no fixed location; because there is nothing to be found, they attain realization.
When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, saying simply "non-existence. Apart from this non-existence, they have nothing further to say. Third, this person...

Observe closely that their minds each have their own locus; because of this, they attain realization. When someone comes to question them, they respond with only a single word, merely saying "it is so.
Apart from this, they have nothing further to say. Fourth, these people perceive both existence and non-existence.
Because their objects of perception are fragmented, their minds are likewise distracted. When someone comes to question them, they answer, "It both exists and does not exist;
yet within that which does not exist, it is not the case that it exists. This is entirely evasive and confused, allowing no room for further inquiry.

By means of such speculative, evasive, and nihilistic reckoning, they fall into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), deluding themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi. This is called the fifth type of non-Buddhist.
The nature of the four perversions (*viparyāsa*).

Regarding the "frivolous and evasive talk of immortality" (*amarāvikkhepa*) and the "reckless theorizing" (*vitanda*), those who harbor views based on birth calculate erroneously according to what they know and see within their meditative attainments (*samādhi*).
The heterodox outsiders (*tīrthika*) themselves have four types of frivolous and evasive discussions regarding immortality, which differ from these; the Blessed One [addressed] these four...

These various types of people establish their own "knowledge" based on their views and knowledge, giving rise to false conceptualizations; therefore, they are rebuked as having fallen into the four kinds of externalist paths.

Within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which is characterized by arising and ceasing, eight meanings are distinguished. "Separate views" refers to divergent perspectives, namely the constant transformation of arising and ceasing, and the increase or decrease of existence and non-existence.
In the response, six of these meanings are briefly cited; [the opponents] are unable to determine the underlying principle, remaining merely between two pillars.
He answered in such a way that the interlocutor could find no logical meaning within the phrases; "mutually non-existent" means that things perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaya*).
Because they are non-existent, one cannot attain realization, which implies that all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-existent. "Each and every thing exists" means that things arise moment by moment.
When he did not say "exists" but rather "is," it was because he considered that each phenomenon possesses its own nature, responding thus according to the question asked.
"None are not thus. He answered in this way. As for "branches": it is like a single tree trunk that divides into two branches;
from two they go to four, and within the preceding eight, there is the differentiation of existence and non-existence. Existence is precisely non-existence, just as ice is water.
Non-existence is not something other than existence, just as water is not something other than ice. To see that which arises and suddenly ceases, and having ceased...
Regarding "non-arising": therefore, to calculate that existence is itself non-existence, or that non-existence is not existence, is incorrect. Question:

The first case involves presenting eight meanings simultaneously, which may be called "evasive confusion" (*vibhrama*). Why is the second case—calculating existence and non-existence individually yet answering with a single word—also called "evasive confusion"?
Answer: To cling to things while failing to accord with principle is "evasiveness" (*vibhrama*); to lack a central, correct standard is "confusion" (*moha*). Now...

Observing the first and fourth [types of speech], their words are both ambiguous; they involve much confused intent and ultimately do not accord with principle, while also being characterized by pretension.
The third and fourth [types] have words that are exclusively one-sided; they involve much pretentious intent and ultimately do not maintain correctness, converging equally upon confusion.
Therefore, they are collectively termed "pretentious confusion" (*kuṭila-vyākarana*). "Vastness" (*śūnyatā*) refers to that which is false and unreal.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi*, their minds are firm, concentrated, and upright, so that Māras find no opportunity.

They exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings and contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Those who harbor speculative calculations regarding this inexhaustible flow fall into the view that there is a "sign" (*nimitta*) after death;
their resolve becomes inverted. Some fixate upon their own bodies, claiming that "form is the self," while others perceive a pervasive "self" within their own roundness.
Pervading the entire realm, one thinks, "I have form," or, as that prior object-condition follows my movements, one thinks, "Form belongs to me";
or again, as the self continues within the succession of formations, one thinks, "I am in form. All such conceptualizations claim that there is a mark after death.

Thus it revolves in a cycle, possessing sixteen characteristics. From this, one may calculate that affliction and enlightenment are ultimately two distinct natures that proceed side by side, never touching one another.
Based on such speculative reckoning, because one asserts the existence of a self after death, one falls into the ranks of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).

This deludes the nature of Bodhi. This is called the sixth heterodox school, which establishes that within the five aggregates there is a "sign of existence after death," a theory of inverted mind, and an inexhaustible flow—this refers precisely to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Because they reckon it to be inexhaustible, they reckon that there is a sign of existence after death. True awakening [is otherwise].
There is no arising. To fully understand that arising itself entails cessation, one sees that even before birth it is empty and signless;

how much more so after death? How could one falsely reckon it as having signs? These latter five types, along with the aforementioned "evasive equivocation regarding non-death," both arise from views concerning existence and non-existence.
However, the four types of evasive equivocation are merely false views; these four are ultimately wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The four "or" characters represent four types of calculation. Regarding "solidifying the self": this refers to firmly maintaining and nurturing [the body].
As for saying "form is the self," the first calculation holds that the self and form are one; the essence of the self is pervasive and complete, and form belongs to me.

The second calculation holds that the self is large and form is small, with form residing within the self. "The former object" refers to the forms currently before one's eyes. "Returning and reversing" refers to the movement...
[This refers to] the usage [of the term]. First, the preceding conditions follow me; thus one thinks, "Form belongs to me. Second, one calculates that the self and form are distinct.

Third, as the formations continue, there is the single [notion of] form; the self resides within these formations, and thus one says, "I am in form. Fourth, one calculates that form is large and the self is small, such that the self is contained within form.
This is because one infers the existence of death in the future from the existence of birth in the present. Therefore...

It is said that there are characteristics after death. This is true for the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); it is likewise so for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Therefore, these are called the "sixteen characteristics.

As for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it is not mentioned because the aggregate of formations has not yet been destroyed, and thus consciousness does not manifest before one's mind.

Because one calculates that the aggregates and the self exist after death, one further calculates that afflictions (*kleśa*) and awakening (*bodhi*) both exist subsequently; thus, defilement and purity proceed side by side.

They mutually invade and extinguish one another. To reckon the various aggregates (*skandha*) as afflictions (*kleśa*) and to reckon the essence of the self (*ātman*) as bodhi—since both dharmas coexist, it is said that "the two natures drive side by side.
As for the term "five aggregates," it generally refers to the five aggregates in their entirety.

Furthermore, among the sons of good family within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, such that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.
They contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source. Among those who, having previously eliminated form, sensation, and perception, give rise to conceptual calculations:
This person falls into the signless state after death. Their resolve becomes inverted; they perceive the cessation of form and see that the physical shape has no cause.

They contemplate the cessation of perception and see that the mind has no attachments. They know that sensation has ceased and there is no further connection. The nature of the aggregates (skandhas) dissolves and disperses.
Even if there were the faculty of life, in the absence of sensation and perception, one would be identical to grass and trees;

since this physical substance cannot even be apprehended while present before us, how could various characteristics possibly exist after death? By investigating and examining it in this way, one finds that characteristics do not exist after death. Thus, the cycle continues.
There are eight kinds of signlessness. From this, some may reckon that the causes and effects of nirvana are entirely empty, existing merely as names, and ultimately subject to total annihilation.
Because they thus speculate that there is nothing after death, they fall into the ways of the external paths and become deluded regarding the nature of bodhi.
This is called the seventh heterodox school’s doctrine of the "signless state after death" established within the five aggregates; it is a theory of inverted mind.

This stands in direct opposition to the previous calculation [of permanence], as it transforms existence into non-existence. It observes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) which has not yet ceased.
Seeing that these three [aggregates] are inexhaustible, one then infers that the preceding three, along with all phenomena, must likewise be inexhaustible.

Having observed that the preceding three have already ceased, one sees them as being without marks (*animitta*); consequently, one infers that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and all phenomena must likewise be without marks.
Since form exists because of matter, when matter ceases, form has nothing upon which to depend. Since the mind is bound by perception (*saṃjñā*), when perception ceases, [the mind...]
The mind has no attachments. Where there is feeling (*vedanā*), it binds and sustains form and mind; therefore, where there is no feeling, there is no connection.

Once the three aggregates (*skandhas*) have dissolved, even if the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra*) remains, it too returns to cessation. The principle of arising is the aggregate of formations. This is explained in terms of the four aggregates.
The present cause perishes; the future fruit ceases. When cause and effect are discussed together, they constitute the eight marks of non-characteristic (*aṣṭānimitta*).
They exist yet are empty; fundamentally, they are unborn from the beginning. Before and after are of one limit; this is the Buddha’s true teaching.

That what existed before is now absent, and that what exists now will be absent later—this is the inverted calculation of arising and ceasing. Based on the preceding three, one should practice so that the aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise extinguished.

[The opponent replies: "No. This [argument] applies to all dharmas alike. The cause and effect of Nirvana are cultivated based on the present aggregates (*skandhas*) and realized through the subsequent aggregates.

Since the aggregates are ultimately unfathomable, how can there be cultivation or realization? [The Master replies: "Those who delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi do so because they fail to realize that the nature of Bodhi does not establish even a single speck of dust, nor does it discard a single dharma.
It is the wondrous existence of true emptiness, for it is neither annihilation nor extinction."

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized and concentrated their right minds, such that Māras find no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

They contemplate that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source; while abiding in the midst of mental formations (*saṃskāra*), they simultaneously suppress sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), dualistically calculating both existence and non-existence.
Their own essential nature is undermined. These people fall into the view that after death there is neither existence nor non-existence, giving rise to inverted doctrines.

Within form, sensation, and perception, they see both existence and non-existence; within the flux of formations, they observe both non-existence and not-non-existence. Thus they cycle through them, exhausting the eight characteristics of "neither" regarding the aggregates and elements.
Encountering any single condition, they all claim that after death there is either a mark or no mark. Furthermore, they calculate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
