Because their natures have undergone transformation and distortion, their minds give rise to a superficial awakening. They hold that both existence and non-existence are not applicable, and they lose their bearings regarding the void and the real.

Based on such conceptualizations, they conclude that after death one is neither existent nor non-existent; being muddled regarding the future limit because there is nothing further to be said, they fall into the ranks of external paths and become deluded about the nature of Bodhi.

This is called the eighth heterodox doctrine established among the five aggregates: the "neither-existence-nor-non-existence after death" theory of inverted mind. Regarding those who perceive existence within the formations (*saṃskāra*):
they see that the aggregate of formations has not yet ceased, and its domain remains intact. Regarding those who perceive the extinction of sensation and perception (*vedanā* and *saṃjñā*):

they see that the preceding three [aggregates] have already ceased, and their substance and characteristics are entirely empty. Regarding those who dualistically calculate both existence and non-existence: they calculate [existence] regarding what persists...
There is. To conceive of cessation as non-existent is to fall into error. As for the mutual subversion of intrinsic natures:

one uses the existence of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) to refute the non-existence of the preceding three aggregates, and uses the non-existence of the preceding three aggregates to refute the existence of the aggregate of formations.

To fall into "neither" is to refute non-existence and thereby find it is not non-existent, and to refute existence and thereby find it is not existent. Although the three aggregates of form, feeling, and perception were previously existent, yet...
Now, because they have been broken and exhausted, it is said that they "are not existent. The same principle applies to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

While the four [aggregates] are non-existent, the *saṃskāra-skandha*—as exemplified previously—is non-existent; yet, as it presently flows and shifts from moment to moment, it is also not non-existent.

Since the *saṃskāra-skandha* is not non-existent, the same applies to the preceding three; thus, the four are not non-existent. By cycling through these four aggregates and exhausting them, one establishes the eight characteristics of "neither existence nor non-existence."
"Whichever single condition is encountered": in each of the aggregates (*skandha*), one calculates these two as "neither. "All formations" (*saṃskāra*) refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Above, one merely contemplates both the already-extinguished and the not-yet-extinguished four aggregates, while correctly calculating eight negations (*apratiṣedha*).

Here, it is further transformed so that one calculates that there is no phenomenon whatsoever that is not subject to this dual negation. Regarding "the shifting and erroneous nature": the existence or non-existence after death mutually sublate one another.
It is a deprivation. One whose mind gives rise to penetrating enlightenment merely expands their own false views and misconceptions.

Regarding "neither void nor real": because it is not non-existent, one cannot say it is void; because it is not existent, one cannot say it is real. Regarding "after death, neither [existent nor non-existent]":
taking the state of being alive as an analogy for after death—the latter limit, that is, after death, extending to the end of the future—[one falls into] darkness.
"Obscure" (*mèng*) means profound darkness; there is nothing that can be spoken of. To say it "exists" is not to say it exists; to say it "does not exist" is not to say it does not exist.
Being neither conscious nor aware, how can it be described? Having not yet attained true knowledge and clear vision, I have merely conjectured and approximated to compose this treatise.
If one were truly to realize the Truth (*satyadarśana*), then whether speaking of existence or non-existence, all would constitute a sublime discourse.

Furthermore, among those good sons within samādhi who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, so that Māra finds no opportunity, they exhaustively investigate the root of all living beings.

Observing that profound, pure, yet eternally agitated source, if they subsequently engage in speculative calculations regarding non-arising, such a person falls into the seven theories of annihilationism.
They may speculate that the body is annihilated, or that desire is annihilated, or that suffering is annihilated, or that ultimate bliss is annihilated.

Or there is the extreme of cessation through relinquishment. Thus, by cycling through these stages until the seven limits are exhausted, they are extinguished before one's eyes; once extinguished, nothing remains.
Based on this calculation, they conclude that after death there is annihilation, thereby falling into the ranks of the non-Buddhists and deluding their nature of Bodhi.
This is called the ninth heterodox doctrine: the inverted theory of mind established within the five aggregates that asserts annihilation after death.
When one observes that the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) perishes moment by moment, this is termed "non-existence in successive succession.
Based on this, they falsely calculate that even if one is born into the seven stations of humans and gods, all will subsequently be cut off and cease.

The difference between this and the seventh [view], "non-existence after death," is that the latter calculates that because there is no self in the present, there is likewise none after death; whereas this [view] merely calculates that there is non-existence through annihilation after death. As for the body...

The two realms of humans and devas in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) constitute one limit; the exhaustion of desire constitutes the first dhyāna; the exhaustion of suffering constitutes the second dhyāna; supreme bliss constitutes the third dhyāna;
and supreme equanimity constitutes the fourth dhyāna and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are called the seven limits. As for "extinguishing before one's eyes":
"Pointing to the extinction of the cause" refers to the cessation of the cause. "Having ceased, there is no further arising" refers to the cessation of the fruit.
"To be deluded regarding the nature of bodhi" means that the nature of bodhi is eternally abiding and does not perish.
Furthermore, among those good sons within *samādhi* who have stabilized their minds in right concentration, the Māras find no opportunity.

They investigate the fundamental source of all living beings, observing that profound, pure, and eternally agitated origin. If, subsequently, they harbor conceptual calculations regarding rebirth, such persons fall into the "Five Theories of Nirvāṇa.
Alternatively, taking the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) as the true basis for transformation, they perceive its perfect luminosity and consequently give rise to attachment and longing for it.
Either because the nature of the first dhyāna is free from sorrow; or because the mind in the second dhyāna is free from suffering;

or because the third dhyāna is accompanied by extreme joy; or because in the fourth dhyāna both suffering and pleasure have perished, and thus one does not undergo the nature of saṃsāric birth and death.
Deluded regarding the heavens of outflows, they take them to be unconditioned. Regarding these five abodes as secure and peaceful, they regard them as a supreme, pure refuge.

Thus circling through these five abodes until their ultimate end, they calculate from this that there is nirvana in the five realms. Consequently, they fall into the ways of external paths and become confused about the nature of Bodhi.
This is called the tenth heterodox school. It establishes the inverted doctrine that within the five aggregates there is nirvana in the present moment.

Because the activity-aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) ceases and then arises again, they speak of "successive existences. The former [school] gave rise to its calculations regarding the point where the activity-aggregate ceases moment by moment;

this [school] gives rise to its calculations regarding the point where the activity-aggregate arises moment by moment. This is because they perceive the activity-aggregate as succeeding moments of mutual succession.
Continued: "Newly and newly there is existence," meaning that because there must be a real fruit [of action], it certainly does not perish into non-existence.
This differs from the sixth view regarding existence after death; for the latter calculates that because there is present existence, there is also existence after death.
This [view] calculates that the present itself is *nirvāṇa*. The term "or" (*huò*) is an indefinite expression used according to their respective perspectives.

It is not that a single person falsely discriminates all five locations. As for "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): it is the transformation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and taking recourse in nirvāṇa.
Because one perceives the perfect clarity [of the higher realms] and gives rise to attachment and longing, this is the cause of false discrimination.

Indeed, because there is neither sorrow nor suffering, and both joy and compliance have vanished, this very false discrimination is itself the correct transformation of the basis. One sees the impurity of the lower realms.
Being turbid, they instead reckon five locations to be supremely pure; these are called the "five present nirvāṇas.

Because they experience pleasure in the present life and do not wait for a future birth, they fail to realize that all of these belong to the outflows (*sāsrava*), are not the fruit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and are not the ultimate state.
Those who delude themselves regarding the nature of Bodhi [do so] because they consider Bodhi and Nirvāṇa to still be far distant.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of deluded realizations in dhyāna all arise because the mind is applied in a state of mutual conflict within the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

Thus, these awakenings manifest. Sentient beings are stubborn and deluded; they do not reflect upon themselves. When they encounter these manifestations before them, they mistake their confusion for realization and claim to have attained the state of a sage.
Having committed this great falsehood, they fall into the Avīci Hell. You must take the words of the Tathāgata as your standard regarding me...

After my parinirvāṇa, transmit and reveal this to the age of the Dharma’s decay, causing all sentient beings everywhere to awaken to and understand this meaning. Do not allow mental demons to give rise to deep afflictions within them;
maintain and protect them, quelling their false views. Teach them so that their bodies and minds may awaken to the true meaning, ensuring they do not encounter divergent paths on the Unsurpassed Way.
Do not let them pray for the heart's desires and consider a small attainment sufficient; rather, become great awakened kings of purity.
The pointing finger:
previously it was said that when *dhyāna* manifests its objects, it is the celestial māras who wait for such an opportunity;

here it is said that when *dhyāna* produces deluded understandings, it is the mental māras that give rise to deep calamities. Whenever one’s realization of the Way is not true, and one follows many divergent paths with false calculations, all of these are instances of madness.

Explanation: This is called the "demon of the mind. These ten types of deluded interpretations all mistakenly take the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) to be the wondrous true *tathatā* (suchness).
Therefore, these divergent views arise. The first, the theory of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*), mistakenly identifies the subtle, brilliant awareness as being neither caused nor conditioned.
The second, third, and fourth—the theories of omnipresence, permanence, and partial permanence—mistakenly identify the profound stillness as eternally abiding.
Furthermore, the fourth extreme, the doctrine of the finite and infinite, mistakenly identifies the pure and fundamental nature as being all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
Regarding the latter six types: the seventh, that there is nothing after death, and the ninth, annihilationism, mistakenly identify the empty Tathāgatagarbha.
The sixth, that there is something after death, and the tenth... [text continues]
To manifest *nirvāṇa* while erroneously identifying it with the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the fifth form of evasive sophistry (*kuhakavāda*).
To erroneously identify the *tathāgatagarbha*—which is free from all marks—as being identical to all phenomena is the eighth, the doctrine of "neither [existence nor non-existence] after death.

As for the "demon of the mind" (*cittamāra*), because the perverted views of the mind are themselves the demon, they constitute a profound calamity; "calamity" (*niyāna*) refers to a portentous evil, which is precisely the demon.

"Calamity. "Branching and diverging" refers to these ten kinds [of views], which are like the branches of a tree rather than its root, or like the forked paths of a road rather than the main thoroughfare.
"Mental seeking" refers to that which the mind pursues. Encountering these branching paths, one falls into external paths (*tīrthika*);
being satisfied with a mere fragment, one falls into the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*). "Pointing finger" is like a finger pointing at the moon.

Ānanda, when those sons of good family practice *samādhi* and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the various natures of the world—those subtle, pure, and turbulent movements that constitute the generative force of commonality—suddenly shatter.
The deep-seated cords and knots, as well as the profound channels through which the *pudgala* repays its karma, are severed; the resonance between cause and effect is suspended.
One is on the verge of awakening to the great radiance of the heaven of *nirvāṇa*, like the crowing of a rooster at dawn, looking back and forth.

In the east, there is already a refined radiance. The six sense faculties are empty and still, no longer wandering or scattering. Internally and externally, all is limpid and bright; one enters that which has no place of entry.

One deeply penetrates the fundamental source of life for the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions. Observing the source through its manifestations, the various classes can no longer summon [the mind].
Having attained identity with the realms of the ten directions, the refined radiance does not sink, but reveals what is hidden and secret. This is...

This is called the realm of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). If, within the collective assembly [of the faculties], one has attained integration and the six gates have been refined away through their harmonious opening and closing, such that seeing and hearing communicate with one another and their mutual functions are purified;

and if the ten directions of the world, as well as one's own body and mind, are like *vaiḍūrya* crystal, transparent and clear both inside and out—this is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness. Such a person is then able to transcend the turbidity of life. Observe this...
The source of this is the formless void and inverted delusive thoughts, which serve as its foundation.
When the nature of action is agitated, it becomes the pivotal axis for the generative impulses of the homogeneous class and the profound conduit for the retribution of karma.
*Pudgala*. This is translated as "one who repeatedly takes on various destinies," meaning that one repeatedly undergoes birth by taking up various realms of existence.
The reason for undergoing birth is to repay past karma; yet, because the underlying connections are deep and hidden, this is what is induced by the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).

"Suspension" refers to the cessation of the causal chain of *paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa* (birth and death in discrete segments), whereby the cause perishes and the fruit ceases. The nature of *nirvāṇa* is the celestial realm, which is [unaffected] by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Obscured, it is as dark as a long night. When the preceding three *skandhas* are exhausted, it is like the first crowing of a rooster;

though it is a sign of dawn, one still remains submerged in the two remaining *skandhas*, and the subtle colors have not yet been distinguished. When this *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, it is like the rooster’s subsequent crowing;

only one *skandha* remains. Thus it is said that one is about to awaken through the Great Illumination. The internal faculties and external objects are transformed into a realm of profound clarity; within, the subject is no longer perceived.
The root of entry: outwardly, one does not see the objects (dharmas) into which one enters. The primary source from which life is received is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
Now, observing that this aggregate of consciousness is the primary source from which the various classes of beings arise, one does not give rise to afflictions nor create new karma.

By maintaining this state, one prevents [the mind] from proceeding toward the fruits [of rebirth]; since there is no longer any portion for taking birth, it is said that "the various classes do not summon" [one], and thus one ultimately comprehends the ten directions.

The environment and its inhabitants are both transformations of consciousness; they share the same single substance of consciousness. Therefore, it is said that one has already attained their identity.

Although the pure radiance of the celestial nature (*dharmadhātu*) is not yet fully clear and penetrating, its subtle and secret characteristics have already begun to manifest. This is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) has not yet been exhausted.

It is profoundly serene yet subtly agitated, corresponding to the shadows of coarse and heavy sensory objects. Previously, the six consciousnesses were extinguished; now, this [seventh] consciousness is extinguished.
"Seven consciousnesses. The phrases "the same portion gives rise to the mechanism of life" correspond to "corresponding with the basis for the simultaneous arising of seeing.

Previously, one could not break through the inability to see; now, for the first time, it is broken. The two phrases "internally and externally serene and luminous" correspond to "the nature enters the primordial clarity.
Previously, there was the shimmering original nature; now, it is transformed into clear water. The phrases "profoundly penetrating the ten directions," and so forth, correspond to...
One perceives the correspondence with the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions;

whereas previously one could see them but could not penetrate their underlying causes, now the primary source of their life-force can be observed and grasped. Within this collective summons, it is precisely the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), the life-source of the twelve classes.
If, within this state, one uses the power of concentration and wisdom to dissolve and refine the six sense-gates, it will be like ice [melting].
Once [the obstructions] have been dissolved, there is no longer any material resistance; once the mirror has been polished, it is free from the category of defilement.

This causes the sense organs to merge without division and the realms to open without separation. Thus, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are like neighboring houses communicating with one another, such that they may be used interchangeably.
Furthermore, the body and mind within the world are no longer subject to obstruction; this is the sign that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been exhausted.
*Vaiḍūrya* is the name of a jewel; it is blue in color and solid in substance. Swords cannot destroy it, and fire cannot melt it;
only spirits possessing supernatural powers can fashion it into vessels. It is also said to be the egg of the *garuḍa*; it is pure, crystalline, and transparently clear. Therefore...

Taking this as a metaphor: the turbidity of life arises dependent upon consciousness; when consciousness is exhausted, one transcends it. Consciousness is but a shadowy manifestation of deluded awareness;
it has no inherent substance from the beginning. Arising from inversion, it is therefore called "phantom-like, void, and false conceptualization."

Ānanda, you should know that these good men have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned formations and returned to the source within consciousness. Having already extinguished birth and death, they have not yet perfected the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction.
They are able to cause their own physical faculties to either remain separated or merge and open, and they can communicate with all classes of beings throughout the ten directions.

Their awareness penetrates everywhere, enabling them to enter the perfect source. If, regarding this place of return, they establish it as the cause of true permanence, [they will attain the stage of the "Light of Wisdom"].
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment to causes and their underlying conditions. They become companions to Śābikāra and his followers who seek the dark realm;
they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the first instance of establishing a mind that clings to attainment.
This constitutes the fruit of one’s ultimate refuge; yet it remains far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of external paths.

When one exhausts all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to find them empty, one clearly perceives that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is empty. These formations leap forth from the ocean of consciousness (*vijñānasamudra*) and undergo successive births;

when their characteristics vanish and they sink back into the ocean of consciousness, this is called "returning to the source. Once the aggregate of formations is emptied, birth has already been extinguished.
It is extinguished; yet it still relies upon the source of consciousness, meaning that this quiescent extinction is not yet perfected.
Quiescent extinction is the wondrous nature of True Suchness, the Tathāgatagarbha; the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is the source of the clarity of seeing.

Thus, the Ālaya-vijñāna is already close to the wondrous nature of True Suchness, but because there remain two kinds of deluded vision—the identical and the distinct—it is said to be "not yet perfected. It does not carry even a hair’s breadth [of further obscuration].
That which arises and ceases is called "subtle" (*jing*). That which remains as a single flavor of quiescent permanence is called "wondrous" (*miao*). This state is not yet perfected;
it is because the *vijñāna-skandha* has not been shattered, and one is still obscured by it. Thus, it appears to be unitary and constant, yet it is neither truly subtle nor wondrous.

As for the roots being separated or joined, and their merging into one, this refers to the dissolution of the six sense bases into a single unity. Regarding the universal awareness shared by all classes of beings, "I" and "sentient beings" are of one and the same awakened nature, like [the light of] a thousand...
The lamp and the chamber share a single space; their light interpenetrates without duality. "Perfect Origin" (*yuan-yuan*) refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
"Perfect" (*yuan*) signifies that all categories are universally contained within it, while "Origin" (*yuan*) indicates that the myriad transformations take their initial footing therein.

For one who can enter this state, the four aggregates are completely dissolved, and they find their ultimate resting place here—just as when the waves have ceased, they subside back into the ocean. These are the extraordinary signs within this meditative concentration; its functional power is temporary.

It is so. If one regards this as truly permanent and establishes it as the cause, capable of producing all things as the ultimate state, then one falls into the attachment to causes and their underlying causes.
For a true cause is not an object; whatever exists as an object is delusory.

The non-Buddhists establish twenty-five principles (*tattvas*), reckoning the *pradhāna* (the primal principle) to be eternal and capable of giving rise to all phenomena; this is precisely the same calculation as the aforementioned view.
Because there is something obtained through causes and something to which results return, both cause and result fall into what is falsely imagined.

Therefore, one contravenes perfect penetration, loses the mind of the causal stage, turns one's back on nirvana, and forfeits the realization of the resultant stage. As previously stated, the arousal of the mind at the causal stage must correspond in name and substance to the state of fruition;
yet now, by establishing a mind that seeks attainment, one does not act according to the principle of non-arising.

The nature of extinction serves as the causal mind of the ground; therefore, the fruit realized is also in correspondence with a false cause, rather than being the fruit of permanence, non-arising, and non-extinction.
Originally, the realization of the fruit was intended as the ground of ultimate repose, wherein both seeds and manifestations are severed.
Now, conversely, one gives rise to the seeds of external paths; not only is the fruit not a true fruit, but furthermore, this false fruit becomes a false cause.
This is what is meant by: "If the ground is not true, the fruit will result in deviation."
Ānanda, furthermore, there may be a son of good family who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death;

yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation (*śamatha*), he has not yet perfected it. If, with respect to that which is the refuge, he perceives it as his own self-substance and develops a resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) that all sentient beings within the twelve categories throughout the entirety of space are but a single class flowing forth from within his own body—this person then falls into the error of "the subject and its object" (*neng-fen*).
The subject-grasping [faculty]: Maheśvara manifests an infinite body and becomes its companion. Thus they become deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision.
This is called the second [stage of] establishing the subject as the mind, whereby the fruit of the subject's activity is accomplished.
It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of the Greatly Arrogant Heaven, where the self is pervasive and complete.
Regarding the "clinging to capacity": this clinging takes the source-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its own essence and regards it as flowing forth from itself to produce all sentient beings.
Consequently, one clings to the notion that "I" can produce them, yet in reality, this is not possible; hence, it is called "clinging to capacity where there is no capacity."
Maheśvara is the celestial king Māra at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*).

He falsely conceives that he can manifest as immeasurable sentient beings, as well as those who are neither sentient nor insentient; he conceives that he can be the mind, the activity, and the fruit, and he calculates that he can serve as their basis.

It is capable of accomplishing those matters. As for the "Greatly Arrogant Deva," this refers to Maheśvara; because he cannot achieve what he considers himself capable of, he is named "Greatly Arrogant.

Regarding "pervasive and complete," this is the calculation that the essence of the self is perfectly round and pervasive throughout the realm of space. This is an erroneous recognition that the ten directions are merely consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), and that immeasurable Tathāgatas flow forth from the nature of consciousness.

Furthermore, a good man may have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.

If, in his place of refuge, he takes something as an object of reliance, he may suspect that his own body and mind flow forth from that source, and that the empty space of the ten directions all arises from it.
Consequently, regarding that ground from which everything issues forth, he conceives of it as a truly eternal body, free from arising and ceasing.
Within the midst of arising and ceasing, they prematurely calculate eternal permanence; thus they are deluded regarding non-arising and likewise confused about arising and ceasing.

Dwelling securely in this infatuation, those who give rise to such a resolute conviction fall into the attachment to permanence and non-permanence, reckoning the Lord of Sovereignty (*Īśvara*) as their companion.
Deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi and having lost their true knowledge and vision, this is called the third: establishing causes based on the mind to produce falsely conceptualized fruits.
This violates and distances one from perfect penetration, turns one's back on the city of nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted perfection.
Taking the fundamental source of consciousness as its point of return, one suspects that it is capable of producing both oneself and all phenomena;

consequently, one calculates that the place from which they arise and flow forth is the true, eternal, and unborn essence. This, along with the aforementioned attachments, all arises from consciousness.
Yet their calculations differ. The former maintains that consciousness itself is the self (*ātman*) capable of producing all phenomena; the latter maintains that the self arises from consciousness.

The former regards it as truly eternal, existing amidst arising and ceasing while falsely calculating it to be permanently abiding. Thus, they are both deluded regarding the nature of true non-arising and confused about the presently manifesting phenomena of arising and ceasing.
Taking what is impermanent to be permanent is called the "grasping at the permanent in the impermanent. They calculate thus...
To claim that the self can produce [all things] is identical to the calculation that Maheśvara can produce all things.

Because one relies on the source of consciousness and falsely calculates it to be permanent, it is said that "the cause is established based on the mind, thereby accomplishing the falsely calculated effect. This refers to the prior calculation that the self is omnipresent and produces all phenomena.
This calculation that the "I" is fully encompassed by that [body] is called "reaching fullness.
This is the erroneous recognition that the physical body, extending outward to the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, are all objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.

Furthermore, there is a good son who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.

Because his knowledge of what is known is all-pervasive and complete, he establishes a view based on that knowledge, such that he regards all grasses and trees throughout the ten directions as sentient beings.
They are no different from others. Grasses and trees become humans; when humans die, they again become grasses and trees of the ten directions.

Those who give rise to a resolute conviction that there is no distinction between them and universal knowledge fall into the attachment of knowing what is unknowable. This is the Pāṭha-Śāṇi attachment to all-encompassing awakening.

They become its companions, deluding themselves regarding Buddha-enlightenment and losing their true knowledge and vision. This is called the fourth calculation: the mind that considers itself perfectly enlightened.
It produces the fruit of false error, strays far from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of inverted knowledge.

That which is known is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) as it manifests. This means that consciousness possesses the capacity for knowing, and all phenomena arise through the transformation of this knowing.

Because they calculate that the essence of knowing is pervasive throughout all phenomena, they subsequently establish divergent interpretations, asserting that even insentient things are everywhere possessed of knowing.
Without making any distinctions, taking ignorance to be knowledge is called the "attachment to the knowledge of ignorance.
Bāṣpa and Śaṇi are the names of two non-Buddhist teachers who maintain that all things are conscious, asserting that everything possesses cognition.
To falsely calculate perfect knowledge as the causal mind is a delusion regarding the result. Taking ignorance to be knowledge is termed "inverted knowledge. Question: Regarding the myriad dharmas...
"Vijñapti-mātra (consciousness-only) is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching. Why, then, do all [of you] here fall back into external seeds? Answer:

"In our internal teaching, the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only, arising through conditions and transformations like dreams or illusions; they are not truly produced. Therefore, one does not establish [the duality of] knowing and seeing, nor does one give rise to attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).
Yet now you say: 'one establishes the mind that is attained,' 'one establishes the mind that is the causal support,' and 'one establishes the mind that acts as the agent.'"
All these are instances of establishing cognition upon what is already known and seen; therefore, they collectively fall into the ranks of the external paths.

This and the fifth [case] both mistakenly identify the appearances of the ephemeral sensory objects and the physical world as real transformations; one should instead contemplate that these are transformed into supreme enlightened awareness.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction is not yet perfected:
if he attains conformity within the mutual functioning of the perfectly interfused sense organs, he will then give rise to all-encompassing, perfect transformation.
They seek the radiance of fire, delight in the purity of water, cherish the circulation of wind, and contemplate the formation of dust;
each venerates their respective element as the fundamental cause from which all arises, establishing a view of eternal permanence. Such a person falls into the attachment to birth within the unborn.
The various Kāśyapas, along with the Brahmins, diligently exerted their minds and bodies, serving fire and venerating water in their quest to transcend birth and death.
They became each other’s companions, becoming lost to the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeiting true knowledge and vision. This is called the fifth [delusion]:

being attached to the veneration of external objects, the deluded mind follows after things. They establish false causes for their seeking and hope for false fruits; thus they remain far removed from perfect penetration and turn their backs on the city of Nirvana.

One who has been born into the lineage of transformation and whose aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted will dissolve and refine the six gates so that the various faculties function interchangeably. At present, this is not yet fully exhausted;

one merely attains compliance, such that according to the mind and following the intent, there is perfect fusion and transformation—like water emerging from the upper part of the body and fire emerging from the lower part, and so forth. First.
When the faculties temporarily attain transformation, one then calculates that all phenomena are capable of such transformation, thereby giving rise to superior fruits.
One claims that fire can manifest radiance, and so forth, up to the claim that atoms can accomplish the receptacle world.

Thus, through perverse seeking and perverse contemplation, one diligently honors and serves these [phenomena], grasping them as being able to produce eternally abiding fruits; yet in reality, they cannot. This is called "arising" (jāti).

Those who hold to the attachment to non-arising are the three Kāśyapas and their like among the various non-Buddhists. Having become deluded regarding the true mind, they seek hope from external objects;
thus both cause and effect are false, and they pervert the principle of transformation. They are called the "species of inverted transformation.
This refers to the mistaken identification of the seven elements as the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha.

Furthermore, a good man may have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.

If, within this perfect luminosity, he reckons the midst of clarity to be empty and regards the non-extinction of the manifold transformations as something to be eternally extinguished, taking that eternal extinction as his refuge, [he will fall into the error of the Unconsciousness Heaven].

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the attachment of taking refuge in that which offers no refuge. They become companions to the *śūnyatā* spirits among the gods of the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their true knowledge and vision. This is called the sixth stage: the Perfectly Empty Mindlessness.

This results in the fruit of emptiness and non-existence. It violates and distances one from perfect penetration and turns one’s back on the city of Nirvana, giving rise to the seeds of annihilationism.

To say that the nature of consciousness is perfectly luminous, yet to falsely calculate it as void and nothingness—"non" here means to destroy—to "destroy the myriad transformations" means to extinguish the heart-mind and extinguish wisdom so that not even a hair's breadth remains.
This eternal extinction of dependence is the Nirvana of the heterodox paths; it leads to...
They are eternally extinguished, yet they do not realize this is an error; this is called "clinging to that which has no refuge. *Śūnyatā* (舜若多) means "emptiness.
Those in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) who cling to nihilistic emptiness take a mind of total voidness as their causal state, thereby producing the fruit of a nihilistic cessation.
This is termed "generating the seed of annihilationism. It is a mistake to misidentify emptiness as being fundamentally non-existent along with the three realms of existence.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth and death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation has not yet reached full perfection: if he forms a resolute conviction that his body will remain eternally fixed within the perfect and constant, remaining as solid and perfect as the essence itself so as never to decay or pass away; This is called the "Samādhi of the Permanence of the Body" (*kāya-nityatva-samādhi*). Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, it is called a "perverse samādhi. Due to this perverse samādhi, he may dwell for eighty thousand great kalpas without passing away. However, because his fundamental nature is not yet liberated, he will eventually fall back into the cycle of birth and death. This is known as the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal" (*pāpa-vidyādhara-bhūmi*). Once he falls from this stage, he will be reborn among humans or devas. If he again encounters a Buddha and cultivates the Way, he may eventually attain liberation; otherwise, he will continue to wander through the realms of birth and death. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for sixty thousand great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for forty thousand great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for twenty thousand great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for ten thousand great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for five thousand great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for two thousand five hundred great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one thousand two hundred and fifty great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for six hundred and twenty-five great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for three hundred and twelve and a half great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one hundred and sixty-two and a half great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for eighty-one and a quarter great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for forty and a half great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for twenty-two and a quarter great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for eleven and a quarter great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for five and a half great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for two and a quarter great kalpas before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for half a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-quarter of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-eighth of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-sixteenth of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-thirty-second of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-sixty-fourth of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation. This is called the "Stage of the Wicked Immortal. Why? Because he perceives permanence where there is no permanence, he is called a "wicked immortal. If he does not encounter a Buddha, he may dwell for one-hundred-twenty-eighth of a great kalpa before falling back into birth and death. If he does encounter a Buddha, he may attain liberation.
Such a person falls into the attachment to "desire" and "non-desire. They become companions to those Āsuras who seek long life;
they lose sight of the Buddha’s Bodhi and forfeit their true knowledge and vision. This is called the seventh attachment: clinging to the source of life, establishing a cause for solidified delusion.
They head toward the long-lasting fruits of toil, distancing themselves from perfect penetration and turning their backs on the city of Nirvana, thus giving rise to the seeds of delusive extension.
Perfect constancy and essential fullness are both the source of consciousness.

Because this essential fullness and constancy do not decline or pass away, one who wishes to firmly preserve the illusory body and coexist with it is following the teaching of the dual cultivation of nature and life, wherein form and spirit are both made subtle.
To give rise to craving and attachment toward that which is not to be craved is called "clinging to craving as non-craving.

All the Ashtakas—namely, the Gods of Long Life—ultimately return to destruction; their efforts have been in vain. This is the erroneous identification of the six sense faculties as blissful, wondrous, and permanent.

The former is an attachment to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); this [latter] is associated with the eighth [consciousness], both being attachments to the ○ (the source). This fundamentally represents the totality of all phenomena.

"Gui" (Returning) signifies that the myriad transformations are contained within it; "Ming" (Clarity) signifies that its essence is transparent and luminous; "Chang" (Constancy) signifies that it is ultimately firm and solid.
Each of these relates to its respective original text, yet they are all equally pervasive throughout the ocean of consciousness; therefore, they are all termed "Perfect" (*yuan*).

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) appears to be unitary and constant, yet failing to realize that these appearances are not real, each falls into their respective perceptions and gives rise to divergent attachments.

Furthermore, a son of good family has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena and has already extinguished birth and death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of cessation, he has not yet perfected it.

Contemplating that life-force is mutually pervasive, he intentionally retains his involvement with worldly defilements, fearing they might be entirely consumed. Thus, at this juncture, he sits within a Lotus Palace.

They extensively acquire the seven treasures and amass many precious concubines, indulging their hearts to the limit. Those who give rise to such superior understanding fall into the attachment to "the real as unreal.
They become companions to the *Ṭakkirāja* demons, becoming deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and losing all true knowledge and vision.

This is called the eighth cause for giving rise to perverse thoughts, which establishes the fruit of blazing afflictions. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana, giving birth to the lineage of celestial demons.
Taking the consciousness-aggregate as the life-source of the twelve classes of beings, one now observes that the origins of each life’s destiny all [proceed from this].

Taking consciousness as primary, that "self" and others interact with one another. If the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is exhausted, the lives of all sentient beings are exhausted, and my life is also exhausted.
Who then can realize the true and eternal? Thus, while in meditative concentration, they transform various objects of desire in order to retain worldly defilements;
relying on such perverse thoughts, they seek to realize the true and eternal. This is called the attachment to the non-existent as being real. Takṣaka, this is the summit of desire itself.
Among the celestial classes, due to his perverse thoughts, he was reborn as a celestial Mara. Gradually, he perceived that sentient beings are of the same essence as himself;
wishing to emulate the Bodhisattvas in benefiting both self and others, he feared that if his afflictions were completely extinguished, he would immediately enter *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, he retained his delusions to sustain his rebirth, establishing a basis for saving sentient beings. He remains like Ānanda until not even a single being has reached completion.
The Buddha will never attain *nirvāṇa* here. While they share the same power of aspiration, the Bodhisattvas intentionally retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) without severing them.
How could this not be a vast expansion? It can be said that even a hair’s breadth of difference results in a gulf as wide as heaven and earth. This is an error:
to mistake all manifested transformations for being non-afflictive and to claim they are all in accord with the pure, wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, a good man who has exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death, yet whose subtle and wondrous state of cessation is not yet perfected, differentiates between the refined and the coarse within the clarity of life, and discriminates between the true and the false.
He regards cause and effect as mutually compensating, seeking only to evoke a spiritual response.

They turn their backs on the path of purity—namely, seeing suffering, abandoning its origin, realizing cessation, and cultivating the path—and having settled into cessation, they rest there, no longer advancing.
Those who give rise to such resolute conviction fall into the category of the śrāvakas of fixed nature; they become companions to those unlearned monks of overweening pride.
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and have lost their wisdom and insight. This is called the ninth stage of perfecting the essence.

This corresponds to the mind. It achieves the fruit of quiescent wandering, deviates from perfect penetration, turns its back on the city of Nirvana, and gives rise to the seeds of entanglement within emptiness.
Of the preceding eight, all have erroneously entered onto bypaths; these two merely bring rest at the illusory city. "Life and clarity" refers to consciousness.

Within the perfect clarity of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), a slight view suddenly arises. Because of this, one discriminates that suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are coarse and false, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are subtle and true.
Furthermore, one knows that the fruit of suffering recompenses the cause of the origin, and the fruit of cessation recompenses the cause of the path.
Thereupon, they perceive suffering and sever its origin, seeking only the Path and Cessation as their response;

having thus given rise to limited views, they turn their backs on the path of perfect fusion—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—and, being ignorant of the Sangha, they falsely cling to the Lesser Vehicle as the ultimate goal.

Furthermore, a good man may have exhausted the emptiness of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and already extinguished birth-and-death; yet, regarding the subtle and wondrous state of quiescent extinction, he has not yet perfected it.
If, within the perfectly interfused, pure, awakened clarity, he investigates its profound subtlety and establishes himself in *nirvāṇa* without proceeding further, [he will remain there].

Those who give rise to such resolute conviction will fall into the fixed nature of the pratyekabuddhas; they become companions of those solitary practitioners who do not turn their minds [toward enlightenment].
They are deluded regarding the Buddha’s Bodhi and lose their true knowledge and vision. This is called the tenth [delusion]: the mind that obstructs Perfect Enlightenment.

This constitutes the fruit of profound clarity. It is far removed from perfect penetration and turns its back on the city of Nirvana. "The arising of awakened perfection and clarity" refers to the non-transformative, perfect seed.
"Perfect fusion" (*yuanrong*) means that, as stated above, it enables one's own physical faculties to merge and open.

"Purity" means that the six sense-faculties are void and still, no longer wandering or dissipating. "Awakened clarity" means that the essential radiance does not sink, manifesting what is deep and secret.
This is the place where the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is pure, brilliant, and profoundly still without wavering.

If one considers this to be profound and subtle, and establishes it as a realized fruit, then one is merely among the ranks of those with fixed natures—the *pratyekabuddhas* (solitary realizers) and *arhats* (worthy ones). Their awakening is limited; they have only attained a partial resonance with true enlightenment.
They realize the perfect luminosity of consciousness-awakening, yet lack the wondrous function of compassionate transformation; therefore, they are called "untransformed seeds.
Ānanda, these ten kinds of *dhyāna* lead to madness midway through the path because they rely on delusion, giving rise to a sense of fulfillment within what is not yet fulfilled.
All of these arise from the interaction of the mind with the *vijñāna-skandha*; thus, this state occurs. Sentient beings are stubbornly ignorant.

Failing to examine themselves, they encounter these [visions] appearing before them; each, according to their own cherished habitual delusions of mind, comes to rest therein, regarding it as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace.
They claim for themselves that they have attained unsurpassed *bodhi*, thereby committing a great falsehood.
Those influenced by external paths and malevolent spirits will, when their karma is exhausted, fall into the Avīci Hell; Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas will fail to achieve further progress.
You all should maintain your resolve and uphold the Way of the Tathāgata, transmitting and revealing this Dharma-gate to the final age after my parinirvāṇa.
May all sentient beings universally awaken to and understand this meaning, so that they do not allow Māra to cause them to create their own ruin. May they be protected, comforted, and rescued;
may their evil conditions be extinguished, and may their bodies and minds enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, attaining fulfillment from the very beginning without encountering divergent paths.

In the interim, one becomes insane. In the former eight mental states (*manas*), there is much that is insufficient for producing realization. In the latter two mental states, there is much that relies on delusion.
The mind encompasses both the preceding and succeeding states; what it loves is its prior habituation—the beginningless *vāsanā*.

Now, when one takes the objective appearances within meditative concentration as real, one strikes at the root of that illness and triggers its chronic malady. Thus, one mistakenly takes the cause of joyful grasping to be the cessation [of suffering].

Ultimate realization is the final attainment. The first eight are collectively termed "external paths" (*bāhyamārga*) and "demonic obstacles" (*mārāntarāya*); alternatively, one may specifically designate the first seven as external paths and the eighth as demonic obstacles.
Since neither has severed their afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that they "fall into hell. The Two Vehicles differ from this, and thus it is said they "do not advance.

Collectively, these are termed the "demon of views" (*dṛṣṭimāra*). "View" is defined by its contravention of principle; the first eight contravene the True [Middle Way], while the middle two contravene the Principle.
The latter two contradict the Middle Way principle; they are collectively categorized as false views because the wisdom of the Two Vehicles is itself ignorance.
Such a Dharma-gate was realized by Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and as many as motes of dust throughout the past aeons, who, by relying upon this mind, attained enlightenment.
One attains the Unsurpassed Way. When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, your present sense faculties will function interchangeably.

From within this mutual functioning, you can enter the Bodhisattva’s adamantine stage of dry wisdom (*kanka-śu*). Your perfectly luminous and refined mind will manifest transformations therein, like a precious moon contained within pure lapis lazuli.
In this way, you transcend the ten stages of faith, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, and the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Mind. The Bodhisattva’s practice of the ten adamantine stages, the perfect clarity of equal enlightenment, enters the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous adornments;
having perfected bodhi, one returns to non-attainment.

The Dharma-gate of Discerning the Five Aggregates as Demons: Those who ride upon the vehicle of the Buddhas and open their minds by means of this, whenever they have not yet opened [their understanding] regarding any one of the aggregates, rely on this discernment;
thus they will not be deluded and shall be able to break through them. To mention "consciousness" alone is to exhaustively encompass all that follows and includes what precedes it.
That which is manifested and transformed within the perfectly luminous and essential mind is accomplished through pure *dhyāna*.

This illuminates and penetrates all stages. "Lapis lazuli" (vaidūrya) is a metaphor for the perfectly luminous, refined mind. "Containing the moon" is a metaphor for the transformative activity arising from within it.
Having transcended the forty-four minds and reached the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), the perfectly luminous transformation reaches its ultimate consummation.
The "Ocean of Sublime Adornments" is the ocean of fruition endowed with ten thousand virtues.
What was previously termed the "Path of Sublime Adornments through the Ten Thousand Practices of Śūraṅgama" is simply the path leading toward this [ocean].

Returning to non-attainment corresponds to that which will serve as the ultimate ground of refuge and peace. Indeed, the state of non-attainment is the true ground of refuge and peace. From the preceding...
The fifty kinds of false objects are all due to the grasping at existence. As for the Dharma-gate of the causal stage, it is shared by the thousand Buddhas;
therefore, one must first gradually exhaust the five aggregates in succession before it can be called the "causal mind.

As for the cultivation and realization of the fruition stage, there are differences in the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties and the thickness or thinness of one's habitual tendencies; each case is distinct.
First: The previous passage spoke of gradual cultivation from this point to establish the stages of the sages;

this refers to those of ordinary capacity who gradually dismantle ignorance—what is called "gradual perfection" (*yuan-jian*). Here, however, one transcends directly to the stage of Equal Enlightenment;

this refers to those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom who suddenly sever the ignorance of phenomenal marks and immediately realize unsurpassed *bodhi*—what is called "perfect perfection" (*yuan-yuan*).
Whether sudden or gradual, there is originally no fixed rule; however, the path upon which one first sets out must by no means be mistaken.
This is the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of the past Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who discerned subtle demonic affairs within the clarity of awareness.
When such demonic realms manifest before you, if you can recognize them, the defilements of the mind will be washed away, and you will not fall into false views.
The māra of the aggregates is extinguished; the celestial māras are shattered; powerful spirits and ghosts lose heart and flee; and goblins and specters no longer arise.
Until the attainment of bodhi, there shall be no lack of anything, and those of inferior capacity will advance. Their minds will not be confused regarding Great Nirvana.
As for the dull-witted sentient beings of the final age who do not yet recognize dhyāna and do not know how to preach the Dharma—
He delights in cultivating samādhi, yet you fear he may fall into heterodoxy. With single-minded devotion, exhort him to uphold my Buddha-uṣṇīṣa dhāraṇī mantra.
If he is not yet able to recite it, write it out and place it in his meditation hall, or carry it upon his person; then no māras whatsoever will be able to disturb him.

You should reverently honor the ultimate cultivation and advancement of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, their final instructions, and the summary of the five aggregates that distinguishes the origins of demons. Within *śamatha*, *vipaśyanā* refers to wisdom within concentration;
"analyzing with awakened clarity" means employing the observational wisdom of concentration and wisdom to analyze all demons.
This is to instruct those of later learning. That which harms meditative concentration is Māra; yet that which brings about Māra is truly due to the master of the five aggregates (*skandha*).
If the mind of this master is pure, then Māra will no longer appear. *Tī* (pronounced as in *chí*) means "to lose" or "to perish. This refers to the inferior *śrāvakas*.
Those who linger at the illusory city and do not hasten toward the Precious Place may advance by means of this [practice].

Since they do not separately cultivate the stages of dhyāna, it is said that they have not yet recognized *dhyāna*. Since they have not yet studied wisdom and skillful means, it is said that they do not know how to preach the Dharma.

If one does not practice both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) but delights only in the tranquility of dhyāna, when demonic realms manifest before them, who can distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox? One should therefore exhort them to maintain the recitation of mantras.
To settle them in correct understanding and guard against their deviant thoughts, they will not fall into the power of Māra;
this is the ultimate definitive teaching of all Tathāgatas and the final discourse spoken at the end of the world’s duration. Therefore, it is called "the final instructions."
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat. Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, he prostrated himself in reverent acceptance and memorized it without omission.

In the midst of the great assembly, he addressed the Buddha once more: "Regarding the five kinds of delusion within the characteristics of the five aggregates that the Buddha has described as being the fundamental root of thought—since we have not previously received such subtle and detailed elucidation from the Tathāgata, and furthermore, as for these five aggregates..."
"May they be extinguished. May they be exhausted in succession. Thus, through these five stages, to what realm do they go?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will manifest great compassion, purifying the eyes and minds of this great assembly, and acting as the future eye for all sentient beings of the末代 (final age)."

The World-Honored One has always taught that the five aggregates arise based on causes and conditions, yet he has never stated that the five aggregates all fundamentally arise from deluded thought—as in the passage where "form" is defined as "solidified deluded thought," and so forth.
[The interlocutor] first asks why these five aggregates are collectively termed "deluded thought.

Furthermore, these two sentences inquire into the sudden and gradual methods of severing and eliminating [delusion]; the phrase "simultaneously dissolving them" refers to the meaning of the sudden method. Next...
This is the gradual intention. These two phrases exhaustively inquire into the ultimate limit.
One observes that the five aggregates and demonic influences all arise at the juncture where each aggregate is about to end and has not yet ended; this is what is called the "limit.
We pray that the Buddha will reveal these three meanings to us, so that our minds and eyes may become clear and bright, enabling us to serve as the true eye for the final age.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "This essential, true, wondrous, and luminous original enlightenment is perfectly pure. It does not harbor birth and death, nor any defilements, even down to empty space;
all these arise from the production of false conceptualization. This is fundamentally the wondrous, luminous, and true essence of original enlightenment."
They falsely give rise to the various vessel-worlds, like Yanjadatta who, being deluded, mistook his own head for a reflection.

This falsity has no original cause; yet within this state of false conceptualization, they establish the nature of causes and conditions. Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call it "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).

That very nature of space is itself produced from a phantom; thus, both causes and conditions and spontaneity are merely the conceptual constructions of the deluded minds of sentient beings. Ānanda, know this as falsity.

Regarding that which arises, I have explained the false causes and conditions. If the falsehood is fundamentally non-existent, then the false causes and conditions are fundamentally non-existent as well;

how much more so for those who, out of ignorance, speculate that it is produced spontaneously? Therefore, the Tathāgata has revealed to you that the original cause of the five aggregates is likewise nothing but false imagination.

This sutra generally clarifies the arising of delusion. First, it establishes its foundation by designating the non-delusory reality; this fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the essence of origination.

This essence is not mixed with conditioned phenomena, thus it is called "subtle" (*praṇīta*); it does not involve any delusions, thus it is called "real" (*tattva*); it is understood to be without form or obstruction, thus it is called "wondrous" (*adbhuta*);

it is far removed from dullness and ignorance, thus it is called "luminous" (*prakāśa*); its pure virtues are fully perfected, thus it is called "perfect" (*paripūrṇa*); and it forever severs all defiled evils.
It is said: "Purity" means not retaining the defilements of birth and death; from the beginning, not a single dharma has been established.
Form and emptiness arise from deluded thought (*vikalpa*), which is itself the manifestation of the false aspect of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Thus, all dharmas are like madness or folly, such as mistaking a reflection for reality. Delusion is fundamentally without cause; yet within this deluded thought, one establishes the nature of causes and conditions. This is delusion.
Those who are deluded regarding causes and conditions call them "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*); this is even more delusory.
That nature of empty space arises from a single moment of obscuration within pure awakening;

it is not even substantially real, let alone causes and conditions or spontaneity, all of which arise from the conceptualization of false imagination—how could they be substantially real? All phenomena arise from the false; if such falsehood...
This means that if one knows there is something that arises, one may speak of causes and conditions. But if delusion is fundamentally non-existent, who would speak of causes and conditions?
Even causes and conditions are established within the midst of delusion; how much more so when one does not realize it is delusion and instead speculates that it is spontaneous (*svabhāva*)?

This is why both views must be rejected: the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) arise from the beginning out of false imagination (*vikalpa*); though they appear to exist, they are eternally non-existent, for they ultimately depend [on the mind].

They dwell upon inverted calculations; though these do not exist eternally, the two types of calculation are never forgotten. Because the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are so solid they cannot be broken, the Tathāgata rebukes deluded thoughts (vikalpa).
He must necessarily rebuke the calculations upon which those thoughts rely. Opening this volume, he points out that the root of human illness lies in the employment of various deluded thoughts.
In this section, he will clarify each of the five layers of deluded thought one by one, forming the grand conclusion of the entire sutra.

Your body was originally produced by the thoughts of your parents; yet your mind is not thought itself. If it were not thought, you would be unable to come into this state of thought to transmit life, as I previously said:
when one thinks of the taste of vinegar, saliva is produced in the mouth; when one thinks of climbing a high place, a tingling sensation arises in the soles of the feet.
The precipice does not exist, and the sour object has not yet arrived; yet your body is certainly not of the same category as empty illusions.
How could saliva emerge from speaking of vinegar? Therefore, you should know that this manifested physical body of yours is called the first solid delusion.
The parents and you achieve the three perceptions (*saṃjñā*), thereby binding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within the womb; hence it is said that "life is transmitted through perception.
The explanations regarding sour plums and the like serve as evidence that the body is bound due to delusion. If it were not for this delusive category, delusion could not produce such an effect.

Various delusions coalesce and solidify to form the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which is termed "solidity. This aggregate of form includes both the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*);
here, however, it refers specifically to the internal body. If it were the external body, what would it have to do with the three perceptions?

Form, sensation, and perception—these three depend upon one another to constitute life, yet they all arise fundamentally from a single consciousness. When consciousness moves, it becomes perception; the perception of "my mind" ought to give rise to the perception of the parents. And yet...
Upon conception, the life-force of the preceding aggregate (*skandha*) is transmuted into the life-force of the succeeding aggregate, continuing without interruption;
this is what is meant by the transmission of life within conceptualization. When deluded thoughts are exhausted, birth and death are likewise exhausted.
This is precisely what has been described: the mind that contemplates from a height can cause your physical form to truly experience astringency and bitterness.

Because sensation arises from causes, it can move the substance of the body. What you now experience as present—both favorable and adverse, driving you back and forth—is called the second false discrimination of "empty luminosity."

The three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception arise through mutual dependence on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and are necessarily inseparable; therefore, it follows upon the preceding discussion of perception and employs the previous analogy.

"In your present state" and below refers to sensation and perception. That which is favorable and beneficial is pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*); that which is adverse and harmful is painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*).

While these are merely empty perceptions arising at the brink of reality, a sense of bitterness and astringency truly manifests. Though both the favorable and the adverse are illusory, they nonetheless produce harm and benefit.
If it were currently racing, then the aggregate of sensation would have no substance; it would be an empty manifestation of clarity.

It is due to your thoughts and deliberations that you cause your physical body to move. Since the body is not of the same category as thought, for what reason does your body follow the dictates of thought?
Various forms are grasped; the mind gives rise to the apprehension of shapes, which corresponds with mindfulness. When awake, this is the conceptualizing mind; when asleep, it becomes various dreams.
Thus, your conceptualizations and the fluctuations of deluded emotions are called the third false discrimination, known as "interfusion."

Thoughts are empty phenomena; the physical body is substantial reality. That the empty and the substantial, being of different natures, can influence one another is due to the integration of mental conceptions (*saṃjñā*).

The mind gives rise to empty conceptions, while the form grasps substantial objects. That the mind and form, though functioning differently, can correspond with one another is due to the penetration of mental conceptions.
This extends even to the shifts and changes between waking and sleeping, which cause the mind to follow its objects. As it is said: [like]... (as above).

It is said that by contemplating the steep cliffs of vinegar, one causes the environment to follow the mind, just as water seeps out when the feet ache; all of this is the interpenetration of deluded thoughts.

The principle of transformation does not abide, shifting secretly and incessantly: the nails grow and the hair sprouts, the vital energy wanes and the face wrinkles, day and night succeeding one another.
"You have never awakened to this, Ānanda. If this were not you, why would its substance undergo change? If it were truly you, why would you lack awareness?
Thus, your various formations (saṃskāra) ceaselessly shift from moment to moment; this is called the fourth subtle and hidden deluded thought."
The two aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) gradually become more subtle, making it even more difficult to perceive their falsity.
Therefore, from above, this points to the subtle shifting of physical form; from below, it points to the seeds receiving perfuming.

This principle of transformation—that is, the *saṃskāra* aggregate—has "constant flux" as its characteristic. It is called "non-abiding. That which "keeps moving" is that which changes again and again.

"Subtle shifting" means shifting in a dense and continuous manner such that people do not perceive it. Nails grow and hair sprouts—this is arising. Qi dissipates and the face wrinkles—this is ceasing.
Arising and ceasing alternate day and night, yet there is not a single person who can awaken to it;

this is precisely what is meant by "subtle shifting. From "If this... onwards, [the text] demonstrates the falsity of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). As for the *saṃskāra-skandha*:
It is not your substance; how could it replace you without ceasing? If it were truly your body, why would you not perceive its arising and perishing?
To say it is not yours is untenable; to say it is yours lacks evidence. Therefore, it is called "hidden delusive thought.
(The aggregates of) feeling, perception, and formations all belong to the mind, yet they permeate the physical body. Feeling enables the body to experience sensations, while perception drives...
