It acts within the body; its activity is able to transform the physical form. You should view the body as belonging to the category of mental constructs rather than as something truly existent.
Furthermore, that which you call "constant"—the place where your clarity and brilliance are profoundly still and unshakable—does not transcend seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing within the body.
If [the mind] were truly pure and authentic, it could not tolerate the practice of delusion. For what reason, then, did you all once in years past behold a strange object?
Throughout the passing of years, there was neither recollection nor forgetting of it; yet later, upon suddenly beholding that former anomaly again, the memory returned as vivid as ever.
It has never been lost or forgotten. Thus, within this state of refined clarity and profound stillness that does not waver, there is the permeation of every thought-moment;

how could it be calculated? Ānanda, you should know that this stillness is not the true reality. It is like a rushing torrent of water that appears tranquil at first glance; because the flow is so rapid, it is not perceived as such.
It is not that they are free from outflows; yet if this were not the source of perception, how could one undergo the habitual tendencies of delusion?

This false conceptualization does not cease at any time through the mutual functioning, opening, or closing of your six sense faculties. Therefore, within your current seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it has become deeply ingrained through repeated habituation.
Thus, it is profoundly clear and internally devoid of any semblance of form, empty and non-substantial. This fifth [stage] involves subtle, refined conceptualization that is inverted.
This consciousness is the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). It is profound and unshakable; it appears to be permanent, yet is not permanent—true permanence is indeed constancy.
If it were truly a refined and constant reality, it would not admit of deluded habituation, just as pure gold does not mix with sand. Now, one is able to...
As for "storing," it is as if nothing is lost; thus, while the profound stillness remains unshaken, it allows for the permeation of delusion—how could this be calculated?
To speak of the depth of this habitual delusion: the profound stillness is not true stillness. This obscure stillness is unaware, like a swift current of water that appears level and waveless.
This obscure stillness flows on, unfathomable; it is the source of recollective thought and the locus where delusion is harbored.
This is the substance. You must simply dissolve the six gates so that deluded habits have nowhere to lodge; only then can they be extinguished.
Now, within your present six sense organs, there is a pervasive resonance, a continuous and uninterrupted state. "Habit" refers to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); "several" refers to subtle traces.
This essence, which is clear, profound, and unwavering, originally arises from a single thought of ignorance.

It exists; therefore, it appears as if it exists though it is not truly non-existent. This is why this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is called the subtle, inverted, and refined perception.
It goes without saying that the Two Vehicles do not know the eight consciousnesses and mistake the state of profound stillness for the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Even Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*) must only eliminate the ignorance of abiding in signs (*nimitta-avidyā*), which they are able to do.
Excluding the two consciousnesses of transformation and manifestation, one has still not yet departed from the state of profound stillness and non-shaking.

Within this state of profound stillness and non-shaking, there remains the delusion of conjunction that serves as the root of birth and death; this is precisely the ignorance of the "phase of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*).

Only a Buddha can perceive and directly point it out, as fully depicted in the four lines regarding the "rapidly flowing water. This is what is meant by the "four entanglements" (*catvāraḥ paryavasthānāḥ*).
As for its profound stillness, it is generally referred to as the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate); however, here it specifically refers to the limit (*paryanta*) of the *vijñāna-skandha*.
When this profound stillness merges with the ultimate profundity, it lies dormant as if formless; yet when stimulated, it arises again.
Only when the six sense faculties attain mutual function and the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted will these deluded thoughts be eradicated—this is precisely the realm of the Buddha.

Ānanda, these five aggregates of clinging are formed by five kinds of deluded conceptualization. If you now wish to know the depth of their causal realms: only form and emptiness constitute the limit of form;
only contact and its cessation constitute the limit of feeling; only recollection and forgetfulness constitute the limit of perception;
only extinction and arising constitute the limit of mental formations; and the profound entry into the merging with the profound constitutes the limit of consciousness. These are the five.

The sense organs arise through successive layers; their arising depends on consciousness, and their cessation follows the removal of form. In principle, there is sudden enlightenment, whereby one attains awakening and simultaneously dissolves [delusions].

In practice, however, things are not suddenly eliminated, but are exhausted through gradual stages. I have already shown you the knots in the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth; what is there that you do not understand? Why do you ask again?
You should take this root of deluded thought and allow your mind to attain penetration; then you may transmit and show it to others.
In the future age of the Dharma-ending period, may all practitioners recognize the nature of delusion, develop a profound weariness with their own arising,
know that there is nirvana, and no longer cling to the three realms.

"Feeling" (*vedanā*) has the meaning of "receiving and experiencing. It refers to the receiving and experiencing of all phenomena, both material (*rūpa*) and mental (*citta*). This applies to all five aggregates (*skandha*); therefore, they are collectively termed "feeling.

This is established through false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and does not exist inherently within the true mind. These two phrases conclude the preceding section. Below, the response addresses the question of what constitutes their respective realms (*dhātu*).

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the shallowest, while the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the deepest. Within the aggregate of form, that which possesses characteristics is "form," and that which lacks characteristics is "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

In the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), grasping is contact (*sparśa*); wearying detachment is disjunction (*vippayoga*). In the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), having mindfulness is recollection; lacking mindfulness is forgetfulness.
In the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), the coarse activity of a distracted mind is arising (*utpāda*); the subtle activity of a concentrated mind is cessation (*nirodha*).

In the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), having an entry is clarity; lacking an entry is merging with clarity. If one exhausts form (*rūpa*) but does not exhaust space (*ākāśa*), and exhausts contact but does not exhaust...

They are separated; though fully recorded, they are not entirely forgotten; though fully produced, they do not entirely perish; though fully entering into stillness, they do not entirely merge with that stillness.
Thus, they have not yet transcended the boundaries of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

The upper instance of the character *zhàn* (stillness) refers to the practice, while the lower instance refers to the fundamental essence. This means that through the practice of clarity and stillness, one enters the stream and returns to the source. And so forth.

The essence of perfect stillness and clarity seems to merge; yet people know only that when the mind flows outward and chases after sensory dust, it divides its own still, perfect nature into consciousness.
They do not realize that the entry of stillness into stillness is likewise the very limit of consciousness. Because stillness perceives the interior, the subtle flow of leakage has not been severed.
This lack of completion allows darkness to grow and nourish itself in secret; from the minute it becomes manifest, relying upon—
The old cycle of saṃsāra. These five [aggregates] below: the answer is that they are eliminated instantaneously yet exhausted gradually. The true analogy is a *kalpavīṭikā* (cloth).
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is like the first knot; form (*rūpa*) is like the final knot. That "birth arises from consciousness" is like the subsequent knot arising in dependence upon the initial knot.
That "cessation proceeds from the removal of form" is like the untying proceeding from the final knot. The arising of the five aggregates proceeds from the subtle to the coarse. By...
Delusion gives rise to consciousness; once there is consciousness, there subsequently arise volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on until form (*rūpa*) appears.

When they cease, it proceeds from the coarse to the subtle. At the time of initial awakening, one ceases form; having ceased form, one then ceases sensation (*vedanā*), and so on until consciousness ceases.

Regarding the cessation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), some can be sudden and some cannot. That which can be sudden is the principle (*li*); that which cannot be sudden is the phenomenon (*shi*).
The principle is of one essence; it is only people who lose their way at the source. By means of this single awakening, all shall merge and be extinguished.

Yet phenomena are manifold, and it is difficult to address them all simultaneously. Therefore, proceed from the shallow to the deep, exhausting them in successive stages. If one attains sudden awakening without gradual elimination, there will be understanding but no practice;
one will cling to the principle while remaining deluded regarding phenomena. This is ultimately not the true Samādhi of authentic cultivation. You—

One should descend [into this realization], so that by means of this principle one may awaken oneself and awaken others, forever severing the source of delusion and together returning to the ultimate fruit.
Knowing that there is nirvana, upon first hearing and seeing it, one recognizes it; hearing the teaching of nirvana as the place of refuge, one pursues it in every thought.
Why linger in the three realms? It is like a destitute son who, knowing he has a hometown, will not long cherish his alien land. One.
The knowledge of full awakening has already attained *nirvāṇa*; true bliss resides within me. Why then should one be attached to the three realms?
It is like a destitute son who has returned to his native land—how could he ever again long for a foreign land?

People today recite the passage on the three realms as a burning house with their mouths, yet in their hearts they remain deeply attached and refuse to let go; it is simply that they do not know there is *nirvāṇa*. This concludes the main portion of the text.

"Ānanda, suppose there were a person who filled all the space throughout the ten directions with the seven treasures to overflowing, and offered them to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a mind that never wasted a single thought. What do you think?
By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, would that person obtain much merit? Ānanda replied, "The space is inexhaustible, and the precious treasures..."
It is boundless. In the past, there was a sentient being who offered seven coins to a Buddha; by relinquishing his body, he still attained the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.
How much more so when one fills the entirety of space before them with precious jewels as offerings to the Buddha-fields—such that even contemplating it for an entire eon could not reach its limit.
How could this merit possibly have any boundary? The Buddha told Ānanda: "The speech of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, is without..."

This is false. If there should be another person who has committed the four grave offenses and the ten *pārājika* transgressions, and in a mere instant passes through the Avīci hells of this world and other worlds, even exhausting all the uninterrupted hells throughout the ten directions without exception;

yet, if they can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa—the karmic obstructions of such a person shall vanish at that very moment.
It shall be extinguished. The causes for the suffering of hell that one has received shall be transformed into a land of peace and bliss.

One shall obtain merit exceeding that of the person who previously made the offering by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, a millionfold, a billionfold, and even to the point that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra as I have extensively explained, [they shall likewise attain such merit].
It will not be exhausted even throughout kalpas. Relying on my teachings and practicing according to them until reaching Bodhi, one will no longer encounter demonic activities.
This concludes the section on the dissemination of the teaching. It compares the excellence of material giving with the even greater excellence of the gift of Dharma, in four parts.
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying constitute the ten *pārājika* offenses; these are precisely the ten grave transgressions (*daśa-guru-apatti*) described in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
These are the most extreme causes of evil. The ten directions of *Avīci* hell are the most extreme fruits of evil.

"A single thought-moment" refers to even a temporary arousal of the mind, provided it is focused with single-mindedness. This dharma gate points to the door for entering deeply into the perfect penetration of Great Samādhi during the final age.
On days when the sages are distant and Māra is powerful, those who have not yet studied—people who find it difficult to advance and easy to retreat—should contemplate their own annihilation;
thus, even the thoughts of propagating the sutras shall all be extinguished. Through the subtle merit of a single thought-moment, one can immediately escape extreme suffering.
Those who are born in Sukhāvatī do so because all phenomena are mind-only; by transforming delusion into awakening, they awaken such that they no longer fall back into delusion.
This allows those who hear it to gain faith and understanding without error, benefiting and bringing joy to others in succession without end. Therefore, the merit obtained is unsurpassed.

Minor offenses and absences of offense; the karmic rewards for propagating the sutras can be known to be exceptionally sublime. "If there are those below" refers to those who exhort others to recite and uphold [the teachings], as well as those who practice according to the instructions.
This brings superior benefit to others and gains merit; this constitutes the fulfillment of one's own path to enlightenment.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās,
and all the devas, humans, asuras, and others from various directions— including bodhisattvas, followers of the two vehicles, noble seers and youths,
as well as powerful spirits who had first resolved their minds— were all greatly rejoiced. They paid homage and departed.

This clarifies the joy and celebration of the Dharma assembly. The youthful sages (ṛṣikumāra), who dwell in the realm of the sages and practice the inner teaching in the hope of attaining the wondrous fruit of perpetual youth (kumārabhūta), have generated the great power of resolve.
Possessing supernormal powers and having attained fearlessness, they have turned their minds to protect the Teaching and sit beneath the seat of the Tathāgata;
all of them are filled with great joy, for they have been granted the opportunity to hear the Great Dharma according to their respective capacities.
Through this realization, one attains great benefit; therefore, the joy and exhilaration are beyond compare.
*The Śūraṅgama Sūtra on the Ultimate Meaning of the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization, and the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*, Fascicle Ten (End).
Preface to the Re-engraved *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* as Spoken:
Regarding the various dharmas spoken by the World-Honored One—whether they be surging waves upon mountain peaks or flying dust at the bottom of the ocean—they are known only by Buddhas and Buddhas.

Only one who can exhaustively investigate [the truth] may fathom this; those of shallow roots and small capacity cannot measure it. Yet the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* alone declares that all phenomena are ultimately firm and solid.
This is because sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind, and thus wander through the various realms of existence.

If they knew that delusion has no fundamental cause, then the sense organs and their objects would pervade the entire Dharma-realm. Upon reaching the point where Ānanda attained awakening, he requested instruction on the "Flower Mansion."
At this gateway, the World-Honored One compassionately bestowed detailed instructions and revealed them with precise clarity.

It is like a great elder at an inn who speaks of poverty and wealth, and compares suffering and joy, to those travelers passing through; he points out the karma inherent within and provides inexhaustible provisions, each according to their own capacity.
The Great Purpose of the Buddha does not depart from the precepts, concentration, and wisdom—this is the ancient [teaching].

Now, there are more than fifty masters who have provided commentaries and annotations. Among the scholar-officials, some trace the resonance of the subtle sound, while others expound upon the words of the tongueless man.
Are they lofty and remote? Are they plain and easy? Do they clap their hands in laughter? Or do they devote themselves with undivided attention?

I cannot enumerate them all. Master Zhou Zi-ne, though a Confucian, would frequently inquire about cause and effect (*hetu-phala*). I instructed him using the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, explaining that Confucianism and Buddhism converge in their ultimate aim and that the principle of cause and effect is fully realized therein.
Thereupon, he took up Master Zhong Bo-jing’s *Reading According to the Teachings* and, sighing in admiration, said:

"Excellent! To find this alone brings joy; to attain it individually brings serenity. Consequently, he wished to circulate it and consulted with me, the mountain recluse, to collaborate upon it together.
I have collated, augmented, and revised this work, and have had it reprinted from my own resources as if protecting a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
May all who see or hear it empty their mundane thoughts and together realize the true mind. Through precepts may they attain concentration, and through concentration may they attain wisdom;
thus, may all matters reach ultimate firmness. In years to come, may I and Master Bojing walk hand-in-hand within the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Within this, both the mundane and the supramundane attain return to the source. Why should I employ many words?
On the sixth day of the Lotus Month in the year Jiwu of the Qing Kangxi era, Jingfan of Dongta respectfully inscribed this.

Having heard that the precious *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* allows one, first, to perceive the nature and achieve Buddhahood, and second, to remain far removed from demonic obstacles, [it encompasses] both the Exoteric and Esoteric...
The divine efficacy is inconceivable; both those within and beyond the mundane world should prostrate themselves before it.

For instance, Du Qi (Du Fu) knew only the Confucian classics and did not believe in the Buddhist scriptures; yet, upon following Zhang Wen-ding, he read this sutra and marveled at it as a sacred book, regretting his belated realization.

Wang Jie-fu was stubborn and perverse throughout his life and could not have understood Perfect Penetration (*yuantong*); only in his later years, when he retired to Mount Zhongshan, did he come to appreciate it.

While conversing with Pan Xingsi about Chan, I repented of my previous errors and misconceptions. Thus, I have composed these annotations for this scripture; from initial confusion to final awakening, it is impossible to describe them all in detail.

I, Dezhui, am most foolish and mediocre, yet I rashly attempted to emulate the "escaping from Chan" (of Hanshan). My primary prayer was to offer merit to my ancestors, while also seeking to chart my own path.

When I first read this scripture, it was like gazing out upon the vast ocean; fortunately, I was able to rely on Master Zhong Bojing’s explanations as they were spoken, and my heart was filled with joy.
Hand-copied. Requesting that it be corrected for the sake of Master Wei. He noted: "This is the *Huìjiě* (Collected Explanations) by Master Tiānrú, with Master Yǔyù harmonizing its tracks;
it may be called 'green surpassing blue. Is this not a case of those who come later excelling those before? However, it contains many errors, such as confusing 'fish' for 'Lu.'"

For this reason, its circulation has not been widespread. To ensure its broad dissemination, the text must be carefully edited. If the meaning is not yet precise, one should cautiously consult various commentaries;
one may only delete or revise, but must not add anything arbitrarily. It is better to be concise than prolix.

Do not list the names of the masters as if they were speaking with one voice; for in assisting the Buddha to proclaim his transformation, there is no need for sectarian distinction. This is because the teachings are expounded through the Sūtras.

I have striven for brevity and clarity. Master De received my instructions and served as the scribe on my behalf. Upon the completion of each fascicle, I requested his authentication so that it might be carved into printing blocks for the public and included in the Tripitaka.
This was all due to Master Zhong’s skillful compilation, Master [De]’s exquisite editorial judgment, the guidance of former masters, and the assistance of various worthies.
Thus, it has become a lamp of wisdom for dark rooms and a precious raft for those lost at the ford. I, De, possess but a glimpse through a tube; [this work is the result of their collective merit].

I have not offered a single word of praise; I merely record the origins and conclusion of this edition carved for printing. My sole hope is that these precious scriptures may circulate widely, so that by relying on the Buddha’s compassionate light, they may shine universally upon this turbid world.
May all beings universally pray that their roots of goodness lead them to realize the fruits of enlightenment through this sutra.
Respectfully recorded by the disciple from Yeongju, Zhou Zhende, in the sixth lunar month of the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era.
